Passive components › Inductors

Air-core coil (Wheeler)

What it computes

The inductance of a coil with no core, from its dimensions, the turns that give a wanted inductance, and what a single-layer coil does at radio frequency: its own capacitance, its self-resonance and its Q. Five pills; the length boxes (form diameter, wire diameter, winding length, pitch, inside diameter, depth, a tube's wall) each have their own mm / cm / in picker, and changing one changes all the others.

The Your inputs heading holds the wire picker: a typed diameter, or a gauge from 6 to 40 AWG. A gauge puts its bare diameter in the wire box (to four figures) and, until you type your own, proposes the close-wound value of the box that depends on the wire (marked close-wound): the solenoid's length (turns × the diameter over the insulation), the pitch of the Turns and Spiral pills (that diameter), and the depth of a layered winding (turns × d² / b). The proposal follows the turns and the length as you change them; typing a diameter puts the picker back to typed.

  • Solenoid: a single-layer coil. The form diameter, the wire diameter, the turns and the winding length. The big result is the Bureau of Standards' inductance: Nagaoka's sheet-of-current value from its exact coefficient K, less the round-wire correction. Cells: Wheeler's formula, how far Wheeler's is from the big result, and K. Rows: the sheet value and the correction, diameter over length and wire over pitch, which of Wheeler's two formulas applies (and whether the coil is outside its range), the length of wire and its DC resistance. The drawing is the coil with its diameter and length.
  • Turns: the inductance wanted (µH), the form diameter, the wire diameter and the pitch (the distance from one turn to the next). The big result is the turns, not rounded; cells: the whole turns, the winding length and how far Wheeler's answer is from it; rows: the inductance of the whole turns, the turns Wheeler's formula would give, the length of wire and its DC resistance. The turns are found by trying: the inductance rises a little faster than the square of the turns, because the coil lengthens.
  • Multilayer: a coil wound in layers with a rectangular cross-section. The picker in the Output heading says what is given. Turns: the inside diameter, the turns, the wire diameter, the length b and the depth c; the big result is Wheeler's formula. Inductance: the inductance wanted, the inside diameter, the length b and the wire; the big result is the turns, with the whole turns, the depth they build and the layers in the cells, and the inductance of the whole turns in a row. Rows for both: how much each of 6a, 9b and 10c takes of the denominator (about equal is the best case), the accuracy, the length of wire and its DC resistance. The drawing is the cross-section of Wheeler's figure.
  • Spiral: a flat coil of round wire: the inside diameter, the wire diameter, the turns and the pitch. The big result is the Bureau of Standards' formula for the equivalent coil, less the round-wire correction; cells: Wheeler's formula, how far it is, and the mean radius; rows: the width c = n D, c / a and wire over pitch, Wheeler's accuracy, the sheet value and the correction, the length of wire and its DC resistance.

  • SRF & Q: the Solenoid pill's coil (the same four boxes, shared: what is typed on one pill is on the other) at a working frequency, with its former: none (air), a tube (its relative permittivity εr and its wall) or a solid rod (its εr). The big result is the self-resonant frequency in a circuit, from L and the coil's own capacitance C (Knight's formula); the line under it gives both. Cells: C, the Q at the working frequency (or "above SRF") and the self-resonance of the coil standing free, connected to nothing (Knight's helical-line model). Rows: the inductance seen at the coil's ends at the working frequency (raised by C) and by how much it differs from L; the AC resistance and how many times the DC resistance it is; the skin depth and Medhurst's proximity factor; Medhurst's own quick Q (his Table IX) and his self-capacitance formula (for coils on polystyrene with one end earthed), to compare; the frequency at which the wire is half a wavelength long. The drawing is the coil with C dashed across its ends, green as calculated.

  • Units: mm, cm or in for every length (the formulas use cm or inches inside); µH for the inductance wanted; kHz or MHz for the working frequency.

  • Remembered: the pill, the length unit, the wire, the way the multilayer coil is given, the frequency unit and the former.

Examples: the Bureau's 400-turn coil, a 10-turn coil on a 20 mm form, a single loop (outside Wheeler's range), 10 µH on a 20 mm form, 1 µH close-wound on 10 mm, the Bureau's 1000-turn multilayer coil, an IF coil, a flat spiral, 20 turns of 22 AWG close-wound, 330 µH in layers of 30 AWG, and on the SRF & Q pill Knight's PTFE-cored coil, his 18-turn air coil, Medhurst's coil No. 31 and a 7 MHz coil of 22 AWG.

Terms

  • Inductance L: the flux a coil links per ampere of current. Air core: no magnetic material, so L depends on the shape alone and grows as the square of the turns n.
  • Mean radius a: the radius to the middle of the winding (to the centre of the wire for a single layer). Length b: the length of the winding. Depth c: the thickness of a layered winding. Pitch D: the distance from the centre of one turn to the next; d / D is the wire diameter over the pitch (1 for wire turns touching).
  • Nagaoka's coefficient K: the number by which a very long solenoid's inductance, 4π² a² n² / b (in cm, in µH, 0.03948 a² n² / b), is multiplied for a coil of finite length. K is a function of 2a / b, the diameter over the length: nearly 1 for a long coil, 0.818 for a length of two diameters, 0.083 for 2a / b = 34.
  • Round-wire correction: Nagaoka's formula is for a sheet of current; wire has gaps and its current does not spread, which lowers the inductance a little. The correction is 0.01257 n a (A + B) µH (a in cm), A from d / D and B from the number of turns.
  • AWG, bare and insulated diameter: the American wire gauge, whose diameter is defined by a formula (NBS Handbook 100: 0.127 mm × 92^((36 − n) / 39)); the copper alone is the bare diameter, which sets the resistance and the round-wire correction; enamelled magnet wire is thicker over its insulation (heavy build here), which sets how close the turns can sit. Close-wound: each turn touching the last, the pitch equal to the insulated diameter.
  • DC resistance: the wire's length over its conductivity times its cross-section, for annealed copper (IACS) 1/58 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C; it rises 0.393 % per °C.
  • Self-capacitance C: a coil behaves as L with a small capacitance across its ends. It does not come from the turns facing each other (Medhurst and Knight showed that theory fails) but from the wire being a transmission line: at the self-resonance the wire is about half a wavelength long. C hardly depends on the spacing of the turns and grows with the coil's length and diameter; a former inside the coil (its relative permittivity εr, 1 for air) raises it, the more so for a short coil.
  • Self-resonant frequency (SRF): where L and C resonate, 1 / (2π √(L C)); above it the coil behaves as a capacitor. In a circuit (a network analyser, a datasheet's SRF) the coil resonates there; a coil standing free, connected to nothing, resonates at another frequency, set by the speed of a wave along its helix (higher for a long coil, lower for a short one).
  • Q: the coil's reactance over its resistance, 2πfL / R: how little energy it loses per cycle. The selectivity and the loss of a tuned circuit follow from it.
  • Skin depth δ: at radio frequency the current flows near the wire's surface, within about δ = √(ρ / (π f μ0)) (21 µm in copper at 10 MHz), so the AC resistance of a wire much thicker than δ is its DC resistance × d / (4δ).
  • Proximity factor: the field of the neighbouring turns pushes the current further, to the inside of the coil and away from the next turns, raising the resistance again: Medhurst's measured ratio of a coil's resistance to that of the same wire straight, from 1 for widely spaced turns to over 5 for touching turns of a short coil. d/s: the bare wire's diameter over the pitch.
  • Pitch angle ψ: the slope of the turns, tan ψ = pitch / (π D); C is divided by cos²ψ, which matters only for widely spaced turns.

Sources

  • Harold A. Wheeler, "Simple Inductance Formulas for Radio Coils", Proceedings of the IRE 16 (10), October 1928, pp. 1398–1400 (the PDF of the issue from worldradiohistory.com; the three pages read as text and rendered, with their figures): L = 0.8 a² n² / (6a + 9b + 10c) µH for a multilayer coil (a mean radius, b length, c depth, in inches), right to about 1 % when the three terms of the denominator are about equal; L = a² n² / (9a + 10b) for a single-layer coil, right to 1 % for b > 0.8 a with a the radius; L = a² n² / (8a + 11c) for a spiral, right to 5 % for c > 0.2 a; the helix formula (9a + 10b) for b > a and the other for a > b > 0.2 a, equal at b = a; the accuracy is lower with few turns, wide spacing, skin effect or capacitance. Wheeler derived them from the formulas and curves of Circular 74.
  • Bureau of Standards Circular No. 74, "Radio Instruments and Measurements" (the 1937 edition, the PDF from nvlpubs.nist.gov; 360 pages as text, pages 252–253, 260–263 and 283–284 rendered): the single-layer coil L = 0.03948 a² n² K / b with K from Table 10 (2a / b from 0 to 100); for round wire L = Ls − 0.01257 n a (A + B) (155), A from Table 11 against d / D, B from Table 12 against the turns; the worked example of 400 turns, a = 10 cm, b = 40 cm, d / D = 0.5: Ls = 12 919 µH, A + B = 0.199, correction 9.99 µH, L = 12 909 µH; the multilayer example (1000 turns, a = b = 10 cm, c = 1 cm) 195.2 mH; the flat spiral of round wire as the equivalent coil of width c = n D and mean radius a = a1 + (n − 1) D / 2, L = 0.01257 a n² {ln(8a / c) − ½ + c² / (96 a²) (ln(8a / c) + 43/12)} (160), with the same correction.
  • David Knight and Rodger Rosenbaum, "Grover's Inductance Calculations: supplementary information and errata" (g3ynh.info, 2012; page 5 rendered): the exact Nagaoka coefficient K(z) = 4 / (3π) (√(1 + z²) / z² (K(m) − E(m)) + √(1 + z²) E(m) − z), z = 2a / b, m = z² / (1 + z²), with the complete elliptic integrals K and E. The tool computes them by the arithmetic-geometric mean; the formula reproduces 13 rows of Table 10 (z from 0.05 to 100) to its four figures.
  • The Radio-Craft article of May 1932 (RF Cafe copy) and Jim Lux's page of Wheeler's formulas (read): both repeat Wheeler's formulas; the 1932 text wrongly says "length greater than four-fifths of the diameter" where Wheeler says 0.8 of the radius (b > 0.8 a, so a length over 0.4 diameters).
  • The wire: the AWG formula and copper's resistivity are NBS Handbook 100's, as the Wire sizing tool uses them (that tool's manual section gives the source); the diameter over heavy-build insulation is Magnetics' wire table (2017 Powder Core Catalog, page 28, the table the Toroid winding tool uses). The resistance per metre from the formula agrees with Magnetics' printed column within 0.5 % from 6 to 27 AWG; from 28 to 40 AWG Magnetics' figures scatter on both sides of it, by up to 2.8 % (40 AWG: 3.44 against 3.54 Ω/m), checked by a script.
  • R. G. Medhurst, "H.F. Resistance and Self-Capacitance of Single-Layer Solenoids", Wireless Engineer 24, February 1947 pp. 35–43 and March 1947 pp. 80–92 (the PDFs of both issues from worldradiohistory.com, read as text; Tables V, VIII and IX and the formula for H rendered and read as printed): about 40 coils of bare copper wire (silk-covered for the closest spacings) on grooved Distrene (polystyrene) rods, 30 to 50 turns, measured with a twin-T bridge; the self-capacitance with one end earthed, C0 = H D pF (D the mean diameter in cm), H = 0.1126 l/D + 0.08 + 0.27 / √(l/D) within 2 or 3 % of his Table V, the curve good to l/D = 0.05 even with two turns and falling off below; Table VIII, the coil's high-frequency resistance over that of the same length of straight wire at the same frequency, against l/D (0 to ∞) and d/s (0.1 to 1), for many turns; Table IX, his ψ in Q = 0.15 R ψ √f for copper (R the mean radius in cm, f in Hz); the worksheet of coil No. 31 (40 turns of 0.0910 cm wire, D 5.10 cm, 7.01 cm long: Q 228 to 236 at 0.78 to 0.86 MHz, 42.37 µH), which shows his ratio taken over the straight wire's high-frequency resistance, d / (4δ) × its DC resistance. The letters of June 1947 (p. 185, Callendar's simpler Q formula) and September 1947 (p. 281, Medhurst's tentative curves for few turns) read.
  • David W. Knight, "The self-resonance and self-capacitance of solenoid coils: applicable theory, models and calculation methods", version 1.00, 4 May 2016 (his site, g3ynh.info, now carries something else: the Internet Archive's copy of the PDF; the 105 pages read as text, pages 52 and 97 rendered): the DAE formula (5.3) for the self-capacitance of a coil in a circuit, C = (4ε0 / π) b [1 + k (1 + εi / εx) / 2] / cos²ψ with k = 0.717439 (D/b) + 0.933048 (D/b)^1.5 + 0.106 (D/b)², ±2.1 %, Medhurst's data refitted with the former's permittivity εi (εx outside, 1 for air); the permittivity inside a tube (8.2), εi = (ri / ro)² + εf (1 − (ri / ro)²), "a very crude correction"; section 10: C with L gives the self-resonance a circuit sees, not that of a free coil; section 11: the free coil's first self-resonance from a helical transmission line terminated in its fringe-field and axial-field capacitances, the procedure of p. 95 and his macro VFnom (p. 97), fitted to 62 measurements (Drude, Jackson, Pettit, his own) within 2.1 %; his PTFE-cored coil predicted at 17.98 MHz (measured 17.939 MHz); the GKMR coil's C, 10.1 pF.
  • David W. Knight, "Solenoid Impedance and Q", part II of his solenoid article, version 0.01, 4 January 2016, a provisional draft (the Internet Archive's copy, read as text): Medhurst's resistance table reprinted with p/d in place of d/s (a few entries differ from Medhurst's print, 1.20 for 1.26 at l/D = 0 and d/s = 0.4, 2.27 for 2.37 at l/D = 10 and d/s = 0.7: the tool uses the printed values), Rac = Rdc Ξ Ψ (N − 1) / N with the two end turns at half the proximity effect, and a doubly-asymptotic form Rdc [1 + (Ξ − 1) Ψ (N − 1 + 1/Ψ) / N].
  • Not read: Butterworth's papers (Medhurst's Table VIII corrects his high-frequency table), Ollendorff's 1926 paper, Drude, Knight's paper on the internal impedance of wires and his worksheets; Wheeler's 1982 paper, Grover's book itself, Rosa's papers, the Bureau's multilayer formula (156) beyond the example, and the Radio Broadcast page of Wheeler's article (refused by its bot check; left alone); the IEEE copies are behind a paywall. Table 11 (A) is replaced by the fit A = ln(d / D) + 0.557, which agrees with the 45 printed rows to the 0.001 they give; Table 12 (B) is the printed table, interpolated straight in ln n. The Bureau's 38-turn ribbon spiral (324.2 µH calculated, 323.5 measured) is for rectangular wire and is not reproduced here.

Why the formulas are these

Solenoid. A long solenoid has the flux density μ0 n I / b inside and so L = μ0 n² π a² / b, which is 4π² × 10⁻³ a² n² / b µH with a and b in cm (0.03948). A finite coil loses flux at its ends: Nagaoka solved it exactly for a sheet of current, and K is the result. The round wire is not a sheet; the Bureau corrects it with two tabulated terms, A (a function of d / D) and B (a function of the number of turns). Table 10 is the exact formula to four figures, so the tool uses the formula, not the table.

Wheeler's formulas. Fits of Circular 74's results by simple fractions: for a long coil 9a + 10b tends to 10b, giving L → a² n² / 10b, the long-solenoid value in inches; the 9a term is the end effect. The second form, for shorter coils, is the spiral's 8a + 11c with the length b in place of the depth c. The tool compares Wheeler's with the exact K and says in the cell by how much they differ; for a single turn of a thin loop (b < 0.2 a) Wheeler's formula is outside its range and reads some 15 % low.

Turns. The inductance, with the length b = n × pitch, is a continuous function of n that rises with n: the tool halves an interval of turns 200 times between 1 and 10 million until it matches the wanted inductance. (Derived here; the same for Wheeler's formula.) The whole turns are the rounded result, and the row below tells what they give.

The wire. With a gauge, the radius of a single layer and the inside radius of a spiral are to the centre of the wire, so they take the diameter over the insulation; the round-wire correction's d / D and the resistance take the bare copper. A typed diameter is used for both. The wire's length is the turns times the circumference at the centre of the wire (π × (form + wire) × n) for a single layer, and 2π a n for a layered winding and a spiral, a their mean radius; the resistance is that length × 1/58 over the bare cross-section. A layered winding of n turns of a wire of diameter d in a length b takes n d² of the cross-section, so its depth is n d² / b with the turns stacked in squares (derived here; the turns nest a little in practice, so the depth is a slight overestimate). Given an inductance, the tool tries turns in Wheeler's formula, with the depth and the mean radius growing with them, until it matches (the same halving as for a single layer).

Multilayer, spiral. Wheeler's (1) and the Bureau's (160) as quoted. For the spiral the tool uses the equivalent coil of the Bureau and the same correction (A and B as for a single layer); the sheet value of (160) for a coil of zero length with width c.

SRF & Q. The self-capacitance is Knight's DAE formula with the mean diameter D (form plus wire), the winding length b and the pitch angle; for a rod εi is its εr, for a tube Knight's area-weighted (8.2) with ro the form's radius and ri = ro − wall; outside is air. The SRF in a circuit is 1 / (2π √(L C)) with the Solenoid pill's L. The free coil follows Knight's VFnom line by line: the Bessel argument x = π D / (2b) + 0.117 exp(−22 exp(−0.75 b/D)), Nagaoka's K (the exact one; Knight's macro uses an approximation good to about 20 ppm), the radial permittivity, Ollendorff's function √(I0K0 / I1K1), the two capacitances, R0 tan ψ, and the nominal velocity factor v found by iteration; the SRF is v c / (2 lw), lw = √((π D n)² + b²) the wire's length along the helix. The modified Bessel functions I0, I1, K0 and K1 come from their integrals by the trapezoid rule (within 1e-14 of scipy's).

The resistance (derived here): the isolated wire's skin effect Ξ is the exact Bessel solution (the Skin depth tool's), and the other turns add (Ψ − 1)(n − 1)/n times Ξ − ¼ − 3/(4Ξ), the high-frequency part of the wire's resistance. At high frequency that part tends to d / (4δ), so the coil's resistance tends to Ψ × d / (4δ) × Rdc, Medhurst's own definition; at low frequency it vanishes with the skin effect, leaving Rdc. Ψ is Medhurst's Table VIII, interpolated straight in l/D (in D/l between 10 and ∞) and in d/s, and straight to 1 below d/s = 0.1; the two end turns have half the effect (Medhurst's rough argument, Knight's (n − 1)/n). Against Medhurst's coil No. 31 this gives his measured resistance within 1.8 % at the nine frequencies of his worksheet; Knight's doubly-asymptotic form reads 5 to 8 % low there, and Rdc Ξ Ψ 6 to 9 % high.

Q and the inductance at the coil's ends come from R + j2πfL in parallel with C: with u = 1 − (2πf)² L C, L' = (L u − R² C) / (u² + (2πf R C)²) and Q = 2πf (L u − R² C) / R. Medhurst's quick Q interpolates his Table IX the same way as Table VIII, and his C = H D uses his formula for H.

Assumptions and limits

  • Round copper wire, the gauge's insulation the heavy-build enamel of Magnetics' table (other insulations are thinner or thicker), a form with no core or shield nearby, and a coil far smaller than a wavelength. The inductance is at low frequency (DC). Near the self-resonance, with skin effect or a core, a real coil differs.
  • The correction table is Circular 74's (A as a fit, B by interpolation); it is for a coil of several turns, B is 0 for one turn, and past 1000 turns B is held at 0.336.
  • Single-layer coils need diameter over length of at most 100 (the Bureau's table); the pitch cannot be less than the wire diameter.
  • Wheeler's formulas are within their stated accuracy only in their ranges; the tool shows both numbers so the difference is visible. The multilayer pill has no second formula to compare. Its depth from the turns assumes square stacking and the length b given; a real winding is a little shallower when the turns nest.
  • DC resistance at 20 °C, for direct current; it rises with temperature. The SRF & Q pill adds the skin and proximity effects.
  • SRF & Q: a single layer at least 0.05 diameters long (Medhurst found the self-capacitance formulas fail below); air outside the coil; copper at 20 °C; no loss in the former, the leads or a nearby shield, and no leads' capacitance. C is for a coil across which the circuit puts a lower impedance than C's own (a tuned circuit); near the SRF the coil behaves as a transmission line and the lumped L and C, and the Q, lose accuracy. Medhurst's table is for 30 turns or more at high frequency (a wire more than about ten skin depths thick); the end correction for fewer turns is rough. L is the low-frequency inductance: at high frequency the current crowds to the inside of the turns and L falls a few per cent (3.5 % for coil No. 31), so Q reads that much high. The tube correction is Knight's crude one, and using it in the free-coil model is an extension he did not test.
  • Display. Three figures; nH, µH or mH as the size asks; the wire length in the length unit, or in metres from 1 m; frequencies in Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz and capacitances in pF.

How it was checked

216 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation (scipy's elliptic integrals and Bessel functions; the tool uses the arithmetic-geometric mean and the integrals) that replays each case's taps and typing with the screen's rules for the wire picker and the close-wound proposals, every figure and label of the drawings: - Solenoid: the opening screen, 24 other coils (long, short, a single loop, 2 to 1500 turns, the three length units, wire as thick as the pitch, very thin wire, diameter over length from 0.0005 to 50, Wheeler's two formulas and the range where it fails), the Bureau's 400-turn example, six refusals; - Units: cm and in on all four pills, the unit remembered and offered, carried from one pill to another; - Turns: the opening, 12 settings, seven refusals (an inductance one turn exceeds, one that needs 10 million turns, thick wire…) and the pill remembered; - Wire: the picker's options, eleven gauges on the Solenoid pill (the bare diameter in the box, the close-wound length and its hint), the length following the turns, a typed length kept, a typed diameter putting the picker back, inches, the heaviest and the finest gauge, the gauge remembered, the close-wound pitch on the Turns and Spiral pills, the depth on the Multilayer pill and its following the turns; - Multilayer: the opening, 12 settings, six refusals; given the inductance: the opening, eight settings (typed wire and four gauges, from 1 µH to the Bureau's 195.2 mH), four refusals and the choice remembered; Spiral: the opening, 12 settings, five refusals; - SRF & Q: the opening and the pickers' options, 29 coils (from 1 kHz to 10 GHz, below and above the SRF; 1 to 600 turns; 0.051 to 60 diameters long; d/s under 0.1 and at 1; tubes and rods of εr 1 to 10; the three length units and kHz), four gauges close-wound, eleven refusals, the tube's and the rod's boxes, inches in the wall, kHz, the choices remembered, the coil shared with the Solenoid pill, Knight's PTFE-cored coil and the GKMR coil; - the fourteen examples and the formula-search cards (by name and by self-capacitance).

1,080 more cases (six batches of 180: random coils, inductances, windings and spirals in the three length units, the later three with random gauges on every pill and layered windings given the inductance), and 540 for the SRF & Q pill (three batches of 180: random coils, frequencies, formers, units and gauges, a tenth of them refused), compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

Passive components › Inductors

Toroid winding

What it computes

The turns, the inductance, the wire, the DC bias and the AC flux, core loss and heating of a wound toroid, from the maker's inductance factor AL. The Core heading holds two pickers: the size (101 Micrometals iron powder sizes, T5 to T650, with their height variants A, B, C, D; the 125 Fair-Rite ferrite toroids, each a part number with its material; or typed) and, for iron powder, the mix (the material: −0, −1, −2, −3, −6, −7, −8/90, −10 … −70, as many as that size is made in). Typed asks for AL and the three dimensions, and works out le, Ae and Ve from them. Five pills:

  • Turns: the inductance wanted (nH, µH or mH). The big result is the turns, not rounded; cells: the whole turns, the inductance they give and the AL tolerance of the mix; rows: that inductance with the tolerance, the inductance of one turn less and more, the core.
  • Inductance: the turns. The big result is L = AL N²; cells: the lowest and highest with the tolerance and AL; rows: one turn less and more, the core.
  • Winding: the turns and the wire gauge (AWG 6 to 49, Magnetics' heavy-build diameters). The big result is the window fill; cells: the wire length, its DC resistance and the turns one layer holds; rows: where the fill falls (low, full, high, impossible), whether the turns fit in one layer, the window area and the wire diameter, the mean length of a turn.
  • Bias: the turns and the DC current (mA or A), for the mixes whose curve fit agrees with the catalog (−1, −2, −3, −6, −7, −8, −10, −14, −15, −17, −30, −63). The big result is the inductance with the current; cells: the field H in oersteds, the percentage of the initial permeability, the flux density B; rows: H in A·T/cm, the inductance without the current, the fit at 200 Oe beside the catalog's own figure, the core. A ferrite part or a typed core is refused: the tool has no DC-bias curve for them.
  • AC: the turns, an AC voltage (V rms) and its frequency (Hz, kHz or MHz). The big result is the peak flux density Bpk; cells: the core loss, the temperature rise in still air and the reactance of the winding; rows: the loss per volume and the fit of the loss curve at 100 kHz and 140 G beside the catalog's own figure, the permeability at that flux and at that frequency, the inductance at that frequency, the current the winding draws with no load, Bpk against the mix's saturation flux density, the drift of permeability with temperature, and the core's volume and surface. The loss, the heating and the two permeabilities are for the Micrometals mixes, and only inside the frequency and flux the catalog's curves cover; outside them, and for ferrite and typed cores, the tool says so and gives Bpk, the reactance and the current only.

The drawing is the core with one continuous wire wound round it (up to 26 turns are drawn) and a lead at each end.

  • Units: nH, µH, mH for the inductance wanted; mA, A for the current; Hz, kHz, MHz for the AC frequency; mm, in for the dimensions of a typed core (all three boxes change together); the diameters and the window of a catalog core are in mm; AL in nH/N²; the AC voltage in V.
  • Remembered: the pill, the size, the mix and the four units.

Examples: 10 µH on a T50-2 and 1 µH on a T37-6; 30 turns on a T68-2; 45 turns of 26 AWG on a T50-2 and 60 of 20 AWG on a T106-2; a current of 5 A through a T50-3 and 3 A through a T106-2; 100 µH on the ferrite 5943002701; 50 V at 100 kHz on a T106-2 and a T50-26 overdriven at 50 kHz.

Terms

  • Toroid, core, mix: a ring of magnetic material; the winding goes through the hole and round the outside, so the field stays inside the core. The mix is the maker's number for the material; it sets the permeability (µ 4 to 100 for iron powder), the useful frequency range, the tolerance and the DC-bias behaviour.
  • AL (inductance factor): the inductance of one turn, in nH, so N turns give AL N². Micrometals and Magnetics give nH/N² (Amidon's older tables give µH per 100 turns, ten times the number: 49 µH/100 turns is 4.9 nH/N²). The catalogs test it at a peak flux density of 1 mT (10 gauss) and 10 kHz on a full, evenly spaced single layer.
  • le, Ae, Ve: the core's effective magnetic path length (cm), cross-section (cm²) and volume (cm³). Window: the hole, of area π ID² / 4.
  • Window fill (winding factor): the wire's cross-section, N times that of one wire with its insulation, over the window area. 20 to 60 % is the range, 35 to 40 % usual; a single layer, low fill (under 30 %), a full winding (30 to 45 %) and high fill (up to about 65 %, by hand only).
  • AWG, heavy build: the American wire gauge; heavy-build enamel is the thick insulation, its outside diameter is what takes room.
  • Mean length of a turn (MLT): the length of wire in one turn. DC resistance: MLT × turns × the wire's resistance per metre.
  • H, oersted, A·T/cm: the magnetizing force of the current, H = 0.4π N I / le in oersteds with le in cm (1 A·T/cm = 1.26 Oe). % initial permeability: the permeability left under the field, a fraction of its value at low field; the inductance falls in the same proportion. B: the flux density in the core; 1 T = 10 000 gauss.
  • Bpk, Bsat: the peak flux density an AC voltage makes, and the flux density at which the material saturates. At radio frequencies the core loss limits Bpk long before saturation.
  • Core loss: the heat the alternating flux makes in the core (hysteresis and eddy currents), in mW per cm³ of core, which rises steeply with Bpk and with frequency; the total is that times Ve.
  • Temperature rise in still air: Magnetics' estimate (total loss in mW / surface in cm²)^0.833 °C. Reactance, current at no load: 2π f L, and the current the winding draws from the voltage with nothing on the other side.
  • Tolerance, ferrite: Fair-Rite gives each part's AL as ±20, ±25 or ±30 %, as +35 / −25 % (higher above than below), or as a minimum only; the ranges the tool gives follow that.

Sources

  • Micrometals, "Iron Powder Cores" catalog (2023; the PDF from micrometals.com, 88 pages read as text; pages 18, 19 and 30 rendered): the toroid table (PDF pages 48 onward), for each part the outside and inside diameter and height in inches and mm, Ae, le, Ve, AL in nH/N², the reference permeability and the mix; the notes that AL is for 10 gauss and 10 kHz on an evenly spaced full single layer and that a few turns not evenly distributed read higher than expected; the typical AL tolerance of each mix (PDF page 47); on each mix page H = 0.4π N I / Le (oersteds, Le in cm), %µi = 1 / (a + b H^c) + d with the coefficients of the table on PDF page 44, and Bpk = Erms 10⁸ / (4.44 Ae N f); and the catalog's own "% perm at DC bias (200 Oe)" of each mix, which the fit is checked against. 616 parts in 101 sizes are in the tool. The AC curve fits of every mix (the equations rendered on pages 18 and 19, the coefficients read from the tables on PDF pages 44 to 46): core loss in mW/cm³ = f / (a / B³ + b / B^2.3 + c / B^1.65) + d B² f² (B in gauss, f in Hz), over curves drawn from 60 Hz to 500 kHz and 10 to 10 000 G; the percentage of the initial permeability at Bpk, 1 / (1 / (a + b B^c) + 1 / (d B^e) + 1 / f), over 10 to 10 000 G; the permeability at a frequency, 1 / (a + b f^c) + d, over 10 kHz to 100 MHz; the change with temperature, a (T − 20) ppm; Bsat; and each mix page's core loss at 100 kHz and 140 G, which the loss fit is checked against.
  • Magnetics, "Powder Core Catalog" (2017; the PDF from mag-inc.com, 112 pages read as text) and its "Powder Core Calculations" page (read): LN = AL N² 10⁻³ (µH, AL in nH/T²) and the turns from it; H = N I / le in A·T/cm with the conversion to oersteds; the winding factor N Aw / WA with WA = π ID² / 4 and its ranges; the wire table, AWG 6 to 49, resistance in Ω/m and heavy-build outside diameter; the single-layer winding tables (turns and DC resistance for each gauge and core size) and the table of the length of a turn against the winding factor; and the worked example of a 600 µH inductor (minimum AL 74.6 nH/T², 90 turns, 127 turns of 17 AWG of 1.177 mm² in a window of 427 mm², 35 %).
  • Fair-Rite Products, "Ferrite Cores" catalog, 17th edition (2013; the CERN copy, read): the 125 uncoated ferrite toroids of the picker, with their dimensions, le, Ae, Ve, AL and its tolerance (see the Toroid/ferrite reference table). Data sheet 5943002721 (read): AL as the inductance divided by N², tested at 10 kHz.
  • Magnetics 2017 catalog, page 15 (rendered): the still-air temperature rise ΔT (°C) = (total losses (mW) / component surface area (cm²))^0.833, which it gives as a useful approximation, its surface areas being those of cores wound to 40 % fill.
  • The Amidon iron powder table (the qsl.net copy, read; used only to cross-check): 140 rows of T-xx cores with O.D., I.D., height, le, Ae, Ve and AL in µH per 100 turns; a few of its printed cells are wrong (for example the inside diameters of the mix-2 rows of T-106, T-130, T-184, T-225 and T-300, and "0.183 cm" for le of the T-30). The Amidon copy at ibselectronics.biz refused the download (403) and was left alone.
  • Not read: Fair-Rite's material curves (permeability, loss and saturation of its ferrites), Ferroxcube's data, the coating thickness of Micrometals cores, Magnetics' leakage-flux formula for few turns (it is for Magnetics' cores and scatters ±50 %). The catalog prints no AL for the T250-8A/90 row, and prints 4.8 nH/N² for the T400-2D (the same as for the T400-0D, probably a typing mistake for 48): both are left out. The row T90-66 has the dimensions of a different size and is its own entry, T90/66.

Why the formulas are these

AL and the turns. AL is defined by L = AL N² (Micrometals, Magnetics, Fair-Rite); the turns for a wanted L are √(L / AL) (Magnetics' N = √(L 10³ / AL) for L in µH and AL in nH). The tool shows the whole turns and the inductance of the turns on each side, because the whole number is what gets wound; the tolerance of the mix gives the range. A typed core has no tolerance.

One layer and the length of a turn (derived, checked). The wire's centre line runs round a circle of diameter ID − d (the hole less one wire), so one layer holds π (ID − d) / d turns. The length of a turn is the perimeter of the core's section, a rectangle HT by (OD − ID) / 2, with the wire's centre line d / 2 outside it all round: 2 (HT + (OD − ID) / 2) + 4 d with square corners. Magnetics' own single-layer tables agree with this (see the table below). The fill is the number of turns times (d / ID)², the wire's circle against the hole's.

DC bias. H = 0.4π N I / le is the field of the current round a path of length le. A powder core's permeability falls as H rises; the catalog gives the curve of each mix and its fit, 1 / (a + b H^c) + d in percent of the initial value. The inductance with the current is AL N² times that percentage, and the flux density is the flux linkage over N Ae: B = L I / (N Ae), derived here.

AC. A sine voltage across N turns makes a flux whose peak density is Bpk = Vrms 10⁸ / (4.44 Ae N f) (Micrometals' equation; 4.44 is 2π / √2). The catalog's loss curve of the mix at that Bpk and frequency gives the loss per cm³, times the volume Ve the core loss; the temperature rise is Magnetics' estimate with the bare core's surface, π (OD² − ID²) / 2 + π (OD + ID) HT (derived here; the wound part has more surface and runs a little cooler). The inductance at the frequency is AL N² times the frequency fit's value there over its value at 10 kHz, the frequency AL is measured at (derived); the reactance and the no-load current follow. The permeability at Bpk is shown as a percentage, not applied to the inductance: the two fits are separate curves.

Assumptions and limits

  • AL is the nominal value at low level. Frequency, the level of the AC signal and temperature move it (the mix pages in the catalog show how); none is modelled. A winding of few turns, or turns crowded on one side, reads higher than AL N² (Micrometals and Magnetics both say so). The result is the inductance for an evenly spread winding.
  • The dimensions are the catalog's, as printed, for the bare core. A finished (coated) core has a slightly smaller hole; Magnetics' tables were made from the coated dimensions and the tool, which uses Micrometals' printed ones, reproduces them when given those. The fill and the length of wire follow from that.
  • The DC-bias percentage is only for the mixes in the list above. For the others (−18, −19, −26, −34, −35, −38, −40, −45, −52, −60, −61, −65, −66, −70) the catalog's coefficients give a figure far from the catalog's own value at 200 Oe (for example 10 % against 55 % for the −26), so the tool says that it has no figure instead of printing one; mix −0 has no curve. The fit is for the field of a DC current only, and the catalog gives the curves a tolerance of +20 %, −10 %.
  • AC: only inside the catalog's curves. The loss and the heating are given from 60 Hz to 500 kHz and from 10 to 10 000 G; the permeability at a frequency from 10 kHz to 100 MHz; at Bpk from 10 to 10 000 G. Outside, the tool gives no figure rather than extending a curve. The loss fit is for a sine voltage; a square wave or a DC current with ripple loses differently. The temperature rise is an estimate for still air (Magnetics), on the bare core's surface; a fan, a board or a box changes it. Ferrite and typed cores get Bpk, the reactance and the current but no loss: the tool has no ferrite curves.
  • No winding capacitance, no AC copper loss. The DC resistance is at the wire table's temperature.
  • Display. Three figures; the inductance in nH, µH, mH or H as the size asks; the wire length in mm or m.

How it was checked

169 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the equations above (every figure and every label of the drawing; the core table built from the catalog text by a program, and the wire table): - Turns: the opening screen, 25 parts (sizes from T5 to T650, a dozen mixes, height variants, the T90/66 entry), 8 inductances in nH, µH and mH, a wanted inductance below one turn, two refusals, a typed core and its three refusals, a typed core in inches; - Inductance: the opening, 15 settings (from 1 turn to 1000, fractions of a turn, mix −0, the largest cores), three refusals; - Winding: the opening, 18 settings (gauges 6 to 40, from 1 turn to 120, a fill of 598 % and one under 1 %), Magnetics' wire-table and worked-example cases, two refusals and a wire too thick for the hole; - Bias: the opening, 14 settings (ten mixes, 0 to 20 A, 100 mA and 800 mA in mA), four mixes with no figure, a typed core and a negative current, each refused; - Ferrite: ten parts in all nine materials for the turns, seven for the inductance (tolerances of ±20, ±25 and ±30 % and minimum-only; the +35 / −25 % one is among the turns cases), a winding, the Bias refusal, the picker's ferrite entries and the missing mix picker; - AC: the opening of the pill, 16 settings (ten mixes, 60 Hz to 100 MHz, the edges of the curves at 500 kHz and 100 MHz and just past them, a saturated core, mix −0, a tiny flux), a ferrite and a typed core, three refusals, the MHz unit; - the pickers (the iron powder sizes, the ferrite parts and typed, the mixes of the T50, the mix falling back when the size has no such mix, the core remembered), the units, the pill remembered, and the ten examples.

1,080 more cases (six batches of 180: random parts and ferrites, inductances, turns, gauges, currents, AC voltages and frequencies, and units) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

Passive components › Inductors

Transformer (turns ratio)

What it computes

The ratio, the voltages and currents and the reflected impedance of a transformer; the turns it needs for a core and a flux density; and its regulation and efficiency under load. Three pills:

  • Ratio: the picker in the Output heading says what is given. Turns: the primary and secondary turns (a = Np / Ns); voltages: the primary and the secondary voltage (a = Vp / Vs); impedances: the impedance the primary must show (a = √(Zin / RL)). Always: the primary voltage and the load RL (Ω). The big result is the turns ratio a : 1; cells: the secondary voltage, the secondary current and the primary current; rows: the load as the primary sees it (a² RL), the power, the kind (step-down, step-up, 1 : 1 isolation), and the turns or the voltages. The drawing is two coils on a core with the voltages, the ratio and the load.
  • Turns: the primary and secondary voltage, the frequency (Hz, kHz, MHz), the core's cross-section Ae (cm² or mm²) and the peak flux density B (mT or gauss); the picker in the Output heading chooses a sine wave (K = 4.44, the voltage rms) or a square wave (K = 4, the voltage its amplitude). The big result is the primary turns, not rounded; cells: the whole turns (rounded up, so B stays under the limit), the secondary turns (rounded to the nearest) and the volts per turn; rows: B with the whole turns, the exact secondary turns, the constant.

  • Loaded: the primary voltage, the turns ratio Np / Ns, the winding resistances Rp and Rs, the load and the core loss (W). The big result is the loaded secondary voltage; cells: the regulation, the efficiency and the output power; rows: the no-load secondary voltage, the currents, the copper loss and the resistance the source sees.

  • Units: V, Ω and W are fixed; Hz / kHz / MHz, cm² / mm² and mT / G are pickers, each in its own box.

  • Remembered: the pill, the way the ratio is given, the waveform and the three units.

Examples: 230 V to 12 V into 8 Ω; matching 50 Ω to 200 Ω; the turns of a 50 Hz mains core of 8 cm² at 1.2 T; a 100 kHz ferrite with a square wave at Magnetics' flux level; a small mains transformer and a heavily loaded one.

Terms

  • Primary, secondary, turns ratio a: the winding the source drives, the winding that feeds the load, and Np / Ns. a above 1 is step-down (the secondary voltage is lower), a below 1 step-up. Some books write the ratio the other way round.
  • Ideal transformer: no losses, no leakage, infinite magnetizing inductance: the voltages are in the ratio of the turns, the currents the other way, and power in equals power out.
  • Reflected impedance: a load ZL on the secondary appears from the primary as a² ZL, which is how a transformer matches a source to a load.
  • EMF equation: the voltage of a winding is its turns times the rate of change of flux. For a sine wave the rms voltage is 2π f N Ae B / √2, about 4.44 f N Ae B, B the peak flux density and Ae the core's cross-section (m², tesla); for a square wave of amplitude V, V = 4 f N Ae B. With B in gauss and Ae in cm², N = V 10⁸ / (K f Ae B).
  • Flux density B, saturation: B can't exceed the core's saturation (ferrite saturates at a substantially lower flux density than laminated steel, Wikipedia), and at high frequency the core loss limits B much lower (Magnetics: 200 mT at 20 kHz down to 70 mT at 250 kHz for a power ferrite).
  • Regulation: how much the secondary voltage falls from no load to load, over the loaded voltage. Efficiency: output power over the output plus the copper and core losses.
  • Copper loss, core loss: the heat in the windings (I² R) and in the core (hysteresis and eddy currents).

Sources

  • Magnetics, "Ferrite Cores for Power: Transformer Design" (the 2013 guide, 9 pages read as text; the PDF from acalbfi.com): Np = Vp 10⁸ / (4 B Ac f) for a square wave with B in gauss, Ac in cm² and f in Hz, Ns = Np Vs / Vp, Ip = Pin / Vin and Is = Pout / Vout, efficiency = Pout / (Pout + wire losses + core losses), voltage regulation = (|V no load| − |V full load|) / |V full load| × 100, K Wa = Np Awp + Ns Aws with K 0.4 for toroids and 0.6 for pot, E and U cores, and the flux density it gives for a power ferrite against frequency (200 mT at 20 kHz, 130 mT at 50 kHz, 90 mT at 100 kHz, 70 mT at 250 kHz). The guide cites A. I. Pressman's "Switching Power Supply Design" for its area-product method; the book was not read.
  • Micrometals, "Iron Powder Cores" catalog (2023; page 18 rendered): the sine-wave flux density Bpk = Erms 10⁸ / (4.44 Ae N f) in gauss, volts, cm² and Hz, the same equation as the tool's.
  • Wikipedia, "Transformer" (the page downloaded and read as text; a secondary source): the ideal transformer identity Vp / Vs = Is / Ip = Np / Ns = a (its equation 5), the load impedance seen from the primary a² ZL (equation 7), the universal EMF equation Erms = 2π f N A Bpeak / √2 ≈ 4.44 f N A Bpeak, and the equivalent circuit: winding resistances and leakage reactances in series, referred to the primary by multiplying the secondary's by a², and the magnetizing branch, which can be moved to the input to give two series impedances that simply add. Its sign convention (step-up a < 1) is the one used here.
  • Fair-Rite data sheet 5943002721 (read): Ae 0.78 cm² of a 43-mix toroid, used for the example of the 100 kHz core.
  • Not read: IEEE C57 and IEC 60076 (power transformer standards), the open- and short-circuit tests, autotransformers, three-phase connections, leakage inductance and winding capacitance formulas. The tool is for single-phase two-winding transformers.

Why the formulas are these

Ratio. Faraday's law gives each winding a voltage proportional to its turns; conservation of power gives the currents the other way; a load RL on the secondary draws Vs / RL, and the primary current is that divided by a, so the primary sees Vp / Ip = a² RL (Wikipedia, Magnetics). When the ratio is given by two voltages or by two impedances the same relations are used the other way: a = Vp / Vs, or a = √(Zin / RL).

Turns. The EMF equation solved for N: V 10⁸ / (K f Ae B) with the units of the printed forms (B in gauss, Ae in cm², the tool converts from tesla and m²). The whole turns are rounded up because fewer turns would raise B above the value asked for; B with the whole turns is shown. The secondary turns are the primary's whole turns times Vs / Vp, rounded to the nearest. K is 4.44 for a sine wave (rms) and 4 for a square wave (amplitude). The exact sine constant is 2π / √2 = 4.4429; the printed 4.44 is used.

Loaded (derived here). In the simplified equivalent circuit (magnetizing branch at the input, leakage reactance ignored) the source drives Rp, the secondary resistance referred as a² Rs and the load as a² RL in series: Ip = Vp / (Rp + a² (Rs + RL)); then Is = a Ip and Vs = Is RL. The no-load secondary voltage is Vp / a. The regulation is (Vno-load − Vloaded) / Vloaded. The copper loss is Ip² Rp + Is² Rs. The core loss is typed in and goes into the efficiency only (the magnetizing current it implies is not added to Ip).

Assumptions and limits

  • A resistive load, one frequency, sine or square-wave drive. The Loaded pill leaves out the leakage reactance and the magnetizing current, so its regulation is the resistive part only; a real mains transformer's leakage reactance adds to it for loads with reactance, and the core loss is a number you supply.
  • No saturation check beyond B. The tool gives B; whether it is acceptable depends on the core and the temperature (the Magnetics levels above are for a power ferrite at a 100 mW/cm³ loss limit).
  • Turns are rounded for the core, not for the winding window. Whether the wire fits is the Toroid winding tool's business (or the area product K Wa = Np Awp + Ns Aws).
  • Skin effect and proximity effect, winding capacitance, tolerances of the turns ratio are not modelled.
  • Display. Three figures; V or mV or kV, A or mA or µA, Ω or kΩ or MΩ, W or mW or kW as the size asks.

How it was checked

81 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation of the equations above (every figure and every label of the drawing): - Ratio: the opening screen, 9 settings by turns (1 : 1 to 1000 : 1, fractions of a turn, 50 mV to 1 kV, 0.1 Ω to 100 kΩ), 8 by voltages, 8 by impedances (equal, 50 Ω to 200 Ω, 1 MΩ to 50 Ω), six refusals; - Turns: the opening screen, 12 settings (sine and square wave, 50 Hz to 1 MHz, 0.25 to 100 cm² and mm² sections, 40 to 1500 mT, and in gauss), five refusals, the constant and the picker; - Loaded: the opening screen, 12 settings (no losses, almost shorted, almost unloaded, 1 : 1, step-up, 1 kV), five refusals; - the pickers and their memory, the units, and the six examples.

540 more cases (three batches of 180: random turns, voltages, impedances, frequencies, flux densities, sections, resistances, loads and core losses, in the three frequency, two flux and two area units) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept. The loaded circuit was also compared, on 2000 random transformers, with the Thevenin form (the no-load voltage Vp / a behind Rs + Rp / a²) and with the power balance (source power = output + copper loss): the differences were at the level of rounding (5 × 10⁻¹⁶).

Passive components › Inductors

Series/parallel (L)

What it computes

The total inductance of two to six inductors, in series or in parallel, by pill.

  • Inputs: each inductor's value, in nH, µH, mH or H, by typing or with its slider, which steps through the standard values. Rows are added and removed.
  • Tolerance: ±5, 10 or 20 %, which sets the E-series offered: E24, E12 or E6. Each row names the nearest standard value.
  • Output: the total, large, with its worst-case spread from the tolerance and the nearest single standard part.
  • Drawing: the coils end to end, or side by side between two rails.
  • Remembered: the connection and the tolerance.

Examples: two 10 µH in series, two 22 µH in parallel, 15 µH made from 10 and 4.7 µH, and 100 µH beside 47 µH.

Source

Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Volume I, DC, 5th edition (2021), chapter 15, read in review: - §15.4: - in series "the total inductance is the sum of the individual inductors' inductances", Ltotal = L1 + L2 + … Ln; - in parallel it is "less than any one of the parallel inductors' inductances", with the formula "the same form as for calculating parallel resistances". - §15.5, practical considerations: - a rated current; - the series resistance of the coil's wire; - mutual inductance when the magnetic fields of two inductors "link" with each other's turns.

Why the formulas are these

series:   L = L1 + L2 + … + Ln
parallel: 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2 + … + 1/Ln
two in parallel: L = L1 × L2 / (L1 + L2)

Inductance is the voltage across a coil for a given rate of change of its current. In series one current changes through every coil, so their voltages add and so do the inductances. In parallel the current divides between them, so the same change in the total makes less voltage: the total is below the smallest. Inductors combine like resistors and unlike capacitors.

Assumptions and limits

  • No coupling: the sums hold only if the coils' fields do not link. Two inductors close together, or wound on one core, add a mutual inductance M: in series the total can be more or less than the sum, depending on how they are wound. That case is not computed here.
  • Ideal coils: each real one also has a resistance and a rated current. In series the lowest rating limits the chain.
  • The spread takes every part at the same tolerance, worst case.

How it was checked

8 cases: - 10 µH + 10 µH in series is 20 µH, ±20 % spanning 16 to 24 µH; - two 22 µH in parallel are 11 µH; - 10 µH + 4.7 µH make 14.7 µH; - 100 µH beside 47 µH is 31.97 µH; - a third 10 µH makes 30 µH; - 10 µH + 10 mH is 10.01 mH; - a negative value is refused; - the remembered connection and tolerance.

Toroid/ferrite reference table

What it shows

741 toroidal cores from two makers' catalogs, with the numbers a winding needs. Two pills:

  • Iron powder: the 616 toroids of Micrometals' 2023 catalog (101 sizes, T5 to T650, with their height variants, in every mix the size is made in).
  • Ferrite: the 125 uncoated toroids of Fair-Rite's catalog (17th edition), in nine materials: the nickel-zinc 43, 52, 61, 67 and 68 and the manganese-zinc 75, 76, 77 and 78.

Each card gives the part number with its material and permeability, the outside diameter × inside diameter × height in mm, AL in nH/N² with its tolerance, the magnetic path length le, the cross-section Ae and the volume Ve, and one line on what the material is for. The heading holds two pickers: the material (all, or one mix) and the order (by size, by AL from low to high or from high to low). The search box finds a part by its number, ignoring spaces and dashes (t50 2 finds T50-2). Thirty cards show at a time; the button under them adds thirty more.

  • Remembered: the pill, the material and the order. Changing the pill puts the material back to all.

Both tables are the Toroid winding tool's core picker, so a core found here can be picked there: an iron powder core by size and mix, a ferrite by its part number.

Terms

  • AL (inductance factor): the inductance of one turn in nH; N turns give AL N² nH. Micrometals tests it at 10 gauss and 10 kHz on a full, evenly spaced single layer; Fair-Rite tests its toroids at 10 kHz.
  • Tolerance: Micrometals gives one tolerance per mix (±5 % for −2, −6, −7, −10 and −17, ±10 % for the others); Fair-Rite gives one per part (±20, ±25, ±30 or +35 / −25 %, or only a minimum: "min").
  • Mix, material, µ, µi: the maker's number for the magnetic material and its (initial) permeability. Micrometals numbers its mixes −0 to −70; Fair-Rite's two digits after the 59 of the part number are the material (5943… is 43 material).
  • le, Ae, Ve: the effective path length (cm), cross-section (cm²) and volume (cm³) of the core.
  • Iron powder, ferrite; NiZn, MnZn: iron powder is carbonyl iron or a powdered alloy pressed with a binder, a distributed air gap; ferrite is a ceramic of iron oxide. Fair-Rite's nickel-zinc ferrites are for higher frequencies (above about 1 MHz) and low flux density; its manganese-zinc ferrites have the highest permeabilities and serve from the low kHz into the broadcast band (the catalog's own summary).

Sources

  • Micrometals, "Iron Powder Cores" catalog (2023; the PDF from micrometals.com, read as text): the toroid table (PDF pages 48 onward: part number, dimensions in inches and mm, Ae, le, Ve, AL, reference permeability, mix), the typical AL tolerance of each mix (PDF page 47), the AL test conditions, and the description of every mix (the materials pages and the selection guide), which the one-line notes paraphrase. Read and built by a program (616 parts in 101 sizes); the T400-2D row (AL printed as 4.8, the same as the T400-0D's, almost certainly 48) and the T250-8A/90 row (no AL) are left out, and the T90-66 row, whose dimensions are not the T90's, is its own entry. Cross-checked with an older Amidon table (the qsl.net copy): AL agrees within 2 % for 89 of the 96 parts in both.
  • Fair-Rite Products, "Ferrite Cores" catalog, 17th edition (© 2013; the copy on a CERN web server, 164 pages read as text): the toroid tables (PDF pages 104 to 112): part number, A, B and C dimensions with tolerances, weight, Σl/A, le, Ae, Ve and AL with its tolerance; the notes that toroids are tested for AL at 10 kHz and that the 9th digit of the part number is 1 for a Parylene coating and 2 for a thermo-set plastic coating (whose rows, 73 of them, have the same magnetic figures and are not listed); the "Soft Ferrites" summary of the nickel-zinc and manganese-zinc families; and the frequency ranges the catalog gives for its materials (43: 25–300 MHz suppression; 52: 250–1000 MHz; 61: 1–40 MHz broadband and inductive, above 250 MHz suppression; 67: 10–100 MHz; 75: 200 kHz–30 MHz). 125 parts, parsed by a program; one row is odd as printed (5943017501: Ve 70.5 cm³ against Ae × le = 75.3).
  • Fair-Rite data sheet 5943002721 (the CERN copy; read): the coated version of 5943002701: AL 885 nH +20 / −25 %, Ae 0.78 cm², le 8.9 cm, Ve 7 cm³. The catalog gives the uncoated part 885 nH ±20 %, 0.79 cm², 8.9 cm and 7 cm³.
  • Not read: Fair-Rite's newer catalogs and its current web data (this edition has no toroids in 31, 33, 73 or 95 to 98 material, which Fair-Rite sells now), Ferroxcube's and TDK's toroids, the material curves (permeability against frequency, temperature and flux) of either maker. The 77 and 78 notes give only the family and permeability: the catalog's toroid pages do not say what they are for.

Assumptions and limits

  • The catalog figures, as printed. Dimensions are the uncoated core's; a coated core is larger outside and smaller inside (Fair-Rite: up to 0.5 mm for thermo-set plastic, 0.038 mm for Parylene).
  • AL is for low level and 10 kHz. At higher frequencies, with a DC current or with a large AC flux the inductance changes (the Toroid winding tool's Bias pill gives the DC effect for the iron powder mixes whose curve fit agrees with the catalog).
  • Editions. Fair-Rite's 2013 edition, and Micrometals' 2023 catalog. Parts come and go: check the maker's current data before ordering.
  • Display. Three figures; part numbers as the makers print them.

How it was checked

64 cases, the expected lists from a Python program that builds the same rows from the same data and filters, sorts and searches them the way the screen should: - Iron powder: the opening list (the count, the first three cards, the 30th, the Show more button and what it adds), each of the 24 mixes (the count and the first two cards), the material picker, both AL orders, ten searches (with spaces and dashes, a mix suffix, a height variant, one that finds nothing), a search within a mix, and the T50-2 card against the catalog's own row; - Ferrite: the opening list, each of the nine materials, the picker, both orders, five searches, and the 5943002701 card against the catalog and the data sheet; - the pill, the material and the order remembered, and the material reset when the pill changes.

Every card checked gives its title, size, AL line, le and Ae line and note.

RC filter

What it computes

The cutoff frequency of a filter made of one resistor and one capacitor — or the resistor or capacitor for a cutoff you want — as a low-pass or a high-pass, with up to six identical stages. It draws the frequency response, and gives the attenuation and phase shift at any frequency you pick.

Source

No standard is needed: the results follow from Ohm's law and the impedance of a capacitor. The derivation is below.

What it means

A filter passes some frequencies and weakens others. A low-pass (resistor in series, capacitor to ground) lets slow signals through and weakens fast ones: it smooths PWM into a steady voltage, or removes noise above the band you care about. A high-pass (capacitor in series, resistor to ground) does the reverse: it blocks DC and passes the signal riding on it, as a coupling capacitor does in audio.

  • Cutoff frequency, fc — where the output has fallen to 70.7% of the input (1/√2). Below it a low-pass passes nearly everything; above it, less and less.
  • Decibels (dB) — a way of comparing two levels on a scale that suits signals: 20 × log₁₀(output ÷ input). −3 dB is 70.7%, −20 dB a tenth, −40 dB a hundredth.
  • Pole — one RC stage. Past fc a single pole weakens the signal by a further 20 dB for every tenfold increase in frequency (20 dB per decade); two poles 40 dB, and so on.
  • Phase shift — how far the output's waveform is behind (lag) or ahead of (lead) the input's, in degrees of a cycle. At fc it is 45°.

Why the formulas are these

A capacitor's impedance falls with frequency: Z = 1 / (2πfC). The low-pass is a voltage divider of R on top and C below, so its output is the part of the input across C:

Vout / Vin = 1 / (1 + j·f/fc),     fc = 1 / (2πRC)

At f = fc the real and imaginary parts are equal, so the magnitude is 1/√2 (−3.01 dB) and the phase −45°. Well above fc the magnitude is fc/f: ten times the frequency, a tenth of the output, −20 dB. The high-pass swaps R and C, and its response is the same with f/fc turned upside down.

Solving fc = 1 / (2πRC) for R or C gives the other two forms the tool uses.

With N identical stages each buffered (an op-amp between them, so none loads the next), the responses multiply: the dB figures and the phase are N times one stage's. At each stage's fc the total is already −3N dB, so the system's own −3 dB point moves in:

f(−3 dB) = fc × √(2^(1/N) − 1)          (low-pass; high-pass divides instead)

For two stages that is 0.644 × fc.

Assumptions and limits

  • Nothing loads the output. A load in parallel with the output changes the divider: keep it well above R (ten times R or more costs under 10%), or buffer it.
  • The source drives it with little resistance of its own. A source resistance adds to R and lowers fc.
  • Several poles here means buffered stages. Unbuffered RC stages in a chain load each other and give a softer knee than this.
  • Parts have tolerances: a ±5% R and a ±10% C move fc by up to about 15%.

What it deliberately does not do

  • RL filters have their own tool; op-amp active filters with gain and sharper shapes (Butterworth, Sallen-Key) are not covered.
  • The time response — how the output settles after a step — is the RC charge/discharge tool.

How it was checked

10 kΩ with 100 nF gives 159.2 Hz; at fc the attenuation is −3.01 dB and the phase −45°. Two buffered poles put the system's −3 dB point at 102.4 Hz, 0.644 × fc. 10 kΩ with 1 µF gives 15.92 Hz, and −35.97 dB at 1 kHz. A high-pass of the same parts is 2.13 dB down at 20 Hz. fc = 20 kHz with 1 kΩ needs 7.958 nF.

The review found the frequency to explore opening at 159.2 Hz, a rounded fc, which showed −45.01°; it now starts at fc exactly. The units offered were cut to those RC filters use: Ω to MΩ, pF to µF, Hz to MHz.

Passive components › Passive filters

RL filter

What it computes

The cutoff frequency of a filter made of one resistor and one inductor — or the resistor or inductor for a cutoff you want — as a low-pass or a high-pass, with up to six identical stages; the frequency response, and the attenuation and phase shift at any frequency you pick.

Source

No standard is needed: the results follow from Ohm's law and the impedance of an inductor. The derivation is below.

What it means

It is the RC filter's counterpart with an inductor in place of the capacitor (see that section for what a filter, fc, a decibel, a pole and a phase shift are). An inductor's impedance rises with frequency, where a capacitor's falls, so the two parts swap places:

  • Low-pass — inductor in series, resistor to ground. The inductor blocks the fast signals. Often the "resistor" is the load itself: a loudspeaker in a crossover, a circuit fed through a choke.
  • High-pass — resistor in series, inductor to ground. The inductor shorts the slow signals to ground and lets the fast ones through, as in RF circuits where the series resistance is the 50 Ω of the system.

Why the formulas are these

An inductor's impedance is Z = 2πfL. The low-pass is a divider of L on top and R below, so its output is the part across R:

Vout / Vin = R / (R + j·2πfL) = 1 / (1 + j·f/fc),     fc = R / (2πL)

This is the same shape as the RC low-pass, so everything that follows from it is the same: −3.01 dB and −45° at fc, 20 dB per decade beyond, and for N buffered stages a system −3 dB point at fc × √(2^(1/N) − 1). The high-pass swaps R and L and turns f/fc upside down. Solving fc = R / (2πL) for R or L gives the other two forms.

Assumptions and limits

  • A real inductor has resistance. Its winding's DC resistance (DCR, in the datasheet) adds to R in a low-pass and flattens the high-pass at low frequencies. For small R — an 8 Ω speaker — it matters.
  • Cores saturate. Past its rated current an inductor with a ferrite or iron core loses much of its inductance, and fc moves up.
  • Every inductor resonates with its own winding capacitance at its self-resonant frequency (SRF, in the datasheet); well below it the model holds, near it the part stops behaving as an inductor.
  • Nothing loads the output, and several poles mean buffered stages, as for the RC filter.

What it deliberately does not do

  • RC filters have their own tool; LC filters (both an inductor and a capacitor, 40 dB per decade from one pair) are not covered.
  • Loudspeaker crossover design beyond one coil — the speaker's impedance is not a pure 8 Ω across the band — is not covered.

How it was checked

100 Ω with 100 mH gives 159.2 Hz; at fc −3.01 dB and −45°. An 8 Ω woofer crossed over at 2.5 kHz needs 509.3 µH. A 10 µH choke into 10 Ω is a 159.2 kHz low-pass, −16.07 dB at 1 MHz. 100 nH to ground in a 50 Ω system is a high-pass at 79.58 MHz.

The review made the same corrections as on the RC filter: the frequency to explore opens at fc exactly, Low-/High-pass take the mode pills, and the resistor units are ohms to megohms. Inductors keep nH to H and frequencies up to GHz, which RF inductors and supply chokes really reach.

Passive components › Passive filters

LC filter

What it computes

A band-pass or a notch made of inductors and capacitors between a source resistance and a load: one resonator (an L and a C), or a ladder of 2 to 5 resonators. Two pills, Band-pass and Notch. The Your inputs heading holds the circuit, Series LC or Parallel LC (for a ladder, the kind of the first section), and the number of poles. Under the drawing of the circuit, the response is plotted in dB around f0, with the −3 dB line, the edges f1 and f2 and a dot at the check frequency.

  • One pole. Band-pass: a series LC in the line, or a parallel LC (a tank) across the load. Notch: a series LC from the line to ground (a trap), or a tank in the line. The Output heading says what is given. f0 and bandwidth: the centre (or notch) frequency, the −3 dB bandwidth, the source and load resistances, the coil's Q (0 for an ideal coil) and a frequency to check; the big result is the inductor and the capacitor. L and C: the two parts instead of f0 and the bandwidth; the big result is the centre frequency, the bandwidth under it. Cells: the loaded Q and the low and high edges. Rows: the loss at f0 (band-pass) or the depth (notch); the reactance of L and C at f0; the coil's loss as a resistance; for a band-pass, the voltage on L and C (series) or the current in them (tank) at f0, in units of the source's; the attenuation at the check frequency.
  • 2 to 5 poles. Designed from f0, the bandwidth and the source resistance; the Output heading picks the response: Butterworth, or Chebyshev with 0.01, 0.1, 0.5 or 1 dB of ripple. The result lists every section, its L and C, and whether it sits in the line or goes to ground; cells: the loss (band-pass) or depth (notch) at f0 with the coils' Q, and the band edges; rows: the ripple or flatness in the band, the load resistance the ladder needs (equal to the source except for an even number of Chebyshev poles), the prototype values g1 to gn, the coils' Q, the attenuation at the check frequency.
  • Units: Hz to GHz for the frequencies (the centre, the bandwidth and the check frequency share one unit), nH to H, pF to µF, Ω or kΩ for the resistances.
  • Proposed: the check frequency follows twice f0, to three figures, until you type it. Switching what is given carries the answer over (the designed L and C, or the centre and bandwidth found, to three figures); asking for more poles after a section given by L and C hands its centre and bandwidth to the ladder.
  • Remembered: the pill, the circuit, what is given, the poles, the response and the units.

Examples: Kuphaldt's four resonant filters (series band-pass, tank band-pass, trap, tank notch), a 7.1 MHz band-pass in 50 Ω, a 1 MHz tank for AM, a trap for 27 MHz, a 3-pole Butterworth for 7 MHz, a 5-pole 0.1 dB Chebyshev for 14 MHz and a 3-pole stop for the FM broadcast band.

Terms

  • Resonance, f0: the frequency where the reactance of L, 2πfL, equals that of C, 1 / (2πfC); f0 = 1 / (2π √(L C)). There a series LC is a short circuit and a parallel LC (a tank) an open circuit; either side of f0 they become a reactance that grows with the distance from it.
  • Band-pass, notch: a filter that passes a band around f0 and blocks the rest, or blocks a band and passes the rest (also called band-stop, band-reject or, for one series LC to ground, a trap).
  • Bandwidth (BW), edges f1 and f2: the band between the frequencies where the output is 3 dB down (half the power; 70.7 % of the voltage); for a Chebyshev ladder, the band inside which the response ripples. The edges are not symmetric about f0: f1 f2 = f0².
  • Loaded Q: f0 / BW, how sharp a single resonator is with the circuit around it; Q = X / R for a series LC against a resistance R in series, Q = R / X for a tank across R, X the reactance of L or C at f0. Coil Q (Qc): the coil's own reactance over its own loss resistance; typical coils have 50 to 300.
  • Pole: for these filters, one resonator; each adds 20 dB per tenfold step in frequency to the slopes far from the band. Butterworth: as flat as possible in the band; Chebyshev: a set ripple in the band for steeper sides. Prototype values g1 to gn: the element values of a low-pass filter with a cut-off of 1 rad/s between 1 Ω resistances, which the band-pass and band-stop designs scale.

Sources

  • Tony R. Kuphaldt, "Lessons in Electric Circuits", volume II (AC), chapter 8 "Filters", section "Resonant filters" (ibiblio.org, read as text): the four circuits, a series LC to pass a signal and a tank to short it (band-pass), a series LC to short it and a tank to block it (band-stop, notch), with their SPICE decks: 1 H and 1 µF into 1 kΩ; 500 Ω, 100 mH, 10 µF and 1 kΩ; resonance at 159.15 Hz; and the remark that the inductor's resistance limits the selectivity. Chapter 6 "Resonance", section "Q and bandwidth of a resonant circuit": Q = X / R, the bandwidth between the 70.7 % (half-power) points, BW = fc / Q, fl = fc − Δf / 2 and fh = fc + Δf / 2 (approximations, see below).
  • Michael Steer, "Microwave and RF Design IV: Modules" (North Carolina State University; the LibreTexts edition, read as its LaTeX text), section 2.7 "Butterworth and Chebyshev Filters": the Butterworth prototype g_r = 2 sin((2r − 1) π / 2n), g0 = g(n+1) = 1; the Chebyshev recursion g1 = 2 a1 / γ, g_k = 4 a(k−1) a_k / (b(k−1) g(k−1)), a_k = sin((2k − 1) π / 2n), b_k = γ² + sin²(kπ / n), γ = sinh(β / 2n), β = ln coth(R_dB / 17.3717793); g(n+1) = 1 for an odd order and, for an even order, tanh²(β / 4) after a series element or coth²(β / 4) after a shunt one; his tables of g for n = 3, 5 and 7. Section 2.9 "Filter Transformations": for a band-pass, a shunt prototype element becomes C = g / (ωBW Z0) across L = ωBW Z0 / (ω0² g) and a series one L = g Z0 / ωBW in series with C = ωBW / (ω0² g Z0); for a band-stop, a shunt element becomes L = Z0 / (ωBW g) in series with C = g ωBW / (ω0² Z0) and a series one L = g ωBW Z0 / ω0² across C = 1 / (ωBW g Z0); ω0 = √(ω1 ω2), ωBW = 2π (f2 − f1).
  • "Analog electronics for beam instrumentation", CERN Accelerator School (arXiv 2005.07422; section 3.2 read as text): the same band-pass recipe in words (a low-pass with the bandwidth as its cut-off, every element resonated at f0) and a 5-pole example at 20 MHz, 2 MHz wide, in 50 Ω.
  • Not used: the 1963 SRI report of Matthaei, Young and Jones (DTIC refused the download, "the request is blocked"; left alone) and Keysight's filter chapter (behind a form). A University of Utah lecture (ECE 5180, L27) was read and not used: it says odd-order Chebyshev filters are unmatched, the reverse of Steer and of the response this tool computes.

Why the formulas are these

One resonator (derived here by circuit analysis). The source and the load make one resistance for the resonator: Rs + RL for a part in the line, Rs RL / (Rs + RL) for a part across it. A series LC has |X| = R at the −3 dB points, X = 2πfL − 1 / (2πfC), so f2 − f1 = R / (2πL) exactly and f1 f2 = f0², which gives f1, f2 = √(f0² + BW² / 4) ∓ BW / 2; Kuphaldt's f0 ∓ BW / 2 is its high-Q approximation. A tank has |B| = G there and f2 − f1 = G / (2πC). The coil's loss is its Q at f0 as a resistance r = 2πf0 L / Qc in series with L in a series LC, and Rp = Qc 2πf0 L across a tank (the usual narrow-band equivalents); the capacitor is lossless. With them the bandwidth and the loss stay in closed form: for a series band-pass L = (Rs + RL) / (2π (BW − f0 / Qc)), so the band cannot be narrower than f0 / Qc, and its loss at f0 is −20 log(1 − QL / Qc), the familiar rule; for the notches the design solves a quadratic. The response is the load's voltage over what it gets with the filter taken out.

Ladders. Steer's prototype and transformations as quoted, with the source resistance as Z0 and the load the prototype's g(n+1) times it. The response is computed by chaining the sections' ABCD matrices (the usual network algebra), as the power the load gets over the most the source can give, with every coil's loss as above; at f0 an ideal Butterworth or odd-order Chebyshev passes everything, an even-order Chebyshev loses its ripple. The tool's check runs compare the ladder with ideal parts against the prototype's own response, 1 / (1 + Ω^2n) or 1 / (1 + ε² Tn(Ω)²) with Ω = (f / f0 − f0 / f) f0 / BW (or −1 / Ω for a band-stop), and they agree to a millionth of a dB.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal capacitors, coils with a loss set by one Q at f0 (as a series or a parallel resistance, a narrow-band model), no stray capacitance, no coupling between the coils, parts far smaller than a wavelength; real coils also self-resonate (see the Air-core coil's SRF & Q pill).
  • Ladders are designed for ideal parts: the coils' Q is in the response and the loss but does not reshape the design (predistortion is not done); with a low Q a narrow Chebyshev loses its ripple and much of its passband. Very narrow ladders give awkward values (a large series L, a small series C); coupled-resonator designs suit them better, and are not here.
  • The load of a ladder is the one it is designed for; for an even number of Chebyshev poles it differs from the source.
  • Display. Three figures; attenuations under 0.00005 dB show as 0 dB; −∞ dB for an ideal notch at f0.

How it was checked

152 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps and typing; for every case the closed forms of one resonator are compared with the circuit solved with complex impedances (the edges found by bisection agree to 1 part in 10⁷), and every ladder with ideal parts with the prototype's response. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; 32 designs (both pills, both circuits, eight settings, ideal and real coils, unequal source and load); 24 sets of L and C; two notches the coil keeps from 3 dB; the check frequency typed, kept and following; the carry-over between what is given; the units; twelve refusals; 40 ladders with ideal parts (2 to 5 poles, every response, both pills and both circuits) and six with real coils; the hand-over from one pole to many and back; the ten examples and the formula-search card.

720 more cases (four batches of 180: random circuits, values, units, coils and ladders, a tenth of them refused) compared every figure with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept. They found that an even-order Chebyshev ladder starting with a shunt element needs the tanh² load, not coth² (the first version had coth² for both), and a lost-precision low edge for very wide bands (now f1 = f0² / f2).

Published answers reproduced:

Example Source Source says Tool gives

the same in series to ground Kuphaldt ch. 8, SPICE notch at 159.15 Hz 159 Hz, −∞ dB with ideal parts, 531 Hz wide
100 mH and 10 µF in the line to 1 kΩ Kuphaldt ch. 8, SPICE notch at 159.15 Hz 159 Hz, 15.9 Hz wide
Butterworth g, n = 4 and 5 Steer, Table 1 0.7654 1.8478 …; 0.6180 1.6180 2 … the same (formula)
