Digital & logic circuits › Number systems

ASCII table

What it computes

The 128 ASCII characters on one screen, as the classic chart of 8 columns by 16 rows. Tap a character, or type it in one of the three live boxes: - Char takes a character, or a control character's name (LF, ESC, XOFF, TAB, SP…); - Dec takes the decimal code, 0–127; - Hex takes the hex code, 00–7F.

The card shows, for the chosen character: - its name, with the standard mnemonic for a control character; - its codes in octal and in binary, the binary grouped as column and row; - the C escape (\n, \t, \0…) and the Ctrl key that sends it, where there is one; - in plain words, what a control character does, how a letter relates to its other case, or a digit to its value.

Source

RFC 20, ASCII format for Network Interchange (October 1969), was read for this. It is based on USAS X3.4-1968, the US standard ASCII, and gives: - the mnemonics and full names of the 33 control characters, NUL to US and DEL. Code 9 is HT, horizontal tabulation, so the tool no longer calls it TAB (it still finds it by that name); - the definitions behind each plain-word meaning; - the chart: bits b7–b5 give the column (0–7), and b4–b1 the row (0–15).

The modern uses are common knowledge, not from RFC 20: - C's escapes; - XON/XOFF serial flow control on DC1/DC3; - Ctrl+C sending ETX and Ctrl+D sending EOT in a terminal; - CR LF line endings; - ESC starting a terminal control sequence.

What it means

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) gives 128 characters a 7-bit code. - Codes 0–31 and 127 are control characters: commands for a terminal, printer or modem rather than symbols. RFC 20 groups some of them: - communication controls frame and acknowledge messages: SOH, STX, ETX, EOT, ENQ, ACK, NAK, SYN, ETB; - format effectors move the print position: BS, HT, LF, VT, FF, CR; - information separators split data, from the largest unit to the smallest: FS, GS, RS, US. - Codes 32–126 are printed characters. 32, the space, is a printed character that prints nothing. - Codes above 127 are not ASCII. Different 8-bit sets give them different characters (Latin-1, Windows-1252…). In UTF-8 they only appear inside multi-byte characters.

Uses worth knowing in electronics: - CR LF ends a line on Windows and on many serial devices. Linux and macOS end a line with LF alone. - XOFF (DC3) and XON (DC1) pause and resume a serial sender: software flow control, Ctrl+S and Ctrl+Q. - ESC [ starts a terminal control sequence, which sets colours and moves the cursor. - SOH, EOT, ACK, NAK and CAN run XMODEM, a simple serial file-transfer protocol.

Why the formulas are these

Hex code      = column digit, then row digit
Lower case    = upper case + 0x20        (bit 5)
Digit value   = code − 0x30              (48)
Ctrl + key    = key's code AND 0x1F      (bits 5 and 6 cleared)
  • The chart's columns are the top three bits and its rows the low four. A column is one hex digit, 0–7, and a row is the other, 0–F. So A, column 4 and row 1, is 0x41.
  • Letters were placed so the two cases differ in one bit. A to Z run 0x41–0x5A, and a to z run 0x61–0x7A: setting bit 5 lowers the case.
  • Digits were placed so the low four bits are the value. 0 to 9 run 0x30–0x39, so subtracting 0x30 (or masking with 0x0F) gives the number.
  • Ctrl clears bits 5 and 6. Ctrl+C is C (0x43) AND 0x1F, which is 3, ETX; Ctrl+[ is ESC.

Assumptions and limits

  • US ASCII only. The national variants of ISO 646 replace a few printed characters, such as # or [, and are not shown.
  • Uses, not rules. The modern uses in the card say what a code usually does today. A particular device may assign its own meanings.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Numbers in other bases have their own tool, Number bases.
  • Turning text into bytes, for example "AT\r\n" into 41 54 0D 0A, was left out on Pierre's choice. It could become a tool of its own.

How it was checked

  • A: 65, 0x41, octal 101, binary 100 0001; column 4, row 1.
  • Code 9: HT, Horizontal tab (RFC 20's name).
  • LF: 10, 0x0A, octal 012, binary 000 1010, \n, Ctrl+J.
  • Hex 7E: 126, the tilde.
  • XOFF typed by name: 19, DC3.
  • ESC: octal 033, binary 001 1011, Ctrl+[.
  • 127: DEL.
  • Out of range: 200 and é are reported as not ASCII.
  • <: shown as a character, and named less-than sign.
  • Space: shown as SP.
  • 7: 55; value = 55 − 48 = 7.
  • The chart's height: constant for all 128 characters. At 375 × 812 it ends 21 px above the tab bar.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the searchable list with RFC 20's chart, and the search with three live boxes. - It named code 9 HT, after the standard, instead of TAB. - It added names and plain meanings for the 33 control codes, C escapes, Ctrl keys, and the case and digit relations. - It escaped <, > and &, which were inserted as raw HTML. - It added examples: CR LF, XOFF/XON, a digit to its number, upper and lower case.

Digital & logic circuits › Timing & interfaces

PWM (duty cycle)

What it computes

For a pulse-width-modulated signal, the tool links six live boxes: - Frequency and Duty, the usual way to specify a PWM signal; - Ton (the pulse) and Toff (the gap), the way it is read off a scope; - High level and Low level, in volts.

From them it computes: - the average voltage, shown large; - the RMS voltage; - the period.

The waveform shows two periods, with the average as a dashed line. The slider under it sets the duty. The high and low levels are remembered.

Source

The formulas follow from the definitions. Two examples were checked against documents: - The Arduino reference for analogWrite() (reference-en, read on GitHub), which gives: - the PWM frequency: 490 Hz on most Uno, Nano and Mini pins, and 980 Hz on pins 5 and 6; - the value range: 0 (always off) to 255 (always on). - An ebm-papst DC fan catalogue page (speed setting, p. 175). It states a four-wire interface "in accordance with Intel specifications for 12 VDC fans, PWM frequency 25 kHz". Intel's own 4-wire PWM fan specification could not be opened (the copies found refused access), so it was not read.

The hobby-servo figures are the common convention, not a standard: - a pulse every 20 ms (50 Hz); - 1 ms to 2 ms wide, with 1.5 ms at the centre.

What it means

PWM, pulse-width modulation, switches a signal fully on and off, fast, and sets how long it stays on. - Ton — the pulse, how long the signal stays high. - Toff — the gap, how long it stays low. - T — the period, Ton + Toff. f = 1 / T is the frequency. - The duty cycle D — the share of each period spent high, from 0 % (always off) to 100 % (always on). - The average — a load too slow to follow the switching responds to the average. That load can be a motor, a heater, the eye watching an LED, or a low-pass filter. This is how PWM sets a speed, a brightness or a DC level with a switch that wastes almost nothing: it is either fully on or fully off. - The RMS — the steady voltage that would heat a resistor the same. With a low level of 0 V, the power into a resistor is D times the full power. - A negative low level — an H-bridge switching between +V and −V. The average then goes from −V to +V as the duty goes from 0 to 100 %.

The boxes work like this: - Typing a frequency rescales the pulse and keeps the duty. - Typing a duty redistributes it and keeps the frequency. - Ton and Toff are independent, so two readings off a scope can be typed one after the other.

Why the formulas are these

D = Ton / T,   T = Ton + Toff = 1 / f
Average = Vlow + D × (Vhigh − Vlow)
RMS     = √(Vlow² × (1 − D) + Vhigh² × D)
  • The average is the time-weighted mean of the two levels: Vhigh for a share D of the time and Vlow for the rest.
  • The RMS is the square root of the time-weighted mean of the squares, by definition.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal edges. The rise and fall times are taken as zero. With real edges the average shifts a little, most at very short pulses.
  • Ideal averaging. The average is what a perfect filter, or an infinitely slow load, would see. How much ripple remains depends on the filter or the load: see the RC filter tool.
  • Frequency is a design choice the tool does not make. It must be high enough for the load to average: no visible flicker, no audible whine (20 kHz is the usual upper limit of hearing). It must also be low enough for the switching losses to stay small.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Timer register values (prescaler, top, compare) are not computed: they differ from one microcontroller family to the next.
  • Filtering the PWM into a DC level is the RC filter tool's job.

How it was checked

  • 1 kHz, 50 %, 5 V / 0 V: Ton 500 µs, average 2.5 V, RMS 3.536 V, period 1 ms.
  • 25 % at 1 kHz: 250 µs on, 750 µs off, average 1.25 V.
  • 2 kHz with the duty kept at 50 %: 250 µs on.
  • Ton 200 µs, then Toff 800 µs: 1 kHz and 20 %.
  • 150 % typed: held at 100 %, Toff 0, average 5 V.
  • +12 V / −12 V at 75 %: average 6 V, RMS 12 V.
  • Examples:
  • servo: 1.5 ms on, 18.5 ms off, 7.5 %;
  • analogWrite(128): 490 Hz, 50.2 %, 2.51 V;
  • PC fan at 40 %: 16 µs at 25 kHz;
  • 12 V motor at 75 %: 9 V.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the two mode pills with six live boxes. - It put the average voltage first and large. - It redrew the waveform: - the pulse in the part blue, not the domain colour; - two periods, with the average dashed in green; - 11 px labels instead of 9 px; - the duty slider under it. - It limited the units to real ones (Hz–MHz, ns–s), and the levels to V with a ± key. - It added plain definitions, examples, and remembered levels.

Switch debounce

(formerly Debounce / RC timing)

What it computes

It sizes the RC debouncer from Jack Ganssle's guide: Vcc through R1 to the switch, R2 from the switch to C, and C feeding a Schmitt-trigger input. - Sizing. Type the bounce time, C, Vcc and the input's worst-case thresholds (VT− at its highest, VT+ at its lowest), and R1 and R2 are sized so that both the press and the release take the bounce time to change the input. - Checking. Type R1 and R2 to check a circuit you have.

The output shows: - the delays of the circuit built from standard values, rounded up to the next value of the chosen series. The shorter delay is shown large, with the press and release delays beneath; - the two resistors in standard values; - the pressed input level caused by input leakage through R2.

Two small graphs show C's voltage after a press, falling through R2, and after a release, rising through R1 + R2. Each is drawn against the bounce window, with a dot where it crosses the threshold: green after the bounce, amber inside it. Vcc, the thresholds and the series are remembered.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; it sets the series the sized resistors are rounded to and the tolerance their spread uses.

Source

  • Jack Ganssle, A Guide to Debouncing, part 2 (ganssle.com) was read for:
  • the circuit;
  • the method: R2 from the press, R1 + R2 from the release, each against the worst-case threshold;
  • his worked example: 20 ms, 74AHCT14 at 5 V; with 0.1 µF R2 = 185 kΩ, and with 1 µF R2 = 18 kΩ, R1 + R2 = 101 kΩ, R1 = 82 kΩ;
  • the leakage concern;
  • his measured bounce times: most switches well under 10 ms, so he designs for 20 ms.

His equations are images on the page and could not be read as text. They were rebuilt from the RC charge law, and reproduce all three of his resistor values. - TI SN74AHCT14 datasheet (SCLS246T, October 2023) was read for the thresholds: - VT+ (rising) is 0.9–1.9 V at 4.5 V, and 1.0–2.1 V at 5.5 V; - VT− (falling) is 0.5–1.5 V at 4.5 V, and 0.6–1.7 V at 5.5 V; - Ganssle's 0.9 V and 1.7 V are the extremes; - the input current is ±1 µA. - Nexperia 74HC_HCT14 datasheet (rev. 10, 29 February 2024), table 10, was read for the 74HC14 thresholds: - at 4.5 V, VT+ is 1.7–3.15 V and VT− 0.9–2.0 V; - the input leakage is ±1.0 µA over temperature.

What it means

  • Contact bounce — a switch's contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when it is pressed or released. A fast input would see every bounce as another press.
  • The RC delay — C slows the input down. Pressing empties C through R2; releasing fills it through R1 + R2. The input changes only once C crosses its threshold, after the bouncing is over.
  • R1 — the pull-up. It also limits the current through the switch while it is held.
  • R2 — sets the press delay, and limits the current the contacts take from C.
  • Without R2 (C straight across the switch), a press registers on the very first contact, and the contacts take C's full discharge.
  • The bounce after that first contact is still filtered: an opening is too short for C to recharge past VT+ through R1.
  • A Schmitt-trigger input — it has two thresholds, VT− for a falling input and VT+ for a rising one, with a gap between them (hysteresis). So a slow, noisy edge switches it only once.
  • Ganssle warns never to feed C straight to a microcontroller input, as few have any hysteresis. An input without it does unpredictable things on a slow edge.
  • Some microcontrollers do have Schmitt-trigger inputs: check the datasheet, and use its thresholds.
  • Worst case — thresholds vary between parts and with the supply. The highest VT− and the lowest VT+ give the shortest delays, so those are the values to design with.
  • Pressed input — the input's leakage (up to 1 µA) flows through R2 while the switch is held, lifting the input up to 1 µA × R2 above ground.
  • Ganssle rejected 180 kΩ (0.18 V, against a lowest threshold of 0.5 V) and moved to 1 µF to bring R2 down to 18 kΩ.
  • The tool cautions from 0.1 V.

Why the formulas are these

Press delay   = R2 × C × ln(Vcc / VT−)
Release delay = (R1 + R2) × C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc)
Sizing:  R2 = t / (C × ln(Vcc / VT−)),   R1 + R2 = t / (C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc))
  • Press: C falls from Vcc toward 0 through R2 alone, following V = Vcc × e^(−t/R2C). It reaches VT− after R2C × ln(Vcc / VT−).
  • Release: C rises from 0 toward Vcc through R1 + R2, following V = Vcc × (1 − e^(−t/(R1+R2)C)). It reaches VT+ after (R1 + R2)C × −ln(1 − VT+ / Vcc).
  • Bounce makes the real delays longer. Each opening during a press lets C climb back a little, so these delays are the shortest the circuit can give, which is what the design needs.
  • Typing the bounce time, C or the thresholds sizes R1 and R2. Typing R1 or R2 checks them, as typed.
  • The standard values are rounded up, so the built circuit never waits less than the bounce time. Ganssle rounded to the nearest values (18 k, 82 k): that gives 19.4 ms and 19.8 ms, a little under his 20 ms, which already doubles the bounce he measured.

Assumptions and limits

  • Full charge and discharge. Each delay starts from C fully charged or fully empty. A press released before C has emptied gives a shorter release delay.
  • Leakage only through R2 is shown. The released input also sits up to 1 µA × (R1 + R2) below Vcc.
  • Bounce time is the switch's. Measure it, or use Ganssle's 20 ms. Some switches bounce far longer.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Firmware debouncing, which Ganssle's guide also covers, is not modelled.
  • The RC charge itself, with any threshold, has its own tool: RC charge/discharge.

How it was checked

  • 20 ms, 1 µF, 74AHCT14 at 5 V (1.7 V, 0.9 V):
  • exact R2 18.539 kΩ and R1 82.242 kΩ, so R1 + R2 = 100.78 kΩ (Ganssle's 101 kΩ);
  • E24, rounded up: 20 kΩ and 91 kΩ;
  • delays: press 21.58 ms, release 22.03 ms;
  • pressed input ≤ 20 mV.
  • 0.1 µF: R2 = 185.39 kΩ (Ganssle's 185 kΩ). With 200 kΩ (E24) the pressed input sits at 200 mV, and the tool cautions.
  • 50 ms: R2 46.347 kΩ, R1 205.6 kΩ.
  • 10 k and 10 k typed with 1 µF: press 10.79 ms, release 3.969 ms, shorter than 20 ms.
  • 74HC14 at 4.5 V (2.0 V, 1.7 V), 1 µF, 20 ms: 27 kΩ and 18 kΩ (E24), shorter delay 21.35 ms.
  • R2 = 0: the press delay is 0 s, and the tool says why.

The review made these changes: - It replaced the single-resistor circuit, C straight across the switch, with Ganssle's two-resistor circuit and his worst-case method. - It made Vcc count. It was an input the result never used, because the threshold was a percentage. - It replaced the guessed 50 % threshold with VT− and VT+ in volts, from the datasheet. - It replaced the unsourced bounce-time table with Ganssle's measurements. - It added the two graphs and the leakage check. - It limited the units to real ones (Ω–MΩ, pF–µF, µs–s, volts). - It put the result first and large, added examples, and remembers the input's thresholds. - The tool was renamed Switch debounce, on Pierre's choice.

Digital & logic circuits › Timing & interfaces

I2C pull-up resistor

What it computes

For an I²C bus, given the speed mode, the supply, the bus capacitance and the number of devices, it computes: - the window of pull-up resistances that work; - a suggested value inside it, snapped to a standard E-series and shown large. The result says which limit sets the top of the window: the rise time, or the devices' leakage; - for the Rp you have: its rise time, the current it asks a device to sink, and how far leakage pulls the high level down through it.

The mode, the series and Vdd are remembered.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; it sets the series the suggested Rp is rounded to and the tolerance its spread uses.

Source

NXP UM10204, I²C-bus specification and user manual, rev. 7.0 (1 October 2021), was read for every limit: - Section 7.1, pull-up resistor sizing: - the rise time is measured between 0.3 and 0.7 Vdd, which gives T = 0.8473 × RC; - Rp(max) = t_r / (0.8473 × Cb); - Rp(min) is set by the minimum sink current: 3 mA for Standard and Fast mode, 20 mA for Fast-mode Plus; - portable, low-power designs "can use a value toward the higher end of the range". - Table 10, the I/O stages: - V_OL1 is 0.4 V at 3 mA when Vdd > 2 V; - V_OL2 is 0.2 Vdd at 2 mA when Vdd ≤ 2 V, for Fast mode and Fast-mode Plus only; - I_OL at 0.4 V is 3, 3 and 20 mA; - each I/O pin is at most 10 pF. - Table 11, the bus lines: - the rise time t_r is at most 1000, 300 and 120 ns; - the bus capacitance Cb is at most 400, 400 and 550 pF; - the high-level noise margin is 0.2 Vdd. - Section 7.4, input leakage: each connection may draw up to 10 µA at the high level, and "due to the required noise margin of 0.2 VDD for the HIGH level, this input current limits the maximum value of Rp."

What it means

  • Open-drain. I²C lines are open-drain: a device can only pull a line low. Nothing drives it high; the pull-up resistor Rp brings it back. That single fact produces the bounds, pulling in opposite directions.
  • I_OL — the current a device is rated to sink while holding the line at the output-low level V_OL. Too small an Rp asks for more.
  • The rise time t_r — the time the line takes to climb from 0.3 to 0.7 Vdd. Too large an Rp makes it too slow for the mode.
  • The bus capacitance Cb — every pin on the bus, up to 10 pF each, plus the wiring. It is the input people are most wrong about, and the whole upper bound scales with it.
  • Leakage — every device may leak up to 10 µA into the line. Through Rp, that pulls the high level down, and it must not cost more than the 0.2 Vdd noise margin. With many devices this, and not the rise time, sets the top of the window.

Why the formulas are these

Rp min          = (Vdd − V_OL) / I_OL        V_OL = 0.4 V, or 0.2 Vdd at 2 V or less
Rp max          = t_r / (0.8473 × Cb)
Rp max, leakage = 0.2 Vdd / (n × 10 µA)
Suggested       = √(Rp min × Rp max), on the E-series
  • The lower bound is the pull-down. When a device asserts the line, its transistor has to hold it below V_OL while the pull-up pushes (Vdd − V_OL) / Rp into it.
  • The upper bound is the rise. Going up, the line is just an RC: the pull-up charging the bus capacitance. An RC charge reaches 0.3 Vdd at RC × ln(1/0.7), and 0.7 Vdd at RC × ln(1/0.3). The difference is RC × ln(7/3) = 0.8473 RC, the factor the spec prints.
  • The leakage bound is Ohm's law. n devices × 10 µA through Rp must drop no more than 0.2 Vdd.
  • The suggestion is the geometric mean of the two bounds: the centre of the window on a logarithmic scale, which is what "equal margin on both sides" means when the ends can differ by a decade. The spec's own advice for low-power designs is the high end instead.
  • Finding Cb. Measure the rise time with a known Rp, and the same formula gives Cb = t_r / (0.8473 × Rp).
  • When the window closes. Rp max falls as the bus capacitance rises, while Rp min does not move. At 3.3 V in Fast mode the two cross at about 366 pF. Past that no resistor rises in time without overloading the pull-down. That is a dead end, not a poor choice. The ways out are:
  • a shorter bus, or fewer devices;
  • a slower mode;
  • a bus buffer that splits the bus into segments (UM10204 section 7.2).

Assumptions and limits

  • Bus capacitance is an estimate. UM10204 gives no capacitance per centimetre of wiring, so the tool does not guess one. Measure it on a long bus, as above.
  • One lumped capacitance and an ideal resistor. At Fast-mode Plus, with long tracks, the line no longer behaves as one RC.
  • Standard mode at 2 V or less has no output-low level in UM10204. The tool keeps 0.4 V at 3 mA and says so.
  • I_OL follows the mode and the supply, unless you type a value: a particular part may be rated differently.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Current-source or switched pull-ups (UM10204 section 7.2.4): a different circuit, with different arithmetic.
  • Bus buffers and repeaters: they split a bus into segments, each with its own capacitance and resistor. Run the tool once per segment.
  • Level shifters: a MOSFET level shifter between two voltage domains puts a pull-up on each side, and the two interact.

How it was checked

  • 400 kHz, 3.3 V, 100 pF, 2 devices:
  • window 966.7 Ω – 3.541 kΩ, 1.8 kΩ suggested;
  • with 2.2 kΩ: rise time 186.4 ns, sink current 1.318 mA, leakage drop 44 mV.
  • 100 kHz, same bus: up to 11.8 kΩ, 3.3 kΩ suggested.
  • 100 kHz with 10 devices: leakage caps Rp at 6.6 kΩ, and 2.4 kΩ is suggested.
  • 1.8 V at 400 kHz: I_OL drops to 2 mA, Rp min is 720 Ω, and 1.6 kΩ is suggested.
  • 1 MHz, 3.3 V, 200 pF: 145–708.1 Ω, 330 Ω suggested.
  • 370 pF at 400 kHz and 3.3 V: no value works.

The review made these changes: - It added the output-low level below 2 V, 0.2 Vdd at 2 mA. The tool used 0.4 V at 3 mA at any supply, which put Rp min too low on a 1.8 V bus (467 Ω instead of 720 Ω). - It added the input-leakage limit (UM10204 section 7.4), with a Devices field. - It replaced the unsourced "a few pF per centimetre of track" with the spec's 10 pF per pin and the measure-the-rise-time method. - It put the suggestion first and large, and named which limit sets the window. - It added examples, remembered the mode, series and Vdd, enlarged the 10 px labels to 11 px, and added plain definitions.

UART baud rate

What it computes

From a peripheral clock and a wanted baud rate, it computes: - the divisor the UART needs, and the divisor actually written once it is rounded; - the rate that divisor gives, and the resulting error, shown large; - the frame time for 8N1.

There are two kinds of divider, each at 16x or 8x oversampling: - 16x / 8x: the integer divider of the AVR, the 16550 family and PIC. - STM32 16x / 8x: the finer divider of STM32's USART.

A table gives the error of every standard rate on the same clock; tap one to try it. The drawing shows the sample points walking off the bits as the error grows. The mode and the clock are remembered.

Source

There is no single standard for baud generation: it is per-device. Three sources were read: - ST's STM32G0 HAL driver (stm32g0xx_hal_uart.h and .c, on GitHub): - UART_DIV_SAMPLING16 is round(PCLK / baud); - UART_DIV_SAMPLING8 is round(2 × PCLK / baud); - the authorized BRR is UART_BRR_MIN 0x10 (16) to UART_BRR_MAX 0xFFFF. - The Arduino AVR core (HardwareSerial.cpp, ArduinoCore-avr on GitHub): - begin() tries U2X, the 8x mode, first; - it falls back to 16x only for 57600 at 16 MHz (for bootloader compatibility), or when the divisor would exceed 4095. - The error budget is derived below from the sampling behaviour, not quoted.

What it means

  • A UART sends bytes one bit at a time, with no clock wire. Both ends agree on a rate, the baud, in bits per second.
  • Its own oscillator — it has none. It divides whatever clock it is given, and the divisor is a whole number, so the rate comes out a little off.
  • Oversampling (16x or 8x) — how many clock periods of the divided clock the receiver counts per bit, to find the middle of each bit.
  • 8N1 — one start bit, eight data bits, no parity, one stop bit: ten bits per frame.
  • Register names:
  • an AVR writes UBRR = divisor − 1;
  • an STM32 writes BRR, which at 16x is the divisor shown. At 8x the HAL computes USARTDIV, shown here, and repacks it into BRR.

Why the formulas are these

Integer:  Divisor = Clock / (Oversample × Baud),  Actual = Clock / (Oversample × round(Divisor))
STM32:    BRR = round(Clock / Baud) at 16x,  round(2 × Clock / Baud) at 8x
          Actual = Clock / BRR,  or 2 × Clock / USARTDIV
Error  = (Actual − Baud) / Baud

Integer dividers. At 16 MHz, 115200 baud and 16x, the divisor comes to 8.681. Written as 9, the line runs at 111,111 baud, 3.55 % slow. - That single fact is why 14.7456 MHz crystals exist: 14,745,600 / 16 = 921,600, which divides exactly into every standard rate. 11.0592 MHz and 18.432 MHz are the same trick at other speeds. - An Arduino Uno does better than that figure. Its core uses 8x mode first: 16 MHz / (8 × 17) = 117,647 baud, 2.12 % fast.

STM32. STM32's USART divides in whole clock cycles per bit, sixteen times finer than an integer 16x divider. The same 16 MHz at 115200 writes BRR = 139: 115,108 baud, −0.08 %.

How much error a link survives. There is no clock shared between the two ends. The receiver finds the falling edge of the start bit, starts its own counter, and samples each bit at what it believes is the middle. Taking the receiver as the reference, it samples bit n at

(n + 0.5) × T_rx

while the transmitter's bit n occupies

[ n × T_tx , (n+1) × T_tx ]

With r = T_tx / T_rx, the sample lands in the right bit only while

n × r  <  n + 0.5  <  (n+1) × r

Nothing resynchronises inside a frame, so the worst case is the last bit. For 8N1 that is the stop bit, n = 9:

9 r < 9.5      →  r < 1.0556
9.5 < 10 r     →  r > 0.95

So the two clocks may differ by about −5.0 % to +5.56 %, usually quoted as ±5 %. - It is slightly asymmetric because the sample point is fixed at mid-bit, while the bit it must land in is what stretches. - That budget covers both ends together. Hence 2 % each as the practical rule: it leaves room for the other end, edge jitter and finite rise time. - The tool's colours: blue up to 2 %, amber to 3 %, red beyond. The caution says "fails outright" only past 5 %.

The error does not accumulate across a message. The receiver re-finds the start edge on every frame, so the drift resets ten bits at a time.

The drawing shows exactly this. The waveform is drawn at the transmitter's real bit width, stretched or squeezed by the error, while the sample marks stay evenly spaced where the receiver puts them. Raise the error, and the marks that fall outside their own bit turn red.

Assumptions and limits

  • 8N1 is assumed. Parity or a second stop bit makes the frame longer and the budget tighter.
  • One end's error. The receiver is taken as exact. In reality both ends have error and the two add, which is why the caution starts at 2 % rather than 5 %.
  • STM32 as ST's HAL writes it, read from the G0 driver only; the other STM32 families' drivers were not read. Other vendors' fractional dividers (SAM, nRF and others) have their own resolution, and are not modelled.
  • Oversampling is a divider stage, not noise immunity. 8x doubles the top speed from a given clock, and halves the margin around each sample.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Auto-baud detection, where the receiver measures a known character.
  • Anything above the physical layer: framing errors, break detection, flow control.

How it was checked

  • 16 MHz, 115200, integer 16x: divisor 8.681, 9 used, 111,111 Bd, −3.55 %.
  • 16 MHz at 9600: 104, +0.16 %.
  • Arduino Uno (8x), 16 MHz at 115200: 17, 117,647 Bd, +2.12 %.
  • STM32 16x, 16 MHz at 115200: BRR 139, 115,108 Bd, −0.08 %. At 8x, USARTDIV 278 gives the same.
  • 14.7456 MHz at 115200: exactly 8, 0.00 %.
  • 8 MHz at 115200, integer 16x: 4 used, +8.51 %, fails.
  • STM32 at 1 MHz and 115200: BRR would be 9, under the HAL's minimum of 16, so the tool refuses it.

The review made these changes: - It added STM32's divider from ST's HAL. The tool modelled only integer dividers, which overstated an STM32's error about fortyfold at 16 MHz and 115200. - It put the error first and large. - It reworded the caution: a single end at 3.55 % does not fail, it uses most of the shared budget; only past 5 % does a frame fail. - It added the Arduino detail (8x first), checked against the core's source, and examples. - It remembers the mode and the clock, and enlarged the 9 px labels to 11 px.

Crystal load

(formerly Crystal load capacitance)

What it computes

For a Pierce oscillator, it computes: - the two capacitors it needs, so the crystal sees the load it was cut for. The pair to buy, in the chosen E-series, is shown large, with the load it really presents and how far that pulls the frequency; - for the pair in the fields: its load, its error and its pull; - start-up, after AN2867: - from the frequency, the crystal's ESR and the MCU's gm, the gain margin, with and without RExt; - RExt's starting value; - from the swing you measure on OSC_IN, the crystal's drive level against its rating, and so whether RExt is needed at all.

The drawing is the oscillator as it is really built: - the MCU, with its inverting amplifier and feedback resistor RF inside; - the OSC_IN and OSC_OUT pins (OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT for a 32.768 kHz crystal); - the crystal Y1, RExt, and CL1 and CL2, with their values.

The crystal type and the series are remembered.

Standard values. The load capacitors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools (the series the CL1 and CL2 suggestions come from).

Source

  • ST AN2867, Oscillator design guide, rev. 10 (DocID15287), was read in a copy hosted by Raltron (st.com reset the connection):
  • figure 5, "Pierce-oscillator circuitry": Inv, the internal inverter working as the amplifier; RF, the internal feedback resistor; Q, the crystal; RExt, an external resistor "to limit the inverter output current"; CL1 and CL2, the load capacitors; Cs, the stray, which is the pin capacitance plus the PCB;
  • section 3.3: CL = CL1 × CL2 / (CL1 + CL2) + Cs, and the worked example: a 15 pF crystal, assuming Cs = 5 pF, needs CL1 = CL2 = 20 pF;
  • section 3.7: pullability from Cm, C0 and CL;
  • section 3.2, typical RF: 10–25 MΩ at 32.768 kHz, down to 0.47–5 MΩ at 20 MHz;
  • section 3.4, the gain margin:
    • gmcrit = 4 × ESR × (2πF)² × (C0 + CL)², and gm / gmcrit should be at least 5;
    • the worked example: an 8 MHz Fox crystal (C0 7 pF, CL 10 pF, ESR 80 Ω) on an STM32F1 (gm 25 mA/V) gives gmcrit 0.23 mA/V and a margin of 107;
    • its LSE table gives gm from 5 to 25 µA/V across the drive modes of the first family listed;
  • section 3.5.3, RExt:
    • it limits the drive level, and with CL2 keeps the oscillator off overtones;
    • it is mandatory only if the crystal would dissipate more than its rated drive level, and otherwise "not recommended", 0 Ω;
    • its initial value is the reactance of CL2, 1 / (2πF × CL2): 1326 Ω at 8 MHz with 15 pF;
    • it is then trimmed with a potentiometer, and added to ESR when the margin is rechecked;
  • section 3.5.2, the drive level from a measurement:
    • the crystal current is the current through CL1, so the swing Vpp measured on CL1 gives DL = ESR × (π F Ctot)² × Vpp² / 2, with Ctot = CL1 + Cs/2 + Cprobe;
    • the probe must add no more than 1 pF;
    • section 3.5.1 gives the other way, a current probe, with I_pp,max = 2√2 × √(DLmax / ESR).
  • The drive-level ratings are Epson's: 0.5 µW max for the FC-135, and 200 µW max (10 µW recommended) for the FA-238, an MHz crystal.
  • Epson FC-13F / FC-135 specification sheet, read for the 32.768 kHz values:
  • C1 3.4 fF and C0 1.0 pF typical;
  • CL 7, 9 or 12.5 pF;
  • ±20 ppm at 25 °C.
  • The pulling expression comes from the crystal's equivalent circuit, the Butterworth–Van Dyke model: a motional arm of L1, C1 and R1 in series, all in parallel with the shunt capacitance C0 of the electrodes and holder.

Why the formulas are these

The two capacitors are in series, not in parallel. This is the step people get backwards. Each one runs from one crystal terminal to ground, so the loop the crystal drives is: out through CL1, along the ground, back through CL2. Two capacitors in series:

CL1 × CL2 / (CL1 + CL2)

which for an equal pair is just half of one of them. Add the stray capacitance of the two tracks and the two oscillator pins — that sits directly across the same nodes, so it adds on:

Load = CL1 × CL2 / (CL1 + CL2) + Stray

Turn it round for a symmetric pair and the capacitors come out at

CL1 = CL2 = 2 × (CL spec − Stray)

A crystal marked 12.5 pF on a board with 3 pF of stray therefore wants 19 pF parts, not 25 pF and not 12.5 pF. Both of those are common mistakes, and the second is the worse one.

Why the load changes the frequency at all. A crystal has two resonances. At series resonance the motional arm is purely resistive; a little above it the arm looks inductive and resonates with everything capacitive across it — C0 and whatever load the circuit adds. The parallel-resonant frequency is

fp = fs × [ 1 + C1 / (2 × (C0 + CL)) ]

A crystal is cut and trimmed so that this lands on the marked frequency for one particular CL. Present a different load and it lands somewhere else, which is the whole reason the number is on the datasheet.

Differentiating that with respect to CL gives the sensitivity, which is what the tool reports as pullability:

d(Δf/f) / dCL = − C1 / (2 × (C0 + CL)²)

The sign is negative: more load, lower frequency. For a typical MHz part with C1 = 8 fF and C0 = 3 pF at CL = 12.5 pF that comes to about 16.6 ppm/pF, so fitting 22 pF where 19 pF was wanted — 1.5 pF too much load — pulls it roughly 25 ppm slow. Epson's FC-135 watch crystal (C1 3.4 fF, C0 1.0 pF) pulls 9.3 ppm/pF at 12.5 pF. In its 7 pF version it pulls 26.6 ppm/pF: the lower the load, the steeper the slope, so a low-load crystal wants the tightest stray.

Where the inputs come from, and what they are called

Three of the inputs are easy to look for in the wrong place.

  • C0 — on the crystal datasheet, as C0, "shunt capacitance" or "static capacitance". Often given only as a maximum; that is usable.
  • C1 — the motional capacitance, C1 on datasheets that give it, after the Butterworth–Van Dyke model. Many do not. When it is missing, look for a pullability figure in ppm/pF, or a "frequency versus load capacitance" curve, and type that into Pullability instead: the tool works C1 back from it. C1 is the one that stays fixed when the load changes — it is the crystal — while pullability is its slope at whatever load is chosen, so changing CL spec recomputes pullability, not C1.
  • Stray — never on the crystal datasheet, because it is not the crystal. It is the capacitance of the two oscillator pins, sometimes listed in the MCU datasheet, plus the two tracks. ST's AN2867 assumes 5 pF in its worked example; take that as an order of magnitude, not a value to copy.

The load capacitors are called CL1 and CL2 rather than C1 and C2, which is how MCU application notes label them and which keeps C1 free for its datasheet meaning. Every capacitance here only ever comes in one unit — pF for load, stray and shunt, fF for motional — so the fields show the unit fixed rather than offering a picker.

When CL says "Series". Some datasheets offer, or list, a series-resonant cut: the crystal is trimmed to its marked frequency with no load at all. A Pierce oscillator cannot present no load, so the part runs above its marking by the whole parallel-resonance offset,

Δf/f = C1 / (2 × (C0 + Load))

which is not a trim but a few hundred ppm: 8 fF against 3 pF + 12.5 pF is +258 ppm. Type 0 in CL spec to see it. The fix is to order the part with a load capacitance, or to use it in a circuit that runs it at series resonance.

Assumptions and limits

  • Stray is an estimate, and it dominates the mistakes. It is a few picofarads for the pins plus short tracks (AN2867's example takes 5 pF), but a long or guarded layout can be well outside that. If the frequency matters, measure.
  • The presets are starting points.
  • The 32.768 kHz preset is the Epson FC-135's typical values.
  • The MHz preset is illustrative: no manufacturer table was found to quote for C0 and C1.
  • Use your crystal's datasheet: a wrong C1 scales the pullability in proportion.
  • The pulling figure is a slope taken at the specified load, so it is exact for small errors and increasingly optimistic for large ones, since the true curve flattens as CL grows.
  • Sizing assumes a symmetric pair. Asymmetric capacitors are legitimate and the tool will report the load they present, but it will not propose them.

What it deliberately does not do

  • RF is drawn, not sized. It is inside the MCU on the parts AN2867 covers. Its section 3.2 gives typical values, from 10–25 MΩ at 32.768 kHz to 0.47–5 MΩ at 20 MHz.
  • The drive level comes from your measurement, not from a model. Type the peak-to-peak swing you read on OSC_IN.
  • The Vpp defaults (1 V, 0.5 V) only illustrate a reading.
  • A probe heavier than 1 pF both loads the oscillator and inflates the figure: a 10 pF probe reads twice the drive of a 1 pF one at 8 MHz here.
  • Temperature and ageing. The load error here is a fixed offset; drift over temperature is the crystal's cut and belongs with the ppm tooling.

How it was checked

Recomputed by hand: 12.5 pF specified with 3 pF stray gives 19 pF capacitors and a presented load of exactly 12.5 pF, 0 ppm. Fitting 22 pF instead presents 14 pF, 1.5 pF over, and pulls −24.97 ppm against 16.65 × 1.5 = 24.98 by hand. Fitting 33 pF presents 19.5 pF and pulls −116.5 ppm against 16.65 × 7 = 116.6. The watch preset (FC-135) returns 9.328 ppm/pF, against 3.4 fF / (2 × (1.0 + 12.5 pF)²) = 9.33 by hand.

Further checks: - AN2867's example (15 pF, 5 pF stray) gives 20 pF each, the same as the note. - The E12 pair for 12.5 pF with 3 pF stray is 18 pF, which presents 12 pF and pulls +8.325 ppm. - The FC-135's 7 pF version needs 8 pF parts and pulls 26.56 ppm/pF. - A Series crystal with 18 pF parts runs +266.7 ppm fast. - Start-up reproduces AN2867: - C0 7 pF, CL 10 pF, 8 MHz, ESR 80 Ω and gm 25 mA/V give a margin of 107; - RExt with CL2 = 15 pF is 1326 Ω. - At the defaults (8 MHz, C0 3 pF, CL 12.5 pF, 19 pF parts): - RExt 1.047 kΩ; - margin 129 without RExt, 9.135 with it. - Drive level at 8 MHz (19 pF parts, 3 pF stray, 1 pF probe, ESR 80 Ω): - 1 Vpp gives 11.68 µW, 5.84 % of the FA-238's 200 µW, so RExt is 0 Ω; - 5 Vpp gives 292 µW, over the rating, so RExt is needed; - a 10 pF probe reads 23.5 µW for the same 1 Vpp. - The FC-135 at 0.5 Vpp: 42.86 nW, against its 0.5 µW rating. - The FC-135 at 15 µA/V: - margin 6.934; - with RExt (255.6 kΩ) it would fall to 1.491, so the tool says to fit 0 Ω; - at the lowest drive, 5 µA/V, the margin is 2.311, too low.

The pullability was wrong by twelve orders of magnitude on first write: C1 / (2(C0+CL)²) is per farad, not dimensionless, because the numerator is first order in capacitance and the denominator is second. It needs multiplying by one picofarad to become per-pF. The hand check is what caught it.

The review made these changes: - It redrew the schematic as the real Pierce oscillator of AN2867 figure 5, on Pierre's request. - It replaced the 32.768 kHz preset (C0 1.5 pF, C1 2.5 fF, from no source) with the Epson FC-135's typical values, and corrected the claim that a watch crystal has "a tenth the motional capacitance" and pulls "around 6 ppm/pF". - It replaced the "2–5 pF" stray range, which AN2867 does not state in what was read, with its worked example's 5 pF. - It put the pair to buy first and large, with what it pulls. - It added the start-up check and RExt's starting value from AN2867, after Pierre asked why RExt was drawn but not calculated. - It added the drive-level check from a scope reading, so the tool says whether RExt is needed at all. - It added examples, remembers the crystal type and the series, and was renamed Crystal load, on Pierre's choice.

Oscillator stability

(formerly Oscillator stability (ppm → Hz))

What it computes

The total frequency error budget of a crystal oscillator — tolerance, temperature, ageing and load pulling combined — as a worst case and as a root-sum-square estimate, then expressed as hertz and as time gained or lost per day and per year. The worst case is shown large, the RSS beneath it. For a 32.768 kHz crystal, the parabola's coefficient B and turnover T0 are fields, taken from the crystal's datasheet. The crystal type is remembered.

For a single ppm figure applied to a single value, the PPM converter under Tools does that; this tool is the budget that produces the figure.

Source

The contributions and their names are the ones on crystal datasheets: frequency tolerance at a reference temperature, frequency stability over the operating temperature range, and ageing, usually per first year. The reference is 20 °C on some datasheets and 25 °C on others — one Petermann-Technik page quotes both for the same part — so the field is labelled Tolerance without a temperature.

The 32.768 kHz temperature curve is a parabola, whose two numbers come from the crystal's datasheet. Epson's FC-135 specification sheet, read for this review, gives: - B −0.04 ppm/°C² max, and a turnover of 25 ± 5 °C; - a tolerance of ±20 ppm at 25 °C; - ageing of ±3 ppm in the first year.

These are the tool's defaults. The −0.034 ppm/°C² often quoted as typical (±0.006) has −0.04 as its worst end.

Why the formulas are these

Two kinds of error, kept apart. Tolerance, temperature stability and ageing are limits: the part is somewhere within ± each of them, and which way it sits is not known. The tuning fork's temperature drift and the load pulling are offsets: they have a known sign and they move the whole window. Mixing the two kinds is how budgets end up either too pessimistic or wrong-signed, so the tool computes

Offset     = Drift + Pulling
Worst case = Offset ± (Tolerance + Temperature + Ageing)

and reports the extreme of that window with its sign. A window of −69 to −23 ppm is a clock that can only lose time, and writing it as ±69 ppm would throw that away.

Worst case and RSS. The worst case adds every limit at full size in the same direction. It is what datasheets call overall stability, and it is the right figure to design against when failure is not an option. If the contributions are independent, all of them sitting at their extremes together is unlikely, and the root-sum-square

RSS = Offset ± √(Tolerance² + Temperature² + Ageing²)

is the likelier spread. Offsets are added directly, never squared: they are not random.

The tuning-fork parabola. A 32.768 kHz crystal is a quartz tuning fork, and its frequency falls off either side of a turnover temperature:

Δf/f = B × (T − T0)²       (FC-135: B −0.04 ppm/°C² max, T0 25 °C)

It only ever goes down. - With the FC-135's worst-case B: −25 ppm at 0 °C (2.2 seconds a day), and −81 ppm at −20 °C (7 seconds a day). - With the typical −0.034: −21 ppm and −69 ppm. That is why a watch or a data logger left outdoors in winter runs slow, and why the tool asks for the temperature the fork will actually see rather than a spec. MHz crystals are AT-cut plates, whose curve is a cubic set by the cut angle; their datasheets fold it into one ±ppm figure over the range, which is what the MHz pill asks for.

Into time. A day is 86 400 s, so 1 ppm is 86.4 ms a day, and a year of 31 557 600 s makes 1 ppm about 31.6 s a year. Twenty ppm is 1.73 s a day or 10.5 minutes a year.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ageing is not linear. It is fastest in the first months and slows roughly logarithmically, so ten years is much less than ten times the first-year figure. Enter the total you expect over the period, not a rate.
  • The parabola uses one B and one T0. The datasheet gives B as a maximum and T0 with a tolerance (±5 °C on the FC-135). Typing the worst B, and the turnover furthest from your temperature, gives the worst case. Near the turnover it barely matters; at the extremes it does.
  • The MHz temperature figure is taken as a symmetric ± limit, which is how it is specified, even though the real AT-cut curve is not symmetric.
  • Pulling is carried in as a signed figure from the crystal load tool and is treated as exact.
  • Tolerance never includes temperature on a crystal datasheet. The temperature stability is a separate line, often a separate ordering table, and the two add: ±20 ppm tolerance with ±30 ppm over −40/+85 °C is up to ±50 ppm before ageing. A packaged XO or TCXO is different: its "frequency stability" is often one all-inclusive figure covering tolerance, temperature, supply and load, sometimes ageing too. Read the footnote; if it is all-inclusive, enter it as Tolerance and leave the rest at zero.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Compensated oscillators. A TCXO or an RTC with digital trimming cancels most of the temperature term; its datasheet gives a residual stability, which can be entered as Temp. stability on the MHz pill.
  • Short-term stability and jitter. Phase noise and Allan deviation are a different question from where the average frequency sits.
  • Protocol limits. Whether a budget meets USB, CAN or Ethernet timing needs those standards' own tolerances and belongs with the tools for each.

How it was checked

By hand, MHz defaults: 20 + 30 + 3 = 53 ppm worst case; √(400 + 900 + 9) = 36.18 ppm RSS; 53 ppm of 16 MHz is 848 Hz; 53 × 86.4 ms = 4.579 s a day; 53 × 31.56 s = 27.88 minutes a year. With −25 ppm of pulling the window becomes −78 to +28 ppm and the worst case reads −78, signed.

32.768 kHz at 0 °C, with the FC-135's B of −0.04: - drift −0.04 × 25² = −25 ppm; - with ±23 ppm of limits the window is −48 to −2 ppm, worst −48 ppm.

At −10 °C it is −49 ppm of drift, −72 ppm worst, 6.221 s a day slow. A typed B of −0.034 at −10 °C gives −41.65 ppm of drift, −64.65 ppm worst. At 25 °C only the limits remain: ±23 ppm, 12.1 minutes a year. Switching pills resets pulling, which on first build carried over from one family to the other.

The review made these changes: - It made B and the turnover fields, defaulting to the FC-135 sheet. The tool hard-coded −0.034 ppm/°C² about 25 °C, which is a typical value and not the datasheet's worst case. - It put the worst case first and large. - It enlarged the 9–10 px chart labels to 11 px. - It added a plain definition of ppm, examples, and the remembered type. - It was renamed Oscillator stability, on Pierre's choice.

Digital & logic circuits › Timing & interfaces

PLL settings

(formerly PLL multiplication factor)

What it computes

Every combination of input divider M, feedback multiplier N and output divider that a chip's PLL allows, walked exhaustively, with the ones that land closest to a target frequency listed first — each with its error in ppm and the frequencies at the phase detector and the VCO, so the limits can be seen being respected. The chosen setting is shown large, with its error and its internal frequencies; tap another row to choose it. Presets cover the STM32F1, F4, G0 and G4 and the RP2040 and RP2350; Generic takes any integer-N PLL's limits from its manual. The chip is remembered.

Source

The limits are taken from the vendors' datasheets and code rather than from summaries, which disagree with each other:

  • STM32F4 — ST's HAL driver (stm32f4xx_hal_rcc.h, stm32f4xx_hal_rcc_ex.h): PLLM 2–63, PLLN 50–432, PLLP 2, 4, 6 or 8, PLLQ 2–15, and the VCO input between 1 and 2 MHz. The VCO output window of 100–432 MHz and the 168 MHz system clock of the F405/407 are from RM0090.
  • STM32F1 (the F103 of the Blue Pill) — DS5319 rev 18, table 27: PLL input 1–25 MHz, PLL output 16–72 MHz. The F1 has no output divider: its PLL output is the system clock. From the F1 HAL: PLLMUL 2–16, the crystal divided by 1 or 2 on its way in (PLLXTPRE), and USB clocked by the PLL output divided by 1 or 1.5 — so USB works only with the PLL at 48 or 72 MHz.
  • STM32G4 (G474) — DS12288 rev 2, table 49: PLL input 2.66–16 MHz, VCO 96–344 MHz, and the R output that clocks the core up to 150 MHz, or 170 MHz with the regulator in Range 1 boost mode (section 3 of the same datasheet). Dividers from the G4 HAL: PLLM 1–16, PLLN 8–127, PLLR 2, 4, 6 or 8.
  • STM32G0 (G071) — DS12232 rev 4, table 43: PLL input 2.66–16 MHz, VCO 96–344 MHz, R output 12–64 MHz. Dividers from the G0 HAL: PLLM 1–8, PLLN 8–86, PLLR 2–8.
  • RP2040 — the Pico SDK's own calculator, vcocalc.py: reference divider 1–63 with at least 5 MHz after it, FBDIV 16–320, VCO 750–1600 MHz, and two post-dividers each 1–7.
  • The RP2040's rated clock is from the Pico SDK 2.1.1 release notes: it is now "certified to run at a system clock of 200Mhz when using a regulator voltage of at least 1.15 volts". The SDK raises the voltage itself when needed, and keeps 125 MHz as the default. Before, 133 MHz was the most that was supported.
  • RP2350 — its datasheet, section 8.6, lists the RP2040's limits again (at least 5 MHz after REFDIV, VCO 750–1600 MHz, FBDIV 16–320, post-dividers 1–7) and gives 150 MHz as the most the RP2350 supports.

The STM32 datasheets were read in the copies distributors host (RS and DigiKey), because st.com refused the download; later revisions exist and were not compared. ST's own code disagrees with these tables: its LL utils files check the VCO from 64 MHz on both families and the G0's PLL input at 4–8 MHz, and the G4's reference manual (RM0440 rev 3) gave a 64–344 MHz VCO and a 2.66–8 MHz input. Asked about it on ST's community forum in April 2020, an ST technical moderator answered that the datasheet's PLL characteristics are the correct values and that RM0440 would drop its numbers, so the tables are used here.

Why the formulas are these

An integer-N PLL has one loop and three dividers:

PFD = Input / M
VCO = PFD × N
Out = VCO / P

The input is divided down to the phase-frequency detector (PFD) rate. The VCO runs at N times that, because the loop compares the VCO divided by N against the PFD reference and steers the VCO until they match. The output is the VCO divided down again. Each stage has a window it must stay inside: the PFD because the detector and its filter are designed for a range, the VCO because the oscillator only tunes over a range. That is what makes this a search rather than a division — the obvious M and N often put one of the stages outside its window.

The STM32F1 has no output divider, so there Out = PFD × N, and its window is the PLL output's. The output divider is P on the F4, R on the G0 and G4, and two dividers in series on the RP2040 and RP2350.

Ranking. Rows are ordered by error first. Among equally good rows:

  • on the STM32F1 and F4, a row that also gives USB exactly 48 MHz comes first, since USB will not work on anything else;
  • then the higher PFD. ST's manual recommends a 2 MHz VCO input on the F4 to limit jitter, and in general a faster comparison lets the loop correct the VCO more often and filter less, which is quieter;
  • then the higher VCO, quieter for the same reason. It costs current: the G0 and G4 datasheets give their PLL 200 µA typical at a 96 MHz VCO and 520 µA at 344 MHz, so pick a lower-VCO row from the table when power matters more.

That is why 8 MHz to 168 MHz on the STM32F4 comes out as M 4, N 168, P 2, Q 7 (PFD 2 MHz, VCO 336 MHz, USB 48 MHz) ahead of the equally exact M 8, N 336, which runs the detector at 1 MHz.

The RP2040's and RP2350's two post-dividers multiply, so the tool offers each distinct product once, as the pair with the larger first divider — the SDK prefers that split for power.

Notes above a plain rating. The RP2040 above 133 MHz needs its core regulator at 1.15 V or more, and the G4 above 150 MHz needs Range 1 boost mode (PWR_REGULATOR_VOLTAGE_SCALE1_BOOST in the HAL); the tool says so under the result. Above the rating itself it says the part is not rated for it.

Assumptions and limits

  • Integer-N only. Many modern PLLs add a fractional part to N, which can hit almost any target but trades it for spurs and depends on each vendor's modulator. Not modelled.
  • The preset limits are for the named parts. Other members of a family can differ — the F401, for one, needs its VCO in 192–432 MHz, and the F105/F107 multiply by 4–9 or 6.5 after a 1–16 prescaler — and the G0 and G4 presets come from the G071 and G474 datasheets, so check another member's own table, or use Generic with the right reference manual when in doubt.
  • The G0 and G4 windows are Range 1's. Range 2, the low-power range, narrows the VCO to 96–128 MHz and the system clock to 26 MHz on the G4 and 16 MHz on the G0; not modelled.
  • Lock time, loop-filter design and phase noise are not addressed; the tool answers only which settings are legal and how close they land.
  • On Generic, the search stops at three million combinations to stay responsive and says so; narrow the ranges for a complete answer.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Vendor clock trees beyond the PLL — AHB and APB prescalers, peripheral clock muxes, flash wait states for the chosen frequency. Those are the next steps after this one, and every family arranges them differently.
  • The G0's and G4's other PLL outputs. P and Q feed peripherals; the tool sets R, the system clock. The G4 can clock USB from its separate 48 MHz oscillator, HSI48, instead of the PLL.
  • Other presets. The Generic pill covers any integer-N PLL given its manual; a preset is only worth adding for a part used often enough to save the reading.

How it was checked

Against the configurations the vendors ship: 8 MHz to 168 MHz on the STM32F4 gives M 4, N 168, P 2, Q 7 with USB at exactly 48 MHz, and from a 25 MHz crystal M 25, N 336, P 2, Q 7 — the standard setting for that crystal. 180 MHz is flagged as above the part's 168 MHz rating and as leaving USB at 45 MHz.

On the STM32F1, 8 MHz to 72 MHz gives M 1, N 9 with USB at 72 / 1.5 = 48 MHz, the setting of ST's own F1 USB examples; at 64 MHz the tool warns that USB cannot get its 48 MHz. On the STM32G4, 16 MHz (HSI16) to 170 MHz gives M 4, N 85, R 2 with the boost-mode note — the setting of ST's NUCLEO-G474RE examples, which switch boost mode on — and 150 MHz gives M 4, N 75, R 2 without it. On the STM32G0, 16 MHz to 64 MHz gives M 1, N 20, R 5 (VCO 320 MHz).

On the RP2040, 12 MHz to 125 MHz gives VCO 1500 MHz with post-dividers 6 and 2, and 133 MHz gives VCO 1596 MHz with 6 and 2 — both exactly the Pico SDK's own default settings. 200 MHz gives VCO 1200 MHz with 6 and 1, and the note about the 1.15 V core voltage; 250 MHz is flagged as above the certified 200 MHz. On the RP2350, 12 MHz to 150 MHz gives VCO 1500 MHz with 5 and 2, the SDK's default in clocks.h; 200 MHz is flagged as above its 150 MHz. The full RP2040 search takes about 3 ms.

The review made these changes: - It raised the RP2040's rating from 133 MHz to the 200 MHz certified in Pico SDK 2.1.1, with the voltage condition shown above 133 MHz. - It put the chosen setting first and large. - It enlarged the 9–10 px diagram labels to 11 px, and moved the VCO frequency clear of the USB branch. - It added plain definitions of the PFD, the VCO and the dividers, examples, and the remembered chip. - It was renamed PLL settings, on Pierre's choice. - It added the STM32F1, G0 and G4 and the RP2350, on Pierre's choice, with limits read from their datasheets, the chips split over two rows of pills. - It fixed a chip switch that carried the RP2040's 1.15 V note over to the next chip. - Without a USB branch, the diagram drops its empty top band, which keeps Generic's result above the tab bar with the second row of pills.

Digital & logic circuits › Data conversion

ADC resolution

(formerly ADC resolution / quantization)

What it computes

For an ideal N-bit converter and its reference: the size of one step (the LSB), shown large since it is the resolution, then the code a given input produces, the voltage that code stands for, and the quantization error between the two, in volts and in LSB. It works both ways: type a voltage to get the code, or type a code — say, one read off a register — to get the voltage. The range of inputs and codes is shown under the fields. The reference and the input can be typed in mV or V; the mode and both units are remembered.

Two pills cover the two ways converters are built:

  • Single-ended — 0 to VREF, codes 0 to 2ᴺ − 1. Every MCU ADC (AVR, STM32, RP2040, ESP32) works this way.
  • Bipolar ± — −FSR to +FSR, codes −2ᴺ⁻¹ to 2ᴺ⁻¹ − 1 in two's complement. Differential converters such as the ADS1115 and the HX711 work this way.

Examples: an Arduino Uno on its 5 V reference, an LM35 temperature sensor on the Uno's 1.1 V reference, an STM32 at 12 bits on 3.3 V, the ADS1115 at its default ±2.048 V, and the HX711 load-cell converter at 24 bits.

Source

  • The ideal transfer function is the one in IEEE Std 1241 and the one MCU datasheets measure their errors against. The ATmega328P datasheet (Atmel-42735B, section 28.6) defines offset error as the deviation of the first transition from its ideal place "at 0.5 LSB", gain error against a last transition 1.5 LSB below full scale, the quantization error as always ±0.5 LSB, and ±0.5 LSB as the ideal absolute accuracy. The same chip is specified at ±2 LSB absolute accuracy, and its internal reference at 1.0 V minimum, 1.1 V typical, 1.2 V maximum.
  • Arduino's analogReference() page gives the Uno's DEFAULT reference as 5 V and INTERNAL as 1.1 V on the ATmega328P.
  • The bipolar pill follows the TI ADS1115 datasheet (SBAS444E): the full-scale range is set by the PGA to ±6.144, ±4.096, ±2.048 (the power-up default), ±1.024, ±0.512 or ±0.256 V; Table 7-1 gives the LSB as 125 µV at ±4.096 V and 62.5 µV at ±2.048 V; output is binary two's complement, clipping at 7FFFh and 8000h.
  • The HX711 datasheet (Avia Semiconductor) gives its full-scale input as ±0.5(AVDD/GAIN), ±20 mV at gain 128 with a 5 V AVDD, 24-bit two's complement output from 800000h to 7FFFFFh, and 50 nV rms input noise at gain 128 and 10 samples a second.
  • The LM35 is 10 mV/°C (TI SNIS159H).

Why the formulas are these

The step. N bits give 2ᴺ codes. Spread over the reference:

Single-ended:  LSB = VREF / 2ᴺ
Bipolar:       LSB = 2 × FSR / 2ᴺ

The bipolar span is twice FSR because it runs from −FSR to +FSR. The ADS1115 datasheet writes its Equation 4 as LSB = FSR / 2¹⁶, but its own table (125 µV at ±4.096 V) only works with FSR as the whole 8.192 V span — the tool asks for the ± figure, as the datasheet's register table quotes it, and doubles it.

The code. Code k stands for k × LSB and covers half an LSB either side, so the ideal converter rounds:

Code = round(Input / LSB)

The first transition, 0 to 1, is at ½ LSB. That is why the quantization error is ±½ LSB rather than 0 to −1 LSB: the steps are centred on the ideal straight line, and the error is the sawtooth between the line and the staircase. The drawing shows eight codes around the input at scale, with the dashed ideal line through the step centres.

The top of the range. The highest code is 2ᴺ − 1, not 2ᴺ, so the largest voltage a code stands for is VREF − 1 LSB: 3.2992 V for 12 bits on 3.3 V. An input at VREF itself reads the top code, a whole LSB short.

Two's complement. A bipolar converter's register holds negative codes as 2ᴺ + code, so −1 reads FFFFh and −FS reads 8000h. The hex in the result shows the register as it would be read, the Code field the signed value it means.

Dividing by 2ᴺ − 1. Arduino's ReadAnalogVoltage example computes code × (5.0 / 1023.0), and ST's LL macro __LL_ADC_CALC_DATA_TO_VOLTAGE divides by __LL_ADC_DIGITAL_SCALE, 4095 at 12 bits. That treats the top code as exactly VREF, stretching the scale: the reading is k / (2ᴺ − 1) instead of k / 2ᴺ of VREF, high by up to one LSB near the top. Small beside a real ADC's errors, but a systematic one, and it is why a 3.3 V input "reads 3.3 V" on those examples and 3.2992 V here.

Resolution is not accuracy. A finer LSB only helps while it stays above the noise and the reference's tolerance. The HX711's 2.33 nV step sits under 50 nV rms of noise, about 21 LSB, so its last four bits or so are noise; SNR estimation turns noise into effective bits.

Assumptions and limits

  • An ideal converter. Offset, gain error, INL, DNL and noise are not modelled; on a real MCU ADC they add up to several LSB, far more than the quantization shown here (the ATmega328P's ±2 LSB, for one). Their datasheet figures are in LSB, which is what this tool gives the size of.
  • VREF is taken as exact. On most MCUs it is the supply, so the supply's own tolerance scales every reading. A 1% regulator is 41 LSB at 12 bits. An internal reference is no cure by itself: the ATmega328P's 1.1 V is 1.0 to 1.2 V from part to part, ±9 %, so measure it once and use that figure.
  • Inputs past the range read the end code; the tool says so and the error then is the overshoot, not quantization. On the ADS1115 the ±4.096 and ±6.144 V settings are scaling only — the pins themselves never go past VDD + 0.3 V or below GND − 0.3 V.
  • Single-ended on a bipolar part. The ADS1115 measuring one input against ground uses only codes 0000h to 7FFFh, so it is a 15-bit converter in that mode. Model it on the bipolar pill with 16 bits, and read only the positive half.

What it deliberately does not do

  • SNR, ENOB, oversampling. The noise that quantization adds, and what averaging buys back, is the next tool, SNR estimation.
  • DAC. The reverse conversion has its own tool.
  • Offset-binary and sign-magnitude codes. Some bipolar converters output these instead of two's complement; they are rare enough on current parts to leave out.

How it was checked

By hand, single-ended 12 bits on 3.3 V: LSB = 3.3 / 4096 = 805.66 µV; 1.2 V / 805.66 µV = 1489.45, code 1489 = 0x5D1, code voltage 1.19963 V, error +366.2 µV = +0.4545 LSB. Code 4095 gives 3.29919 V; 4 V reads 4095 and is flagged as over range.

The examples: 3.3 V on the Uno's 5 V reference reads 676 (4.883 mV steps, −0.16 LSB); an LM35 at 25 °C, 250 mV, reads 233 on the 1.1 V reference, in steps of 1.074 mV, 0.11 °C, against 0.49 °C on 5 V; −1 V on the ADS1115 at ±2.048 V reads −16000, 0xC180; 5 mV on the HX711 at ±19.53 mV reads 2147484, 0x20C49C, in steps of 2.328 nV.

The review made these changes: - It was renamed ADC resolution, on Pierre's choice; the old name still finds it in search. - The LSB became the large result, with the code, its voltage and the error on the line under it. - The reference and input fields take mV or V, remembered with the mode. - The drawing's labels went from 9–10 px to 11 px, with a left margin that grows with the code's digits. - It added the five examples, checked against their datasheets. - In formula search, the cards of renamed tools had lost their link to the tool; they now find a tool by its old name too.

Digital & logic circuits › Data conversion

DAC resolution

What it computes

For an N-bit DAC, its reference and its output gain: the step between neighbouring output levels (the LSB), shown large since it is the resolution, then the code to write for a target voltage, the voltage that code really puts out, and how far that is from the target, in volts and in LSB. It works both ways — type the voltage you want, or type a code to see what it outputs. The output range is shown under the fields. The target and VREF can each be typed in mV or V, each with its own picker; the divisor pill and both units are remembered.

Examples: an MCP4725 on 5 V, an MCP4822 at ×2, an STM32 DAC set to 0.7 V, the ESP32's 8-bit DAC and the SAMD21's 10-bit DAC (the Arduino Zero's).

Source

Divided by 2ᴺ, the top code one LSB under VREF:

  • Microchip MCP4725 (DS22039D): Equation 4-1 gives the ideal LSB as VREF / 2ⁿ, which equals (full-scale − zero-scale) / (2ⁿ − 1); VREF is VDD on this part.
  • Microchip MCP4802/4812/4822 (DS20002249B): VOUT = VREF × D / 4096 with the GA bit at 1 (×1), and 2 × VREF × D / 4096 with GA at 0 (×2), from the internal 2.048 V reference; its table gives 0.5 mV per step at ×1 and 1 mV at ×2.
  • TI DAC7311 (SBAS442D): Equation 1, VOUT = AVDD × D / 2ⁿ, read in TI's HTML datasheet viewer.
  • STM32. On ST's community forum, a user quotes RM0444 (STM32G0) as dividing by 4096, and in a 2017 thread on the STM32F373, whose reference manual also writes 4096, ST engineer K.Oku explains why: the DAC "is kind of R-2R implementation", and its top code "has one resistor (corresponds 1LSB) under the VREF". RM0444 itself was not read; st.com refused the download. The STM32G071 datasheet (DS12232 rev 4, table 59) gives the output as 0 to VREF+ with the buffer off and 0.2 V to VREF+ − 0.2 V with it on.

Divided by 2ᴺ − 1, the top code at VREF:

  • SAMD21 (Atmel-42181, the Arduino Zero's microcontroller): VDAC = DATA / 0x3FF × VREF.
  • ESP32 (technical reference manual, section 31.4.3): DACn_OUT = VDD3P3_RTC × PDACn_DAC / 255, with VDD3P3_RTC typically 3.3 V.

And ST's software, against its own manuals: the STM32G0 HAL's comment writes DAC_OUTx = VREF+ × DOR / 4095, with the example (3.3 × 868) / 4095 = 0.7 V, and its LL driver's DAC_DIGITAL_SCALE_12BITS is 4095, which __LL_DAC_CALC_VOLTAGE_TO_DATA multiplies by.

Why the formulas are these

One level per code. A DAC puts out one voltage for each code and nothing in between:

Vout = Code × LSB

so a target that is not exactly a level gets the nearer one, at most half an LSB away. That is why the picture is points, not a staircase: eight levels around the target at scale, the target a line between two of them, the chosen one in green.

Two divisors, and why it matters. How big the step is depends on what the datasheet divides by:

÷ 2ᴺ:        LSB = VREF × Gain / 2ᴺ         top code = VREF × Gain − 1 LSB
÷ (2ᴺ − 1):  LSB = VREF × Gain / (2ᴺ − 1)   top code = VREF × Gain exactly

A resistor string or R-2R ladder makes 2ᴺ equal steps between ground and VREF, of which the top code uses 2ᴺ − 1, so the output stops one LSB short: that is the ÷ 2ᴺ datasheets, the STM32 among them. The SAMD21 and ESP32 documents divide by 2ᴺ − 1 instead. The difference is under one LSB, but it is systematic, largest near the top of the range. Pick the pill your part's datasheet uses.

ST's 4095. ST's HAL and LL code divide by 4095, so a code they compute is up to one LSB low near the top on a DAC that, by ST's manuals, divides by 4096. At 0.7 V on 3.3 V, the HAL comment's 868 puts out 0.69932 V; 869, the nearer level on the 4096 scale, puts out 0.70012 V.

An earlier version of this tool took the STM32 to be ÷ 4095, on a forum user's bench readings from a NUCLEO-G071RB. Those readings cannot decide it: on the 2.5 V reference used there, the two divisors give the same code, or codes one LSB (0.61 mV) apart, at the 400, 800 and 1200 mV targets, yet the readings differ by about 4 mV, six or seven LSB, so something else changed between the two runs.

Gain. Many DACs follow the ladder with an amplifier. On the MCP4822 the GA bit picks ×1 or ×2 from its internal 2.048 V reference, which is how a 2.048 V reference makes a 4.095 V range at 1 mV a step.

Assumptions and limits

  • The output cannot reach the rails. The MCP4822's amplifier swings from 10 mV to VDD − 40 mV, and its accuracy holds only between those. The STM32 DAC with its output buffer on spans 0.2 V to VREF+ − 0.2 V. The top and bottom few codes on the tool's range are therefore not really available on those parts, and with ×2 gain the range can exceed VDD, which the output will not follow either.
  • An ideal DAC. Offset, gain error, INL and DNL are not modelled; they are specified in LSB, which is what this tool gives the size of.
  • VREF is taken as exact. When it is VDD, as on the MCP4725, the supply's tolerance scales every output.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Bipolar DACs (±VREF output with offset-binary or two's-complement codes) are rare on current general-purpose parts; the bipolar pill on the ADC tool covers the arithmetic if needed.
  • PWM as a DAC. Resolution there is set by the timer and the filter, not a ladder; it is a different calculation.
  • SNR and ENOB are the next tool.

How it was checked

÷ 2ᴺ, 12 bits, 3.3 V: LSB 805.66 µV; 1.2 V gives code 1489 (0x5D1), output 1.19963 V, error −366.2 µV = −0.4545 LSB. Code 4095 outputs 3.29919 V, one LSB short of VREF.

÷ (2ᴺ − 1): LSB 3.3 / 4095 = 805.86 µV; code 4095 outputs exactly 3.3 V; 1.2 V gives code 1489, output 1.19993 V.

The examples: the MCP4725 on 5 V puts 3.3 V at code 2703, 0xA8F, 0.44 mV low; the MCP4822 at ×2 steps exactly 1 mV, so 3 V is code 3000; the STM32 at 0.7 V gets 869, +122 µV; the ESP32's 8 bits ÷ 255 step 12.94 mV, so 1.5 V is code 116 at 1.501 V; the SAMD21's 10 bits ÷ 1023 put code 310 at exactly 1 V.

The review made these changes: - The STM32 moved from the ÷ (2ᴺ − 1) side to ÷ 2ᴺ, after reading ST's engineer's answer and its manuals' 4096; the second pill now rests on the SAMD21 and ESP32 documents, and the forum bench test is no longer cited as evidence. Analog Devices is no longer named: none of its datasheets was read. - The LSB became the large result, with the code, its output and the error on the line under it. - The target field takes mV or V, remembered with the pill. - The drawing's labels went from 9–10 px to 11 px. - It added the five examples, the first cases (13), and in every tool's examples a value now stays on one line with its unit.

Digital & logic circuits › Data conversion

SNR estimation

What it computes

Two things, one per pill.

  • Estimate — the signal-to-noise ratio an ADC can reach from the noises that can be calculated: quantization, the process gain of oversampling, and sampling-clock jitter. Each is shown on its own, then added as noise powers into one SNR and expressed as an effective number of bits (ENOB).
  • ENOB ↔ SINAD — the conversion between the two figures ADC datasheets quote, both ways, with how many of the converter's bits noise and distortion take away.

The total SNR is the large result on Estimate, with the ENOB it is worth and its three terms on the line under it; on ENOB ↔ SINAD the effective bits are large, with the bits lost and the noise floor. The pill and the units of the sample rate, bandwidth, input frequency and jitter are remembered.

The picture is a level diagram in dBFS: full scale at the top, the signal, and each noise floor as a line. The gap from the signal down to the total floor is the SNR, and the highest noise line is the one worth fixing.

Examples: 16-bit audio at 44.1 kHz, ×16 oversampling, 1 ps of jitter at 100 MHz, a signal at −20 dBFS, and the ADCs of the RP2040 and the STM32G0.

Source

Walt Kester's Analog Devices tutorials:

  • MT-001, "Taking the Mystery out of the Infamous Formula, SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB": the ideal SNR of an N-bit converter for a full-scale sine measured over dc to fs/2, and the correction 10 log(fs / 2BW) it calls process gain.
  • MT-003, "Understand SINAD, ENOB, SNR, THD, THD + N, and SFDR": ENOB from SINAD, and its Equation 2, which adds the level below full scale so ENOB is normalised to full scale.
  • MT-007, "Aperture Time, Aperture Jitter, Aperture Delay Time": the SNR limit set by jitter, and that the total jitter is the root-sum-square of the sampling clock's and the ADC's own aperture jitter.

analog.com refused a re-read of these during the review, so the formulas were checked again elsewhere:

  • TI's SLYT379, part 1 of an Analog Applications Journal series on clock jitter: its Equation 2 is SNR = −20 log(2π × fIN × tJitter), its Equation 1 adds the quantization, thermal and jitter SNRs as noise powers, and its Equation 3 combines the clock's and the ADC's aperture jitter as a root-sum-square.
  • Wikipedia's article on ENOB quotes MT-003's ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76) / 6.02.
  • National Semiconductor's note on aperture time and jitter (TI SNAA018) agrees that doubling the sample rate and filtering gains 3 dB. Its jitter example does not agree with the formula: it gives 73 dB for 10 ps at 10 MHz, where −20 log(2π × 10 MHz × 10 ps) is 64 dB, because it divides by the full-scale range where the sine's rms value belongs (20 log 2√2 = 9 dB).

Datasheet figures:

  • RP2040, section 4.9.3, table 566, typical, measured at 250 ksps with the input spanning codes 1 to 4094: SNR 61.5 dB, THD −55 dB, SFDR 59.9 dB, SINAD 54.0 dB, ENOB 8.7. These are the ENOB pill's defaults.
  • STM32G071, DS12232 rev 4, table 58: SINAD 63 dB typical (62.5 dB minimum) and ENOB 10.2 (10.1) at VDDA = VREF+ = 3 V and 25 °C.

Why the formulas are these

Quantization. Rounding to the nearest code leaves an error spread evenly over ±½ LSB, whose rms value is q / √12. A full-scale sine has an rms value of 2ᴺ q / (2√2). Their ratio, in dB, is

SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB

— 6.02 dB per bit, which is 20 log 2, plus a constant from the shape of a sine. 12 bits: 74.0 dB. 16 bits: 98.1 dB.

Level. The quantization noise stays where it is when the signal gets smaller, so the SNR falls one dB for every dB below full scale. A 12-bit ADC reading a signal at −20 dBFS has 54 dB of SNR, the same as an ideal 8.7-bit one. That is the most common way resolution is wasted.

Process gain. Quantization noise is spread evenly from dc to fs/2. Filter the result digitally down to a bandwidth BW and only the share of the noise inside BW remains:

PG = 10 log(fs / 2BW)

Four times the bandwidth needed is 6.02 dB, one extra bit. MT-001's example: a 65 MSPS ADC with channels 30 kHz wide gains 30.3 dB, 65 dB becoming 95.3 dB.

Jitter. If the instant of sampling wanders by tj rms, the error it causes is the signal's slope times that wander. For a full-scale sine at fin the result is independent of amplitude:

SNR(jitter) = −20 log(2π × fin × tj)

It depends on the input frequency, not the sample rate. 100 ps is harmless at 1 kHz (124 dB) and ruinous at 100 MHz (24 dB). MT-007 notes that 14-bit performance at 100 MHz needs under 0.1 ps; the tool gives 84 dB at exactly 0.1 ps, just under the 86 dB of 14 bits.

Adding them. Uncorrelated noises add as powers:

SNR = −10 log(10^(−Q/10) + 10^(−J/10))

so the total is always a little worse than the worse of the two, and a term 10 dB better than the other barely counts. When jitter is the lower one, the tool says so — more bits will not help.

What ENOB means. ENOB, the effective number of bits, answers the question "how many bits is this converter really worth?". The resolution on the datasheet, 12 bits say, only counts the codes the ADC can output. A real ADC also adds its own noise and distortion, so the last few bits are buried in them: they change from reading to reading without telling you anything about the signal. ENOB is the resolution of a perfect converter that would be exactly as noisy as the real one. A 12-bit ADC with an ENOB of 8.7 gives, on a changing signal, the same quality as a flawless 8.7-bit ADC; the bottom 3.3 bits are noise. ENOB is not a whole number, because it is worked back from a measured ratio, not counted.

What SINAD means. SINAD, the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, is that measured ratio: a pure sine is fed in, and the power of the sine is compared with the power of everything else in the output — noise and the harmonics that distortion adds. SNR is the same measurement leaving the harmonics out, which is why a datasheet's SNR is always the higher of the two. Because a perfect N-bit converter has an SINAD of 6.02N + 1.76 dB, the two figures are the same fact in different units, and datasheets quote either.

ENOB from the ratio. The SNR equation solved for N, with the level term of MT-003:

ENOB = (SNR − 1.76 − Level) / 6.02

On the ENOB pill SINAD takes the place of SNR, as the datasheets do. The RP2040's 54.0 dB gives 8.68 bits, and its datasheet says 8.7: of its 12 bits, 3.3 are lost to noise and distortion. Its noise alone, an SNR of 61.5 dB, would leave 9.9; its THD of −55 dB — its INL and DNL errors (the DNL spikes are erratum RP2040-E11) — costs more than the noise. The STM32G071's 63 dB gives 10.17 bits, its datasheet's 10.2.

Assumptions and limits

  • Oversampling needs noise. Process gain assumes the quantization error is random. A clean, slow signal on a quiet ADC can give the same code every time, and averaging a constant gives nothing. MT-001 warns about this correlation; the cure is noise or dither of about an LSB at the input.
  • Thermal noise and distortion are not estimated. They are the ADC's own and only its datasheet knows them. The Estimate pill gives the ceiling the architecture allows; the ENOB pill gives what the part actually does.
  • No noise shaping. Delta-sigma converters push quantization noise out of band and gain far more than 10 log per octave of oversampling. Their datasheets give SNR directly.
  • SINAD at other levels. MT-003's level correction assumes the noise does not change with level. Distortion usually drops at lower levels, so ENOB normalised from a −6 dBFS measurement can read better than at full scale.

What it deliberately does not do

  • THD, SFDR, THD + N. Read from the datasheet, not calculated.
  • Noise-free resolution and effective resolution from rms input noise, the measure for dc and slow signals. MT-003 warns not to confuse them with ENOB; they are a different calculation from different data.

How it was checked

Default Estimate: 12 bits, 1 MSPS, 500 kHz, 0 dBFS, 100 kHz, 100 ps. Q = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74.0 dB; J = −20 log(2π × 10⁵ × 10⁻¹⁰) = 84.04 dB; total 73.59 dB; ENOB 11.93 bits.

MT-001's process-gain example: 65 MSPS and 30 kHz give 30.35 dB. MT-007's jitter example: 14 bits, 100 MHz, 0.1 ps give J = 84.04 dB, total 81.91 dB, with the jitter warning. 40 MHz of bandwidth at 65 MSPS is refused as past fs/2. With no jitter at −1 dBFS, 14 bits give 85.04 dB and an ENOB of 14.0, normalised.

ENOB pill: SINAD 54.0 dB at 0 dBFS gives 8.678 bits — the RP2040's 8.7 — with 3.32 bits lost; ENOB 10 gives SINAD 61.96 dB.

The examples: 16 bits over the whole band with no jitter, 98.08 dB; 12 bits keeping 31.25 kHz of a 1 MSPS band, process gain 12.04 dB, total 86.04 dB, 14 bits; 14 bits at 250 MSPS with 1 ps at 100 MHz, jitter 64.04 dB, total 64.01 dB, 10.34 bits, with the warning; 12 bits at −20 dBFS, 54 dB and an ENOB still of 12; the STM32G0's 63 dB, 10.17 bits.

The review made these changes: - The total SNR and the ENOB became the large results, with their terms on the line under them. - Rates, frequencies and jitter are kept in hertz and seconds, so a remembered unit only changes how a field shows them; the pill and units are remembered. - The Estimate fields went from three to a row to two: at 375 px the sample rate's unit was cut to "MS…". - The diagram's labels went from 8–9 px to 11 px, with values to one decimal. - It added the six examples, the first cases (12) and a formula-search card.
