Path loss

What it computes

How much of a radio signal gets from one antenna to another, three ways (pills):

  • Free space: the frequency and the distance give the free-space path loss in dB, between isotropic antennas. In three cells: the wavelength, the distance in wavelengths and the power ratio (the share of the power that arrives). Under them: what each doubling adds (6.02 dB), the loss at ten times the distance, the loss at 1 m, and a warning when the distance is under 5 wavelengths. The drawing is the loss against distance on a logarithmic axis, your distance marked.
  • Link budget: the transmitter's power, the transmitting antenna's gain and line loss, the receiving antenna's gain and line loss, the receiver's sensitivity, the frequency, the distance and the exponent γ. The big result is the received power in dBm, with the margin over the sensitivity in the line under it ("the link closes" or "no link"). In three cells: the EIRP, the path loss and the margin. Under them: the EIRP in watts, the received power in watts (pW, fW) and the field strength, in free space, for that EIRP at that distance (V/m and dBµV/m). The drawing is the received level against distance, the sensitivity dashed, your distance marked with its margin.
  • Range: the same equipment, and the margin you want instead of the distance. The big result is the distance at which the signal falls to the sensitivity plus that margin, with that level and the other system's unit (miles for metres and kilometres, the other way round for miles) in the line under it. In three cells: the path loss allowed, the EIRP and γ. Under them: the range in free space (γ 2) and with γ 3 and γ 4. The drawing is the level against distance with the sensitivity (grey) and the level needed (green) dashed, the range marked.
  • Units: frequency kHz, MHz or GHz; distance m, km, mi, nmi or ft; the transmit power dBm, mW or W; the antenna gains dBi or dBd (the two boxes change together).
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: a Wi-Fi link across a field, a geostationary satellite, how far a LoRa node reaches, and what each doubling of distance costs.

Terms

  • Path loss: how much weaker a signal is at the receiving antenna than at the transmitting one, in dB. In free space, the free-space path loss (the ITU's "free-space basic transmission loss") is between isotropic antennas, the reference ones that radiate and receive equally in every direction.
  • dBi, dBd: an antenna's gain in dB over an isotropic antenna, or over a half-wave dipole; dBd = dBi − 2.15, the dipole's own 2.15 dBi.
  • EIRP: the effective isotropic radiated power: the transmitter's power less its line loss, plus the antenna's gain; the power an isotropic antenna would need to radiate the same in the antenna's best direction.
  • Line loss: what the cable and connectors between the radio and its antenna take, in dB (the Coax cable standards tool gives it for a cable).
  • Sensitivity: the weakest signal at the receiver's input that it can use, in dBm; it depends on the bandwidth and the data rate.
  • Link margin (fade margin): how many dB the received power is above the sensitivity: the cushion against fading, rain, bodies and misalignment.
  • Path-loss exponent γ: how fast the loss grows with distance, 10 γ dB for each tenfold distance: 2 in free space, larger where walls, trees and buildings are in the way.
  • Far field, Fresnel zone: the region well beyond the antennas (the distance much more than the wavelength) where the formula holds; and the ellipsoid round the straight path in which obstacles take signal away.

Sources

  • Recommendation ITU-R P.525-3, "Calculation of free-space attenuation" (09/2016; read as PDF text): the field of an e.i.r.p. p (watts) at a distance d (metres), e = √(30 p)/d V/m (eq. 1); the free-space basic transmission loss between isotropic antennas, Lbf = 20 log (4π d/λ) dB with d and λ in the same unit (eq. 3), and the same for f in MHz and d in km, 32.4 + 20 log f + 20 log d (eq. 4). The constant is 32.4478, so the rounded 32.4 reads up to 0.05 dB low (2.4 GHz at 1 km: 100.004 dB by eq. 4, 100.052 by eq. 3): the tool uses eq. 3 with c = 299 792 458 m/s. Later versions of the recommendation were not read (the address tried for version 4 did not exist).
  • Wikipedia, "Free-space path loss" (last edited 20 July 2026; read through a text-extraction tool): FSPL = (4πd/λ)² between isotropic antennas, the definition credited to IEEE Std 145; that the term is "a little misleading", the frequency dependence belonging to the receiving antenna's aperture and not to the path; valid with the antennas in each other's far field (d ≫ λ) and the path clear of obstructions out to 0.6 of the first Fresnel zone; the dB forms 20 log d + 20 log f − 147.55 (metres, hertz) and 20 log d + 20 log f + 92.45 (km, GHz), which the tool's constant agrees with.
  • Wikipedia, "Link budget" (11 October 2026; read): Prx = Ptx + Gtx − Ltx − Lfs − Lm + Grx − Lrx, and the link margin as "a safety margin between the received power and minimum power required by the receiver"; it cites Pozar, Microwave Engineering, 4th ed. (not read). The tool's margin is the cushion left over, so it has no separate Lm.
  • Wikipedia, "Log-distance path loss model" (15 July 2026; read): L = L0 + 10 γ log (d/d0) + Xg, L0 the loss at the reference distance d0 from close-in measurements or the Friis model, d0 typically 1 to 10 m for a microcell, Xg a zero-mean Gaussian term (the shadowing). Its table of measured exponents γ (and standard deviations σ), credited to Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice (Prentice-Hall, 2002; not read): vacuum 2.0; grocery store at 914 MHz 1.8 (σ 5.2 dB); retail store at 914 MHz 2.2 (8.7); office with soft partitions 2.4 at 900 MHz (9.6) and 2.6 at 1.9 GHz (14.1); with hard partitions 3.0 at 1.5 GHz (7); textile or chemical works 2.0 at 1.3 GHz (3.0) and 2.1 at 4 GHz; offices 2.2 and commercial buildings 1.7 at 60 GHz (3.92 and 7.9). The tool takes d0 = 1 m and L0 the free-space loss there, so γ = 2 is exactly free space, and does not model Xg: its σ, 3 to 14 dB in that table, is why a margin is wanted.
  • Not read: Friis' "A Note on a Simple Transmission Formula" (Proc. IRE, 1946), Pozar, Rappaport's book, IEEE Std 145, ITU-R P.341 and P.526. The 2.15 dB between dBi and dBd is the textbook directivity of a half-wave dipole (10 log 1.64); no source was read for it. The 5 wavelengths at which the tool warns is its own rule of thumb: the sources say only "far field, d ≫ λ".

Why the formulas are these

An isotropic transmitter of power P spreads it evenly over a sphere, so at a distance d the power density is P/(4π d²). An isotropic receiving antenna collects it over the aperture λ²/(4π), so what arrives is P (λ/(4π d))² and the loss is (4π d/λ)², 20 log (4π d/λ) in dB: 6.02 dB for each doubling of the distance, and for each doubling of the frequency, which comes from the aperture, not from the path. With f in MHz and d in km the constant is 20 log (4π × 10⁹/c) = 32.448; with d in metres and f in MHz, −27.55; for hertz and metres, −147.55.

The field of an EIRP p at d follows from the power density: S = p/(4π d²) = e²/(120 π) (the 120 π Ω of free space), so e = √(30 p)/d, ITU-R P.525's eq. 1.

The link budget adds what the equipment does in decibels: the power the antenna is given is Ptx − Ltx, its gain adds Gtx (EIRP = Ptx − Ltx + Gtx), the path takes PL, and the receiver gets EIRP − PL + Grx − Lrx; the margin is that less the sensitivity. For a path that loses more than free space the loss is PL(d) = FSPL(1 m) + 10 γ log (d / 1 m), the log-distance model with d0 = 1 m: for γ = 2 it is eq. 3 itself, since 20 log (4π d f/c) = 20 log (4π f/c) + 20 log d. Solving it for the distance at which the margin is a given M:

d = 10^((EIRP + Grx − Lrx − sensitivity − M − FSPL(1 m)) / (10 γ))   metres

Assumptions and limits

  • Free space or a fitted exponent. The tool has no terrain, ground reflection (the two-ray model), diffraction, atmospheric absorption, rain or foliage; γ is yours to choose, and a real path varies round it by the shadowing σ.
  • Far field, clear path. Closer than about 5 wavelengths the formula is not reliable, and the tool says so (its own rule of thumb); for a large antenna the far field starts much farther out, at about 2D²/λ (D the antenna's largest dimension: 13.9 m for a 0.6 m dish at 5.8 GHz), which the Beamwidth & gain tool gives. The path must be clear of obstructions out to 0.6 of the first Fresnel zone for the free-space figures to apply: the Fresnel zone tool is where to check it.
  • Antennas aligned and the polarization matched. The gains are in the direction of the link; a misalignment or a polarization mismatch is margin you must keep.
  • The sensitivity is yours. It depends on the bandwidth, the data rate and the noise figure; the receiver's data sheet gives it for each setting.
  • The field strength is the free-space far-field figure for the EIRP, whatever γ you give.

How it was checked

26 cases. The expected values come from a Python implementation of the same formulas: - Free space: 1 km at 2.4 GHz, 100.05 dB (λ 12.5 cm, 8006 wavelengths, a power ratio of 9.88 × 10⁻¹¹, 40.05 dB at 1 m); a geostationary satellite, 12 GHz over 35 786 km, 205.11 dB; 100 m 80.05 dB and 200 m 86.07 dB; a mile, 104.18 dB; 868 MHz over 1 km, 91.22 dB; 0.5 m flagged as under 5 wavelengths; a missing distance or frequency refused; - Link budget: 2.4 GHz over 1 km with 20 dBm, 2 dBi at each end, 0.5 dB lines and −90 dBm: EIRP 21.5 dBm (141 mW), −77.05 dBm (19.7 pW), +12.95 dB, 2.06 mV/m; a −70 dBm receiver (7.05 dB short); the power in watts; the antenna in dBd (−76.90 dBm); γ 3 (−107.05 dBm, 17.05 dB short); a negative line loss and a zero exponent refused; - Range: 103 dB allowed, 1.4 km (0.872 mi), with γ 3 and 4 125 m and 37.5 m (411 ft); a LoRa node at 868 MHz, 14 dBm, −130 dBm, 10 dB margin, 137 dB allowed: 195 km in free space, 3.36 km at γ 3, 441 m at γ 4; no margin, 4.44 km; in miles; a missing margin refused; - the four examples.

The Python twin also showed that the log-distance form with γ = 2 equals eq. 3 to 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ dB over 110 combinations of frequency and distance (30 cm to 384 000 km, 100 kHz to 120 GHz), that solving the range and then running the link budget at it returns the margin asked for to 10⁻¹⁴ dB, and that e²/(120 π) equals p/(4π d²).

Radio wavelength

(formerly Wavelength (RF), then Wavelength ↔ frequency)

What it computes

A frequency and its free-space wavelength, each from the other — type either — with the period of one cycle and the ITU band the frequency falls in: its symbol and number, its full name, and the name ITU gives its wavelengths (metric waves for VHF, decimetric for UHF). The band is the large result, since the wavelength already sits in its field, and the drawing carries the wavelength's value. A row of buttons jumps to the middle of each named band, and a table gives the wavelengths of common allocations.

The units are remembered. When typing one field leaves the other unreadable in its unit — 100 Hz is 2 997 925 000 mm — that field moves to the unit that reads best, without changing the remembered choice.

Examples: FM radio at 100 MHz, AM radio at 1 MHz, Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz, GPS L1, a 1 m wavelength typed as such, and exactly 30 MHz, on a band edge.

Source

  • c = 299 792 458 m/s, exact: the metre has been defined from the speed of light since 1983.
  • The bands are ITU-R Recommendation V.431-8 (08/2015), table 1, which follows No. 2.1 of the Radio Regulations: band N runs from 0.3 × 10ᴺ to 3 × 10ᴺ Hz, "lower limit exclusive, upper limit inclusive", with the symbols ULF (band 3) to EHF (band 11) and a metric name for each band's wavelengths, from hectokilometric to decimillimetric waves. Band 12, 300 GHz to 3 THz, has no symbol in the table.
  • The reference rows are US allocations from the FCC: the AM broadcast band, 535 to 1705 kHz (47 CFR 73.14); the FM broadcast band, 88 to 108 MHz (73.310); and Wi-Fi's 6 GHz band, 5.925 to 7.125 GHz (15.407), all read through Cornell's copy of the CFR. GPS L1, 1575.42 MHz, is 154 times the 10.23 MHz reference that IS-GPS-200 section 3.3.1.1 specifies: the change notice read here gives the 10.23 MHz, and the multiplier comes from secondary sources.

Why the formulas are these

λ = c / f
f = c / λ
T = 1 / f

A wave travels at c and repeats every period T, so one cycle covers c × T, which is the wavelength. In free space only: in a cable or on a PCB the wave is slower, by the velocity factor, and so its wavelength is shorter.

Bands by decade. ITU's bands are decades of frequency, and since λ = c/f each is a decade of wavelength too: band N spans 10^(8−N) to 10^(9−N) m, which is where the metric names come from — VHF, 30 to 300 MHz, is 1 to 10 m, the metric waves. The decades are nominal: c is not quite 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so 30 MHz is 9.993 m rather than 10.

Edges. Each band includes its upper limit and excludes its lower one, so exactly 30 MHz is HF, band 7, and anything above it is VHF.

Assumptions and limits

  • Free space. Air is close enough to it for this purpose; coax, twisted pair and PCB traces are not, and need their velocity factor.
  • ITU bands 3 to 12 only. Below 300 Hz and above 3 THz the tool shows no band. V.431 also lists URSI's extension to lower bands and bands 13 to 15 up to 3000 THz, which reach the infrared; light has its own tool, Wavelength ↔ color.
  • The reference table is the US's. Other regions allocate these bands differently.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Antenna lengths. A quarter-wave or half-wave antenna is a fraction of this wavelength, shortened further by end effects: that is the Antenna length tool's job.
  • Velocity factor. Its own future tool.
  • Band plans. Amateur, cellular and microwave allocations are reference tools of their own.

How it was checked

100 MHz gives 2.997925 m: VHF, ITU band 8, metric waves 1–10 m, period 10 ns. Exactly 30 MHz gives HF and 9.993082 m, and 30.001 MHz gives VHF. A 1 m wavelength gives 299.7925 MHz. GPS L1 keeps its decimals: 1575.42 MHz, 19.02937 cm. The EHF button lands on the band's geometric middle, 94.86833 GHz. 1 kHz is ULF, hectokilometric waves, 100–1000 km; 500 GHz is band 12; 100 Hz is outside the bands, its wavelength shown as 2997.925 km.

The review made these changes: - It was renamed Radio wavelength, on Pierre's choice: with the examples bulb, "Wavelength ↔ frequency" wrapped. - Band edges now follow ITU, the upper limit in the band: the tool had put exactly 30 MHz in VHF. - ULF (band 3) and band 12 were added, with each band's number and ITU wavelength name. - The AM row read 525 kHz, which is not the US band's edge; it is now the FCC's 535–1705 kHz, and the rows say US. - The band and the period became one result; the wave on the drawing went from the domain colour to part blue and carries the wavelength's value. - Frequency and wavelength are kept in hertz and metres with remembered units, shown to seven figures so GPS's .42 survives. - It added six examples and the first cases (11).

Beamwidth & gain

What it computes

How strongly an antenna beams its power and how wide the beam is, from whichever of the antenna's figures you have (pills):

  • Diameter: a dish's diameter and the frequency, with its aperture efficiency, a beamwidth constant k and an aiming error, give the gain. The big result is the gain in dBi; under it the same as a power ratio and in dBd. In three cells: the half-power beamwidth, the effective area and the distance from which the far field starts. Under them: D/λ; the ITU-R F.699 rules of thumb for the same dish (its gain and its beamwidth); the loss from the aiming error and the gain left; and the side lobe peaks (the level they stay under, and how far below the main beam that is). A dish under one wavelength across is flagged. The drawing is the antenna's gain against the angle off its axis, the angle on a logarithmic scale: the main lobe, then the reference pattern of ITU-R F.699 for the side lobe peaks. The −3 dB point is a green dot with a dotted line down to its angle, the aiming error a ring; both are named, with their values, in the row above the plot.
  • Gain: the gain as a data sheet gives it (dBi or dBd) and the frequency. The big result is the beamwidth; in three cells the equivalent dish's diameter, its effective area and the far-field distance; under them the same rows. It is the circular dish that would give that gain at the efficiency you assume.
  • Beamwidths: a sector antenna's horizontal (azimuth) and vertical (elevation) half-power beamwidths; the frequency is optional. The big result is its gain by the sectoral rule of ITU-R F.1336, 31 000 / (θH × θV). In three cells: the directivity by F.1336's own formula (the gain with no losses in the antenna), the gain in dBd and the equivalent D/λ (the dish that would give that gain, by F.699's rule). Under them: the equivalent dish (needs the frequency), how much of the sphere the beam covers, the loss from the aiming error in each plane, and a flag when the horizontal beamwidth is over about 120° or the vertical one over about 45°, where the rule is outside its range or rougher. The drawing is the two beams as sectors, each as wide as its beamwidth: the horizontal one seen from above, the vertical one from the side.
  • Omni: an omnidirectional antenna, one that radiates alike in every direction round the horizon and squeezes its beam in elevation, like a doughnut: a whip, or a collinear array of stacked dipoles. Its vertical beamwidth and its gain are linked: type either and the other is calculated (the box that is calculated carries the word "result"). The efficiency is the antenna's radiation efficiency (100 % is the ITU's assumption), the side-lobe k is the parameter of the ITU's pattern (0.7 for typical antennas below 3 GHz, 0 for ones with improved side lobes and for 3 to 70 GHz), and the elevation is the angle off the horizon. The big result is the gain (when the beamwidth is typed) or the vertical beamwidth (when the gain is). In three cells: the directivity, the gain in dBd and how much of the sphere the beam covers. Under them: the simplified rule of F.1336 for the same antenna (its gain, 10 log (107.6 / θ), or its beamwidth, 107.6 × 10^(−0.1 G)), the loss at the elevation angle and the gain left, how far down the far side lobes stay (12 − 10 log k dB; "falling away" for k = 0), and a flag when the gain is outside the 8 to 13 dBi the ITU states its pattern for. The drawing is the gain against the angle off the horizon, to 90°, the angle on a logarithmic scale: the main lobe, then the ITU's side lobe peaks, marked as in the Diameter pill.
  • Units: frequency kHz, MHz or GHz; the diameter in m, cm, ft or in; the gain in dBi or dBd (in the Gain and Omni pills). The "lengths in" picker at the Output heading is the diameter's own: the diameter box, the diameter result, the effective area (in that unit squared) and the far-field distance (metres and kilometres, or feet and miles) follow it, and choosing a unit there changes the box.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: a 2 ft dish at 13 GHz (CommScope's data sheet), a 2° miss on a 1.2 m dish, how big a 30 dBi antenna is, a 90° by 30° sector panel, and the ITU's measured 5.8 GHz omnidirectional antenna.

Terms

  • Gain (dBi, dBd): how much more power an antenna sends, or picks up, in its best direction than an isotropic antenna, which treats every direction alike. In dB: dBi against the isotropic antenna, dBd against a half-wave dipole (dBd = dBi − 2.15, the dipole's own gain).
  • Directivity: the same figure for an antenna with no losses; the gain is the directivity times the radiation efficiency, the share of the power given to the antenna that it radiates.
  • Half-power beamwidth (beamwidth, −3 dB beamwidth): the angle between the two directions, one each side of the best, where the power has fallen to half, 3 dB, of the peak.
  • Aperture, effective area: the area through which an antenna collects a wave. A dish's physical area is πD²/4; its effective area, A_e = G λ²/4π, is the area that really counts.
  • Aperture efficiency (η): the effective area over the physical area: what uneven illumination, spill-over past the edge, the feed's shadow and surface errors take away. 55 to 70 % is usual.
  • Beamwidth constant (k): the number in θ = k λ/D, in degrees: about 70 for a typical dish, 58.96 for an evenly lit aperture.
  • Sectoral antenna: one that covers a sector of the horizon, up to about 120° wide in the ITU's rules, with a narrow beam in elevation: a base-station panel.
  • Omnidirectional antenna: one with the same gain in every direction of azimuth; only its elevation pattern is shaped. Its vertical (elevation) beamwidth, θ3 in ITU-R F.1336, is the angle between the directions above and below the horizon where the power is half the peak.
  • Side-lobe k (F.1336): how high the side lobes of an omnidirectional antenna stand above what an improved design would give: 0.7 for typical antennas below 3 GHz, 0 for improved ones and for 3 to 70 GHz.
  • Main lobe, side lobes: the beam, and the weaker lobes beside it. The side lobe peaks are what interference studies use.
  • Far field: the region far enough out that the pattern no longer changes with the distance, beyond about 2D²/λ; nearer, the formulas for a distant receiver do not hold.
  • Off axis: the angle between the direction the antenna points and the one in question; the aiming error (the angle off the horizon, for an omni).
  • Beam solid angle (Ω): the beam's size as an angle in space, in steradians; Ω = 4π/D, a share 1/D of the whole sphere (what the tool calls "sphere covered").

Sources

  • Recommendation ITU-R F.699-9, "Reference radiation patterns for fixed wireless system antennas ... 100 MHz to 174.8 GHz" (02/2026; read as PDF text, and the pages with the equations rendered and read as printed): recommends 3 gives the maximum gain from the diameter, G_max ≈ 20 log (D/λ) + 7.7 dBi (about 48 dBi for D/λ = 100) and the reverse; recommends 4 gives D/λ ≈ 70/θ and G_max ≈ 44.5 − 20 log θ for the −3 dB beamwidth θ in degrees. Recommends 2 is the reference pattern of the side lobe peaks: the main lobe G_max − 2.5×10⁻³ (D φ/λ)² up to φ_m = (20 λ/D) √(G_max − G₁), with G₁ = 2 + 15 log (D/λ); then G₁ up to φ_r = 15.85 (D/λ)^−0.6 (D/λ over 100) or to 100 λ/D (100 or less); then 32 − 25 log φ or 52 − 10 log (D/λ) − 25 log φ; then a floor, −10 dBi from 48° (1 to 70 GHz; 10 − 10 log (D/λ) for D/λ up to 100), or −20 dBi and −10 log (D/λ) from 120° (70 to 174.8 GHz), and for 100 MHz to 1 GHz (D/λ over 0.63) −2 − 5 log (D/λ) from φ_s = 144.5 (D/λ)^−0.2. Its notes say the pattern is for rotationally symmetric antennas and can be used for square or polygonal reflectors and flat panels through an equivalent D/λ found from the maximum gain (Note 5), that a real antenna may be worse than it over some angles and that it should not be read as a limit (Notes 2, 3), and that it models some practical antennas poorly from 5° to 70° (Note 9); Annex 1 says measurements confirm it to D/λ of about 180.
  • Recommendation ITU-R F.1336-5, "Reference radiation patterns of omnidirectional, sectoral and other antennas ... 400 MHz to about 70 GHz" (01/2019; read as PDF text, and pages 4, 9, 12 and 29 rendered and read as printed): recommends 2.1 gives the elevation pattern of the side lobe peaks of an omnidirectional antenna: G₀ − 12 (θ/θ3)² up to θ4 = θ3 √(1 − log (k + 1) / 1.2), G₀ − 12 + 10 log (k + 1) up to θ3, then G₀ − 12 + 10 log ((θ/θ3)^−1.5
  • k) to 90°, with θ3 = 107.6 × 10^(−0.1 G₀) (G₀ the gain in dBi, θ3 the beamwidth in degrees); 2.3 and 2.4 set k to 0.7 for typical antennas from 400 MHz to 3 GHz and to 0 for antennas with improved side lobes and all those from 3 to 70 GHz. Annex 1 builds the pattern on a collinear array of dipoles spaced 3λ/4, states it for 8 to 13 dBi (further work being needed above), gives the directivity from the beamwidth, D = 10 log [191 √(0.818 + 1/θ3) − 172.4] dBi (5a), says k = 0.7 stands for side lobes about 13.5 dB below the peak and k = 0.5 for about 15 dB, and compares a measured 9.4 dBi antenna at 5.8 GHz, θ3 = 8.7°, with it. Annex 2 derives the directivity from an exponential elevation pattern: D = 107.64 e^(θ3²/36400) / θ3 for an omnidirectional antenna (23a, θ3 in degrees; Table 2 compares it with the directivity of a cos^2N pattern, to within 0.062 dB), the same with the exponential set to 1 (23b, under 6 % error below 45°), and for a sector D = k e^(θ3²/36400) / (φs θ3) with k = 36 400 up to φs = 120° and 38 750 above (34, 35; the transition said to need study). Its measured sectoral antennas (25 to 29.5 GHz: 90° by 2.5°, directivity 22.1 dBi, gain 20.5 to 21.4 dBi) lead to the provisional gain G₀ = 10 log (31 000 / (φs θ3)) of recommends 3.3 (28a), for a sector of about 120° or less and an elevation beamwidth under about 45°.
  • Condon and Ransom, "Essential Radio Astronomy", chapter 3 (NRAO; the first 100 000 of its 174 658 characters, read through a text-extraction tool): the beam solid angle Ω_A = 4π/G (eq. 3.34), the average effective area λ²/4π (3.41) and A_e = λ² G/4π (3.46), a half-power beamwidth of 0.89 λ/D for a uniform one-dimensional aperture (3.82) and about 1.2 λ/D for a cosine taper, "typical of most radio telescopes" (3.96), the aperture efficiency as the effective over the geometric area (3.111) and its being 70 % or less for most radio telescopes, and the far-field distance R ≈ 2D²/λ, defined by a path error of less than λ/16 at the edge (3.64). The coefficient for a uniform circular aperture is not on that page.
  • Wikipedia, "Parabolic antenna" (read through a text-extraction tool): G = e_A (π d/λ)², an aperture efficiency of 0.55 to 0.70 for typical dishes (0.7 to 0.8 for offset feeds), and θ = k λ/d with k about 70 for a typical dish; it gives 57.3 for an ideal uniform one, which the exact value below, 58.96, corrects. "Near and far field": d_F = 2D²/λ, with d_F much greater than D and than λ.
  • Köppen, "Notes and Tools about Paraboloidal Antennas" (Kiel; read through a text-extraction tool): the half-power beamwidth of a uniformly illuminated circular dish as 58.95701° × λ/D. It cites Hansen (1976) and Baars (2007) for how the constant grows with the edge taper; neither was read.
  • CommScope, "VHLP2-13-2WH/A" product specifications (revised 23 October 2015; read from a distributor's copy of the PDF): a 0.6 m (2 ft) dish, 12.700 to 13.250 GHz; gain 35.8, 36.0 and 36.2 dBi at the low, middle and top of the band; beamwidth 2.7° both ways; front-to-back ratio 61 dB.

The 41253 mentioned below is derived, not quoted, and dBd = dBi − 2.15 is the textbook figure, as in Path loss.

Why the formulas are these

Gain from the size. An isotropic antenna receives from a wave over an area λ²/4π; the gain of an antenna with effective area A_e is the ratio, G = 4π A_e/λ² (NRAO 3.41, 3.46). A circular dish of diameter D and efficiency η has A_e = η π D²/4, so

G = η (π D / λ)²

and in dB, G = 20 log (D/λ) + 20 log π + 10 log η = 20 log (D/λ) + 9.94 + 10 log η. The ITU's 7.7 is that with 10 log η = −2.24 dB, an efficiency of 59.7 %: its rule G = 20 log (D/λ) + 7.7 is within 0.025 dB of η = 60 % for any D/λ from 1 to 1000.

The beamwidth. The far field of a circular aperture is the transform of its illumination. For an evenly lit one it is 2 J₁(u)/u with u = π D sin φ/λ; the −3 dB point is at u = 1.6163, a full width of 1.0290 λ/D radians, 58.96° × λ/D (Köppen's 58.95701°); the first null is at sin φ = 1.2197 λ/D and the first side lobe is 17.57 dB down. A taper that lights the middle more than the edge lowers the side lobes and widens the beam, to about 70° × λ/D for a typical dish (the ITU's and Wikipedia's figure; NRAO's 1.2 λ/D is 68.8°). The tool's default k is 70.

The far field. From a point at distance R the path to the edge of an aperture of diameter D is longer than to its centre by about D²/(8R). Asking for no more than λ/16 gives R ≥ 2D²/λ (NRAO 3.64).

Aiming. Near the peak the pattern is a parabola in dB, G(φ) = G_max − 12 (φ/θ)², which is 3 dB down at φ = θ/2. The ITU's main lobe is the same parabola for θ = 69.28 λ/D, since 12 / 69.28² = 2.5×10⁻³: at 1° for D/λ = 11.6 both give 0.33686 dB. The ITU's omnidirectional main lobe is the same parabola again, with θ3 the full beamwidth. The tool writes it with the beamwidth you use, so k changes it, and continues with the ITU's pattern beyond φ_m.

Omnidirectional antennas. F.1336 takes the elevation pattern as e^(−aθ²), half the peak at θ3/2, which fixes the constant, a = 4 ln 2 / θ3² = 2.7726 / θ3² (θ3 in radians). The directivity is 4π over the integral of the pattern over the sphere; round the horizon the integral is 2π, and in elevation it is the integral of e^(−aθ²) cos θ, which the ITU evaluates as the infinite integral √(π/a) e^(−1/(4a)). That gives D = 107.64 e^(θ3²/36400) / θ3 with θ3 in degrees. The tool's numerical integration of the same pattern agrees with it to 0.0005 dB up to a 60° beam, 0.0055 dB at 78° and 0.021 dB at 90°. The exponential is 1 for narrow beams and 1.06 at 45°; leaving it out gives the simple 107.6 / θ3, and θ3 = 107.6 × 10^(−0.1 G). A half-wave dipole's 78° gives 2.12 dBi, against its own 2.15. The gain is the directivity times the radiation efficiency, G = η D; the ITU takes η = 100 %, but its measured 9.4 dBi antenna, 8.7° wide, has a directivity of 10.93 dBi, so its efficiency is 70 %: the tool's efficiency box is for such an antenna. To go from the gain to the beamwidth the tool solves the equation for θ3 (D falls steadily with θ3 up to 90°, so there is one answer; a directivity under 1.74 dBi, a 90° beam, has none).

Sector antennas. The same integral with a flat azimuth pattern of width φs gives D = 38 750 e^(θ3²/36400) / (φs θ3) (the 107.64 above is 38 750/360, the omnidirectional case), and an exponential azimuth pattern gives 36 400, within 0.3 dB of it; F.1336 takes 36 400 up to φs = 120° and 38 750 above. Numerical integration of the flat case agrees with its formula to 0.001 dB. The practical rule, 31 000 / (φs θ3), comes from measurements: with the gain 0.7 dB under the directivity and the exponential dropped, the ITU fits 31 000 to its first set of antennas and 34 000 to the second. For a 90° by 30° sector that is 10.6 dBi against a directivity of 11.4 dBi. The familiar 41253 / (θH θV), the sphere's 41 253 square degrees (4π (180/π)²) over a rectangle, is the same idea without the shape of the beam or any losses: 11.8 dBi for that sector.

Assumptions and limits

  • A dish-like aperture. The gain, beamwidth and pattern rules of the first two pills are for a circular aperture lit smoothly from the middle; flat panels and horns follow only through an equivalent dish (F.699 Note 5).
  • The efficiency is yours. 55 to 70 % is typical for a dish, 60 % matches the ITU's rules, and it falls where the dish surface is rough compared with the wavelength (the Ruze loss, which the tool does not model). The data sheets below imply 56 to 60 %.
  • The sector rule is provisional. F.1336 gives 31 000 / (φs θ3) for sectors of about 120° or less and elevation beamwidths under about 45°, on two sets of measurements at 25 to 29.5 GHz, and says the transition at 120° needs study; the tool flags beamwidths beyond those limits.
  • The omnidirectional rules are for a collinear array of dipoles and an elevation beam up to 90° (a directivity from 1.74 dBi); the ITU's pattern is stated for 8 to 13 dBi, from 400 MHz to 70 GHz, and further work is said to be needed above that, particularly above 3 GHz; the tool says so outside 8 to 13 dBi. The efficiency of a real antenna is below the ITU's 100 %: its beam is narrower for its gain.
  • The pattern is the ITU's reference. It is a line through the side lobe peaks, for interference studies, not a measured pattern; real antennas can be worse over some angles (F.699 Notes 2, 3 and 9). The dish pattern is defined from 100 MHz to 174.8 GHz; its printed ranges follow one another only above D/λ of 100/48 (1 to 70 GHz), 100/120 (70 GHz and up) and 0.63 (under 1 GHz, the limit F.699 states), so the tool draws the main lobe only below those, and outside the frequencies. Its pieces meet to 0.031 dB (the printed constants are rounded).
  • The aiming loss is the parabola inside the main lobe and the pattern beyond; for the Beamwidths pill, per plane, the parabola only, to an angle of the beamwidth.
  • The far field is for the largest dimension of the antenna, and holds when the distance is also much larger than D and λ.
  • Under one wavelength across the aperture formulas do not apply (the tool's own flag), and a beam wider than 180° is not a beam.

How it was checked

69 cases. The expected values come from a Python implementation of the same formulas: - Diameter: 0.6 m at 5.8 GHz, 29.0 dBi (a ratio of 798, 26.9 dBd), 6.03°, 0.17 m², far field from 13.9 m, the ITU rules 29.0 dBi and 6.03°, 0.33 dB lost 1° off axis, side lobes up to 18.0 dBi, 11.0 dB down; the CommScope dish at 12.7, 12.975 and 13.25 GHz (35.8, 36.0 and 36.2 dBi; 2.75°, 2.7°, 2.64°); a 1.2 m dish 2° off axis (35.0 dBi, 3.02°, 5.28 dB); 11.7 GHz (35.1 dBi, 2.99°); 70 % efficiency; k = 58.96; the diameter in cm and in ft; a 3 m dish at 11 GHz (D/λ over 100, 16.56 dB lost 1° off axis); 80 GHz; 500 MHz; far off axis; frequencies and sizes outside the pattern; a flag under one wavelength; the missing figures refused; - Gain: 30 dBi at 5.8 GHz (0.672 m, 5.39°, 0.213 m², the ITU's 0.674 m and 5.31°), 36 dBi at 12.975 GHz, the gain in dBd, 70 % efficiency, feet, a low gain flagged, a missing gain refused; - Beamwidths: 90° by 30° (10.6 dBi, 8.4 dBd, directivity 11.4 dBi, D/λ 1.4, 7.24 % of the sphere), 60° by 60°, 6° by 6°, 120° by 90° and 150° by 30° flagged, no frequency, 50° off axis, feet, missing and over-large beamwidths refused; - Omni: a 14° beam (8.9 dBi, 6.7 dBd, 12.9 % of the sphere, the ITU rule 8.9 dBi, 1.53 dB lost 5° off the horizon, side lobes 13.5 dB down); a 9 dBi gain (a 13.6° beam, the other box following, and the "result" tags); the ITU's measured antenna (9.4 dBi at 70 % efficiency and k 0: 8.67°); the gain in dBd; k = 0; 30° and 0° off the horizon; beams of 3°, 40° and 70 % efficiency, which fall outside 8 to 13 dBi; the 90° and 78° beams; the missing, over-large and too-low figures refused; - the length unit linked between the diameter box and the Output heading, the pills and the units remembered, the five examples, and the formula-search card.

Against data sheets, with η 60 % and k 70:

Antenna Data sheet This tool
CommScope VHLP2-13-2WH/A, 0.6 m, 12.7 GHz 35.8 dBi 35.8 dBi
the same, 12.975 GHz 36.0 dBi, 2.7° 36.0 dBi, 2.7°
the same, 13.25 GHz 36.2 dBi 36.2 dBi
Ubiquiti RD-5G30-LW, 650 mm square, 5.5 GHz 30 dBi, 5.8° for 30 dBi: a 0.708 m dish, 5.4°

The CommScope sheet implies an efficiency of 59.6, 59.8 and 60.1 % at its three frequencies, and the ITU's rule gives 35.99 dBi at mid-band. The Ubiquiti dish is square: its sheet's 30 dBi at 650 mm implies 56 % efficiency, the equal-area circle is 0.733 m across (the tool's equivalent dish 0.708 m), and 70 λ over the 650 mm side is 5.87°, the sheet's 5.8°.

Against the ITU's own numbers (F.1336-5): - Fifteen of the rows of its Table 2 (2N from 2 to 74) are reproduced: the beamwidths 2 arccos (0.5^(1/2N)) and the directivities (2N + 1)!! / (2N)!! of the cos^2N pattern to the printed digits, and eq. 23a to 0.0001 dB; - its sector example, 90° by 2.5°, gives a directivity of 22.09 dBi by eq. 34 (the text says 22.1 dBi) and 21.39 dBi by the gain rule (the measured gain is 20.5 to 21.4 dBi); - its measured omnidirectional antenna (9.4 dBi, 8.7°) has a directivity of 10.93 dBi by eq. 23a, an efficiency of 70.2 %; a 9.4 dBi gain at 70 % gives 8.67°; the lossless rule would say 12.4°; - the pattern's three regions meet to 10⁻⁸ dB at θ4 and θ3 for k of 0, 0.3, 0.7 and 1, and solving eq. 23a for the beamwidth and then computing the directivity again returns the beamwidth to rounding; - for a half-wave dipole, 78°, eq. 23a gives 2.12 dBi (2.15 dBi); 14° gives 8.88 dBi, and a 9 dBi omnidirectional antenna 13.6° by eq. 23a and 13.5° by the simplified rule.

The Python implementation also showed that the dish pattern's pieces meet at their boundaries to 0.031 dB at most (the main lobe meets G₁ exactly), that 44.5 − 20 log θ is within 0.10 dB of 20 log (70/θ) + 7.7, and that the 2.5×10⁻³ of the ITU's main lobe is 12 (φ/θ)² with θ = 69.28 λ/D.

RF & microwave › Antennas & propagation

Fresnel zone

What it computes

How much room a radio path needs round the straight line between two antennas, and what an obstacle in that room costs, three ways (pills):

  • Zone radius: the frequency, the path length, a point on the path (its distance from the transmitting antenna) and the zone number give the radius of that Fresnel zone at that point. The point starts at the middle of the path and follows it when the path changes, until you type one; the "mid" beside the box says so, and becomes a button that takes you back. In three cells: the wavelength, 60 % of the first zone's radius there (the clearance to keep) and the path length in wavelengths. Under them: the radii of zones 1, 2 and 3 there, and the widest radius of the zone you chose, at mid-path. The drawing is the path seen from the side: the zone as an ellipse, the 60 % one dashed (zone 1 dashed instead when you chose a higher zone), the radius marked in green.
  • Clearance: the two antennas' heights, the top of an obstacle and its distance from the transmitting antenna, the Earth radius factor k and the share of the first zone you want kept clear. The big result is the loss in dB the obstacle causes, taken as a knife-edge; the line under it says how much of the first zone is clear and how that compares with what you want, or "blocked" when the top is above the line of sight. In three cells: the clearance, its share of the first zone's radius and that radius there. Under them: the height of the line of sight at the obstacle, the obstacle's height with the Earth's bulge added, and the clearance from which the loss is nil (55.2 % of the radius, with its length). The drawing is the same path with a hill whose top is where the clearance puts it, the clearance in green.
  • Mast height: the same problem solved the other way: for the transmitting antenna you give, the height the receiving antenna needs so that the line clears the obstacle by the share you want. The big result is that height. In three cells: the height if both ends are alike, the clearance wanted in length, and the Earth's bulge. Under them: the line's height at the obstacle as a sum (the obstacle, the bulge, the clearance) and the first zone's radius there; and a note when the receiving antenna comes out below the datum, which means the transmitting antenna alone clears the obstacle.
  • Units: frequency kHz, MHz or GHz; distances m, km, mi, nmi or ft; heights m or ft. A distance unit and the height unit go together: miles or feet for the distances put the heights in feet, metres or kilometres put them in metres, and the other way round (nautical miles leave the heights as they are). Both distance boxes change together, and so do the three height boxes. The zone radius is given in the height unit, with the other unit in the line under it.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: a 5.8 GHz link across 5 km, the masts needed over a 20 m hill, the Earth's bulge on a 50 km hop, and a hill just inside the zone.

Terms

  • Fresnel ellipsoid, Fresnel zone: the radio energy from one antenna to another does not follow a line but fills a region round it. Take the points M whose path through them, AM + MB, is longer than the straight one AB by n half-wavelengths: they form an ellipsoid, the n-th Fresnel ellipsoid, with the antennas at its foci. The zone of order n is the part between ellipsoids n − 1 and n; the first zone is inside the first ellipsoid.
  • Zone radius (r): the radius of the n-th ellipsoid at a point: the distance from the line of sight to its edge there, widest at mid-path and nil at the antennas. "F1" or "r1" is the first one.
  • Clearance: how far the line of sight passes above the top of an obstacle there; negative when the top is above it (blocked).
  • The 60 % rule: keep the path clear of obstacles to 60 % of the first zone's radius, and the path behaves as if it were free space.
  • Datum: the level the heights are measured from: sea level, or the level ground both antennas stand on.
  • Earth bulge: how far the Earth's surface rises between two points on it, above the straight line joining them: d1 d2 / (2 a), the product of the distances to the two ends over twice the Earth's radius.
  • k, the effective Earth radius factor: the atmosphere bends radio rays slightly toward the ground, so a ray can be treated as straight if the Earth is made larger by the factor k: the effective radius is k × 6371 km. 4/3 is the usual value; 1 means no bending.
  • Knife-edge, ν, J: an idealised obstacle with a sharp top and no thickness. ν (nu) packs its geometry into one number, √2 × (how far its top is above the line of sight) / r1; J(ν) is the loss in dB the obstacle causes, by diffraction.

Sources

  • Recommendation ITU-R P.526-15, "Propagation by diffraction" (10/2019; read as PDF text; the extraction dropped the Greek letters and the root signs, so each equation was read with its dimensions checked, and the numbers below were checked against it): § 2.1 defines the ellipsoids by AM + MB − AB = nλ/2 (eq. 1) and gives the radius of the n-th at a point d1 and d2 from the ends as an approximation, R_n = √(n λ d1 d2/(d1 + d2)) (eq. 2), and in metres for f in MHz and d in km as 550 √(n d1 d2/(f (d1 + d2))) (eq. 3); it calls the part between ellipsoids n − 1 and n the zone of order n, and takes a path as line-of-sight, with negligible diffraction, when nothing lies inside the first ellipsoid. § 2.3 starts the diffraction zone where the clearance falls to 60 % of the first zone's radius, and § 2.5 lists among the conditions for an isolated obstacle a clearance of at least 0.6 of it on both sides. § 4.1 gives the knife-edge parameter, ν = h √(2 (d1 + d2)/ (λ d1 d2)) (eq. 26, h the top's height above the straight line, negative below it; eq. 33 is the same in practical units, with 0.0316 for h and λ in metres and d in km), the loss J(ν) as Fresnel integrals (eq. 30) and, for ν above −0.78, the approximation J = 6.9 + 20 log (√((ν − 0.1)² + 1) + ν − 0.1) dB (eq. 31), which the tool uses. It assumes a diffraction angle under about 0.2 rad (12°) and says the data are mainly for VHF and shorter waves (above 30 MHz). § 3.2 gives the clearance for zero diffraction loss as h_req = 0.552 √(λ d1 d2/d) (eq. 23). Attachment 2 gives the ray's height at a point of the path, (h_u d_iv + h_v d_ui)/d_uv (eq. 123), the terrain's, h_i + d_ui d_iv/ (2 a_e) (eq. 124), the clearance h_z as their difference (eq. 121), F1 = √(λ d_ui d_iv/d_uv) (eq. 122), the normalised clearance C_F = h_z/F1 (eq. 120) and ν = −√2 C_F (eq. 125). The text before eq. 44 gives a_e = k × 6371 km, and § 1 suggests an equivalent Earth radius of 8 500 km when nothing better is known (k = 1.334, 0.06 % above 4/3).
  • Recommendation ITU-R P.526-14 (01/2018; read as PDF text): the same eq. 2 and 3 and the same 60 % statements.
  • Not read: later versions of P.526; ITU-R P.530 (the design of terrestrial line-of-sight links, where clearance criteria with several values of k are given), P.310 (the definition of k) and P.834 (refraction); any textbook derivation of the Fresnel zones or of the knife-edge loss. The 5 wavelengths at which the tool warns is its own rule of thumb (see Assumptions and limits).

Why the formulas are these

The zone radius. A point M at a distance r off the line, d1 from one antenna and d2 from the other along it (r much smaller than d1 and d2), is √(d1² + r²) ≈ d1 + r²/(2 d1) from the first antenna and d2 + r²/(2 d2) from the second. The path through it is longer than the straight one, d1 + d2, by r²/2 × (1/d1 + 1/d2) = r² d/(2 d1 d2). Setting that to n λ/2 gives

r = √(n λ d1 d2 / d)      d = d1 + d2

(eq. 2). It is widest at mid-path, r = √(n λ d)/2, nil at the antennas, symmetric about the middle, and the n-th is √n times the first. With f in MHz λ = 299.792 458/f, and with d1 and d2 in km the factor 1000 turns km into m: r = √(299.792 458 × 1000) √(n d1 d2/(f d)) = 547.53 √(n d1 d2 /(f d)). P.526's eq. 3 rounds the 547.53 to 550, which reads 0.45 % high; the tool does not round it.

The clearance and the loss. The ray passes at a height (h1 d2 + h2 d1)/d over the datum at a point d1 from the first antenna, a linear mix of the two antennas' heights (eq. 123). The Earth's surface, seen from a straight line between two points on it, lies d1 d2/(2 a_e) above that line (the chord theorem for a circle of radius a_e, a small sagitta, eq. 124), so the top of an obstacle at height h_o sits at h_o + d1 d2/(2 k a) over the straight line; the clearance is the difference. In the knife-edge formula ν = h √(2 (d1 + d2)/(λ d1 d2)) = √2 h / r1, where h is the top's height above the line: h = −clearance gives ν = −√2 × clearance/r1 (eq. 125). J(ν) comes from the Fresnel integrals (eq. 30); eq. 31 is a simple fit to it.

Eq. 31 is exactly 0 dB at ν = −0.7806 (√(u² + 1) + u = 10^(−6.9/20) with u = ν − 0.1 gives u = −0.8806), and −0.7806/(−√2) = 0.552: the clearance of 0.552 r1 in P.526's eq. 23 is the point where the knife-edge loss starts. The tool takes no loss at or above it. The 60 % rule has some margin over that: at 60 % the exact knife-edge field is 0.37 dB above free space.

The mast. The line's height at the obstacle must be h_o + bulge + (share wanted) × r1 = T. With the transmitting antenna at h1 and the receiving one at h2 it is (h1 d2 + h2 d1)/d, which equals T for

h2 = h1 + (T − h1) × d / d1

and with the same height at both ends the line is level and the height is T.

Assumptions and limits

  • One thin obstacle. The tool looks at the one obstacle you describe and treats its top as a knife-edge. A real hill is rounded, which loses more (P.526 § 4.2 adds a term for it), and a path with several obstacles, or trees and buildings, needs the methods of its later sections (Bullington, Epstein-Peterson, Deygout, ...), none of which the tool has. The figures are an estimate to within a few dB for a single sharp ridge, and a minimum for anything else.
  • No ground reflection and no fading. A path clear to 60 % of the first zone can still fade from a reflection off the ground or water; the 60 % rule is about diffraction by obstacles only.
  • The approximation of eq. 2. It holds when the point is many wavelengths from either antenna. The exact ellipsoid of eq. 1 is a little wider: +0.0002 % at mid-path of 10 km at 2.4 GHz, +0.25 % at 50 wavelengths from an antenna, +2.5 % at 5 wavelengths (+7.2 % for zone 3), +12 % at one wavelength. The tool flags a point under 5 wavelengths from an antenna; that limit is its own, and the Fresnel picture itself, which assumes the paraxial limit, stops meaning much there.
  • J below its zero. Under 55.2 % of clearance the tool says 0 dB. The exact knife-edge curve there ripples round 0 dB: −1.4 dB (a gain) at ν = −1.22 (a clearance of 86 % of r1) and +1.1 dB at ν = −1.87 (132 %). A real path has a ground and other things that move such ripples; the tool does not model them.
  • Eq. 31 against the integrals. The approximation is within 0.12 dB of eq. 30 over ν from −0.78 to 20 (the worst at ν = 4.6).
  • k is yours. The real value changes with the weather, and a link is usually checked at a smaller k as well; the tool takes the one you give. P.530, which has the criteria for that, was not read.
  • Heights share a datum. If the antennas are on ground of different levels (or the obstacle is), add each one's elevation to its height first; the Earth bulge is measured from the straight line between the antennas' bases.
  • Small angles and VHF and up. P.526's knife-edge formulas are for diffraction angles under about 12° and frequencies above 30 MHz; the tool does not stop you outside them.
  • The distances are along the ground. The tool uses d1 and d2 as the distances to the ends and does not correct for a steep path.

How it was checked

51 cases. The expected values come from a Python implementation of the same formulas (with the Fresnel integrals of scipy for the check of eq. 31): - Zone radius: 2.4 GHz over 10 km, mid-path, 17.7 m (58 ft; λ 12.5 cm, 80 060 wavelengths, 60 % 10.6 m; zones 1, 2 and 3: 17.7, 25 and 30.6 m); 2 km from the transmitter 14.1 m; zone 2 and 3 at mid-path 25 m and 30.6 m; 5.8 GHz over 5 km 8.04 m; 145 MHz over 30 km 125 m; a 5-mile path in feet and a 600 m one in metres; nautical miles; a point 0.5 m from an antenna flagged; a missing frequency or path, a position off the path and a zone number that is not whole refused; - The position: it follows the middle when the path changes (10 km on a 20 km path), stays where it was typed, and goes back with the "mid" button; - Clearance: 2.4 GHz over 10 km, 30 m antennas, a 20 m hill mid-path, k 4/3: bulge 1.47 m, clearance +8.53 m, 48.3 % of the zone, 0.66 dB; a 5 m hill (133 %, no loss); a 35 m hill (blocked by 6.47 m, 10.43 dB); antennas of 10 and 50 m with the hill 2 km from the lower one (the line 18 m there); k = 1 (bulge 1.96 m); a 50 km hop at 6 GHz (bulge 36.8 m, 9.34 dB); 100 % and 0 % wanted; the same path in miles and feet; the missing heights, k = 0, 200 % wanted refused; a flag near an antenna; - Mast height: 34.1 m at the receiving end (32.1 m at both) for the same hill; 54.1 m with the transmitting antenna at 10 m; 100 % wanted; a 100 m transmitting antenna, which leaves the receiver below the datum; the 50 km hop (104 m, 81.8 m); a hill 9 km along; k = 1; - the unit links (miles put heights in feet, feet put distances in miles, metres put them in kilometres, nautical miles leave the heights), the pill and the units remembered, the four examples, and the formula-search card.

The Python implementation also showed that: - eq. 31 is 0 dB at ν = −0.78062, a clearance of 0.55198 r1 (P.526 eq. 23: 0.552); - eq. 31 stays within 0.123 dB of eq. 30 for ν from −0.78 to 20 (the worst at ν = 4.57), for example 6.03 against 6.02 dB at ν = 0 and 13.93 against 13.86 dB at ν = 1; - running the mast height and then the clearance at the height it gives returns the share wanted to 2 × 10⁻¹³ over 2000 random paths (10 MHz to 100 GHz, 100 m to 316 km, k from 2/3 to 2), and the same with a level line at the same height at both ends; - the loss against the clearance, from eq. 31 (the exact value in brackets):

Clearance (share of r1) Loss, dB
60 % 0 (−0.37)
50 % 0.49 (0.42)
40 % 1.48 (1.37)
20 % 3.65 (3.60)
0 (grazing) 6.03 (6.02)
blocked by 25 % 9.08 (9.04)
blocked by 100 % 16.34 (16.33)
blocked by 200 % 21.92 (22.02)
  • the Earth's bulge at mid-path, k = 4/3 (k = 1): 1.47 m (1.96 m) at 10 km, 5.89 m (7.85 m) at 20 km, 36.8 m (49.1 m) at 50 km.

RF & microwave › Antennas & propagation

Antenna length

(formerly Antenna length (dipole/monopole))

What it computes

How long to cut a wire antenna for a frequency, or the frequency a wire of a given length is cut for:

  • Three kinds (pills):
  • a half-wave dipole, fed in the middle;
  • a quarter-wave vertical over a ground plane;
  • a long wire of N half waves, fed at one end.
  • Two live boxes: the frequency and the length. Type either and the other follows.
  • The correction factor k: 0.95 by default. Outside 3 to 50 MHz it is flagged, because that is the only range FM 24-18 gives it for. The long wire uses N − 0.05 half waves instead, and its box takes a whole number.
  • The big result: the length, in metres, centimetres or feet. Below it:
  • the same length in feet and inches (to the quarter inch), or in metres when feet are shown;
  • each leg of a dipole;
  • the free-space wavelength, with its half or quarter.
  • Drawing: the antenna (the calculated part, green) with its length; insulators and the ground plane are blue, the feed is grey.
  • Remembered: the kind of antenna and both units.

Examples:

  • a 40 m band dipole at 7.1 MHz;
  • a CB quarter-wave whip at 27 MHz;
  • FM 24-18's 468 / f rule at 10 MHz;
  • FM 24-18's worked long wire, 3 half waves at 7 MHz.

Terms

  • Wavelength (λ): the distance a radio wave travels during one cycle, c / f. At 7 MHz it is 42.8 m.
  • Half-wave dipole (Hertz antenna): a wire half a wavelength long, cut in the middle where the feed line connects. It resonates there: it looks like a plain resistance, about 73 Ω in free space, to the transmitter.
  • Quarter-wave (Marconi) antenna: half a dipole, standing over ground or a ground plane (a metal sheet, or radials). The ground acts as a mirror and supplies the missing quarter wave, so it resonates at the same frequency as the full dipole.
  • End effect: a real wire seems electrically longer than it is, because of its thickness and the capacitance at its ends and supports. So a wire resonates shorter than the free-space half wave.
  • Correction factor (k): how much shorter to cut it, as a share of the free-space length; 0.95 means 5 % shorter.
  • Long wire: a wire several half waves long, used on harmonics; the end effect matters only at its ends, so FM 24-18 takes 0.05 of a half wave off the total rather than 5 %.

Source

  • FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques, Headquarters, Department of the Army, 30 September 1987, §3-8 "Antenna Length" (read, the EverySpec copy):
  • an antenna's physical and electrical lengths are "never the same": the reduced velocity of the wave on the wire and the end effect make it seem longer electrically. The diameter-to-length ratio and the insulators and clamps contribute;
  • use a correction of 0.95 between 3.0 and 50.0 MHz;
  • a half-wave antenna is 150 × 0.95 / f = 142.5 / f metres, or 492 × 0.95 / f = 468 / f feet, f in MHz;
  • a long wire (one wavelength or longer, for harmonic operation) is 150 (N − 0.05) / f metres, or 492 (N − 0.05) / f feet, N being the number of half waves. Its example is 3 half waves at 7 MHz: 150 × 2.95 / 7 = 63.2 m;
  • §3-8 later gives 468 / f feet again for the half-wave doublet.
  • NEETS Module 10, Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, NAVEDTRA 14182, September 1998, chapter 4 (read):
  • Hertz antennas are half a wavelength long and insulated from ground;
  • Marconi antennas are a quarter wavelength, grounded at one end or worked against a counterpoise, which "provides the equivalent of an additional 1/4 wavelength";
  • a grounded quarter-wave antenna resonates at the same frequency as the ungrounded half-wave, because ground acts as an electrical mirror image;
  • a half-wave antenna in free space has a radiation resistance of 73 Ω; over a ground plane, anything from 0 to about 100 Ω.
  • c = 299 792 458 m/s, exact. FM 24-18 rounds c / 2 to 150 m·MHz and 492 ft·MHz; the tool uses c itself. That is why it gives 46.72 ft where 468 / 10 gives 46.8 ft, and 63.17 m where the manual's example gives 63.2 m.

The quarter-wave applies FM 24-18's 0.95 to half the dipole. FM 24-18 states the factor for half-wave and long-wire antennas only, and NEETS gives the quarter-wave as half the dipole; the factor is not separately sourced for it.

Why the formulas are these

λ = c / f
Half wave:     L = k × c / (2f)       (k = 0.95: 142.5 / f m, 468 / f ft)
Quarter wave:  L = k × c / (4f)
Long wire:     L = c × (N − 0.05) / (2f)

A wire resonates when a wave goes to its end and back in step with the source: half a wavelength, end to end. The end effect makes the wire seem longer, so it is cut short by k. A quarter wave over ground resonates like the full dipole, because its mirror image in the ground supplies the other half. A long wire is N half waves end to end, but the end effect acts only at its two ends: it loses a fixed 0.05 of a half wave, not 5 % of the whole.

The length box works the formula backwards: f = (the factor in front) / L.

Assumptions and limits

  • Thin wire in the clear. The real factor depends on the ratio of the wire's diameter to its length and on the insulators and clamps (FM 24-18), and also on its height above ground and what is near it. 0.95 is FM 24-18's figure for HF wire antennas.
  • 3 to 50 MHz for k = 0.95. Outside it the tool flags the factor and still computes. Type another k if you have a better figure for your antenna, from its maker or from measuring it.
  • Cut long, then trim. Cut the wire a little long, then trim it on the air with an SWR meter or an antenna analyser.
  • The feed point. The tool gives the resonant length only. It does not match the feed-line impedance: a dipole in free space is 73 Ω (NEETS), less or more near the ground; a quarter-wave is fed at its low-impedance grounded end; an end-fed long wire is high and needs a tuner.
  • Ground plane. A quarter-wave needs a good ground or radials (each about a quarter wave long). Their length is not computed here.

What it deliberately does not do

  • The wavelength alone: Radio wavelength has the bands and the period.
  • Loaded or shortened antennas (coils, capacitance hats), Yagis and loops: each would be its own tool.
  • Coax stubs and velocity factor: a cable's length per wavelength is a different correction, for a future Velocity factor tool.

How it was checked

8 cases:

  • 7.1 MHz half wave: 20.06 m, 65 ft 9.75 in, legs of 10.03 m, λ 42.22 m.
  • 27 MHz quarter wave: 2.637 m, 8 ft 7.75 in; λ/4 2.776 m.
  • FM 24-18's long wire, 3 half waves at 7 MHz: 63.17 m (the manual's rounded 150 gives 63.2 m).
  • 20 m typed in the length box: 7.1201 MHz.
  • 144 MHz flags the 0.95.
  • A correction of 0 and 2.5 half waves are refused.
  • 468 / f at 10 MHz: 46.72 ft, 14.24 m, legs of 23.36 ft.

RF & microwave › Transmission lines

VSWR / Return loss

What it computes

How much of a wave a load sends back, and what that costs:

  • Two pills: Convert (the six usual measures of a mismatch, linked) and From a load (a line's Z0 and a load R + jX).
  • Convert: six boxes, VSWR, return loss, |Γ|, mismatch loss, the reflected and the delivered share: type in any one, the five others follow; the box typed in keeps its text until you leave it. With the forward power, the big result is the reflected power in watts; below it the voltage range along the line, and the two resistive loads that give this VSWR on 50 Ω (50 × VSWR and 50 / VSWR).
  • From a load: Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0) for Z = R + jX; the big result is the VSWR, then |Γ| and its angle, return loss, Γ as re + j im, mismatch loss, reflected and delivered power.
  • Units: mW, W or kW for the forward power; the rest fixed (dB, %, Ω, : 1).
  • Drawing: the standing wave along the line, |1 + Γ e^(−j2βd)| over a wavelength and a half back from the load (a zigzag, US style), Vmax and Vmin dashed: their ratio is the VSWR. From a load, Γ's angle sets where the peaks fall (a short puts a null at the load, an open a peak).
  • Remembered: the pill and the power unit.

Examples: a 2:1 VSWR, 20 dB return loss, a 75 Ω load on 50 Ω coax, a short antenna of 25 − j50 Ω.

Terms

  • Reflection coefficient Γ: the reflected wave over the incident one at the load, complex: 0 matched, magnitude 1 for an open, a short or a pure reactance.
  • VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio, SWR): the incident and reflected waves add into a standing wave; VSWR is its maximum over its minimum, (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|): 1 matched, infinite for total reflection.
  • Return loss: how many dB the reflected wave lies below the incident one, −20 log |Γ|; positive, larger is better.
  • Mismatch loss: the power that does not reach the load because of the reflection, in dB, −10 log (1 − |Γ|²), for a source matched to the line.
  • Forward power: the power travelling toward the load, as a directional wattmeter reads it.

Sources

  • Keysight AN 1449-3, "Fundamentals of RF and Microwave Power Measurements (Part 3)", literature number 5988-9215EN (read): Γ = b/a (eq. 2-1), Γ = (Z − Zo)/(Z + Zo) (2-5), |a|² the incident power, |b|² the reflected (2-2, 2-3); SWR = (|a| + |b|)/(|a| − |b|) = (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ), "VSWR is shortened to SWR"; the "Zo mismatch loss", the ratio of its equations 2-22 to 2-21 in dB: with a Zo generator (Γg = 0), 10 log(1/(1 − |Γ|²)) (its printed equations 2-25 and 2-26 did not survive the text extraction; the tool derives them from 2-21 and 2-22).
  • Keysight 5965-7707EN, "Understanding the Fundamental Principles of Vector Network Analysis", 10 August 2022 (read): "Return loss = −20 log(ρ)", "the number of decibels that the reflected signal is below the incident signal", "always expressed as a positive number", infinite at the characteristic impedance, 0 dB for an open or short; VSWR = Emax / Emin = (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ).

Assumptions and limits

  • One frequency, lossless line: a lossy line attenuates the reflected wave on its way back, so the VSWR read at the transmitter is better than at the load.
  • Mismatch loss with a matched source: with a mismatched source the power transferred depends on both reflections (AN 1449-3's mismatch uncertainty).
  • Resistive loads on 50 Ω: the two pure resistances with this VSWR; a complex load has the same VSWR on a circle of impedances.

How it was checked

7 cases, the expected values from the formulas above: - VSWR 2: |Γ| 0.3333, return loss 9.542 dB, mismatch loss 0.5115 dB, 11.11 % reflected, 11.1 W of 100 W, loads 100 Ω or 25 Ω; - return loss 20 dB: VSWR 1.222, mismatch loss 0.04365 dB, 1 W; - a VSWR under 1 is refused; - 75 Ω on 50 Ω: Γ 0.2, VSWR 1.5, return loss 14 dB, 0.177 dB, 4 W; - 25 − j50 Ω on 50 Ω: Γ = (625 − j5000)/8125 = 0.0769 − j0.615, VSWR 4.27, return loss 4.15 dB, 38.5 W; - a short: |Γ| 1 at 180°, VSWR ∞, return loss 0 dB, 100 W back; - kW re-expresses the forward power.

RF & microwave › Transmission lines

Velocity factor

What it computes

How much slower than light a wave travels on a cable or trace, and the lengths that follow:

  • Three pills:
  • From εr: the Material picker (air, PTFE, solid and foam PE at Belden's 66 % and 82 %), εr and the velocity factor as linked boxes (typing one sets the other), a Cable picker (Coax impedance's seven Belden cables, which set εr; typing a value returns it to Custom);
  • Cut a length: the same line plus a frequency: the quarter-wave length λg/4 as the big result, then the half and whole guided wavelength, the free-space wavelength and the quarter wave's delay;
  • Measure: a cable's length, its one-way delay and the frequency of its first resonance, linked (resonance = 1/(4 × delay)); type the delay or the resonance and the velocity factor of the cable follows.
  • The big result: VF in % (or the quarter-wave length); below it the delay per length (ns/m and ps/in), the speed, and the dielectric it looks most like (solid PE, foam PE, PTFE).
  • Units: mm, cm, m, in or ft for lengths (the order of metric and imperial in the results follows the one picked); kHz, MHz or GHz.
  • Drawing: a wave in free space (grey) over the same wave in the line (green), λg = VF × λ, with λg/4 marked in Cut a length.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: RG-58 at 66 %, a quarter wave of it at 100 MHz, Wadell's PTFE resonator, a 10 m cable measured by its resonance.

Terms

  • Velocity factor (velocity of propagation): the wave's speed on the line as a share of the speed of light: 1/√εr, εr the dielectric's (εeff for a microstrip).
  • Guided wavelength λg: the wavelength in the line, λ × VF.
  • Quarter-wave section or stub: a line λg/4 long; it turns a short into an open and the reverse, and is the usual length of a balun or a matching section.
  • Resonance: with the far end shorted, the input impedance of a lossless line is j Z0 tan(2π l/λg), which is infinite where l = λg/4: the first peak, which a network analyser or a grid-dip meter finds.
  • TDR (time-domain reflectometer): an instrument that sends a pulse down a cable and times its echo; half the round trip is the delay.

Sources

  • Brian C. Wadell, Transmission Line Design Handbook, 1991 (Pierre's scan, read): §2.8.3 (p32–35): Zsc = j Z0 tan(2πl/λ) (2.8.3.2), infinite at l = λ/4 (2.8.3.7), λg = c/(f √εr) (its example); the example 2.8.3.1: PTFE (εr 2.10) at 402 MHz, λg/4 = 0.1287 m = 5.07 in with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • Belden technical data sheets (see Coax impedance): "velocity of propagation" 66 % (PE), 70 % (PTFE), 82 % (foam PE).
  • c = 299 792 458 m/s (SI), so the tool's 402 MHz example reads 0.12865 m = 5.065 in, rounding to Wadell's 5.07 in.

Assumptions and limits

  • Lossless, no dispersion: one εr; a cable's VF varies a little with frequency and with its braid and jacket.
  • Open ends and connectors add a little capacitance and length, so a measured quarter-wave resonance reads slightly low; trim on the air.
  • Shortening of antennas (the 0.95 end-effect factor of Antenna length) is a different effect, for a wire in air.

How it was checked

8 cases, the expected values from the formulas above and a Python check: - RG-58: 66 %, 5.05 ns/m, 128 ps/in (128.37), 198 × 10⁶ m/s, solid PE; - typing VF 0.82: εr 1.487, foam PE, 4.07 ns/m, 103 ps/in, cable picker Custom; - a quarter wave of RG-58 at 100 MHz: 49.5 cm, half 98.9 cm, whole 1.98 m, free space 3 m; - Wadell's PTFE resonator: 5.07 in (12.9 cm), VF 69 %; - a 10 m cable resonating at 4.95 MHz: 66 %; a 50 ns delay: 66.7 % and 5 MHz; a delay faster than light is refused; - inches put the imperial figure first.

RF & microwave › Transmission lines

Coax impedance

What it computes

The impedance and the other line constants of a round coaxial cable, from its dimensions, or the dimensions for an impedance:

  • Inputs: the inner conductor's diameter d, the dielectric's diameter D (the inside of the shield), the dielectric (Material picker, εr or the velocity factor, linked: typing either sets the other), a listed cable, and a frequency for the loss.
  • Impedance is a live box: type an impedance and D is set to give it (d and εr kept), D drawn green; leave the box and it shows Z0 again.
  • Cable picker: seven Belden cables; picking one sets d, D and εr (1/VF², the maker's velocity of propagation), and the results add its construction and Belden's own impedance, velocity and capacitance, and at 100 MHz or 1 GHz its attenuation. Typing a dimension or εr returns the picker to Custom.
  • The big result: Z0 (or D for the impedance typed); below it D/d and εr.
  • Below it: C and L per metre, the velocity factor and the delay per metre, the frequency where TE11 starts, the loss of smooth copper (per 100 m, or per 100 ft in inches or beside Belden's figure).
  • Units: mm or in for the diameters, linked; MHz or GHz.
  • Drawing: the cable cut across: shield, dielectric, inner conductor, drawn to the D/d entered (kept between 1.5 and 8), with D and d in mm and in.
  • Remembered: the units.
Cable (Belden) d, D (in) Belden Z0, VF, pF/m from the sizes dB/100 ft at 100 MHz, 1 GHz
RG-58, 8259 0.035 (19×33), 0.117 PE 50, 66 %, 101 47.8 Ω, 106 pF/m 5.4, 22.8
RG-58, 9201 0.033 solid, 0.116 PE 52, 66 %, 93.5 49.7 Ω, 102 pF/m 3.8, 14.5
RG-174, 8216 0.019 (7×34), 0.060 PE 50, 66 %, 101 45.5 Ω, 111 pF/m 8.4, 34.0
RG-316, 83284 0.020 (7×34), 0.060 PTFE 50, 70 %, 95 46.1 Ω, 103 pF/m 8.3, 29.0
RG-213, 8267 0.089 (7×21), 0.285 PE 50, 66 %, 101 46.1 Ω, 110 pF/m 1.9, 8.0
RG-59, 8241 0.023 solid, 0.146 PE 75, 66 %, 66.9 73.1 Ω, 69.1 pF/m (sheet's table empty)
RG-6, 1694A 0.040 solid, 0.180 foam PE 75, 82 %, 53.1 73.9 Ω, 55.0 pF/m 1.95, 6.3

The formula, exact for a smooth line, reads 1 to 9 % low from the nominal sizes, most with stranded conductors: a stranded conductor's outline is larger than its effective diameter, and a braid's inside diameter is not the insulation's nominal one. Belden's figures are the measured truth for its cables; the formula is the one to design with.

Terms

  • d, D: the inner conductor's outside diameter, and the dielectric's diameter, which is the inside diameter of the shield.
  • Characteristic impedance Z0: the ratio of voltage to current of a wave on the line; set by D/d and εr only.
  • Velocity factor VF: the wave's speed as a share of light's, 1/√εr; makers give it as "velocity of propagation", 66 % for solid PE.
  • TE11: the first wave pattern other than the normal (TEM) one; above its cutoff a cable can carry two kinds of wave at different speeds, which spoils it.
  • Skin effect: at high frequency current flows in a thin skin at the conductors' surface, so their resistance, and the loss, rise with √f.
  • Solid, foam PE, PTFE: the usual dielectrics: polyethylene solid or foamed with gas (lower εr, faster), and PTFE for heat and high frequency.

Sources

  • Brian C. Wadell, Transmission Line Design Handbook, Artech House, 1991 (Pierre's scanned copy, read):
  • §3.2.1 (p47–49): Z0 = η0/(2.0 π √εr) ln(D/d) (3.2.1.1), "exact for the case of an infinitely long line"; the TE11 cutoff λc ≈ π (D + d)/2.0 (3.2.1.12), "generally accurate to 3% for 50 Ω lines"; the example (§3.2.1.1): 50 Ω around a 0.040 in pogo pin needs D = 0.092 in in air and 0.134 in in PTFE (εr 2.1);
  • §2.7.1 (p25): Rs = 1/(σδ) = √(π f μ/σ) (2.7.1.3) and α ≈ R/(2.0 Z0) (2.7.6); its printed δ = 1/√(ωμσ) (2.7.1.5) is √2 short of the δ its own Rs implies, 1/√(π f μ σ); the tool works from Rs. Its coax loss shortcuts (3.2.1.2 and 3.2.1.3) do not state their units, so the tool does not use them.
  • Copper: IACS, 1/58 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C, as in Wire sizing (NBS Handbook 100).
  • The cables: Belden technical data sheets 8259, 9201, 8216, 83284, 8267, 8241 and 1694A (catalog.belden.com, read, revisions dated February to May 2026): nominal conductor and insulation diameters, materials, impedance, velocity of propagation, capacitance, attenuation in dB/100 ft. 8241's attenuation table is printed empty. Times Microwave's LMR-400 sheet could not be downloaded, so LMR cables are not listed.
  • Solid and foam PE's εr: 1/VF² from Belden's 66 % and 82 %: 2.30 and 1.49; PTFE 2.1 as Wadell's example.

Assumptions and limits

  • Smooth, round, concentric, uniform: the formula; eccentric or partly filled lines (Wadell 3.2.2, 3.2.3) differ.
  • Loss: solid smooth copper only, no dielectric loss, no braid, plating or stranding: a lower bound, often half a real cable's.
  • TE11: the simple estimate, within about 3 % (Wadell).

How it was checked

9 cases, the expected values from the formulas above (a Python check of the same formulas): - RG-58, Belden 8259: 47.8 Ω, 106 pF/m, 241 nH/m, VF 0.66, 5.05 ns/m, TE11 from 32.6 GHz, smooth copper 3.36 dB/100 ft at 100 MHz against Belden's 5.4; - Wadell's pin: 49.9 Ω in air, 50.0 Ω in PTFE; 50 Ω typed gives D = 0.0921 in (his 0.092); - RG-213 at 1 GHz: 46.1 Ω, TE11 from 13.3 GHz, 4.38 against 8.0 dB/100 ft; - RG-6: foam PE, 73.9 Ω, 4.07 ns/m; - inches re-express both diameters; - at 50 MHz the maker's loss row goes and the copper loss reads 7.8 dB/100 m; - D smaller than d is refused.
