RF & microwave › Transmission lines

Smith chart matching

What it computes

A load sits at the end of a transmission line. When its impedance is not the line's, part of the wave is sent back. The tool shows how bad that is and gives three ways of curing it (pills). You give the load as a resistance R above zero and a reactance X (negative for a capacitor), both in ohms, and the line's impedance Z0.

The drawing is the same for the four pills: the Smith chart with the load on it and whatever the tool found, and under it the circuit that was calculated, the line coming in on the left and the load, ZL, on the right. The parts you gave are blue, the ones the tool calculated green, the wires grey. Tap the drawing and the chart fills the box while the circuit goes; tap again and it comes back.

  • Load: how well the load matches the line. The big result is the VSWR (3.91 : 1) with |Γ| and its angle under it. In three cells: the return loss, the mismatch loss and the share of the power reflected. Under them: the normalized impedance z and admittance y; "Same as", the load as its resistance in series with an inductor or a capacitor at the frequency (the frequency is optional here, and only this row waits for it); the distance from the load to the first voltage maximum, in wavelengths, and to the first minimum. The chart has the load, L, and the dashed circle of constant |Γ| through it; the circuit is the line ending in that resistance and reactance.
  • L-match: a series part and a shunt part, ordinary inductors or capacitors at the frequency, that match the load. The big result is the two values ("92.7 fF · 6.08 nH"); under it which part is which ("shunt C at the load, then series L") and which solution of how many. In three cells: the loaded Q, the band where the return loss stays at 15 dB or better, and the load as its resistance with an inductor or capacitor. Under them, every solution on a row, sorted by loaded Q (up to four); tap a row to pick it: the chart draws its path, from the load through "1", the point after the first part, to the centre, and the circuit shows its parts numbered from the line (L1, C1; C1 and C2 when both are capacitors). A load whose resistance equals Z0 needs only a series part, and that one is listed once.
  • Stub: a length of line from the load, then a stub, a short length of line with its far end shorted or open, across the line (shunt) or in series with it. The Output heading holds the choices: shunt or series, short or open, and the unit for lengths. The big result is the distance from the load to the stub in wavelengths, with the same in length units and "solution 1 of 2" under it. In three cells: the length of a short stub, of an open stub, and the lumped part that does the same job ("shunt L 2.7 nH"). Under them: the two solutions on rows to tap, the stub lengths in the length unit, and the 15 dB band for the short stub and for the open one. The chart draws both solutions, the one you picked bright. The circuit shows the line, the stub you chose and the load: a shunt stub hangs from the line and ends in ground (short) or in the air (open); a series stub breaks the line and runs out and back, closed at its end (short) or not (open). Its label carries the stub's length and, with a frequency, the same in the length unit.
  • λ/4: a quarter-wave section of another impedance, placed where the line shows a real impedance. The big result is the section's impedance; under it its length, where it goes (at the voltage minimum or maximum) and the impedance the line shows there. In three cells: the section's impedance, the length of line before it in wavelengths and the 15 dB band. Under them: the two places (sorted by distance from the load) on rows to tap, and the line's length before the section in the length unit. The circuit is line, section, the line of that length, the load; with the load already at the voltage maximum (a real load above Z0) there is no line before the section and the drawing leaves it out.
  • Units: frequency kHz, MHz or GHz; lengths mm, cm, m, in or ft, set in the Output heading. The velocity factor (Stub and λ/4) turns wavelengths into lengths: λ in the line is c × VF / f.
  • Remembered: the pill, the frequency unit, the length unit, shunt or series and short or open. The enlarged chart is not.

Examples: a 60 − j80 Ω load on 50 Ω, an L-match from 200 − j100 Ω to 100 Ω, a shunt stub and a series stub, and a quarter-wave match for 100 Ω.

Terms

  • Impedance Z = R + jX: what a load presents to a signal at one frequency, in ohms. R, the resistance, dissipates power; X, the reactance, stores and returns it, positive for an inductor and negative for a capacitor. The j marks a quantity a quarter of a cycle out of step with the other.
  • Z0, the line's impedance: the impedance a wave meets travelling along the line, set by its construction (50 Ω and 75 Ω are the usual ones). A load of exactly Z0 sends nothing back.
  • Normalized z = Z / Z0 = r + jx: the load in units of the line's impedance. The chart is drawn for it, so one chart serves every Z0.
  • Admittance Y = 1 / Z = G + jB, y = Y / Y0 = g + jb: the same load seen as how easily current flows, in siemens: G the conductance, B the susceptance, positive for a capacitor and negative for an inductor. Parts in parallel add their admittances, parts in series add their impedances, which is why a matching job switches between the two.
  • Reflection coefficient Γ: the share of the voltage wave sent back by the load, with its phase: Γ = (Z − Z0) / (Z + Z0). |Γ| runs from 0 (a match) to 1 (everything reflected, as from a short, an open or a pure reactance).
  • VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio): incoming and reflected waves add up to a standing wave on the line; the VSWR is its highest voltage over its lowest, (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|), and 1 when matched.
  • Return loss, mismatch loss, power reflected: the same |Γ| in other words. Return loss, −20 log |Γ| dB, says how far down the reflected wave is; mismatch loss, −10 log (1 − |Γ|²) dB, the power the mismatch costs the load; power reflected is |Γ|².
  • Smith chart: the disk of every Γ with |Γ| ≤ 1, which holds every load with R ≥ 0. Its grid shows, at each Γ, the load's r and x: circles of constant resistance all touching at the right-hand edge, and arcs of constant reactance (the top half inductive, the bottom half capacitive). The centre is the match, Γ = 0.
  • Moving along the line: towards the generator, Γ keeps its size and turns clockwise round the centre, a full turn for every half wavelength. A point therefore stays on its dashed circle of constant |Γ|.
  • Voltage maximum, minimum: places on the line where the standing wave peaks or dips. There the impedance is real, Z0 × VSWR at a maximum and Z0 / VSWR at a minimum, a quarter wavelength apart.
  • Series part, shunt part: a series part sits in the line, a shunt part joins the line to ground. Adding series reactance moves the load's point along its circle of constant resistance; adding shunt susceptance moves it along its circle of constant conductance.
  • L-match: two lumped parts, one series and one shunt, drawn like an L or a turned L. Loaded Q: how sharply it is tuned, the reactance over the resistance at its middle point; the lower, the wider the band.
  • Stub: a length l of line, shorted or open at the far end, used as a reactance. Across the line it adds susceptance −cot βl (short) or tan βl (open); in series, reactance tan βl (short) or −cot βl (open), in units of 1 / Z0 and Z0, with βl = 2π l / λ. A shorted stub a quarter wave long is an open circuit; an open one is a short.
  • Quarter-wave section, λ/4: a line a quarter wavelength long, of impedance ZT, turns a real impedance R into ZT² / R. With ZT = √(Z0 R) it makes R look like Z0.
  • Velocity factor (VF): how fast the wave travels in the line, as a fraction of the speed of light; a wavelength in the line is c × VF / f.
  • 15 dB band: the frequencies around the design frequency over which the return loss stays at 15 dB or better, |Γ| ≤ 0.178, about 3 % of the power reflected. 15 dB is this tool's own yardstick, not a standard.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, "Smith chart" (read through a fetch tool): the chart as a plot of Γ with z = (1 + Γ)/(1 − Γ) and the circles of constant resistance and reactance; the admittance chart as the same chart turned half a turn; movement along the line as rotation on the outer wavelength scale, the angle changing by 2π over λ/2; and a worked example the tool reproduces: a 50 Ω line at 800 MHz and a load of 17.5 Ω in series with 6.5 nH, z = 0.35 + j0.65, matched either by 0.079 λ (29.6 mm) of line and a 2.6 pF series capacitor, or by 0.329 λ (123 mm) of line and a 6.5 nH shunt inductor. The article does not say in which direction the rotation goes; that comes from the line equations below.
  • Michael Steer, Fundamentals of Microwave and RF Design, § 10.4 "The L matching network" (LibreTexts page, read through the fetch tool): the L-match between two real resistances, with Q = √(R_high / R_low − 1), and two examples: 100 Ω to 1700 Ω at 900 MHz (Q 4, 70.7 nH, 0.416 pF) and 50 Ω to 75 Ω (Q 0.7071, a series reactance of 35.35 Ω and a shunt one of 106.1 Ω). That page has no method for a complex load.
  • Lecture slides "Impedance Matching and Tuning", Çankaya University (ece358.cankaya.edu.tr; PDF text extracted and read): L-sections: the load 200 − j100 Ω to 100 Ω at 500 MHz, read off the chart as 0.92 pF with 38.8 nH or 46.1 nH with 2.61 pF, and z = 0.5 + j0.3, with a series x = 0.2 and a shunt b = 1.0, or x = −0.8 and b = −1.0; single-stub tuning: a short shunt stub for 60 − j80 Ω on 50 Ω at 2 GHz (0.110 λ and 0.095 λ, or 0.260 λ and 0.405 λ) and an open series stub for 100 + j80 Ω (0.120 λ and 0.397 λ, or 0.463 λ and 0.103 λ); the loads modelled as 200 Ω + 3.18 pF, 60 Ω + 0.995 pF and 100 Ω + 6.37 nH to plot |Γ| against frequency; short stubs preferred on coaxial cable (a short radiates less) and open stubs on a printed board (no via to ground). Their title is also that of the matching chapter of Pozar's Microwave Engineering (from memory; the book was not read) and they do not cite it. Their quarter-wave formula is an image the extraction lost; it is derived below.
  • University of Tennessee, ECE341 lecture notes 9, "Impedance matching: lumped elements and single stub" (Fall 2021; PDF text extracted and read): y_L = 0.4 + j0.8: a line of 0.178 − 0.115 = 0.063 λ where y = 1 + j1.58, a short stub of 0.09 λ, and a second place, the mirror image, at 0.322 − 0.115 = 0.207 λ where y = 1 − j1.58 (the extracted text lost that minus sign).
  • Not read: Pozar's book itself, Smith's papers, and anything on double-stub tuning (the tool does not do it) or on stubs in microstrip, where junction and open-end effects are modelled.

Why the formulas are these

The chart. With Γ = u + jv, z = (1 + Γ)/(1 − Γ) gives r = (1 − u² − v²) / ((1 − u)² + v²) and x = 2v / ((1 − u)² + v²). Setting r constant and completing the square gives (u − r/(1 + r))² + v² = 1/(1 + r)², a circle of centre (r/(1 + r), 0) and radius 1/(1 + r); setting x constant gives (u − 1)² + (v − 1/x)² = 1/x², a circle of centre (1, 1/x) and radius 1/|x|, of which only the part inside the unit circle is drawn. The chart shows r and x at 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2 and 5. Seen as y = 1/z the same chart has its points turned half a turn: Γ(y) = −Γ(z).

Along the line. A wave on a lossless line has Γ(d) = Γ_L e^(−j2βd) at a distance d from the load toward the generator, β = 2π/λ. The size stays, the angle falls by 4π d/λ: clockwise, a full turn at d = λ/2. At a voltage maximum Γ(d) is real and positive, so the first one is where the angle has fallen to 0, d = (arg Γ_L mod 360°) / 720° wavelengths, and a minimum is a quarter wavelength from it. There z = S at a maximum and 1/S at a minimum, S the VSWR.

The L-match. Series first (at the load): adding jx to z = R + jX gives R + j(X + x). Its admittance must have conductance 1/Z0: R / (R² + (X + x)²) = 1/Z0, so (X + x)² = R (Z0 − R), which has solutions only for R ≤ Z0:

x = −X ± √(R (Z0 − R))

What is left is the susceptance −(X + x) / (R Z0), which a shunt part cancels:

b = (X + x) / (R Z0)        Q = |X + x| / R

Shunt first: the load's admittance is G + jB_L with G = R / (R² + X²) and B_L = −X / (R² + X²); adding jb gives G + j(B_L + b), whose impedance must have resistance Z0: G / (G² + (B_L + b)²) = Z0, so (B_L + b)² = G (Y0 − G), possible for G ≤ Y0 = 1/Z0:

b = −B_L ± √(G (Y0 − G))    x = Z0 (B_L + b) / G    Q = |B_L + b| / G

Up to four solutions, two per order. A series x is an inductor L = x/ω if positive, a capacitor C = −1/(ωx) if negative; a shunt b is a capacitor C = b/ω if positive, an inductor L = −1/(ωb) if negative, ω = 2π f. For a real load the shunt-first Q is √(Y0/G − 1) = √(R/Z0 − 1), Steer's formula. When R = Z0 exactly, the series-first root is single (x = −X, b = 0) and the shunt-first one ends in the same lone series part, which is listed once.

The stub. With a = y_L (shunt stub) or z_L (series stub) = g + jb, a line of electrical length βd changes it to a(d) = (a + jt) / (1 + j a t), t = tan βd: the same law for an admittance as for an impedance. Its real part is g (1 + t²) / ((1 − bt)² + g² t²); setting it to 1 gives

(b² + g² − g) t² − 2 b t + (1 − g) = 0
t = (b ± √(g ((1 − g)² + b²))) / (b² + g² − g)

and d/λ = atan(t) / 2π, taken in [0, ½). When b² + g² − g is 0 (a on the circle through 0 and 1) one root is t = ∞, d = λ/4, and the other is t = (1 − g) / (2b). Moving along the line from a gives a(d) = 1 + j b_d; the stub must add s = −b_d. A shunt stub, shorted, has −cot βl = s, so l/λ = atan2(1, −s) / 2π; open, tan βl = s, so l/λ = (atan s mod π) / 2π. A series stub has the two swapped. The lumped part with the same s: shunt, C = s / (ω Z0) if s > 0 and L = −Z0 / (ω s) if s < 0; series, L = s Z0 / ω if s > 0 and C = −1 / (ω s Z0) if s < 0. The distance d is of the line's wavelength, so d × c × VF / f is its length.

The quarter-wave section. A line of impedance Zt and electrical length θ turns Z_L into Zt (Z_L + j Zt tan θ) / (Zt + j Z_L tan θ), which at θ = 90° is Zt² / Z_L. For the line to see Z0 the section needs Zt² = Z0 R, with R the real impedance at that point: Z0 × S at a voltage maximum, Z0 / S at a minimum, so Zt = Z0 √S or Z0 / √S. With Zt² = Z0 Z_L the reflection coefficient at any θ is

Γ = (Z_L − Z0) / (Z_L + Z0 + j 2 Zt tan θ)

so its size, (Z_L − Z0)² / ((Z_L + Z0)² + 4 Z0 Z_L tan² θ) under a root, is smallest at θ = 90°.

The band. For the design frequency f0 the lines and stubs keep their length in wavelengths at f0, so their electrical length is proportional to f/f0; a lumped part keeps ωL or −1/(ωC); the load is its resistance in series with X f/f0 (an inductor, X > 0) or X f0/f (a capacitor), as the slides model theirs. |Γ| is computed at steps of 0.2 % of f0 from f0 downward and upward until it passes 10^(−15/20) = 0.178, and each crossing is refined by halving 50 times. A band that has not closed within ±80 % is given as "wider than ±80 %".

The drawing. A series part x moves z to z + jx along the circle of constant resistance; a shunt part b moves y to y + jb along the circle of constant conductance; a length of line d moves Γ clockwise round the dashed circle by 720° per wavelength. The tool samples those paths and draws them. A dotted green circle that appears is the circle of conductance 1, g = 1 (the mirror image of the r = 1 circle): a shunt stub's line, and an L-match that starts with its series part, must bring the load onto it, from where one shunt move reaches the centre.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal parts. Lines lose nothing; inductors and capacitors have no resistance, no stray capacitance and no self-resonance. At gigahertz that is often untrue: the default L-match at 2 GHz asks for a 92.7 fF capacitor, less than the stray capacitance of a solder pad or a via. The tool solves the circuit; it does not know what can be built.
  • Stubs and junctions. The stub and the line have the same Z0 and velocity factor. A T-junction adds a little discontinuity and an open end behaves as if the line went a little further (its fringing field), so a real open stub is cut slightly shorter; neither is modelled.
  • One frequency. Every design is exact at the design frequency and narrow-band. The 15 dB band shows how narrow, for the load model above; a real antenna or device has an impedance that varies in its own way.
  • A match to the line. The tool brings the load to Γ = 0 on a line of Z0, the usual aim. It does not conjugate-match a source with a reactance of its own.
  • R above zero. A negative resistance (an active load) is outside the chart. A load of exactly Z0 is "already matched".
  • Numbers, not pictures. Everything is calculated, not read off the chart; chart readings in the sources differ from the exact values by up to about 2.5 % (2.6 against 2.55 pF, 6.5 against 6.38 nH, 38.8 against 39.0 nH).
  • L-match choices. Up to four networks match one load; the first listed has the lowest loaded Q and so the widest band. The tool does not say which is a low-pass or a high-pass, nor which of them can be built with parts that exist.
  • The λ/4 section matches only a real impedance, so for a load with reactance the tool first moves along the line to the voltage maximum or minimum, and the line before the section counts in the band.
  • The circuit is a diagram. Boxes and parts are not drawn to scale; the numbers beside them are the sizes.
  • The 15 dB and the ±80 % limit are this tool's choices; three digits are shown.

How it was checked

74 cases and the formula-search card. The expected values come from a Python implementation of the same formulas, written apart from the JavaScript, and cover every figure and every label of the circuit: - Load: 60 − j80 Ω on 50 Ω (3.91 : 1, |Γ| 0.593 ∠ −46.8°, 4.54 dB, 35.1 %, z 1.2 − j1.6, y 0.3 + j0.4, 60 Ω + 0.995 pF, voltage maximum at 0.435 λ), 100 Ω and 25 Ω (VSWR 2, the maximum at the load and at 0.250 λ), a match, a near short and a short, the load as 6.5 nH, 3.18 nH, 1.99 nF and 99.5 fF, with and without a frequency, a 75 Ω line; - L-match: the slides' two examples, Steer's two, a load with four solutions, a lone series part, 10 Ω to 50 Ω at 14 MHz, a 10 + j5 Ω load at 500 kHz, picking each row, and the numbering of the parts on the circuit; - Stub: shunt and series, short and open, both solutions, velocity factor 0.66, lengths in cm and in inches, no frequency, a stub right at the load, and a load on the circle through 0 and 1 (one stub exactly a quarter wave away); - λ/4: 60 − j80, 100 Ω at 1 GHz in a 0.66 line, 25 Ω, 300 Ω on 75 Ω, both rows, no frequency; - the refusals (Z0, R, X, frequency, velocity factor, a matched load), the units and the remembered choices, the five examples, and the tap that enlarges the chart.

About 1 200 more cases, on 240 random loads (R 0.5 Ω to 1.5 kΩ, X ±600 Ω, Z0 10 to 400 Ω, 100 kHz to 20 GHz) through all four pills, compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

RF & microwave › Transmission lines

Skin depth

What it computes

How deep a high-frequency current flows in a conductor, and what that does to a wire's or a foil's resistance:

  • Three pills:
  • Skin depth: δ at a frequency, with the surface resistance Rs (ohms per square) and the depth within which 99 % of the current flows (δ ln 100 = 4.6 δ);
  • Round wire: a wire's diameter gives the AC resistance as a multiple of its DC resistance, the two in mΩ/m, the frequency where δ equals the radius (where the skin effect begins) and the share of the wire's area that carries the current;
  • PCB copper: a foil's thickness (oz, µm or mil) gives the frequency where δ equals it; and at the frequency typed, δ, t/δ, Rs and the foil's DC resistance per square.
  • Inputs: the frequency (Hz to GHz), the material, its resistivity ρ in µΩ·cm and relative permeability μr (typing ρ sets the picker to Custom).
  • Materials (ρ at 20 °C): copper as wire is sold (IACS) 1.7241; pure copper 1.678; silver 1.587; gold 2.214; aluminum 2.650.
  • Units: the wire's diameter in mm or mil, the foil's thickness in oz, µm or mil, linked as in the impedance tools.
  • Drawing: the current density e^(−x/δ) against depth with 37 % at δ marked; the wire's section with its green ring δ thick; the foil seen on edge with δ from each face.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: copper at 1 MHz, silver at 1 GHz, a 1 mm wire at 1 MHz, 1 oz copper on a PCB.

Terms

  • Skin effect: at high frequency the changing magnetic field inside a conductor pushes the current toward its surface; the resistance rises.
  • Skin depth δ: the depth at which the current density has fallen to 1/e (37 %) of its surface value.
  • Surface resistance Rs: ρ/δ, in ohms per square: the resistance of a square of the skin, whatever its size.
  • Rac/Rdc: the wire's AC resistance over its DC resistance.
  • μr: the relative permeability; 1 for copper, silver, gold and aluminum, hundreds for iron, which has a much shallower skin.
  • Proximity effect: current crowding caused by a neighbouring conductor (turns of a coil); not included.

Sources

  • Brian C. Wadell, Transmission Line Design Handbook, 1991 (Pierre's scan, read): §2.7.1 (p25): Rs = 1/(σδ) = √(π f μ/σ), δ = "the depth at which the current density is reduced to 1/e"; its printed δ = 1/√(ωμσ) (2.7.1.5) is √2 short of the δ its own Rs implies, 1/√(π f μ σ); the tool uses the latter (copper 66.1 µm at 1 MHz).
  • David Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I, ch. 12, "Specific resistance at 20 °C" (ibiblio copy, read): copper 1.678, silver 1.587, gold 2.214, aluminum 2.650 µΩ·cm. Other sources list gold at 2.44; copper as wire is sold is the IACS value 1.7241 (1/58 Ω·mm²/m, NBS Handbook 100 / Copper Development Association), as in Wire sizing: 1.3 % deeper than pure copper.
  • The round wire: the textbook solution of Maxwell's equations for an isolated straight round wire, Z/Rdc = (z/2) J0(z)/J1(z), z = (1 − j) r/δ, real part Rac/Rdc. It is not from a page read; the tool computes it by power series up to r/δ = 12 and by r/(2δ) + 1/4 + 3δ/(32r) above, and both agree with scipy's Bessel functions to 6 figures (r/δ = 7.566: 4.04524; 23.93: 12.21687).

Assumptions and limits

  • A smooth, uniform, isolated conductor at 20 °C: resistivity rises 0.4 % per °C; surface roughness (PCB copper) adds loss.
  • Foils and planes: the foil's DC resistance and Rs are per square for current in the plane; a trace's current runs on one face as well as the edges, so its loss needs a field solver.
  • Magnetic metals: μr is taken as constant, and iron's falls with frequency.

How it was checked

12 cases, the expected values from the formula and a Python check (scipy for the Bessel ratios): - copper at 1 MHz: 66.1 µm (2.6 mil), 0.261 mΩ per square, 99 % within 304 µm; silver at 1 GHz 2.005 µm, 7.92 mΩ per square; gold 74.9 µm and aluminum 81.9 µm at 1 MHz; - μr 100 with ρ typed: the picker goes to Custom; - a 1 mm copper wire: at 1 MHz × 4.05, 22 and 88.8 mΩ/m, skin effect from 17.5 kHz, 24.7 % of the area; at 100 kHz × 1.45; at 10 MHz × 12.2 (the large-wire form), 268 mΩ/m; - 1 oz foil: 3.61 MHz; t/δ 0.527 at 1 MHz and 5.27 at 100 MHz; - a zero frequency and a μr under 1 are refused.

Coax cable standards

What it computes

The common RG coaxial cables and the Times Microwave LMR family: what each one is, and how much signal it loses. 23 cables, each from a maker's data sheet: 14 RG types that have a row in the M17 table (RG-174A, 316, 58C, 142B, 223, 400, 402, 213, 214, 393 on 50 Ω; RG-59B, 6A, 11A on 75 Ω; RG-62A on 93 Ω), RG-8A/U and RG-8X (no M17 row), and LMR-100A, 195, 200, 240, 400, 600 and the 75 Ω LMR-400. Three pills:

  • Specs: the cable cut across, to scale (jacket, shield, dielectric, inner conductor, with their diameters). The big result is the impedance, with the M17 standard's own line for that type under it (slash sheet, impedance and tolerance, velocity, capacitance). In three cells: the velocity, the capacitance and the diameter. Under them: the inner conductor, the dielectric, the shield, the jacket, what the sheet rates it for (voltage, temperature, top frequency) and its bend radius. A note says what the cable is for, where a source says (L-com's guide, Times' sheet for LMR-400), and where the sheet differs from the standard.
  • Loss: the cable, the frequency (MHz or GHz), the length (m, ft, cm or in) and the power in (mW or W). The drawing is the cable's loss against frequency on logarithmic axes, the sheet's figures as dots, the frequency of the run marked. The big result is the loss of the run in dB, with how it was read from the sheet. In three cells: dB per 100 ft, dB per 100 m and the power out. Under them: the sheet's two nearest figures, the output level in dBm, the largest CW power the sheet allows at that frequency, the delay of the run, and a warning when the frequency is over the sheet's top frequency.
  • Compare: every cable of one impedance (50, 75 or 93 Ω) for the frequency and length you give, best first, with a bar for each. A "~" marks a loss beyond the cable's sheet (an estimate); the cable you picked last is in white.
  • Remembered: the pill, the cable, the impedance and the three units.

Examples: 30 m of RG-58 at 100 MHz, LMR-400 against RG-213 at 144 MHz, a GPS antenna lead of RG-316, and what RG-6 is.

Terms

  • RG: the prefix of the old American military coax series. Today a loose name for a cable of that size and kind, not a specification (see Sources).
  • /U, A, B, C: "universal", for general use; the letters are revisions of the type (RG-58, RG-58A, RG-58B, RG-58C).
  • MIL-DTL-17 (formerly MIL-C-17), M17 slash sheet: the military specification for flexible and semi-rigid coax; each cable it defines has a slash sheet, M17/28-RG58 for RG-58, giving its construction and limits.
  • Impedance Z0: the ratio of voltage to current of a wave on the line; 50 Ω for radio and test gear, 75 Ω for video and cable TV, 93 Ω for some data links.
  • Velocity of propagation (VP, velocity factor): the share of light's speed at which a wave travels on the cable, 1/√εr; the dielectric sets it.
  • Capacitance: per metre; with Z0 it fixes the velocity, C = 1/(Z0 VP c).
  • Loss (attenuation): how much weaker the signal is at the far end of a matched cable, in dB, for 100 ft or 100 m, rising with frequency.
  • Typical, maximum: a sheet's typical loss is what a sample usually does; a maximum (Pasternack's RG-59B) is a limit it should stay under.
  • CW power: the largest continuous (not peak) power the cable can carry at that frequency without overheating; it falls as the loss rises.
  • Dielectric withstanding voltage: the voltage the insulation survives in a test (Times' sheets); not an operating voltage.
  • Bend radius: how tightly the cable may be bent, once when installing and repeatedly.

Sources

  • The standard: the M17 table (a distributor's reprint, "MIL-C-17", from Sycor; no date or author; read): each slash sheet's M17 number and QPL number, conductor, dielectric, shield, jacket, impedance with its tolerance, velocity, capacitance in pF/ft and pF/m, maximum operating voltage, temperature range and test frequency; 14 of its rows are used. It is a transcription, not the specification: it has misprints (RG-58's capacitance reads 38.8 pF/ft beside 101.1 pF/m, RG-11's 20.8 beside 67.6; only 30.8 and 20.6 fit), so the pF/m column is used, and every row's capacitance was checked against 1/(Z0 Vp c): all within 0.5 %. The abbreviations (BC, TC, SC, CCS, SCCS) are not defined in it; they are read in the usual sense (bare, tinned, silver-plated copper; copper-clad steel, silver-plated). The slash sheets themselves, and the DLA's qualified products list, were not read.
  • What "RG" is: Wikipedia, "Coaxial cable" (read through a text-extraction tool, the first 100 000 characters; no edit date seen): RG was "originally a U.S. military designation from World War II", the numbers listed in MIL-HDBK-216 (1962), "/U" for universal and A, B, C for revisions, superseded by the M17 designation, and no standard guarantees a cable sold as an "RG-# type". Military & Aerospace Electronics, "MIL-DTL-17 Requirements for Hi-Rel/MIL-SPEC Coaxial Cable Assemblies and a Note on RG Coax" (4 March 2019, no byline shown; read): MIL-DTL-17 was MIL-C-17; RG is "a generalized industry term, and not a standardized set of cable specifications"; a cable meets MIL-DTL-17 only if it meets every category, and a MIL-DTL-17 supplier should be on the qualified products list, which readily available RG coax is not.
  • What each is for: L-com, "RG Coax Cable Applications" (a one-page technical brief, no date; read): typical use, best feature and trade-off of RG174, 188A, 316, 58C, 142B, 59A/B, 6, 223, 213, 179B and 187; used, paraphrased, for the cables it covers (not RG-188A, 179B, 187, 59A, which are not listed here). For LMR-400, Times' own sheet ("Replacement for Air Dielectric type RG8 cable").
  • The cables, Pasternack: the data sheets of RG174A/U-BULK, RG316/U-BULK, RG58C/U-BULK, RG142B/U-BULK, RG223/U-BULK, RG400/U-BULK, RG402/U-BULK, RG393/U-BULK, RG213/U-BULK, RG214/U-BULK, RG59B/U-BULK, RG6A/U-BULK, RG11A/U-BULK, RG62A/U-BULK, RG8A/U-BULK and RG8X-BULK (PDFs, read as text; revision 1.0 and later as printed): impedance, velocity, capacitance, the typical loss at 3 to 10 frequencies (a maximum for RG-59B), the largest CW power where given, construction, ratings.
  • The cables, Times Microwave: the LMR-100A (as Fairview Microwave's LMR-100A-PVC, with its -FR and -FR-FT sheets), LMR-195, LMR-200, LMR-240, LMR-400 (REV 1.3, 2020), LMR-600 and LMR-400-75 sheets as Fairview Microwave prints them (read as PDF text): loss and largest CW power at ten frequencies from 50 MHz, and the construction. Times' own site refused automated downloads, so its sheets were not read.
  • Not read: the MIL-DTL-17 slash sheets; Belden's sheets again (the Coax impedance tool lists seven of them); the MIL-HDBK-216 table.

Slips found in the sheets, and what was done

  • Pasternack RG-142B: capacitance "96.45 [316.44] pF/ft [pF/m]"; the 96.45 is the pF/m figure (29.4 pF/ft). Used as pF/m.
  • RG-316 and RG-400: 32 pF/ft (105 pF/m), where their 50 Ω and 69 to 70 % imply 96.7 and 95.3 pF/m. RG-62A: 83 % with 47.57 pF/m, where 83 % implies 43.2 (the standard has 81 % and 44.3). Shown as the sheets print them, with the differences from the standard pointed out in the note.
  • RG-6A and RG-62A at 10 MHz: 0.08 and 2.7 dB per 100 ft. Both break the √f law and their own other figures (it gives about 0.86 and 0.82); the two lines are left out and the loss below the first remaining figure goes as √f.
  • LMR-100A-PVC's first line (50 MHz: 3.9 dB, 230 W) is LMR-400's 900 MHz line; the -FR and -FR-FT sheets say 5.1 dB and 180 W, which are used.
  • RG-8X: no velocity on the sheet; taken from 1/(Z0 C c) = 78.2 % and starred.
  • LMR sheets give no shield diameter (except LMR-400): the shield ring is drawn at a default thickness there.
  • Pasternack's RG-316 loss at 1 GHz (38 dB) sits about 10 % above the √f and f law through its other figures, and RG-8A/U's 400 MHz figure about 9 % under it: left as printed.

How the loss is read

Loss in a coax has two parts: the conductors, from the current crowded into their skin, which grows as √f, and the dielectric, which grows as f. Times prints it as K1 √f + K2 f dB per 100 ft, f in MHz (their 75 Ω LMR-400: 0.115570 √f + 0.000260 f). The tool does not fit that law: it reads the maker's own figures, exactly at each, and between two figures it follows a straight line on logarithmic axes (a power law):

a(f) = a1 × (a2/a1)^(ln(f/f1) / ln(f2/f1))

so the number at a sheet's frequency is the sheet's. Below the first figure the loss goes as √f from it (the conductor term dominates there); above the last it continues along the last segment's slope, held between 0.5 and 1 (the two terms' limits). Those two ranges are estimates and are flagged ("~", and a line saying so). The loss of the run is the loss per 100 ft times the length in feet over 100; the power out is Pin × 10^(−loss/10); the delay is the length over VP × c. The largest CW power is read the same way between the sheet's powers (a single figure is shown as one), and not outside them.

Between the figures the reading differs from the K1 √f + K2 f law through the same figures by 4.1 % or less for 18 of the 23 cables; the other five scatter more in their own figures (RG-316/U 10.2 %, RG-8A/U 8.7 %, LMR-600 6.7 %, LMR-100A 6.0 %, RG-8X 5.3 %). Against Times' own formula for the 75 Ω LMR-400 it stays within 3.6 % (the sheet rounds to 0.1 dB, and the formula and the sheet's lines differ by up to 3.8 % at their own points).

Assumptions and limits

  • Typical figures, not guarantees. A cable, even from the same maker, differs between samples and batches; the standard sets maxima.
  • The same name is not the same cable. RG-58's loss at 100 MHz is 4.9 dB per 100 ft on Pasternack's sheet, 5.4 on Belden's 8259 and 3.8 on its 9201 (the Coax impedance tool lists them): the plain name fixes no loss. The M17 row is the only thing that does.
  • A matched line, no connectors. A mismatch (VSWR) adds loss and connectors add some; the VSWR / Return loss tool counts the first.
  • Power ratings are the sheet's, for a matched load and ordinary conditions; they are not derated for heat, altitude or mismatch.
  • Frequency ranges are the sheets': beyond a sheet's top frequency the loss is an estimate and the cable may not be usable (higher modes).
  • 23 cables only; semi-rigid RG-402 is the one tube; no connectors, twin-ax, hard-line or fibre.

How it was checked

31 cases. The expected values come from a Python twin of the loss maths and the sheets' own figures: - Specs: RG-58C/U (50 Ω, 65.9 %, 101 pF/m, 4.95 mm; M17/28-RG58's line; construction, ratings, bend radius, use), LMR-400 (no M17 row, 85 %, 78.4 pF/m, a withstand voltage), RG-8X (velocity from the capacitance, starred), RG-316/U and RG-62A/U (the differences from the standard named), RG-6A/U (agrees), RG-402/U (a tube); - Loss: RG-58C/U, 10 m at 100 MHz: 4.9 dB/100 ft, 1.61 dB, 691 mW, 28.4 dBm, 50.6 ns; 100 ft: 4.9 dB; 100 mW in; zero length; 1 MHz (√f, 0.443 dB/100 ft, flagged) and 6 GHz (68 dB/100 ft, 22.3 dB, flagged); LMR-400 at a sheet frequency (2.7 dB, 830 W) and at 300 MHz between two (2.21 dB/100 ft, 2.18 dB over 30 m, 1.02 kW); RG-59B's maximum; RG-213/U at 2 GHz over its sheet; RG-6A/U at 10 MHz without the bad line; RG-316/U at 1.575 GHz over 3 m (45.3 dB/100 ft, 4.45 dB); LMR-100A at 50 MHz (5.1 dB, 180 W); RG-8X (3.66 dB, 252 W, 130 ns); no frequency refused; - Compare: 50 Ω at 100 MHz over 10 m (LMR-600 0.254 dB first, RG-316/U 3.61 dB last, three estimates marked), 75 Ω, 93 Ω, 144 MHz over 30 m (LMR-400 1.45 dB, RG-213/U 2.66 dB) and 1.575 GHz over 3 m; - the four examples.

Every cable's figures were also checked before use: its loss figures against the K1 √f + K2 f law (19 of the 23 within 4.5 %; LMR-100A 6.4 %, LMR-600 7.2 % because its 50 MHz line is a rounded 0.5 dB, RG-8A/U 9.0 %, RG-316/U 9.3 %; after the slips above), its capacitance against 1/(Z0 VP c), and, for the M17 rows, the impedance recomputed from the conductor and dielectric diameters and the velocity (1 to 9 % under the stated impedance, as stranding and air spaces make an effective diameter differ: no diameter is grossly misprinted).

RF & microwave › Power & gain

RF cascade

What it computes

The gain, noise figure and compression of a chain of amplifiers and losses, seen from its input (it takes the place of the planned "Cascade gain, noise figure, P1dB"):

  • Stages: up to five, each a row: Amp (gain in dB, noise figure in dB, OP1dB in dBm, left blank when unknown) or Loss (an attenuator, a filter or a cable: its loss in dB; its noise figure is its loss and it does not compress). "+ add stage" adds one, × removes one. A mixer is an Amp with a negative gain (its conversion loss) and its noise figure.
  • System: the input level (dBm) and the bandwidth (Hz to GHz).
  • The big result: the chain's noise figure, with its noise temperature and the stage that adds most of the noise and its share.
  • Three cells: the chain's gain, its OP1dB (output-referred 1 dB compression point) and its IP1dB (input-referred).
  • Below them: the noise floor at the input in that bandwidth, the dynamic range from the floor to the input P1dB, the output level for the input level, and the stage closest to compressing with its margin, or a warning when one is over its OP1dB.
  • Drawing: the chain as boxes, each stage's own gain inside (dashed for a loss), and under each, the cumulative gain (blue), noise figure (green) and OP1dB (grey) up to and including that stage.
  • Remembered: the bandwidth unit.

Examples: Rohde & Schwarz's two amplifiers, a 3 dB cable before and after a low-noise amplifier, and a receiver front end.

Terms

  • Noise factor F, noise figure NF: F is how much a stage worsens the signal-to-noise ratio, as a ratio; NF = 10 log F, in dB. A noiseless stage has NF 0 dB.
  • Gain G: output over input power; in a chain, gains multiply (their dB add). A loss L dB is a gain of −L dB.
  • Friis equation: how the stages' noise factors combine: each is divided by the gain ahead of it, so the first stage dominates.
  • Noise temperature Te: the same noise as a temperature, Te = 290 K × (F − 1); unlike F it adds across stages.
  • Noise floor: the thermal noise k T B in the bandwidth, raised by the noise figure, referred to the input (−174 dBm/Hz + 10 log B + NF).
  • P1dB: the power at which gain has dropped by 1 dB. OP1dB is measured at the output, IP1dB at the input: OP1dB = IP1dB + G − 1 dB.
  • Dynamic range: here, from the noise floor up to the input P1dB.

Sources

  • Rohde & Schwarz, application note 1SL378, "The Cold Source Technique for Noise Figure Measurements", Mike Leffel and Christopher Stumpf, version 0e, December 2021 (read): the Friis cascade equation (39), F = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + … + (FN − 1)/(G1 … GN−1), in linear noise factor and gain; the noise-temperature form Te = T1 + T2/G1 + … (40) and Te = T0 (F − 1) (9) with T0 = 290 K; NF = 10 log F (3); the noise density −174 dBm/Hz (21); "a 3 dB attenuator has −3 dB of gain, or +3 dB of loss" (8); and its example 3.7.2, 20 dB at 2 dB then 20 dB at 11 dB, 2.31 dB, which the tool reproduces. It also notes that equations (38) and (39) hold only when the input noise is the standard N0 = k T0 B.
  • A loss's noise figure: the note says a passive device's noise temperature is its physical temperature (so at 290 K, Te = T0 (L − 1), and F = L): the equality NF = loss is derived from it, not quoted.
  • The P1dB cascade: RF Essentials, "What is Cascaded P1dB?" (a web glossary page, no author or date shown; read): the reciprocal sum of the stages' output compression points, each divided by the gains after it, "≈", for "worst-case in-phase compression", the last stages dominating, and OP1dB = IP1dB + Gain − 1 dB; RF Cafe, "Cascaded P1dB" (undated; read, its formula is an image): apply the cascaded intercept-point equation to each device's P1dB as an estimate, the same conversion, and "a well-known rule-of-thumb is to subtract 10 to 15 dB to the IP3 value to estimate the P1dB value". These are website pages, not standards or application notes: the formula is the standard cascaded-intercept sum.
  • Not read: Friis's original paper (1944), and Analog Devices' "System Noise-Figure Analysis for Modern Radio Receivers" (gated; only its summary, which warns that the cascade equation changes with mixers).

Why the compression formula is this one

Taking the chain stage by stage from the input, with Gk the linear gain of stage k and OPk its OP1dB in mW:

1/OP(1) = 1/OP1
1/OP(k) = 1/OPk + 1/(OP(k−1) × Gk)

so an earlier stage's limit counts for less when the stages after it have gain (it is referred to the output, 1/(OP(k−1) × Gk)), and a stage with no limit (a loss, or a blank) adds nothing but still scales the earlier ones.

Assumptions and limits

  • Matched, linear in the small-signal sense: gains and noise figures are the available gains and noise figures into 50 Ω with the source at 290 K; mismatch between stages changes them.
  • A loss is at 290 K. A warmer pad adds more noise.
  • The noise figure of a mixer depends on whether the image is filtered (single-sideband) or not (double-sideband, 3 dB lower): enter the one that matches your receiver.
  • The P1dB cascade is an estimate, pessimistic by assuming every stage compresses in phase; it holds only when none of the stages operates far into compression. Check each stage's own margin (the last row).
  • Dynamic range here is to P1dB; spur-free dynamic range uses the third-order intercept (see Intercept point).

How it was checked

12 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation of the same formulas, and Rohde & Schwarz's example: - the default chain, an LNA (15 dB, 1.5 dB, +10 dBm), a 3 dB loss and an amplifier (20 dB, 6 dB, +20 dBm): NF 2.13 dB (2.1275), 183 K, 32 dB, OP1dB +19.21 dBm, IP1dB −11.79 dBm, floor −111.8 dBm in 1 MHz, 100 dB range, +2 dBm out for −30 in, stage 3 18 dB below its OP1dB; - Rohde & Schwarz's two amplifiers: 2.31 dB, 40 dB; - a 3 dB cable before a 1 dB LNA, 4.0 dB; after it, 1.03 dB (1.0342); - LNA, 3 dB pad, mixer (−6 dB, 6 dB, +5 dBm), IF amplifier (18 dB, 4 dB, +15 dBm): NF 3.04 dB, 24 dB, OP1dB +13.08 dBm and IP1dB −9.92 dBm. RF Essentials' table for the compression of the same chain reads +10.00, +7.00, −0.55 and +13.15 dBm per stage where the sum gives +10.00, +7.00, −0.455 and +13.08: a rounding difference of under 0.1 dB; - a first-stage noise figure of 3 dB: 3.45 dB; 0 dBm in flags stage 3, 12 dB over its OP1dB; adding then removing a stage; a blank gain, a noise figure under 0 dB and a zero bandwidth refused; kHz re-expresses the bandwidth.

Intercept point

What it computes

How linear an amplifier, or a whole chain of stages, is, summed up by its third-order intercept point (IP3), three ways (pills):

  • Measure (you have run a two-tone test): the level of each tone at the output and the level of one third-order product (IM3), both in dBm, and the gain in dB (optional). The big result is the output intercept point (OIP3), with how far the product sits below each tone. Under it: the input intercept point (IIP3, needs the gain), the estimated 1 dB compression points OP1dB and IP1dB, how far the tone is below that compression, and how far down the product would be for 10 dB less tone.
  • Predict (you know the IP3, say from a data sheet): IIP3, Gain and OIP3 are linked boxes (type any two and the third follows; the intercept you typed last is the one held when the gain changes), the level of each input tone and the IM3 rejection you want, in dB. The big result is the IM3 product at the output, with its rejection. Under it: the output tone, the product as it appears at the input, OP1dB; then the largest tone that still gives the rejection you asked for (at the output and at the input), and how far the tone is below its compression.
  • Chain (several stages): up to five rows, each Amp (gain in dB, OIP3 in dBm, left blank when unknown) or Loss (an attenuator, a filter or a cable: its loss in dB, with no distortion of its own); "+ add stage" adds a row, × removes one. Then the input tone level and the noise floor at the input, in dBm. The big result is the chain's OIP3, with the stage that adds most of the distortion and its share. Under it: the gain, the IIP3 and the spur-free dynamic range (SFDR); the IM3 product for that input level (at the output and in dBc) and the tone at the output. Each row shows the chain's OIP3 up to and including that stage.
  • Drawing: Measure and Predict: the tone line (blue, 1 dB per dB) and the IM3 line (green, 3 dB per dB) meeting at the intercept, with the tone and product levels marked and the gap between them, the rejection; not to scale. Chain: the stages as boxes (dashed for a loss), each stage's own gain inside, and under each the cumulative gain (blue) and OIP3 (green).
  • Remembered: the pill.

Examples: Keysight's amplifier (−10 dBm in, 20 dB gain, OIP3 +38 dBm), the same figures worked backwards from a two-tone test, a receiver's input IP3 with two −40 dBm interferers, and an LNA, a pad and an amplifier in a chain.

Terms

  • Two-tone test: two equal sine waves, close in frequency (f1 and f2), applied to the device. The output shows the two tones and, beside them, their intermodulation products.
  • IM3: the third-order products, at 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1. Their level rises 3 dB for every 1 dB the tones rise (the tones rise 1 dB).
  • dBc: dB relative to the carrier, here to each tone: an IM3 of −56 dBc is 56 dB below the tone.
  • Third-order intercept point (IP3, TOI): the level at which the tone line and the IM3 line, each extended along its small-signal slope, would meet. It is never reached, because the device compresses first: a figure of merit, the higher the more linear.
  • OIP3, IIP3: the intercept read on the output power axis or on the input one. They differ by the gain: IIP3 = OIP3 − G.
  • P1dB: the power at which the gain has fallen by 1 dB. OP1dB is read at the output, IP1dB at the input: OP1dB = IP1dB + G − 1 dB.
  • Spur-free dynamic range (SFDR): the range of input tone levels from the noise floor up to where the IM3 product reaches that floor.
  • Noise floor: the noise power in the bandwidth of interest, referred to the input (the RF cascade tool computes it).

Sources

  • Agilent (now Keysight) application note 1408-9, "Amplifier and CW Swept Intermodulation-Distortion Measurements" (publication 5988-9474EN; read): the products at n f1 + m f2; the third-order ones as the concern because they sit beside the tones and rise three times as fast; and, for two equal tones, IP3 (dBm) = the output power of a tone + ½ × (that power − the larger third-order product), in dB. It requires the measurement to be made in the amplifier's linear region. Its measured examples (a −1.258 dBm tone with a −42.03 dBm product: 19.13 dBm; −0.6 and −39.3: printed as 19, this gives 18.75) are reproduced. Its example amplifier has a 1 dB compression point of +3 dBm and an intercept of +14 dBm, 11 dB apart; the model here puts them 10.6 dB apart.
  • Keysight application note 1408-17, "Making Accurate Intermodulation Distortion Measurements with the PNA-X Network Analyzer" (5989-7265EN; read), appendix B: an amplifier with an OIP3 of +38 dBm and 20 dB of gain, driven at −10 dBm per tone: +10 dBm out, the product at −46 dBm, −56 dBc. The tool reproduces it (the first example).
  • The compression point: Wikipedia, "Third-order intercept point" (an encyclopedia page, not a standard; read): for a weakly nonlinear odd-order power-series model, the 1 dB compression point lies about 9.6 dB below the intercept (a factor 0.10875, −9.636 dB), and "approximately 10 dB" below it as a rule of thumb for many amplifiers; the page cites no source for either. The 9.636 dB is re-derived below and used as is. RF Cafe, "Cascaded P1dB" (read, see RF cascade) gives the rule of thumb as 10 to 15 dB below the IP3.
  • The cascade: RF Essentials, "What is Cascaded IP3?" (a web glossary page, no author or date shown; read): 1/OIP3 = 1/OIP3,n + 1/(OIP3,n−1 × Gn) + 1/(OIP3,n−2 × Gn × Gn−1) + …, in linear power; products adding in phase degrade the linearity fastest, and design tools assume that worst case. Its worked table for four stages (an LNA of 16 dB and +22 dBm, a filter of −1.5 dB, a mixer of −6 dB and +18 dBm, an IF amplifier of 12 dB and +25 dBm) lists the cumulative OIP3 as +22.00, +20.50, +12.65 and +10.90 dBm. The first two follow its formula; the third is 0.25 dB under the formula's +12.90 and the last 11 dB under its +21.94. The tool follows the formula and treats the table's last entry as an error. The page was read through a text-extraction tool, not as raw HTML, so a transcription slip cannot be ruled out.
  • Derived here, not quoted: the relations in the next section, the share of each stage, and the SFDR = ⅔ (IIP3 − noise floor), a form in common use for which no source was read.
  • Not read: Analog Devices' tutorial 749, "Use Selectivity to Improve Receiver Intercept Point" (the fetch failed), and any standard that defines the intercept point.

Why the formulas are these

For a weakly nonlinear stage, output = a1 x + a3 x³ with a3 < 0 (it compresses). Two equal tones of amplitude A give a fundamental a1 A and an IM3 product of amplitude ¾ |a3| A³, so product over tone = ¾ (|a3|/a1) A², which grows with the square of the tone: 2 dB per dB of amplitude, 3 dB per dB of power against the tone's 1. It reaches 1 at A² = 4 a1 / (3 |a3|), the intercept. In dB, with P the tone level and IP3 the intercept on the same axis, the product sits 2 (IP3 − P) below the tone:

IM3 = 3 P − 2 IP3
IP3 = P + (P − IM3) / 2        (Keysight's formula)

A single tone is compressed by the same term: its gain falls by the factor 1 − A²/A_IP². For 1 dB, 1 − A²/A_IP² = 10^(−1/20), so A²/A_IP² = 0.10875, which is −9.636 dB. Hence IP1dB = IIP3 − 9.636 dB and, with the 1 dB of gain lost, OP1dB = OIP3 − 10.636 dB.

For a chain, stage k with input intercept IIP3,k and the gain Gprev ahead of it puts a distortion voltage at the chain's output proportional to Gprev / IIP3,k, which is 1/(OIP3,k × the gain after k) once referred to the output. Taken in phase (the worst case), the voltages add, and so do these terms:

1/OIP3 = Σ 1 / (OIP3,k × G(k+1) × … × Gn)

A stage with no limit (a loss, or a blank OIP3) adds no term, but its gain still weighs the stages before it. Taken from the input, stage by stage:

1/OIP3(k) = 1/OIP3,k + 1/(OIP3(k−1) × Gk)

which gives the cumulative figure on each row. A stage's share is its term over the sum.

The product referred to the input is 3 P − 2 IIP3. It reaches the noise floor N when P = (2 IIP3 + N)/3, so the range from N up to there is (2 IIP3 + N)/3 − N = ⅔ (IIP3 − N).

Assumptions and limits

  • Two equal tones, close together, in a device without memory (the intercept does not depend on their spacing).
  • The 3:1 slope holds only well below compression. Near the P1dB the product stops following the line. The tool flags a tone within 10 dB of its estimated P1dB, and one over it, in amber.
  • The compression point is an estimate. The cubic model puts it 10.6 dB under the OIP3; real amplifiers are 10 to 15 dB under, Keysight's example 11 dB. If the data sheet gives the P1dB, trust that.
  • Third order only. Fifth-order terms bend the product's line near compression and are not modelled.
  • The chain sum is the in-phase worst case. If the stages' products had random phases they would add less: for two equal contributions the root-sum-square would give 1.5 dB more OIP3 than the in-phase sum.
  • A loss has no limit here. A passive part is far more linear than an amplifier (RF Essentials' example gives its filter +100 dBm) and is entered as no limit. A mixer is an Amp with its conversion loss as a negative gain and its own OIP3.
  • The noise floor is yours to choose, and the SFDR follows it: take it for the bandwidth you need (the RF cascade tool gives it).

How it was checked

14 cases; the expected values come from a Python implementation of the same formulas and from the published examples: - Measure, +10 dBm tones with a −46 dBm product and 20 dB of gain: OIP3 +38 dBm, 56 dB below the tone, IIP3 +18 dBm, OP1dB +27.36 dBm, IP1dB +8.364 dBm, the tone 17.4 dB under its P1dB, the product 76 dB down for 10 dB less tone; the same without the gain (the input figures show "—"); a +25 dBm tone with a +20 dBm product flagged 8.14 dB over its estimated P1dB; a product as strong as the tone refused; - Keysight AN 1408-9's example, −1.258 dBm and −42.03 dBm: +19.13 dBm; - Predict, Keysight's amplifier: −46 dBm product, 56 dB down, −66 dBm at the input, the largest tone for 50 dB +13 dBm out and −7 dBm in; typing an IIP3 of 18 with 20 dB gives an OIP3 of 38, and a gain of 10 then keeps the IIP3 and moves the OIP3 to 28; a receiver with an IIP3 of −10 dBm and −40 dBm tones: −100 dBm, 60 dB down; a blank gain refused; - Chain, an LNA (15 dB, +25 dBm), a 3 dB loss and an amplifier (20 dB, +30 dBm): 32 dB, OIP3 +29.73 dBm, IIP3 −2.266 dBm, SFDR 71.8 dB for a −110 dBm floor, 94.1 % of the distortion from stage 3, a −83.47 dBm product (−75.5 dBc) for −40 dBm in; RF Essentials' four stages: +21.94 dBm by the formula (the table says +10.90), +20.5 and +12.9 dBm after stages 2 and 3, IIP3 +1.438 dBm; no OIP3 entered shows "—" and "nothing limits the chain"; a negative loss refused; adding then removing a stage.

Intermodulation

What it computes

What two signals leave behind in anything not perfectly linear, and which pair of signals lands on a channel. Two pills:

  • Products: the frequencies of two tones f1 and f2 (in either order; one unit picker, Hz to GHz, sets both). The big result is the third-order products, 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1, with how far outside each tone they sit (one tone spacing). Under it: the fifth order (3f1 − 2f2, 3f2 − 2f1), the seventh order (4f1 − 3f2, 4f2 − 3f1), the second order (f2 − f1, f1 + f2), the harmonics (2f1, 2f2) and the third-order sums (2f1 + f2, f1 + 2f2). A product that falls below 0 Hz is shown at its mirror image, marked *.
  • Interferers: the channel you listen on (f0) and one interferer (f1). The big result is the frequency of a second interferer that puts a third-order product on the channel: 2f1 − f2 = f0 gives f2 = 2f1 − f0 (A, as far beyond f1 as f1 is from the channel) and 2f2 − f1 = f0 gives f2 = (f1 + f0)/2 (B, halfway between the channel and f1); a value at or below 0 Hz shows "—". Under it: the fifth-order partners, (3f1 − f0)/2 and (f0 + 2f1)/3. With the receiver's IIP3, the level of each interferer and the noise floor (all in dBm, at the receiver's input): the product's level at the input (3 × level − 2 × IIP3), how far it sits above or below the floor, and how far the floor rises when the product adds to it ("unchanged" under 0.05 dB).
  • Drawing: Products: the spectrum as lines, the tones (blue), IM3 (green), IM5 and IM7 (grey). Interferers: the channel (green), the interferer (blue), and the partners A and B (dashed blue).
  • Remembered: the pill and the frequency unit.

Examples: two close tones at 100 and 101 MHz, Keysight's PNA-X tones (5.00001 and 5.00011 GHz), and an interferer at 100.2 MHz near a 100 MHz channel.

Terms

  • Intermodulation: the mixing of two or more signals in a nonlinear device (an amplifier, a mixer, a diode, a corroded joint): the output holds signals at the sums and differences of their multiples.
  • Product, order: n f1 + m f2 for whole numbers n and m, of order |n| + |m|. IM3, IM5 and IM7 are the odd orders with the tones' difference (2f1 − f2, 3f1 − 2f2, 4f1 − 3f2 and their mirror images).
  • Harmonic: a multiple of one tone alone (2f1, 2f2).
  • Interferer: an unwanted signal near the channel; two of them can put a product on it.
  • Mirror image (*): a product at −f is the same tone as one at +f, so it is shown at f with a star.
  • IIP3: the receiver's input intercept (see Intercept point).

Sources

  • Agilent (now Keysight) application notes 1408-9 and 1408-17 (see Intercept point; read): the output holds signals at n f1 + m f2 for whole n and m; the third-order products 2f2 − f1 and 2f1 − f2 are the concern because they sit close to the tones and so cannot be filtered out. Their example, tones at 5.00001 and 5.00011 GHz, gives products at 4.99991 and 5.00021 GHz, which the tool reproduces. For tones of different level, note 1408-17 gives the high-side product as P(f1) − 2 × (IP3 − P(f2)) and the low-side one as P(f2) − 2 × (IP3 − P(f1)), at the receiver: the tool's level for equal interferers is the same formula.
  • Derived here, not quoted: the definition of the order as |n| + |m| (the notes name the third-order products and give n f1 + m f2 but do not define the order), the fifth- and seventh-order products, the second-order products and sums, and the partner frequencies of the Interferers pill (the third-order equation solved for the second tone).
  • Not read: a standard that defines intermodulation orders.

Why the frequencies are these

A nonlinearity of order N makes terms of the form (A cos ω1t + B cos ω2t)^N. Each product of cosines splits into cosines at the sum and the difference of their frequencies, so the output holds n f1 + m f2 with |n| + |m| up to N. With Δ = f2 − f1, the odd-order products with opposite signs land at

2f1 − f2 = f1 − Δ        2f2 − f1 = f2 + Δ
3f1 − 2f2 = f1 − 2Δ      3f2 − 2f1 = f2 + 2Δ
4f1 − 3f2 = f1 − 3Δ      4f2 − 3f1 = f2 + 3Δ

equally spaced by Δ either side of the pair: the picture the tool draws. That is why no filter that passes the tones can stop them.

Backwards, a second interferer f2 puts IM3 on the channel f0 when 2f1 − f2 = f0, so f2 = 2f1 − f0, or when 2f2 − f1 = f0, so f2 = (f1 + f0)/2. The same for the fifth order: 3f1 − 2f2 = f0 gives f2 = (3f1 − f0)/2, and 3f2 − 2f1 = f0 gives f2 = (f0 + 2f1)/3.

The product at the receiver's input, for two interferers of level P each and an input intercept IIP3, is 3 P − 2 IIP3 (see Intercept point). The floor is the noise N plus that product in power: the rise is 10 log(1 + 10^((IM3 − N)/10)), which is 3 dB when the product equals the noise and 10.4 dB when it is 10 dB above it.

Assumptions and limits

  • Equal levels: both interferers are taken at the same level; for unequal ones the product is 2 P1 + P2 − 2 IIP3 for 2f1 − f2 (two of the tone whose frequency is doubled).
  • The 3:1 rule holds below compression only; with strong interferers the real product can differ.
  • The intercept is the receiver's, at its input. If a filter before the first nonlinear stage removes an interferer, it makes no product; if the gain ahead of that stage is high, use the chain's IIP3 (Intercept point).
  • Orders above the third are listed by frequency only; their levels are not computed. Second-order products (f2 − f1, f1 + f2) and harmonics need the second-order intercept, which the app does not compute.
  • The tool does not know your receiver's passband, so it does not say whether a product falls in it.

How it was checked

10 cases; the expected values come from a Python implementation of the same equations and from Keysight's example: - 100 and 101 MHz: IM3 at 99 and 102 MHz, IM5 at 98 and 103, IM7 at 97 and 104, second order 1 and 201, harmonics 200 and 202, third-order sums 301 and 302; the tones typed in the other order give the same; - Keysight AN 1408-17's tones, 5.00001 and 5.00011 GHz: 4.99991 and 5.00021 GHz (and IM5 4.99981 · 5.00031, IM7 4.99971 · 5.00041); - 10 and 100 MHz: an IM3 below 0 Hz shown as 80* and the other at 190 MHz; two equal tones refused; - a 100 MHz channel with an interferer at 100.2 MHz: 100.4 or 100.1 MHz, fifth order 100.3 and 100.1333, with −40 dBm interferers and an IIP3 of −10 dBm an IM3 of −100 dBm, 10 dB over a −110 dBm floor, which rises 10.4 dB; at −60 dBm the product is −160 dBm, 50 dB under the floor, which does not move; an interferer at 30 MHz has no partner below the channel, only 65 MHz; one on the channel refused; kHz re-expresses the frequencies.

Attenuator

What it computes

The resistors of a pad that cuts a signal by a set number of dB while looking like the line's impedance Z0 from both ends:

  • Three pills: Pi (a series resistor and a shunt resistor to ground at each end), T (a series resistor in each arm and one to ground) and Bridged T (two arms of Z0, a bridge across them and a shunt).
  • Inputs: the attenuation (dB), the impedance Z0 (50, 75 or 600 Ω typically) and the input power (mW or W). The resistors' tolerance is picked in the "Your inputs" heading, as in the Passive components tools: Exact values, or ±0.1 % to ±10 %, each with its E series (±1 % is E96, ±5 % E24, ±10 % E12).
  • The big result: the two values that define the pad (T: R1 and R2, Pi: R3 and R4, Bridged T: Rb and Rs, whose two arms are Z0).
  • With a tolerance picked: the big result is the nearest values of its E series; below it come the ideal values, then the pad's real loss and its input return loss with the standard parts (the analysis of the actual circuit); the bridged T's arms of Z0 are rounded too.
  • Below it: the output power in W and dBm, the hottest resistor and its dissipation (to pick the resistors' rating), and the heat in the whole pad; over 20 dB, a warning to split the pad in two.
  • Drawing: the pad as a schematic, US zigzag resistors in green with their values (the standard ones when picked), ports in blue.
  • Remembered: the pill, the series and the power unit.

Examples: a 10 dB Pi pad on 50 Ω, the T pad of the same loss (Kuphaldt's), the Pi pad in E96 values, a 20 dB bridged T on 75 Ω.

Pad (Z0) T: R1, R2 Pi: R3, R4 Bridged T: Rb, Rs
3 dB (50 Ω) 8.55, 141.9 Ω 292.4, 17.61 Ω 20.63, 121.2 Ω
10 dB (50 Ω) 25.97, 35.14 Ω 96.25, 71.15 Ω 108.1, 23.12 Ω
20 dB (50 Ω) 40.91, 10.10 Ω 61.11, 247.5 Ω 450, 5.556 Ω
6 dB (75 Ω) 24.92, 100.4 Ω 225.7, 56.03 Ω 74.64, 75.36 Ω

Terms

  • Attenuation A (dB): the power ratio's 10 log; N = 10^(A/20) is the voltage ratio Vin/Vout (3.16 at 10 dB, 10 at 20 dB).
  • Constant-impedance pad: a pad whose input sees Z0 when its output has a Z0 load, and the reverse; T and Pi pads are symmetric, so they work either way round.
  • Return loss: how many dB the reflection at the pad's input is below the incident wave (see VSWR / Return loss); infinite for an exact pad.
  • Shunt, series: a resistor to ground, and one in the signal's path.
  • Heat: the power that does not reach the load is dissipated in the resistors, mostly the one nearest the input.

Sources

  • Ian Poole, "Resistive Attenuator Pads: Pi & T Circuit Design", Electronics Notes (read): N = Vin/Vout; T: R1 = R0 (N − 1)/(N + 1) and R2 = R0 · 2N/(N² − 1); Pi: R3 = R0 (N + 1)/(N − 1) and R4 = R0 (N² − 1)/(2N); the advice not to attempt more than about 20 dB in one section, and that bridged T pads suit PIN-diode variable attenuators.
  • Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits Vol. III ch. 1, "Attenuators" (ibiblio copy, read; its formulas are images, so the text gives only the values): the pads from the voltage ratio K, the 50 Ω, 10 dB T pad of R1 = 25.97 Ω and R2 = 35.14 Ω, and Zin = R1 + (R2 ‖ (R1 + Z)) = 25.97 + 24.03 = 50 Ω, which the tool reproduces; and "multiply all R values by the ratio (600/50) to correct for 600 Ω matching".
  • Bridged T: the arms R0 = Z0, the bridge Rb = Z0 (N − 1) and the shunt Rs = Z0/(N − 1) were not found in readable text; they are derived here and checked by nodal analysis of each pad at 1, 3, 6, 10, 20 and 30 dB: the input impedance is Z0 and the loss A to every figure shown. The same analysis gives the power in each resistor and the results with standard values.

Assumptions and limits

  • Equal source and load impedance Z0, resistive: no minimum-loss pad between different impedances.
  • Ideal resistors: at high frequency a resistor's stray inductance and capacitance, the board's layout and the shielding between sections set the real loss; use small non-inductive surface-mount parts.
  • Power ratings: the hottest resistor's dissipation at the input power entered; derate for temperature and for peaks.
  • The T pad's heat sits mostly in R1 (52 % of the input at 10 dB), the Pi pad's in the input shunt, R3.

How it was checked

11 cases, the expected values from the formulas above and a Python nodal analysis (input impedance and loss at 10, 20 and 30 dB): - the 10 dB Pi pad on 50 Ω at 1 W: 96.2 and 71.2 Ω, 100 mW (20 dBm) out, 519 mW in the input shunt, 900 mW of heat; - Kuphaldt's T pad: 26 and 35.1 Ω; - the Pi pad in E96 (95.3 and 71.5 Ω): 10.05 dB and 53.8 dB return loss; the T pad in E24 (27 and 36 Ω): 10.2 dB and 36.4 dB; - the 20 dB bridged T on 75 Ω at 100 mW: 75, 675 and 8.33 Ω, 1 mW out, 81 mW in the input arm; - 600 Ω: 312 and 422 Ω; 1 dB T: 2.88 and 433 Ω; 30 dB in one Pi pad: 53.3 and 790 Ω, flagged; - mW re-expresses the power; 0 dB and over 100 dB are refused.
