Power divider

What it computes

How to split one signal into two or more shares, and combine them back, with every port matched to Z0. Three pills:

  • Resistive: a star of resistors: the input and each of 2 to 16 outputs are joined to one centre node through a resistor R. The big result is R, the same in every leg. In three cells: the loss from the input to each output, the isolation between two outputs and the worst return loss. Under them: the power out of each output, the hottest resistor (the input leg) and the power lost as heat, for the input power you give.
  • Wilkinson: 2 to 8 equal outputs on quarter-wave arms. The big result is the arm impedance, with the quarter-wave length for your frequency and line (millimetres and inches, or centimetres, metres and feet for long lines). The cells: the isolation resistor (one resistor for two outputs, a star of N resistors of Z0 for more), the loss (the split itself, 10 log N dB) and the 20 dB band as ± a percentage of the centre frequency. Under them: the return loss and isolation at the centre frequency (∞ with exact values), the band as a frequency range, and the heat in the resistor if an output opens or shorts.
  • Unequal: a two-way Wilkinson with the split you ask for, P3/P2 from 0 to 20 dB (port 3 gets the larger share). The big result is the two arm impedances (to port 2 and to port 3); the cells: the isolation resistor and the two output lines Z04 and Z05 that bring each output back to Z0; under them: the loss to each port, the match and isolation, the 20 dB band and the heat as above.
  • Inputs: the number of outputs (type it, or step it with the − and + in its box; hold to repeat; a Wilkinson takes 8 at most, so a larger count comes down to 8 when you change pill) or the split, Z0, the power in (mW or W) and, for the two quarter-wave pills, the frequency (kHz to GHz) and the line's εeff and velocity factor (linked boxes: VF = 1/√εeff). To combine signals instead of splitting one, the outputs are the inputs. The tolerance at the top of the inputs picks the E series for the resistors: "Exact values" shows the ideal ones, any series shows the loss, the match and the isolation the standard resistor really gives.
  • Drawing: the circuit, ports numbered, the resistors and quarter-wave lines in green. Up to four outputs are drawn; more are drawn as two, dots and the last.
  • Remembered: the pill, the tolerance and both units.

Examples: a 2-way resistive divider on 50 Ω, the same in E24 resistors, a Wilkinson for 1 GHz on 50 Ω, a 3-way Wilkinson on 75 Ω at 100 MHz and a 2:1 unequal split.

Terms

  • Divider, splitter, combiner: one network. Run backwards, the outputs are inputs and the input is the output.
  • Port: a connection to the outside, each matched to Z0. Port 1 is the input, ports 2 and up the outputs.
  • Loss (insertion loss): how much weaker the signal is at an output than at the input, in dB. It includes the unavoidable split: 3.01 dB for two equal outputs, 10 log N for N.
  • Isolation: how much weaker a signal is at one output when it is applied to another. High is good.
  • Return loss: how much weaker the reflected wave is than the wave that entered a port, in dB. ∞ is a perfect match.
  • Quarter-wave line: a line a quarter of a wavelength long at the centre frequency (90°). It turns a load R into Z²/R, Z being its own impedance.
  • Isolation resistor (Wilkinson): the resistor across the outputs. It carries no current while the outputs are equal and in step, and absorbs the difference when they are not.
  • εeff, velocity factor: the effective dielectric constant a line sees, and the share of light's speed a wave travels at: VF = 1/√εeff.
  • K: √(P3/P2), the unequal split's amplitude ratio (K² = P3/P2).
  • 20 dB band: the frequencies round the centre where every return loss and every output-to-output isolation is at least 20 dB.

Sources

  • Marki Microwave, "6 Ways to Make an N-Way Power Splitter" (application note, posted 24 June 2015, modified 13 July 2023; read): the direct N-way wye resistive splitter, R = Z0 (N − 1)/(N + 1), N the number of outputs; the branched resistive splitters lose 6 dB per split and the direct wye as much; and the Wilkinson dissipates nothing in its isolation resistors in splitting use. It gives no isolation figure for the resistive types and no N-way Wilkinson impedances.
  • University of Utah, lecture notes L23, "ECE 6130 Wilkinson Power Divider", text section 7.3 (a PDF with no author name in its metadata, created 11 October 2006; read): the equal Wilkinson is matched at all ports, with complete isolation between the outputs, lossless when the outputs are matched and lossy when they are not (only reflected power is lost); by even and odd modes S11 = S22 = S33 = 0, S21 = S31 = −j/√2, S23 = 0, and all the odd-mode power is lost in the resistor. It leaves the unequal split as an exercise.
  • Benha University, ECE 344 Microwave Fundamentals, Lecture 08, "Power Dividers and Couplers, Part 1" (Dr. Sherif Hekal, 30 April 2018; read, but the equations in its text layer are garbled, so only its statements and examples were used): the resistive three-port divider has all ports matched, but half of the input power is dissipated in the resistors and the outputs are not isolated; no lossless divider can match all three ports; the Wilkinson is matched at all ports, isolates the outputs and loses no power between port 1 and ports 2 and 3 (50 Ω, 70.7 Ω arms, 100 Ω).
  • Maloratsky and London, "Quarter-wavelength N-way power dividers/combiners: historical aspects and new modifications", Microwave Journal, 1 September 2003 (read; its general equations are images and did not come through as text): for N outputs, line impedance Z1 = Z0 √N; the resistors go to a floating common node; theoretically infinite isolation between any two ports at the centre frequency; the bandwidth narrows as N grows; planar layouts are difficult for N > 2.
  • Wikipedia, "Wilkinson power divider" (last edited 20 August 2025; read): the unequal split with K² = P3/P2 and R = Z0 (K + 1/K); its arm equations came out garbled, and it cites Pozar, Microwave Engineering, 3rd ed. (2005) for them, and Wilkinson's paper, IRE Trans. MTT, vol. 8, pp. 116–118, January 1960.
  • Huettner et al. (Nuvotronics), "How Hot Do Those Isolation Resistors Get?", Microwave Journal, 13 May 2025 (read): with the amplifier pairs in phase no power goes to the isolation resistor; with a phase difference all the mismatched power goes to one resistor. It gives no formula.
  • RF Essentials, "Wilkinson Divider" (a web glossary page, no author or date; read through a text-extraction tool): 70.7 Ω and 100 Ω for two ways, 10 log N for the split, and a one-section bandwidth of about 25 to 30 % (criterion not given; the 36 % here is for 20 dB). Its unequal-split equations (K² = P2/P3, arms Z0 √(K (1 + K²)) and Z0 √((1 + K²)/K)) were simulated as given, resistor across the arm ends, and leave a 15 dB match at K² = 2, so they are not used.
  • Derived here and checked by simulation: every equation in the next section, the heat in the resistors, and the bands.
  • Not read: Pozar, Microwave Engineering, §7.2 and §7.3 (the book); Wilkinson's 1960 paper; Microwaves101's Wilkinson page (it returned "not found").

Why the formulas are these

Resistive. With every leg R and the M outputs ended in Z0, the input sees R + (R + Z0)/M. Setting that to Z0 gives R (M + 1) = Z0 (M − 1), so R = Z0 (M − 1)/(M + 1). Every port sees the same star, so the transmission between any two ports, input to output or output to output, is 1/M: the loss and the isolation are both 20 log M dB (6.02 dB for two outputs, 9.54 for three, 12.0 for four). The input leg carries the input current and dissipates (R/Z0) of the input power, (M − 1)/(M + 1) of it; each output leg (R/Z0)/M² of it; together (M − 1)/M of it is heat.

Wilkinson, N equal outputs. Each arm, a quarter wave of impedance Z1 loaded with Z0, looks like Z1²/Z0 from the input; N in parallel look like Z1²/(N Z0), which is Z0 when Z1 = Z0 √N. For the isolation, send signals of opposite signs to the outputs, adding up to zero: the arms' input ends are then a virtual ground, a quarter-wave line shorted at one end looks open at the other, and each output sees only its star resistor: matched when that resistor is Z0. (Between any two outputs that is 2 Z0, the 100 Ω of the two-way, so for two outputs one 2 Z0 resistor does.) Signals in step leave the common point at the outputs' voltage: no current in the resistors.

Unequal, K² = P3/P2. Load the arm ends with R2 = K Z0 and R3 = Z0/K (any pair with the ratio K² would do; this one has R2 R3 = Z0² and keeps the output lines near Z0), brought back to Z0 by quarter-wave lines of Z04 = √(Z0 R2) = Z0 √K and Z05 = Z0/√K. Driven from port 1, the arm ends must be at the same voltage (no current in R), which gives R2/Z02 = R3/Z03 and, for the power split (R3/Z03²)/(R2/Z02²) = K², R2/R3 = K². Matching the input, Z02²/R2 ‖ Z03²/R3 = Z0, then gives Z02 = Z0 √(K (1 + K²)) and Z03 = Z0 √((1 + K²)/K³). For the isolation, drive port 2 and ask for no voltage at the end of arm 3. The voltage V2 at the end of arm 2 sends a current V2/R through R into the end of arm 3; that end, held at zero, is a short, which a quarter-wave line passes on as a current V1/Z03 (V1 the voltage at the input node); and with port 1 ended in Z0, V1 = Z0 V2/Z02. Equating the two currents gives R = Z02 Z03/Z0 = Z0 (K + 1/K) = R2 + R3. R goes between the arm ends, ahead of the transformers. For K = 1 these are 70.7 Ω, 100 Ω and no transformers.

Heat with an output open or shorted. The output k that fails reflects all the power it was given, P_k. Of that, the fraction |S1k|² goes back to the input, none to the other outputs (they are isolated), and the rest to the resistors: P_k (1 − |S1k|²). For N equal outputs that is (P/N)(1 − 1/N) = P (N − 1)/N² of the input power P; for the unequal split, either port gives K²/(1 + K²)² P. In the star of N resistors the failed output's resistor takes (N − 1)/N of it and each other 1/(N (N − 1)).

The band. The arms' length is 90° × f/f0. The solver computes the S-parameters round the centre, and the band is the span where every return loss and every output-to-output isolation is at least 20 dB. For two equal outputs it is 0.819 to 1.18 f0; it narrows with the outputs (±11.1 % for three, ±8.56 % for four, ±5.18 % for eight) and with the split (about ±15 % for 3 dB, ±9.4 % for 6 dB, ±2.3 % for 20 dB).

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal lossless lines. The loss shown is the split only. A real line adds its own loss, and the resistors and junctions add parasitics that matter at GHz. No discontinuity is modelled.
  • One section. Wider bands need several sections; they are not computed.
  • The same εeff for every line, though lines of different impedance have different widths and so slightly different εeff: use the figure for the trace you mean (the microstrip tool gives it).
  • N > 2 needs a floating common point. On a PCB that takes crossovers or vias (Maloratsky and London); the tool computes the ideal circuit.
  • The heat is the worst case: total reflection at one output, the others matched, at the centre frequency. For a combiner, two inputs of unequal amplitude or phase give the resistor |a1 − a2|²/2 (the odd-mode power).
  • Power in is the power a matched source can deliver.
  • Standard values: one value for every leg or resistor, the nearest in the series to the ideal one.
  • Unequal: port 3 gets the larger share; swap the ports for the other way round. Splits over 20 dB are refused (the transformers get extreme).
  • Not covered: hybrid and directional couplers and the two-resistor "leveling" splitter of test equipment.

How it was checked

32 cases. The expected values come from a Python S-parameter solver (numpy, nodal analysis with quarter-wave line matrices) and the app's own solver agreed with it to the digits shown: - Resistive: 2 outputs on 50 Ω, 16.7 Ω, 6.02 dB (loss and isolation), matched, 250 mW out of 1 W, 333 mW in the input leg, 500 mW lost; in E24, 16 Ω: 5.93 dB, a 39.9 dB match, 490 mW lost; 4 outputs, 30 Ω, 12 dB, 750 mW lost; 3 outputs on 75 Ω, 37.5 Ω, 9.54 dB; 8 outputs in E96, 39.2 Ω, 18.1 dB, 49.1 dB; 100 mW in; one and 17 outputs refused; - Wilkinson: 2 outputs on 50 Ω at 1 GHz, VF 66 %: 70.7 Ω, 49.5 mm, 100 Ω, 3.01 dB, ±18.1 %, 250 mW; 3 outputs on 75 Ω at 100 MHz: 130 Ω, 49.5 cm, 4.77 dB, ±11.1 %, 222 mW (148 mW in one resistor); 4 outputs (100 Ω, ±8.56 %, 187 mW) and 8 (141 Ω, ±5.18 %, 109 mW); E12 star resistors, 47 Ω: a 33.7 dB match and 39.7 dB isolation; 10 MHz, 4.95 m; VF 1, 74.9 mm; VF 0.5 and εeff 4 linked; nine outputs and no frequency refused; - Unequal: 3 dB: 103 and 51.5 Ω, 106 Ω, 59.4 and 42.1 Ω, 4.76 and 1.76 dB, 0.852 to 1.15 GHz, 222 mW; 4:1: 158 and 39.5 Ω, 125 Ω, 70.7 and 35.4 Ω, 160 mW; 0 dB: the equal Wilkinson; 20 dB; 6 dB in E24 (120 Ω for 125 Ω: a 36.1 dB match, 42.1 dB isolation); 25 dB refused; - the outputs' − and + (to 4, stopping at 2 and at 16 and, for a Wilkinson, at 8, and a count of 12 coming down to 8 on changing pill); - three of the examples.

The solver also confirmed, to numerical zero at the centre frequency, the equal and N-way Wilkinson (every port matched, every pair of outputs isolated), the unequal one for K² from 1 to 100 with the exact split, and that the resistor placed after the output transformers, or the transformers left out, or RF Essentials' arms, do not give a matched and isolated divider.

↑ Index · Open the tool

RF & microwave › Mixing & conversion

IF calculator

What it computes

A mixer moves a signal from one frequency to another by combining it with an oscillator of the receiver's own, the LO. The tool plans that move: from two of the three frequencies, the RF (the signal's), the LO and the IF (the one the mixer delivers), it finds the third, then the image that would give the same IF and the other inputs that would come through. Four pills:

  • Find LO: the RF, as one frequency or as a band (the band's other end in "RF to"), and the IF give the LO. The picker in the Output heading says on which side of the RF the LO sits: "LO above RF" is high-side injection, the usual choice, "LO below RF" is low-side. The big result is the LO (a band gives a range). In three cells: the image, the half-IF response, and the tuning ratio (the highest LO over the lowest, for a band; the LO over the RF for one frequency). Under them: the LO on the other side, with its ratio for a band; the spacing of the image, 2 × IF; and, for a band, the part of the image that falls inside the RF band.
  • Find IF: the RF (a band if you like) and the LO give the IF, IF = |RF − LO|. A band gives an IF band, as in a satellite dish's LNB, which turns 10.70 to 11.70 GHz into 0.95 to 1.95 GHz with a 9.75 GHz LO. In three cells: the image, the half-IF response, and RF + LO, the other product the mixer makes, which a filter removes. The line under the big result says which side the LO is on, and a band that holds the LO is said to fall through 0 Hz.
  • Find RF: the IF (a band if you like) and the LO give the wanted RF, LO − IF with the LO above it and LO + IF with the LO below, the up-converter's case. The same three cells, and the spacing of the image.
  • Spurs: the inputs, other than the wanted one, that put a product of the input and the LO on the IF, m × n responses up to an order you set, 2 to 9. The big result is the closest one to the RF, and under it its order and how far above or below the RF it is. In three cells: the image, the half-IF response and the number of responses. Under them: the eight closest, each with its frequency and its offset from the RF.

Under the inputs, chips set the IF to one of the usual values: 455 kHz, 10.7 MHz, 21.4 MHz, 45 MHz or 70 MHz.

The drawing of the first three pills is the plan: a row each for the RF, the LO, the image and the IF, on one scale of frequency. A value you gave is blue, one calculated green, the image amber; a single frequency is a dot, a band a bar, and where the image lies inside an RF band it is shaded across the rows. The IF is far to the left of the others, so the axis is broken where that saves room; the scale is the same on both sides of the break, so the distance from 0 to the IF is the distance between the RF and the LO. The Spurs pill draws a window round the LO: the RF and the image either side of it, and the responses that fall within 1.35 IF of it, which are the 2 × 2 pair, 3 × 3 pair and so on, crowding up to the LO.

  • Units: Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz, one for every frequency box and for the results: changing it in one changes them all. A value is shown to nine figures at most and to 1 Hz.
  • Remembered: the pill, the unit and the side.

Examples: the FM band with a 10.7 MHz IF, the AM band with 455 kHz, a Ku-band LNB, a 70 MHz IF up-converted, and a half-IF blocker.

Terms

  • RF (radio frequency): the frequency of the signal that is to be received or, for an up-converter, produced.
  • LO (local oscillator): the oscillator the mixer combines the RF with. It is tuned so that it differs from the RF by exactly the IF.
  • IF (intermediate frequency): the fixed frequency the mixer's output is filtered and amplified at. A sharp filter is easier to make at one fixed frequency than to tune across a band, which is why receivers move everything to one.
  • Mixer: a circuit that multiplies two signals. The product holds the sum and the difference of their frequencies; the difference is the IF of a receiver (down-conversion), the sum or the difference the output of an up-converter.
  • High-side and low-side injection: the LO above the RF, or below it.
  • Image: a second input frequency that gives the same IF: on the far side of the LO, as far from it as the RF is, so RF ± 2 IF. After the mixer it cannot be told from the wanted signal, so it has to be stopped before it; the farther it is from the RF, the easier that is, so the image is 2 × IF away. In an up-converter it is the other sideband.
  • Half-IF response: an input halfway between the RF and the LO, half an IF from the RF, which lands on the IF through the mixer's second harmonics (2 × 2). The IF filter cannot remove it, since it is on the IF.
  • m × n response, order: an input at f that puts m f ± n LO on the IF, for whole m and n; the order is m + n. The wanted signal is 1 × 1.
  • Tuning ratio: the highest LO frequency over the lowest as the receiver tunes across a band; the oscillator is easier to build the smaller it is.
  • Sideband: an up-converter's two products, LO + IF and LO − IF; one is wanted.
  • Direct conversion: an IF of 0 Hz, the LO on the RF.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, "Superheterodyne receiver" (read through a fetch tool, the first 100 000 of its 135 500 characters): the IF as |f_LO − f_RF|; high-side injection (the LO above the RF) as the usual choice for broadcast because of the oscillator's tuning range; the medium-wave example, 531 to 1700 kHz with a 455 kHz IF, an LO of 986 to 2155 kHz ("slightly greater than 2:1") and images of 1441 to 2610 kHz, against 76 to 1245 kHz for low-side injection ("a much wider ratio"); a 660 kHz station with the LO at 1115 kHz and the image at 1570 kHz; an input at 955 kHz with a 1455 kHz LO giving a spur on the 455 kHz IF (2 × 955 − 1455); and a double-conversion receiver, a 1 MHz input with a first IF of 81.4 MHz and the LO at 82.4 MHz, whose image is at 163.8 MHz.
  • Wikipedia, "Intermediate frequency" (read through a fetch tool): the usual IFs: 455 kHz for AM broadcast, 10.7 MHz for FM, 38.9 and 45.75 MHz for analogue television, 70 MHz for satellite and terrestrial microwave equipment, 950 to 2150 MHz from a satellite dish's LNB, 30 MHz for radar.
  • Wikipedia, "Low-noise block downconverter" (read through a fetch tool): the universal Ku-band LNB: LO 9.75 GHz for 10.70 to 11.70 GHz (IF 950 to 1950 MHz) and LO 10.60 GHz for 11.70 to 12.75 GHz (IF 1100 to 2150 MHz), the LO below the RF.
  • Stephen Long, "Introduction to Receivers" (University of California, Santa Barbara, ECE145A; PDF text extracted and read): a mixer multiplies, and its output holds the sum and the difference; two inputs, the RF and the image, give the same IF, f_RF − f_LO = f_LO − f_IM = f_IF; where the image lies with the LO above and below the RF; the usual IF filters, 455 kHz, 10.7 MHz, 21.4 MHz, 45 MHz and 70 MHz; the FM band (88 to 108 MHz, IF 10.7 MHz, the image always outside the band) and the AM band (the LO's tuning ratio 16.6 : 1 low-side against 2.2 : 1 high-side, the image often in the band); and a dual conversion, 900 MHz with a first IF of 400 MHz (LO 1300 MHz, image 1700 MHz) and a second of 10.7 MHz (LO 410.7 MHz, image of the second conversion 421.4 MHz).
  • Marki Microwave, "Mixer Basics Primer" (2010; PDF text extracted and read): a mixer's output holds products ± n f_LO ± m f_RF for whole n and m, the wanted one n = m = 1; in a double-balanced mixer only odd n and odd m survive at the IF port; the manufacturer's spur tables give their levels.
  • Microwaves & RF, "Match Mixers To BTS LTE Receivers" (read through a fetch tool): the half-IF response, 2 f − 2 f_LO = ±IF, an input half an IF from the RF on the side of the LO: RF 2510 MHz, LO 2860 MHz and IF 350 MHz put it at 2685 MHz; spurious responses inside the IF band are not attenuated by the IF filter.
  • Not read: Analog Devices' technical articles on the half-IF and 2 × 2 responses (their pages timed out; their content reached me only as a search summary, which agrees with the article above), any mixer's datasheet spur table, any textbook, and any standard for IFs.

Why the formulas are these

The mixer. Multiplying two cosines gives cos a · cos b = ½ cos (a − b) + ½ cos (a + b), so an RF and an LO give terms at |RF − LO| and RF + LO: the IF is the difference.

The LO and the image. An input f gives |f − LO| on the output, which is the IF for f = LO + IF and for f = LO − IF: two inputs, the wanted RF and the image, symmetric about the LO. With the LO above the RF (σ = +1) the RF is LO − IF and the image LO + IF; with the LO below it (σ = −1) the RF is LO + IF and the image LO − IF. In both:

LO = RF + σ IF      image = LO + σ IF = RF + 2σ IF = 2 LO − RF

so the image is 2 × IF from the RF, on the side of the LO. A band moves the LO and the image with it, each shifted by a constant, so the band's width and the tuning ratio follow: LO = RF + σ IF for the two ends gives (RF_high + σ IF) / (RF_low + σ IF); 531 to 1700 kHz with 455 kHz is 2155/986 = 2.19 with the LO above and 1245/76 = 16.4 with it below, the figures of Wikipedia and Long. An image below 0 Hz does not exist; the tool cuts the image band at 0 Hz.

The half-IF response. The mixer's second harmonics make 2 f − 2 LO = ±IF, so f = LO ± IF/2: on each side of the LO, half an IF away. The one nearer the RF is (RF + LO)/2, RF + σ IF/2.

The responses. An input at f puts a product on the IF when m f + a n LO = b IF, with a and b each +1 or −1, so

f = (b IF − a n LO) / m      m, n ≥ 1, order m + n

and only positive f count. With a = −1 these are f = (n LO ± IF)/m, the differences of the product ± n LO ± m f. Whether the mixer makes a given product, and how strongly, depends on its design: an ideal multiplier makes only 1 × 1, a double-balanced mixer only the odd ones, and the levels come from the maker's spur table. The tool lists where responses can be, not how big they are. The wanted signal (1 × 1, at the RF) is left out. The list is sorted by distance from the RF, the lower order first on a tie.

The image in the band. For an RF band [a, b] and an image band [c, d] the overlap is [max (a, c), min (b, d)] when that is not empty, and its share is its width over b − a.

The drawing. The scale is k = (axis length) / (length shown), the length shown being the cluster of RF, LO and image with a margin, plus the stretch from 0 to the IF when the axis is broken. The axis is broken when the gap between the IF (with a quarter more) and the cluster is over 35 % of the highest frequency drawn.

Assumptions and limits

  • The difference product only. The IF is |RF − LO|. A plan whose IF is the sum of the RF and the LO (an LO below the IF) is not covered.
  • Where, not how much. The Spurs list says which inputs can reach the IF, for every m and n up to the order; a real mixer makes only some, at levels in its datasheet's spur table (typically falling quickly with the order), and a preselector before the mixer helps against the ones that are not too close to the RF.
  • Responses from m or n of zero are not listed: an input at the IF itself or at a submultiple of it getting through, the LO leaking to the IF port, harmonics of the RF. Keep the IF outside the RF band.
  • No filter widths. A response counts whatever its distance from the IF in frequency; the tool does not ask how wide the IF filter is. A response that falls within it (the closest rows here show how far each is) is a whistle or a desensitised channel.
  • One conversion at a time. A receiver with two conversions is planned stage by stage, the first IF being the second stage's RF.
  • Positive frequencies. An image band that lies below 0 Hz is shown as none, and one that reaches below it is cut at 0 Hz.
  • Frequencies are the nominal ones. An LO's own spurs and phase noise, the oscillator's accuracy and the filters' shapes are outside the tool.
  • Display. Nine figures at most and to 1 Hz.

How it was checked

58 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation of the same relations (every figure, every label of the drawing, the rows of the Spurs list in order): - Find LO: an FM station at 98 MHz; the FM band; Wikipedia's medium-wave band with the LO above (986 to 2155 kHz, images 1441 to 2610 kHz, 22.2 % of the band reached) and below (76 to 1245 kHz, 16.4 : 1); the 660 kHz station (LO 1115, image 1570 kHz); Long's dual conversion (LO 1300 MHz, image 1700 MHz; the second stage, LO 410.7 MHz, image 421.4 MHz); Wikipedia's double conversion (LO 82.4 MHz, image 163.8 MHz); GHz units; a band typed backwards; a band end equal to the start; a high IF; an image below 0 Hz; - Find IF: the LNB's two bands, a station and an LO, an LO inside the band, an LO below the RF, the refusals; - Find RF: the 70 MHz up-converter, the receiver's view, an IF band, the refusals; - Spurs: Microwaves & RF's blocker at 2685 MHz, Wikipedia's 955 kHz input, an LO below the RF, order 2, 6 and 9, GHz units, every refusal of the order; - the linked units, the side picker, the remembered choices, the chips, the five examples, and the formula-search card.

About 700 more cases, on 180 random plans (an RF from 100 kHz to 20 GHz, an IF from 0.4 % to 250 % of it, bands, both sides, orders 2 to 9) through all four pills, compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

RF & microwave › Mixing & conversion

Image frequency

What it computes

A mixer gives the same IF for two inputs: the wanted RF, and the image, on the far side of the LO and 2 × IF from the RF (the IF calculator finds it). Once they are mixed nothing can tell them apart, so the image has to be dealt with before the mixer: stopped by a filter, kept out of the band by the choice of IF, or cancelled by the mixer itself. One pill for each:

  • Filter: how much a filter ahead of the mixer, a preselector, stops the image. The RF, the IF, the filter's loaded Q or its 3 dB bandwidth (type one and the other is calculated, marked "result"), and the number of poles. Two pickers in the Output heading: the side of the LO, which puts the image above or below the RF, and how several poles behave, "tuned circuits" for tuned circuits that do not load one another (the Q and the bandwidth are each circuit's), "Butterworth" for an n-pole Butterworth band-pass (the Q and the bandwidth are the whole filter's). The big result is the rejection in dB at the image. In three cells: the image, the detuning ρ, and the bandwidth (the Q when the bandwidth was typed). Under them: the amplitude ratio at the image, how many bandwidths from the RF the image is, and for tuned circuits the dB each one gives and, from two circuits up, the 3 dB bandwidth of all of them together; for Butterworth the bandwidth as a share of the RF.
  • Needed: the other way round, the rejection a receiver needs. The wanted signal's level and the image's at the antenna, both in dBm, and S/I, the ratio the wanted signal must keep over what is left of the image. The big result is the rejection. In three cells: the loaded Q that one, two or three poles must have; under them the bandwidth for each and where the image is. If the image is already weaker than the wanted signal by more than S/I, no filter is needed and it says so.
  • IF choice: the least IF that keeps the image out of a band. The band's two ends and a guard, the room to leave between the band and its image (optional, 0 if empty). The big result is the IF, (band + guard) / 2. In three cells: the band, the Q of a filter that just passes it, and the image band. Under them, what each of the usual IFs, 455 kHz, 10.7 MHz, 21.4 MHz, 45 MHz and 70 MHz, leaves between the band and its image: "gap … · clear", "gap … · too close" (under the guard), "touching" or "overlap …" (the image reaches into the band). An IF of your own, in "Your IF" (optional), adds a row and is the one the drawing shows.
  • IR mixer: what an image-reject (quadrature) mixer leaves, from the gain imbalance in dB and the phase error in degrees between its two paths. The big result is the rejection. In three cells: the same by the small-error formula, the gain error as a percentage, and the phase error in radians. Under them, for a target (40 dB at the start; optional): the phase error that alone would give it, the gain imbalance that alone would, and the phase error that is left when the gain imbalance is the one typed ("not possible" if that gain imbalance already costs more than the target).

The drawing of Filter and Needed is the response of the filter round the RF, 0 dB at the top and the attenuation going down, on a scale chosen to fit: the RF is a blue stem, the image an amber dashed one that ends on the curve at the rejection, the response green. Needed draws the curves of one, two and three poles, told apart by their dashes, which all pass through the image at the rejection needed. IF choice draws the band (blue) and its image band (amber) on one scale, with the gap between them marked in green and, where the image reaches into the band, the overlap shaded; the IF drawn is written in the corner. IR mixer draws the wanted signal (green) and the image (amber) with its stem cut at the rejection.

  • Units: Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz, one for every frequency box and for the results: changing it in one changes them all. A frequency is shown to nine figures at most and to 1 Hz; the dB, the Q and the ratios to three figures.
  • Remembered: the pill, the unit, the side and the model.

Examples: a tuned circuit on FM, an AM station and its image, stopping a strong image, an IF for the FM band, and an image-reject mixer.

Terms

  • Image: the second input frequency that gives the same IF, RF ± 2 IF: above the RF with the LO above it, below with the LO below.
  • Preselector: the filter between the antenna and the mixer, tuned to the RF; its job is to stop the image.
  • Image rejection: how far down the image is, against the wanted signal, after the filter or the mixer, in dB.
  • Loaded Q: the filter's centre frequency over its 3 dB bandwidth, with its source and load counted. It is lower than the Q of the bare inductor and capacitor, and it is the one that sets how fast the response falls.
  • 3 dB bandwidth: the width between the two frequencies where the response is 3 dB below its peak.
  • Pole: one tuned circuit (resonator) in the filter; a filter of n poles has n.
  • Detuning ρ: how far off the RF the image is, f_image / f_RF − f_RF / f_image, the form a tuned circuit's response is written in. It is 0 on the RF.
  • Butterworth: the filter whose passband is as flat as it can be: its response falls as 1 / (1 + Ω^2n) in power, 3 dB down at Ω = 1.
  • S/I (signal to interference): the ratio the wanted signal must keep over the image that is left, in dB; how much is enough is the receiver's requirement, which the tool does not know.
  • Guard: the room left between the RF band and the band of its images.
  • Gap: the distance from the top of the band to the bottom of its image band (for an LO above), 2 × IF − band; below 0 the two overlap.
  • Band filter Q: a filter that just passes the band, centre over width.
  • Image-reject mixer (quadrature, Hartley, Weaver): two mixers fed by the LO 90° apart and a 90° shift after them, so the wanted signal adds and the image cancels.
  • Gain imbalance, phase error: how far the two paths are from equal gain (their ratio γ, in dB) and from exactly 90° (φ). Either leaves a part of the image.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, "Image response" (the formula lines of its wikitext, quoted by a fetch tool; the page's rendered text summarised by the same tool): a single tuned circuit's image rejection IRR = √(1 + ρ² Q²), with ρ = f_IMAGE / f_RF − f_RF / f_IMAGE and Q the quality factor, characterised by the RF filter and found from the response of a parallel tuned circuit (the article does not say whether the value is a ratio or in dB; the tool takes it as an amplitude ratio, which is derived below); and IMRR = (γ² + 1 − 2γ cos φ) / (γ² + 1 + 2γ cos φ) ≈ (ε² + φ²) / 4, γ the gain imbalance, ε = γ − 1 and φ the phase imbalance, a formula the article credits to dsplog.com. The article's own example is a 100 MHz signal with a 110 MHz LO and a 10 MHz IF, whose image is at 120 MHz.
  • Wikipedia, "Butterworth filter" (read through a fetch tool): the gain of the n-th order Butterworth low-pass, |H|² = G0² / (1 + (ω/ω_c)^2n), ω_c the cut-off, about the −3 dB point, and a slope of 20 n dB per decade.
  • Wikipedia, "Prototype filter" (read through a fetch tool): the change from a low-pass prototype to a band-pass, iω/ω_c′ → Q (iω/ω_0 + ω_0/iω), with Q = ω_0/Δω, Δω the bandwidth and ω_0 the geometric mean of the band edges; the article gives no Butterworth response itself.
  • Wikipedia, "Superheterodyne receiver" (read through a fetch tool, as for the IF calculator): a 1000 kHz input with a 1455 kHz oscillator and a 455 kHz IF, whose image, at 1910 kHz, also translates to 455 kHz.
  • Edwin Kan, "Chapter 8, Frequency Strategy" (Cornell University, ECE 4880, Fall 2016; PDF text extracted and read): a single-side-band superheterodyne with f_IF > BW_RF / 2 and a filter of width BW_RF as the first way to reject the image (the second, up-conversion, the third, quadrature); f_IF > BW_RF / 4 for dual-side injection; the FM band 88 to 108 MHz with f_IF = (108 − 88) / 2 + 0.7 = 10.7 MHz and a band filter of Q = 98 / (108 − 88) = 4.9; the AM band 530 to 1610 kHz with an IF of 455 kHz, below the 540 kHz that is half the band; the choice of IF, low (a better filter is needed round BW_RF, a larger tuning range for the LO) against high (easier image rejection, less LO phase noise, harder processing); and the Hartley and Weaver quadrature schemes.
  • RF Design Tools, "Hartley IRM" (the documentation page of its image-planning tool; read through a fetch tool): the rejection of a Hartley image-reject mixer as a function of the amplitude mismatch (ε = 10^(G/20) − 1) and the phase mismatch, in the form of Wikipedia's, the printed cosine term lacking the factor 2 that the page's own derivation has (the tool's summary corrected it with the factor and the correction agrees with Wikipedia's); the small-error form, 6.02 − 10 log (ε² + φ²) dB; and the statement that about 6° of phase mismatch alone gives roughly 25 dB. The summary also listed worked examples, 0.1 dB and 1°: 39.6 dB; 0.5 dB and 2°: 29.5 dB (29.3 by the small-error form); 1 dB and 5°: 22.8 dB (22.5). The tool gives the same, but I cannot say whether the page prints those figures or the fetch tool worked them out from the corrected formula, so they count as agreement with the formula, not as published answers.
  • Not read: Analog Devices' article on image rejection in receivers (its fetch failed), McGill's superheterodyne notes (the connection was reset), any textbook, any datasheet of a preselector or an image-reject mixer, and any standard. The rejection of several tuned circuits one after another and the Butterworth form applied to the image are derived here from the single-circuit formula and the two articles above; the allowed errors of the mixer are derived from the exact formula.

Why the formulas are these

The image. With the LO above the RF the image is at RF + 2 IF, with the LO below it at RF − 2 IF (the IF calculator's derivation). Below 0 Hz there is none: the tool refuses an IF of half the RF or more with the LO below.

One tuned circuit. An inductor, a capacitor and the loss resistor R in parallel, fed by a current, have the admittance (1/R) (1 + j Q (f / f0 − f0 / f)), with Q = R / (ω0 L) = ω0 R C the loaded Q, so the voltage across them is 1 / √(1 + Q² δ²) of its peak, δ = f / f0 − f0 / f. Tuned to the RF, f0 = RF: the gain is 1 there and 1 / √(1 + Q² ρ²) at the image, ρ being δ at f_image. The ratio of the two is Wikipedia's IRR = √(1 + ρ² Q²), an amplitude ratio, and in dB

rejection = 20 log √(1 + Q² ρ²) = 10 log (1 + (Q ρ)²)

For the FM example, RF 98 MHz and IF 10.7 MHz: the image is at 119.4 MHz, ρ = 1.2184 − 0.8208 = 0.3976, and Q = 20 gives 10 log (1 + 63.2) = 18.1 dB.

Several tuned circuits. Circuits that do not load one another (an amplifier between them) multiply their gains, so their dB add: n × 10 log (1 + (Q ρ)²). Their 3 dB bandwidth together is narrower than each one's: (1 + x²)^n = 2 at the edges, with x = Q (f / f0 − f0 / f), which gives x = √(2^(1/n) − 1) and a width BW_each × √(2^(1/n) − 1), 0.644 of it for two and 0.510 for three. The edges are exact: f / f0 − f0 / f = ±x / Q puts them x f0 / Q apart.

An n-pole Butterworth band-pass. The prototype is the low-pass |H|² = 1 / (1 + Ω^2n); the band-pass substitution turns Ω into Ω = Q (f / f0 − f0 / f), Q = f0 / BW, so at the image Ω = Q ρ and

rejection = 10 log (1 + (Q ρ)^2n)

One pole is the single tuned circuit; more poles fall faster, as 20 n dB per decade of Ω. The two models agree at n = 1. Beyond it the Q means something else in each: each circuit's in the tuned model, so that the circuits together have a narrower 3 dB bandwidth than any one of them, and the whole filter's (f0 over its 3 dB bandwidth) in the Butterworth model. Typed alike they give nearly the same (36.2 dB and 36.0 dB for two poles and Q 20 at the FM image); for the same 3 dB bandwidth of the whole filter the Butterworth one rejects more, by about 7.7 dB at two poles (17.6 dB at three) when Q ρ is large, since its poles are coupled to be as flat as they can be at the centre and fall steeply after it.

The rejection needed. A filter that is 0 dB at the RF and A dB down at the image leaves the image at P_image − A and the wanted signal at P_wanted; to keep S/I the wanted signal must be that far above:

P_wanted − (P_image − A) ≥ S/I
A = P_image − P_wanted + S/I

The Q for a given A comes from inverting the two forms, with R = A:

tuned:        Q = √(10^(R / 10 n) − 1) / |ρ|
Butterworth:  Q = (10^(R / 10) − 1)^(1 / 2n) / |ρ|

At the FM image (ρ = 0.3976), R = 60 dB takes Q = 2515 for one pole, 79.5 for two tuned circuits (79.5 as well for two Butterworth poles) and 25.0 for three (25.2).

The IF. The band of width BW, from lo to hi, has its image band from lo + 2 IF to hi + 2 IF with the LO above, from lo − 2 IF to hi − 2 IF below. The gap between a band and its image band is the same either way, 2 IF − BW. To leave a guard G the IF must be at least (BW + G) / 2; with no guard the least IF is BW / 2, Cornell's f_IF > BW_RF / 2. Cornell's FM numbers are this with G = 1.4 MHz: (108 − 88) / 2 + 0.7 = 10.7 MHz. A filter that just passes the band has Q = centre / BW, Cornell's 98 / 20 = 4.9. The AM band, 530 to 1610 kHz, is 1080 kHz wide: half of it, 540 kHz, is more than the 455 kHz IF, so the gap is 2 × 455 − 1080 = −170 kHz and the image falls in the band. An image band that is below 0 Hz is shown as none, and one that reaches it is cut there.

The image-reject mixer. With the gain ratio γ and the phase error φ of the two paths, the image leaves as the fraction (γ² + 1 − 2γ cos φ) / (γ² + 1 + 2γ cos φ) of the power (Wikipedia's IMRR), so the rejection in dB is

IRR = 10 log [(γ² + 1 + 2γ cos φ) / (γ² + 1 − 2γ cos φ)]
γ = 10^(G/20)

It is the same for γ and 1 / γ. For small errors it is 10 log [4 / (ε² + φ²)] with ε = γ − 1 and φ in radians. The allowed errors for a target of T dB (R = 10^(T/10)):

phase alone (γ = 1):   R = cot² (φ/2)
                       φ = 2 atan (10^(−T/20))
gain alone (φ = 0):    R = ((γ + 1) / (γ − 1))²
                       G = 20 log ((1 + x) / (1 − x)),  x = 10^(−T/20)
phase with a given γ:  cos φ = (R − 1) (1 + γ²) / (2 γ (R + 1))
                       (possible only while that is at most 1)

For 40 dB: 1.146° alone, 0.174 dB alone; with 0.1 dB of gain imbalance 0.937°.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal filters. The filters are tuned circuits or a Butterworth band-pass, centred on the RF, with no loss. The tool says what a loaded Q buys, not what a particular filter does: a real preselector has its own shape (Chebyshev, one with traps or zeros, a helical or ceramic resonator), a loss at the RF that has to be added to the noise figure, and a Q that depends on its parts.
  • Isolated circuits. The "tuned circuits" model adds the dB of circuits that do not load one another. Circuits coupled to each other respond as a filter does, which is the Butterworth model's case, or another design's.
  • Loaded Q, one frequency. The rejection is at the image's one frequency; a preselector's Q changes as it is tuned across a band, and a fixed filter has to pass the whole band.
  • One image, one conversion. The image of the first conversion only. The other inputs that reach the IF (the half-IF response, the m × n responses) are the IF calculator's Spurs, and a receiver with two conversions has an image at each.
  • The IF rule is for a filter that passes the band. Dual-side injection (the LO below the lower half of the band and above the upper half, which Cornell says needs only f_IF > BW_RF / 4) and up-conversion are not drawn.
  • The mixer's two errors only. The rejection is from the gain imbalance and the phase error of the paths (the error of the 90° shift after the mixers counts as phase error). It is at one frequency; the paths' mismatch changes across the band, and the LO and RF leakage and noise are not included.
  • No noise figure. Noise at the image frequency also reaches the IF (Wikipedia's superheterodyne article says so); how much a rejection saves in noise is not calculated.
  • Over 300 dB is not counted: it shows "over 300 dB", and a needed rejection of 300 dB or more is refused.
  • Display. Frequencies to nine figures at most and to 1 Hz; dB, Q and ratios to three figures, never in exponent form.

How it was checked

84 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation of the same relations (every figure, every label of the drawing): - Filter: the FM front end (18.1 dB at 119.4 MHz), a Q typed and a bandwidth typed (the other follows), two and three tuned circuits, Butterworth with two and three poles, one pole the same in both, Wikipedia's AM image (1910 kHz) with Q 50, the LO below, an image just above 0 Hz, GHz units, Q of 0.5, Q past 300 dB, ten poles, the linked units, the pickers, every refusal; - Needed: 60 dB at the FM image (Q 2515, 79.5, 25.0), Butterworth, an image weaker than the wanted signal, exactly 0 dB, a small need, the LO below, a negative S/I, 120 dB, the 300 dB refusal, GHz units, every refusal; - IF choice: the FM band (10.7 MHz, Q 4.9), Cornell's AM band (−170 kHz with 455 kHz), the LO below, an image below 0 Hz and one that straddles it, an IF tried that overlaps, that is too close, that touches, no guard, a band typed backwards, GHz, every refusal; - IR mixer: 0.5 dB and 2°, 0.1 dB and 1°, 1 dB and 5°, perfect paths, gain alone, phase alone (6°: 25.6 dB), negative errors, a target of 40 and of 60 dB, no target, every refusal; - the five examples, the remembered choices and the formula-search card.

About 1 900 more cases, on 465 random plans (an RF from 100 kHz to 30 GHz, an IF from 1 % to 150 % of it, both sides, both models, 1 to 6 poles, bands, guards, levels, errors), through all four pills, compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

RF & microwave › RF components

Common mode choke

What it computes

A common-mode choke is two identical windings on one core. A current that goes in on one line and comes back on the other (the wanted, differential one) makes opposite fluxes that cancel; a current that goes the same way in both (common mode, the noise that leaks to earth) makes fluxes that add and meets the whole inductance. The tool does two jobs with one. Two pills:

  • Filter: the capacitors that go with the choke in a mains EMC filter, by the procedure of Schaffner's application note. The inputs, three to a row: the frequency of the noise to be cut (kHz), the limit and the safety margin (dBµV, dB); the common-mode and the differential-mode noise at that frequency (dBµV) and the rated voltage (V); the choke's nominal inductance LN and stray inductance LS per path (mH, µH) and the rated frequency (Hz). The picker in the Output heading fills LN and LS from one of Schaffner's 24 RB chokes (typing either goes back to "typed values"). The big result is the Y-capacitor of each line; in three cells the X-capacitor, the differential corner frequency and the leakage current of the Y-capacitor. Rows: the attenuation needed in each mode (noise − limit + margin); the next E6 value above each capacitor with the attenuation it gives at the frequency (and, for the Y-capacitor, its leakage current); and, for a listed choke, its current rating and its saturation limits as the note prints them. A mode whose noise is already under the limit needs no capacitor. The drawing is the filter: the choke's two windings on one core (blue), the X-capacitor across the lines and a Y-capacitor from each line to earth (green).

  • Choke: the choke alone. The inductance (mH), the winding capacitance in parallel with it (pF, 0 for none), the frequency (kHz or MHz) and the resistance of the source and load together (Ω). The big result is the impedance at the frequency; in three cells the resonance, the ideal impedance ωL and the attenuation the impedance makes between that source and load. It says whether the choke is inductive or capacitive there. The drawing is the inductor with its capacitance in parallel.

  • Units: kHz and MHz for the Choke pill's frequency; the other numbers have a fixed unit.

  • Remembered: the pill and the Choke pill's frequency unit.

Examples: Schaffner's 1.6 kW converter, the 3 mH choke RB8522-16-3M0, the same on 120 V and 60 Hz, a common mode already under the limit, a measured choke (19.6 mH, 45.9 pF) and 1 mH at 1 MHz.

Terms

  • Common mode, differential mode: common-mode noise is the same on both lines and returns through earth; differential-mode noise is opposite on the two lines, like the wanted signal.
  • Nominal inductance LN: the inductance of one winding path, tested by Schaffner at 1 kHz; the choke's inductance for common mode. Stray inductance LS: the part of the flux the two windings do not share, the choke's inductance for differential mode; about 1 % of LN (0.6 to 1.1 % in the table below).
  • X-capacitor, Y-capacitor: a capacitor across the two lines (X) holds back differential noise; one from each line to earth (Y) holds back common-mode noise and lets a leakage current flow to earth at the mains frequency, which the safety standards limit. PE: protective earth.
  • Conducted emissions, quasi-peak limit: the noise a device puts on its mains cable, limited from 150 kHz (9 kHz for some products) by standards such as IEC/EN 61000-6-3; the quasi-peak (QP) is the detector the limit is written for. dBµV: decibels above one microvolt.
  • Harmonic; corner frequency: the filter is designed at the first harmonic of the switching frequency above 150 kHz (the 9th of 20 kHz is 180 kHz). A second-order LC low-pass passes everything below its corner frequency fc and attenuates 40 dB per decade above it, A = 40 log(f / fc).
  • Saturation; ICM max, IDM max: a core saturates when too much flux drives it. Schaffner gives, per choke, the largest current through one winding that does not (ICM max, common mode) and the largest peak current back and forth through both (IDM max, differential).
  • Winding capacitance, self-resonant frequency (SRF): the capacitance between the turns, in parallel with the inductance; at 1 / (2π√(LC)) the pair resonates and the impedance peaks, below it the choke is inductive, above it capacitive.
  • E6: the series of preferred values 1.0, 1.5, 2.2, 3.3, 4.7, 6.8 (and ×10).
  • Bifilar, sectional winding: the two wires wound side by side (low leakage inductance, for signal lines) or in separate sections (more separation for high voltage, higher leakage inductance) (Arar, from Würth's figure).

Sources

  • Schaffner, "EMC/EMI Filter Design with RB Common-Mode Chokes", application note (07/2013; the PDF, from simpex.ch, read): the choke and its windings; LN tested at 1 kHz and the stray LS (about 1 % of LN); CM noise held back by LN and the Y-capacitors, DM noise by LS and the X-capacitor; the saturation limits ICM max and IDM max; Z = ωL (equation 2) and the resonance 1 / (2π√(L CWI)) (equation 3), for a copper resistance under 10 Ω and an iron loss over 1 MΩ; the design example (1.6 kW half-bridge on 115 V AC, 20 kHz, IEC/EN 61000-6-3, the QP limit of 65 dBµV at the 9th harmonic, 180 kHz, a margin of 3 dB): A = An − LQP + m (equation 6), A = 40 log(f / fc), fc = f · 10^(−A/40) (7), fc,DM = 1 / (2π√(2 LS CX)), fc,CM = 1 / (2π√(2 LN CY)) and C = 1 / (8π² L fc²) (8), Ilk = 2π fR UR CY (9), with its numbers; the table of 24 RB chokes. Equations 7 to 9 are pictures in the PDF whose text came out in pieces: I put them together and checked them against every number the example prints, to the digit.
  • Dr. Steve Arar, All About Circuits, "Common-Mode Chokes: From Working Principles to Important Performance Parameters" (5 May 2024; the page, read): fluxes cancel for a differential current and add for a common-mode one, so the core does not saturate on the wanted current; Zdm = jωL − jωM + R, about R, and Zcm = jωL + jωM + R, about jω 2L for each winding when L = M; the winding capacitance makes a parallel resonance, inductive below it and capacitive above; bifilar and sectional windings.
  • Omicron Lab, Bode 500 application note "Modeling Multi-Resonance Common-Mode Chokes" (the PDF, read): the common-mode impedance of a choke is measured with terminals 1 and 3 joined and 2 and 4 joined (the two windings in parallel), the differential one by exciting between 1 and 3 with 2 and 4 shorted (through both windings); for a Würth WE-CMB 744824220 the fitted first stage is L = 19.636 mH and C = 45.872 pF, which resonate at about 168 kHz (f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC))), against a first measured peak at 164.8 kHz.
  • Not read: Würth's application notes and Coilcraft's note (both servers refused the download and were left alone); IEC/EN 61000-6-3, CISPR 17 and the safety standards (the 65 dBµV and the 3.5 mA are the note's); Stevanovic's behavioural model; other makers' chokes and the signal-line chokes (USB, CAN, Ethernet), whose datasheets give the common-mode impedance at 100 MHz.

Why the formulas are these

The attenuation needed. The first harmonic above 150 kHz carries the noise An; the filter has to bring it under the limit LQP with a margin m: A = An − LQP + m. 108 − 65 + 3 is 46 dB for common mode and 101 − 65 + 3 is 39 dB for differential mode in Schaffner's example.

The corner. A second-order LC low-pass attenuates 40 dB per decade above its corner (Schaffner), so A = 40 log(f / fc) and fc = f · 10^(−A/40): 19.07 kHz and 12.74 kHz.

The capacitors. For common mode the two windings are in parallel, which gives the choke's LN (Omicron's measurement, Arar's Zcm per winding 2L over two windings), and the two Y-capacitors are in parallel, 2 CY: fc = 1 / (2π√(2 LN CY)). For differential mode the current goes through both windings, 2 LS, with the X-capacitor across the lines: fc = 1 / (2π√(2 LS CX)). Solving, C = 1 / (8π² L fc²) for each. A capacitor off the list gives A = 40 log(f / fc) = 20 log(8π² L C f²), which the tool uses for the E6 values.

The leakage. Ilk = 2π fR UR CY is the reactive current of the Y-capacitor at the rated voltage and frequency (250 V at 50 Hz: 33 nF leaks 2.6 mA, 100 nF 7.9 mA).

The choke alone. Schaffner's Z = ωL and f = 1 / (2π√(L C)) are the first two lines. With the winding capacitance in parallel the impedance is jωL / (1 − ω² L C), inductive under the resonance and capacitive over it (derived; Arar and Schaffner describe the shape). Between a source and a load of R in all and a reactance of impedance Z, the voltage across the load falls by |R + jZ| / R, an insertion loss of 10 log(1 + (Z / R)²) (derived from the definition; none of the sources gives it).

Assumptions and limits

  • An ideal second-order filter. Schaffner's own measurements are close at the designed frequency (45 and 44 dBµV of common-mode attenuation measured for 46 designed; 39 dBµV of differential measured for 39 in the first design, 30 for 39 in the second, until a load-side X-capacitor made 63) and then fall away above 300 kHz from parasitics. The note says so; the tool is the design step, not the verification.
  • Single-phase, two-wire. The equations are those of the note's single-phase example. The three-wire chokes (RBxx32) are listed with their data, but the note gives no three-phase filter equations and none is computed.
  • LN is the 1 kHz value. The permeability of the core falls with frequency (the note's Figure 4): the inductance at 180 kHz is lower, which the tool does not know. Real attenuation can be less.
  • The levels are yours. The noise levels and the limit are typed; the tool does not know the standard or estimate the noise (the note does it by hand with a Fourier series and an envelope).
  • Leakage and safety. The leakage current is for one Y-capacitor at the rated values; the limits (the note's second design aims at 3.5 mA) are not stored. X and Y capacitors have to be of the safety classes the application needs (the note says X2 and Y2 for class I), which the tool does not check.
  • The E6 value shown is the next one above the computed capacitance, so the attenuation is at least the one asked; Schaffner picked 100 nF and 4.7 µF in the first design, 33 nF and 1.5 µF in the second, choosing by leakage and by availability.
  • The choke's table is Schaffner's as printed. Its last column, the common-mode limit at 100 °C, is headed IDMmax by mistake. RB6532-50-0M5 prints 0.18 mH although its code says 0.5 mH (the RB6132-50-0M2 has 0.18). The example uses LS = 6.3 µH for the RB6522-16-1M0 where the table prints 6.2. The tool takes the table's values. Only the saturation limits at 25 °C are shown; the heating (I²R) and the line current are not computed.
  • The rounding in the example. Schaffner rounds the corner frequencies to 19 and 12.7 kHz before taking the capacitors and prints 5.6 µF and 79 nF; the tool keeps the unrounded corners and gives 5.53 µF and 78 nF (with 19 and 12.7 kHz: 5.57 µF and 78.5 nF).
  • The Choke pill is the first resonance only. A real choke has several (Omicron's fit has four stages) and losses; the impedance at the resonance is then finite, the tool's model has none and says "no limit" at it. The common-mode and the differential impedance of a datasheet, the bandwidth of a signal-line choke and its signal integrity are not here.
  • Display. Three figures; capacitances in pF, nF or µF, impedances in Ω, kΩ or MΩ.

How it was checked

85 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the formulas above (every figure and every label of the drawings; the parts table and the notes read out of the tool): - Filter: Schaffner's example; each of the 24 chokes; frequencies from 9 kHz to 1.5 MHz, other limits, margins and noise levels, three mains voltages and frequencies, two other inductances, a mode under the limit, both under, exactly 0 dB and a negative need; the picker and its return to typed values; nine refusals; - Choke: Omicron's pair at 100 kHz, without capacitance, just under and just over the resonance, at 1 kHz and 10 MHz, other loops, the frequency unit picker, six refusals and the remembered choices; - the six examples and the formula-search card.

About 1 200 more cases (four batches of 300: random frequencies, limits, margins, noise levels, voltages, chokes and inductances, random inductances, capacitances, frequencies and loops) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

Balun

What it computes

A balun joins a balanced circuit (two lines carrying equal and opposite voltages: a dipole, a twisted pair) to an unbalanced one (a signal and a ground: coax). It can also change the impedance. The tool covers three things a designer asks of one. Three pills:

  • Ratio: the unbalanced side's impedance Zu (50 Ω) and the balanced side's Zb (200 Ω), both in ohms; chips set the balanced side to 50, 73 (a dipole in free space), 100 and 200 Ω. The big result is the impedance ratio needed, 1 : Zb/Zu, with the turns ratio of a flux-coupled transformer under it. In three cells, for the ratio chosen: the turns ratio, the VSWR left on the unbalanced side and the mismatch loss. Below, the ratios in common use (1:1, 1:2, 1:4, 1:9, 1:16), each with the impedance it brings the load to and the VSWR; the best is chosen, and a tap on another draws it. Typing an impedance goes back to the best. The drawing is the transformer with its centre tap, the unbalanced port at the left (its ground at the bottom) and the balanced load at the right; the transformer and the ratio are green.
  • Lines: a transmission-line balun, one of Guanella 1:1, 1:4, 1:9, 1:16 (one, two, three or four lines), Ruthroff 1:4 or the half-wave coax 1:4, from the source impedance Zu. For Guanella's and Ruthroff's: the line impedance Z0 each line should have, the balanced impedance it is made for (ratio × Zu) and the voltage gain; the drawing shows how the lines are joined. For the half-wave balun, a frequency and a velocity factor (typed, or the cable picker in the Output heading, with the Belden cables of the Coax tool): the length of cable, the free-space wavelength and the wavelength in the cable.

  • Balance: how well the two outputs match, and what that leaves of the rejection of a common-mode signal. The inputs are the two imbalances (the amplitude imbalance in dB, the phase imbalance in degrees from 180°; chips for ±1 dB and ±10°, ±0.2 dB and ±2°, ±0.1 dB and ±1°), or, with the picker in the Output heading, the S-parameters S21 and S31 (magnitude, linear or dB, and phase). The big result is the CMRR; in three cells the two imbalances and the common-mode part of the signal as a percentage of the wanted part; from S-parameters also Gdm and Gcm. An optional target CMRR gives the largest phase imbalance, the largest amplitude imbalance, and the largest phase imbalance at the amplitude given, that still reach it. The chart is the CMRR against the phase imbalance, the green curve for the amplitude imbalance typed, grey ones for 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2 dB, a blue stem at the phase.

  • Units: ohms; the frequency in kHz, MHz or GHz; S-parameter magnitudes linear or dB (changing the picker converts the numbers typed).

  • Remembered: the pill, the balun, the frequency unit, the given picker and the magnitude unit.

Examples: 50 Ω coax to a 200 Ω load, a 73 Ω dipole on 50 Ω coax, a Guanella 1:4 from 50 Ω, a half-wave balun at 145 MHz, Arar's worked S-parameters, and a good balun (0.1 dB and 1°).

Terms

  • Balanced and unbalanced: a balanced circuit has two conductors carrying equal and opposite voltages, neither at ground (a dipole's two arms, a twisted pair); an unbalanced one has a signal conductor and a ground (coax, whose outer conductor is the ground). The balanced impedance is the one between the two lines, twice the impedance from one line to ground (Marki).
  • Balun: short for balanced-unbalanced. Ideally a three-port device whose two balanced outputs are equal and 180° apart, S21 = −S31 (Marki, Arar). The unbalanced port is port 1, the two balanced terminals ports 2 and 3.
  • Impedance ratio, turns ratio: for a transformer with N1 turns on the unbalanced side and N2 on the other, n = N2 / N1; the voltage is n times, the current 1 / n times and the impedance n² times (Mini-Circuits; Marki). The impedance ratio is the square of the turns ratio: 1 : 2 in turns is 1 : 4 in impedance.
  • Flux-coupled (conventional) transformer: two windings on a magnetic core; it can have any ratio, gives DC isolation, and is limited in frequency (Marki: under about 1 GHz; Mini-Circuits: 2 GHz for the core-and-wire kinds). A centre tap on the balanced winding, to ground, improves the balance (Marki; Mini-Circuits).
  • Transmission-line transformer; bifilar coil: a transformer whose windings behave as a transmission line: two wires wound side by side (or a coax) on a ferrite core. Wider band than a flux-coupled one; no DC isolation (Mini-Circuits). Guanella's: n lines, inputs in parallel, outputs in series, so 1 : n². Ruthroff's: one line, a 1:4 with less bandwidth. A half-wave balun takes one output straight from the cable and the other after a half wavelength of cable (Arar; Creative Science).
  • Unun: an unbalanced-to-unbalanced transformer (Ruthroff's 1:4 without the balun connection). Not computed here.
  • Amplitude imbalance, phase imbalance: the difference of the two outputs' magnitudes in dB, 20 log(|S21| / |S31|), and the deviation of their phase difference from 180° (Mini-Circuits; Arar).
  • Differential and common-mode gain: Gdm = (S21 − S31) / √2 and Gcm = (S21 + S31) / √2 (Arar). CMRR: the common-mode rejection ratio, |Gdm / Gcm| in dB: how much the wanted differential signal exceeds the unwanted common-mode part that leaks through the imbalance.
  • VSWR, mismatch loss: for the impedance Zin a balun brings the load to, on the unbalanced side Zu: Γ = (Zin − Zu) / (Zin + Zu), VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|), the larger impedance over the smaller; the mismatch loss is −10 log(1 − Γ²), the power not delivered.
  • Velocity factor (VF): how fast the wave travels on the cable compared with light; a half wave of cable is c · VF / (2 f) long.

Sources

  • Marki Microwave, "Balun Primer" (Jorgesen and Marki; the PDF edited 2026; read): a balun is a three-port device with S12 = −S13 = S21 = −S31 and S11 = −∞; phase and amplitude balance and the CMRR set by their vector addition; "low performance" baluns ±1 dB and ±10° at 15 to 20 dB of CMRR, Marki's own up to 45 dB; the impedance ratio (stated 1:1, 1:2, 1:4) is the square of the turns ratio, and the differential impedance is twice the impedance to ground; the centre tap; the transmission-line types, its Figure 5 (1:1, Guanella 1:4, Ruthroff 1:4, looked at). Its Figure 2, CMRR against the amplitude and phase balances, was read from the picture.
  • Mini-Circuits, "Application Note on Transformers", AN-20-002 Rev. B (2015; the PDF, read): n = N2 / N1, V2 = n V1, I2 = I1 / n, Z2 = n² Z1 (its example: n = 2 on 50 Ω is 200 Ω); the definitions of amplitude and phase unbalance, and that a well designed transformer might have 0.1 dB and 1°; the table of configurations (frequency ranges, impedance ratios, which have no DC isolation: the transmission-line ones).
  • Dr. Steve Arar, All About Circuits, "Balun Basics and Practical Performance Parameters" (21 January 2024; the page, read): S21 = −S31; Gdm = (S21 − S31) / √2, Gcm = (S21 + S31) / √2, CMRR = |Gdm / Gcm| = |(S21 − S31) / (S21 + S31)|; the worked example S21 = 0.66 at 0°, S31 = 0.75 at −170°: 1.11 dB, 10°, Gdm −0.06 dB, Gcm −19.4 dB, CMRR 19.3 dB; ±1 dB and ±10° typical of a low-performance balun, ±0.2 dB and ±2° of a higher-performance one. "Understanding the Guanella Transmission Line Balun" (4 February 2024, read): the 1:4 balun from two lines, Z0 = RL / 2; the 1:n² balun from n lines, Z0 = RL / n and RS = RL / n²; the half-wavelength balun as a narrowband 1:4. "A Brief Introduction to Ruthroff Transmission Line Transformers" (7 April 2024, read): the 1:4 unun and balun from one bifilar coil, Z0 = √(RS RL); no DC isolation; less bandwidth than Guanella's. I looked at the figures of the last two to get the connections right (Guanella 1:4, Ruthroff 1:4 balun); the drawings are my own.
  • L. B. Cebik, W4RNL, "The Impedance-Transformation Properties of Common 4:1 Balun Types", part 1 (the PDF, read): a 4:1 balun is made to transform a 200 Ω load to 50 Ω, normally over 3.5 to 30 MHz; baluns divide into voltage and current types.
  • Dr. Jonathan Hare, The Creative Science Centre, "The 4:1 half-wave coax balun" (the page, read): one output from the cable, the other after a half wave of cable, the shields joined at one point; 180° apart, twice the voltage, 4:1.
  • Keysight (HP) 5988-5635EN, balanced measurements (the PDF, read): the mixed-mode S-parameter naming; that the balun method of measuring a balanced device cannot show mode conversion.
  • For the antenna feed point: the 73 Ω of a dipole in free space is NEETS's, as in the Antenna length tool. RF Essentials' glossary page on baluns (read) gives CMRR ≈ −20 log(√(ΔA² + Δφ²)) with ΔA = dB / 20 and Δφ in radians, and an example, 0.5 dB and 5° giving 25 dB; the formula gives 20.8 dB, so it was not used.
  • Not read: Jerry Sevick's books and his High Frequency Electronics article (its address returned 404), nor Trask's there; Ruthroff's 1959 paper and Guanella's patents; the IEEE standards; Texas Instruments' and Analog Devices' balun notes. Two servers refused or hid their pages (Mouser's copy of a Marki note, and Pasternack's blog, behind a bot check) and were left alone.

Why the formulas are these

Ratio. The ideal transformer gives Z2 = n² Z1 (Mini-Circuits), so a balanced load Zb seen through a balun of impedance ratio r is Zin = Zb / r on the unbalanced side. The VSWR of a real impedance Zin against Zu is the larger over the smaller; the reflection is Γ = (Zin − Zu) / (Zin + Zu), the mismatch loss −10 log(1 − Γ²). The best of the ratios in common use is the one with the least VSWR (the smaller wins a tie), which for a need of 1 : 1.46 (73 Ω on 50 Ω) is 1 : 2, with 1.37, not 1 : 1, with 1.46.

Lines. Arar's Guanella 1:4 gets twice the voltage from two lines, and each line sees half the load, so Z0 = RL / 2; with n lines Z0 = RL / n and RS = RL / n², which makes Z0 = √(RS RL), the form Arar gives for Ruthroff's. The half-wave length is c · VF / (2 f) with c = 299 792 458 m/s.

Balance. Put S21 = 1 and S31 = r at 180° + ψ (r the ratio of the magnitudes, ψ the phase imbalance). Then |S21 − S31|² = 1 + r² + 2 r cos ψ and |S21 + S31|² = 1 + r² − 2 r cos ψ, and Arar's CMRR is

CMRR = 10 log [(1 + r² + 2 r cos ψ) / (1 + r² − 2 r cos ψ)]

which the tool evaluates as [(1 + r)² − 4 r sin²(ψ/2)] / [(r − 1)² + 4 r sin²(ψ/2)] so that it does not lose its digits near perfect balance. For small imbalances it is about 20 log (2 / √(ε² + ψ²)) with ε = ln r (0.115 per dB) and ψ in radians. From the S-parameters directly the tool computes Gdm and Gcm as Arar does. A target T dB gives, with x = 10^(−T/20): the phase alone ψ = 2 atan x (r = 1), the amplitude alone r = (1 + x) / (1 − x), and, for a given r, sin²(ψ/2) = [(1 + r)² − K (r − 1)²] / [4 r (1 + K)] with K = 10^(T/10); these three are derived, not published.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal parts. The transformer ratio and the line impedances are the lossless ideal. A real balun has insertion loss, a lowest and a highest frequency, and finite coupling (Marki, Mini-Circuits); none of that is computed. The "wide" and "narrow" of the notes are those of Arar, Marki and Mini-Circuits.
  • The ratios in common use are the three Marki states (1:1, 1:2, 1:4) and Guanella's 1:n² (1:9 and 1:16 with three and four lines). A flux-coupled transformer can be made with any ratio (Marki; Mini-Circuits give 1 to 16, 25 or 36); the big result is the exact one.
  • Guanella's and Ruthroff's Z0 are the optimum Arar gives for an ideal, lossless line; a cable of that impedance may not exist (100 Ω for a 1:4 from 50 Ω), and what is used instead mismatches a little. Not computed.
  • The half-wave balun is exact at one frequency. At exactly half a wavelength the line's matrix is minus the identity, so the far end is the exact opposite of the near end whatever the load or the cable's impedance (derived); away from that frequency the balance depends on both, and the tool does not compute it. The velocity factors of the cable list are the Belden sheets' of the Coax tool; a real length is trimmed.
  • Marki's CMRR figure. Its Figure 2 reads 2 to 3 dB below Arar's formula (about −19 dB at 1.2 dB and 7°, where the formula gives 21 dB). Arar's worked example reproduces to the digit, as do Marki's and Arar's round numbers (about 20 dB for ±1 dB and ±10°), so the formula was kept; I could not tell why the figure differs.
  • CMRR is of the balun alone. The imbalance of the antenna or the load, and a choke's common-mode impedance, are not here (Common mode choke is its own tool).
  • The antenna feed point is not computed: the 73 Ω chip is a dipole in free space, and a real one is anything from 0 to about 100 Ω over a ground plane (the Antenna length tool's manual).
  • Display. Three figures; a CMRR of 300 dB or more is "no limit", and outputs in phase leave no differential signal ("none").

How it was checked

111 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the formulas above (every figure and every label of the drawings): - Ratio: the example, the dipole, 1:2, 1:9, 1:16, equal, a balanced side below the unbalanced, 2 kΩ and 5 Ω, and the middles between two ratios; a tap on each of the five rows; the chips; a pick dropped when an impedance is typed; the refusals; - Lines: the six baluns from 50 and 75 Ω; the half-wave balun at five frequencies and velocity factors; each of the seven cables; the pickers; the refusals; the remembered choices; - Balance: the low-performance and the good balun, ideal, phase only, amplitude only, negative and wrapped imbalances; five targets; eight S-parameter sets in linear and dB, and the conversion of the picker; the two edges (90° of phase imbalance is 0 dB, outputs in phase leave no differential signal); - the six examples and the formula-search card.

About 1 800 more cases (600 random plans in each of three batches: random impedances and picks, random baluns, frequencies and velocity factors, random imbalances and S-parameters with and without a target) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept. One batch found the rounding noise at exactly 0 dB (shown as 0.0000000000000019 dB) and the in-phase case (a logarithm of zero), both now handled.
