RF & microwave › RF components

SAW filter

What it computes

A surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) filter is two metal combs, interdigital transducers (IDTs), on a piezoelectric crystal. A voltage on the first comb launches a wave along the surface of the crystal; the second comb turns it back into a voltage. The wave is slow, 2 000 to 5 000 m/s (the standard), so the structure is small and a long delay fits on a chip. The tool does four jobs, one per pill. The picker in the Output heading chooses the crystal (the six of the standard's table, each with its wave speed); the first three pills use it.

  • Transducer: one comb of a filter of two identical uniform combs. The inputs, three to a row: the centre frequency (MHz), the finger pairs N of each comb, the aperture in wavelengths (the standard's own way of giving it); then the resistance of the source and of the load (Ω, the same at both ends). The big result is the period λ of the fingers, one wavelength, v / f0, with the width of a finger and of a gap, λ/4, under it. Cells: the −3 dB width of the response, the static capacitance CT of the comb and the shunt coil that tunes it out. Rows: the relative bandwidth; the radiation resistance Ra of the comb (what the power that leaves as sound looks like to the circuit) and its Q; the loss at the centre in that source and load; the aperture that would make Ra equal to R; the size of the comb; and the widest bandwidth the crystal can be tuned for, met or not. The drawing is one comb, tuned: the source (blue), then the coil, CT and Ra across it (green), and the sound leaving.
  • Echoes: the distance between the two combs (mm), the insertion loss of the filter (dB) and, if you have it from a data sheet, the echo level (dB); left empty, the rule 2 IL + 6 gives it. The big result is the delay t = distance / wave speed. Cells: how much later than the wanted signal the echo comes (2t), the period of the ripple the echo makes in the passband, 1 / (2t), and of the one the direct leakage makes, 1 / t. Rows: the echo level; the ripple it makes, peak to peak; and the group-delay ripple. The drawing is the two combs on the crystal, the wanted signal crossing once (green) and the echo crossing twice more (amber).
  • Drift: how far the response moves over a temperature range. The frequency (MHz), the cold and the hot end (°C), the reference temperature at which the frequency is given (25 °C), and, for the two crystals whose response is a parabola (ST quartz and Li₂B₄O₇), the turnover temperature. The big result is the span of the shift over the range; cells: the shift at the cold end and at the hot end from the reference, and the coefficient (ppm/K, or ppm/K² for a parabola). The drawing is the shift against temperature.

  • Resonator: the equivalent circuit of a one-port SAW resonator. The picker in the Output heading chooses what you know. Given: R, L, C: the motional resistance Rm (Ω), inductance Lm (µH) and capacitance Cm (fF), the static capacitance C0 and a series load capacitance CL (pF); the big result is the series resonance fs; cells: the antiresonance fp, Q and the capacitance ratio C0 / Cm. Given: fs, fp, Q: the two resonances (MHz) and Q, with C0 and CL; the tool finds Rm (big result), Lm, Cm and the ratio. In both, rows: the split fp − fs, the coupling K², the resonance with CL in series and the pulling CL makes. The drawing is the Butterworth-Van Dyke circuit, the parts you typed in blue and the ones found in green.

  • Units: fixed (MHz, mm, °C, pF, fF, µH, Ω); the crystal and the way into the Resonator are the two pickers.

  • Remembered: the pill, the crystal and the way into the Resonator.

Examples: 100 MHz on 128° LiNbO₃, 433.92 MHz on ST quartz, too wide for quartz, a 40 dB echo (the standard's example), 5 mm and 20 dB of loss, −40 to 85 °C on LiNbO₃ and on quartz, a measured resonator at 435 MHz and the same from its frequencies.

Terms

  • SAW, Rayleigh wave: an acoustic wave that travels along the surface of a solid, its amplitude falling off exponentially with depth (IEC), so its energy stays within about a wavelength of the surface. Lord Rayleigh described it in 1885 (Hribšek et al.).
  • IDT, finger, pair, period: a transducer is two comb-shaped metal electrodes with interleaved fingers on the crystal; a finger of each comb makes a pair; the period 2d is the distance between two fingers of the same comb, and it is one wavelength: f0 = v / (2d). With equal lines and spaces a finger and a gap are λ/4 each; in a split-finger comb, four fingers to the wavelength, λ/8 (the standard's Figure 9).
  • Aperture: the width over which the fingers overlap; in the standard, the width of the beam in wavelengths. Apodization: varying the overlap along the comb to shape the response (not computed here; the tool's combs are uniform).
  • Coupling coefficient k² (K²): the relative change of the wave's speed when metal shorts the surface, times two: k² = 2Δv / v. It is the share of the electrical energy the crystal turns into sound: the larger, the wider and the lower-loss the filter can be.
  • Effective permittivity εr: of an anisotropic crystal, √(ε11 ε33 − ε13²) (the standard). It sets the capacitance of the comb.
  • Radiation conductance Ga, resistance Ra = 1/Ga: at the centre frequency the power that leaves the comb as sound is, to the circuit, a conductance in parallel with the comb's capacitance. Shunt coil: an inductor across the comb that resonates its capacitance at f0, leaving only Ga. Q of the comb: ω0 CT / Ga.
  • Insertion loss; bidirectional loss: a comb sends the wave both ways, so each comb loses 3 dB and a filter of two loses 6 dB at least; the standard says so.
  • Triple-transit echo (TTE): the wave reflected by the output comb and again by the input comb arrives three transits after launch, two delays behind the wanted signal. Feed-through: the signal that goes straight across by capacitance, with no delay. Both ripple the passband.
  • Group delay: the derivative of the phase with respect to angular frequency.
  • TCF, TCD, turnover: the temperature coefficient of frequency (ppm per kelvin) and of delay (the same size, the opposite sign). Quartz and Li₂B₄O₇ have a turnover temperature where it is zero, and a response that bends like a parabola about it.
  • Motional branch, static capacitance C0: the Butterworth-Van Dyke circuit of a resonator is a series Rm, Lm, Cm (the vibration: loss, mass, stiffness) in parallel with the capacitance C0 of the comb. fs, fp: the series resonance, where the branch is a short, and the antiresonance just above it, where it and C0 resonate. Q = ωs Lm / Rm. Capacitance ratio C0 / Cm. Load capacitance, pulling: a capacitor in series with a crystal or a SAW resonator in an oscillator moves the frequency from fs towards fp.
  • Ladder, lattice, coupled-resonator, unidirectional, three-IDT and IIDT filters; shape factor: the other filters and specifications of the standard, not computed (the loss of an IIDT filter is 10 log((N + 1) / N) dB for N output and N + 1 input combs, the standard says).

Sources

  • IS/IEC 60862-2 : 2002, "Surface acoustic wave (SAW) filters of assessed quality, Part 2: Guidance on use" (the Bureau of Indian Standards' identical copy, posted by Public.Resource.Org on law.resource.org; all 58 PDF pages read as text; pages 19, 46, 47, 48 and 49 also rendered and read as printed): the definitions (SAW, IDT, aperture, k² = 2Δv/v, the shape factor, the group delay, the triple-transit echo, the reflection coefficient); f0 = v / (2d) (5.1 and 7.1 a); the response of two uniform identical transducers T(f) = (sin x / x)², x = Nπ (f − f0) / f0 (equation 3); 3 dB lost at each transducer and so 6 dB at the least (5.3); CT = w N (1 + εr) ε0 for equal lines and spaces (7.1 d); the comb is capacitive and is tuned with coils, and it can be matched when k² > (π / 4) (Δf / f0)² (7.2 a, rendered: the extracted text had lost the square), otherwise the conversion loss is limited, as the minimum loss curves of Figure 37 show; the echo is 2t behind the main signal and ripples the passband with period 1 / (2t), the feed-through with 1 / t (Figure 39); an echo 40 dB down gives about ±0.1 dB of ripple and ±0.02 t of group delay; the echo is suppressed twice as much as the loss is increased (7.2 c); Table 1, the substrates. The 2002 edition; I did not read a later one.
  • Spectrum Control, "Introduction to SAW Filter Theory & Design Techniques" (white paper, 16 pages; Table 1 rendered): seven substrates with their speed, temperature coefficient and coupling; the response of all but quartz shifts up at low temperature and down at high temperature; quartz is a downward parabola with a turnover temperature; the loss of a bidirectional filter is 3 dB at each transducer; the triple transit TT = 2 IL + 6 dB (its own example: 6 dB of loss, about 18 dB).
  • COMSOL blog, "Leveraging the mBVD Circuit Model for MEMS Resonator Design" (read in full): Cm = C0 ((fp / fs)² − 1), Lm = 1 / ((2π fs)² Cm), Rm = √(Lm / Cm) / Q, fs = 1 / (2π √(Lm Cm)); the gap between fs and fp sets the coupling and so the achievable bandwidth.
  • Westrelin, Abdallah, Debavelear, Lefebvre, Lmimouni, Stienne and Hafsi, "Design and Fabrication Of Multiplexed One-Port SAW Resonators On A Single Chip" (arXiv 2506.13788, 9 pages, read): the Butterworth-Van Dyke circuit of a resonator (fr from Lm and Cm, Q = ωr Lm / Rm, fa = fr √(1 + Cm / C0)), the finger width of a quarter wavelength, and the measured values of two ST-quartz resonators near 435 MHz (its Table 2).
  • Wang, Lee, Yang and Park, "Design Optimization of SAW Pressure Sensor with Equivalent Circuit Model", Sensors and Materials 18 (2006) 301 (read; page 4 rendered): the crossed-field circuit of a comb, with the radiation conductance g_a = (4/π) K² ω0 N Ct, Ct = N Cs W λ the total static capacitance, and the susceptance. The paper prints the conductance as g_a (sin x / x), without the square the model has (and the standard's two-comb response T = (sin x / x)² needs); I took the square. K² is the 2Δv/v of the standard (17.2 % for 41° YX LiNbO₃ from its 4 792.2 and 4 379.7 m/s).
  • Hribšek, Ristić, Živković and Tošić, "Modelling of SAW biosensors" (BIODEVICES 2009, read): the delta-function model is the simplest and fast, but its use is limited to small loads and substrates of lower coupling; Lord Rayleigh's 1885 discovery.
  • Asakawa et al. (IEEE IUS 2019) and Gomi et al. (Symposium on Ultrasonic Electronics 2016) (read): K² = 2(vf − vm)/vf, the same definition; their subjects (bonded thin plates) are not used.
  • Agilent Application Note 1373-5, "Balanced Measurement Example: SAW Filters" (read): a SAW filter is most conveniently designed for high port impedances, and one for 350 Ω per terminal (700 Ω differential) measured in 50 Ω shows 14.5 dB single-ended against 8.9 dB in its own system. Not used in the numbers.
  • Read and not used: the next.gr tutorial "Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) Filters" (its radiation conductance has CT N² where the model has N CT, its aperture W = N p and 1/QL = 1/Qu + K² are not in any source I read), and a vendor page that gives f = v / λ with v about 3 100 m/s.
  • Not read: IEC 61019-1 and -2 (SAW resonators; only the contents, foreword and scope pages of the previews), Hashimoto's lecture notes at Chiba University (the host name did not resolve), Morgan's and Campbell's books, the makers' data sheets. Four pages refused the download (urgentcomm.com, core.ac.uk, zenodo.org, and a PMC table behind a robot check) and were left alone.

Why the formulas are these

The period. The wave crosses one period of the comb in one cycle of the signal, so f0 = v / λ with λ the period (IEC equation 2: f0 = v / (2d), 2d the period). 128° LiNbO₃ at 100 MHz: λ = 4 000 / 100 · 10⁶ = 40 µm, a finger 10 µm.

The bandwidth. One comb of N pairs has the response sin x / x, x = Nπ (f − f0) / f0; two identical combs give T = (sin x / x)² (IEC equation 3). I read T as an amplitude ratio, which is what a transfer function is (the standard does not say so in words), so the −3 dB points are where (sin x / x)² = 10^(−3/20), at x = 1.00025: the width is 2 x f0 / (π N) = 0.637 f0 / N (derived here; the standard prints the response, not this width. The null-to-null width is 2 f0 / N and the −6 dB one 0.884 f0 / N). Twenty pairs at 100 MHz: 3.18 MHz.

The capacitance and the conductance. CT = w N (1 + εr) ε0 for an aperture w = (aperture in wavelengths) × λ and the standard's εr (7.1 d). The crossed-field circuit gives the conductance at the centre Ga = 8 k² f0 N CT, which is (4/π) k² ω0 N CT of Wang et al. Check: the comb's Q is ω0 CT / Ga = π / (4 k² N), and it can be tuned across the band when its bandwidth 1 / Q is at least the acoustic one, f0 / N (to a factor of order one): k² ≥ (π / 4) / N² = (π / 4) (Δf / f0)², the condition the standard prints. That the two agree is the reason to trust the 8 in Ga. The widest bandwidth that can be tuned perfectly is that condition solved for Δf / f0: √(4 k² / π): 4.5 % for ST quartz, 9.0 % for X-112° LiTaO₃, 24.8 % for YZ LiNbO₃ and 26.6 % for 128° LiNbO₃, where the four curves of the standard's Figure 37 leave 0 dB at about 4, 9, 20 and 25 % (read by eye on the rendered page). Beyond it the standard says the conversion loss is limited and inversely proportional to k²; the tool does not compute it (the figure shows about 40 dB more per decade of bandwidth).

The coil. The comb is capacitive (the standard); a shunt coil L resonates it at f0, L = 1 / (ω0² CT) (derived; the standard says the comb is tuned with coils and gives an example, "a shunt wire wound inductor of 200 nH" at 97.3 MHz, which is 13.4 pF).

The loss at the centre (derived). A tuned comb is, at f0, the conductance Ga. With a source or a load of conductance GL = 1 / R, y = GL / Ga = Ra / R, a comb that sends the wave both ways couples a fraction 4y / (1 + y)² of the power to or from half of the sound, so each comb loses 3 dB plus 10 log((1 + y)² / 4y), and two with the same R lose 20 log((1 + y)² / (2y)). It is 6.02 dB at y = 1, the standard's 6 dB at the least, and grows as Ra and R part. 433.92 MHz on ST quartz with 100 pairs and 50 λ has Ra = 1.02 kΩ: 21 dB between 50 Ω ends, 6.02 dB between 1 kΩ ones.

The aperture for Ra = R. Ga is proportional to the aperture, so Ra = R at the aperture (typed aperture) × Ra / R.

The delay and the echoes. t = distance / v. The echo has crossed the filter three times, so it is 2t late; its ripple has the period 1 / (2t) and the feed-through's 1 / t (IEC Figure 39). An echo of ratio a to the main signal makes a wave of amplitude 1 + a e^(−jω·2t): the response swings between 1 + a and 1 − a, 20 log((1 + a) / (1 − a)) dB peak to peak, and the group delay by a · 2t either way. For 40 dB (a = 0.01) that is 0.174 dB peak to peak (±0.087 dB) and ±0.02 t: the standard gives about ±0.1 dB and ±0.02 t for it. The echo level from the loss is the rule of Spectrum Control, TT = 2 IL + 6 dB; the standard only says the suppression improves twice as much as the loss is increased.

The drift. Δf / f = TCF · ΔT for the straight-line crystals (IEC 7.1 c, Table 1); for ST quartz and Li₂B₄O₇ the first-order term is zero and the second is −34 and −270 ·10⁻⁹ per K² about the turnover, Δf / f = c2 ((T − T0)² − (Tref − T0)²). The span is the highest minus the lowest shift over the range (the turnover itself when it is inside).

The resonator. fs = 1 / (2π √(Lm Cm)), fp = fs √(1 + Cm / C0) (the antiresonance of Lm and Cm in series with C0 in parallel), Q = ωs Lm / Rm (the paper's equations). From measurements the COMSOL formulas give Cm, Lm and Rm. The coupling (π² / 8) Cm / C0 is the relation that gives the 0.29 and 0.22 % of the paper's Table 2 from its Cm and C0 (it is not printed there). With a capacitor CL in series the resonance of the whole is where the branch has the reactance 1 / (ω (C0 + CL)), which gives fL = fs √(1 + Cm / (C0 + CL)) exactly for the lossless circuit (derived; CL = 0 gives fp and a large CL gives fs). The pulling is (fL − fs) / fs.

Assumptions and limits

  • Two uniform, bidirectional combs with equal lines and spaces. Real filters are weighted (apodized or with fingers withdrawn) to shape the passband, unidirectional or resonator-based to lose less; their bandwidth, loss and echoes are not these. The −3 dB width is that of the uniform response; the shape factor, the passband ripple and the stop band are not computed.
  • The loss is the ideal minimum. Propagation, diffraction, bulk-wave, resistive and package losses, and the reflection of the fingers, are not in it; the standard lists them. The radiation conductance is the delta-function / crossed-field model, which the 2009 paper says is limited to small loads and lower coupling: for the very large k² of 41° YX or 64° YX LiNbO₃ it would be rough (and their rows are not in the picker anyway).
  • R is the same at both ends and the tool designs no matching network. The comb is tuned with a shunt coil, so Ra is what the source sees. A real filter is specified for its own terminating impedance, often 200 to 700 Ω (Agilent), or comes with a matching network; the "Aperture for Ra = R" row can be very large on a weakly coupled crystal (about 1 000 wavelengths for the quartz example in 50 Ω), which is why quartz filters are not made for 50 Ω ends. The Smith chart tool does the network.
  • The substrate table is the standard's, as printed. Others differ: Spectrum Control has 3 992 m/s for 128° LiNbO₃ (the standard 4 000), 0.116 % for quartz (0.16 %) and 0.75 % for 112° LiTaO₃ (0.64 %); the standard's column "temperature coefficient" is not marked TCF or TCD: its values are negative and Spectrum Control says the frequency falls as the temperature rises, so I read it as the TCF (an inference). Two rows are left out: LST quartz (its temperature law is third order) and 64° YX LiNbO₃ (the table gives no permittivity). Spectrum Control's 41°, 64° and 42° cuts are not in the tool.
  • The turnover temperature is yours. The standard gives none for quartz or Li₂B₄O₇ (it says the cut angle sets it). The default is 25 °C, an assumption. The second-order terms are the standard's; a real quartz device with heavy electrodes differs (the arXiv paper measured 18 ppm/K).
  • The echo rule is a rule. For two matched combs (6 dB of loss) it says 18 dB; an ideal tuned three-port model of the combs (derived here, not in a source) gives 12 dB there, and 22.5, 28.2, 40.2, 51.1 dB for 8, 10, 15, 20 dB of loss where the rule says 22, 26, 36, 46. It is a good guide from 8 dB up and a little pessimistic above 10 dB. A typed echo level replaces it.
  • The echo ripple is small-echo arithmetic (one echo, no further bounces), exact for the amplitude and the delay of that echo.
  • The resonator is the single-resonance circuit. No series resistance of the busbars, no spurious modes, no package capacitances; the paper's own fit adds them, and its printed fr of the second resonator (436.960 MHz) is a fit that the parts alone do not give (436.990 MHz). Q is the unloaded one. The coupling row is an estimate from Cm / C0. The load capacitor is in series, as for a crystal; the IEC 61019 sections on load capacitance and pulling were not read.
  • Display. Three figures; the resonator frequencies seven; capacitances in fF, pF, nF; lengths in µm or mm; times in ns, µs, ms.

How it was checked

152 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the formulas above (every figure and label of the drawings; the substrate table read out of the tool and compared with a second typing of the standard's, the notes read out of the tool; the −3 dB constant solved there, the loss built from its two terms): - Transducer: the default, each of the six crystals, 22 other settings (frequencies from 10 MHz to 2.45 GHz, 1 to 300 pairs, half a pair, other apertures and resistances, a match that is met and one that is not), the crystal picker, eight refusals and the opening values; - Echoes: the default, the standard's 40 dB, each crystal, 15 other distances, losses and typed levels, an empty level back to the rule, a typed level without a loss, five refusals; - Drift: the default, each crystal (the turnover field only on the two parabolas), 16 other ranges, references, turnovers above, under and inside the range, six refusals; - Resonator: the paper's two resonators, from the frequencies, other load capacitances, resistances and values from 10 MHz to 900 MHz, the picker, fourteen refusals, and the remembered pill, crystal and way in; - the nine examples and the formula-search card.

600 more cases (three batches of 200: random crystals, frequencies, pairs, apertures, resistances, distances, losses, echo levels, temperatures, resonator parts and frequencies) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

RF & microwave › RF components

RF diode types

What it computes

Diodes at RF are built for one job each. The tool is a reference of ten families and a calculator for the three whose behaviour is a formula. Four pills:

  • Types: the picker in the Output heading chooses the family (PIN, PIN limiter, Schottky, varactor, step-recovery, Gunn, IMPATT, TRAPATT, tunnel, point-contact). The big result is its name and what it is; in three cells what controls it, what it acts as and what it is used for; rows: the parameter that matters, its range or limit, and which pill (if any) calculates it; and a short description. The drawing is the diode symbol with what controls it and what it becomes.
  • PIN: a PIN diode in a line of system impedance Z0, as a switch or an attenuator. The inputs, three to a row: the frequency (MHz), the system impedance (Ω) and the RF power (W); the series resistance RS (Ω) and the capacitance CT (pF). The picker in the Output heading fills RS and CT from the Skyworks SMP1320 series at a bias current (mA, a field that appears with the part); typing RS goes back to typed values. The big result is the loss of a series switch when it is on (forward biased); cells: its isolation when off, the loss of a shunt switch when it is on (reverse biased) and its isolation when off (forward biased). Rows: the power the on-state diode dissipates in each switch, and for the SMP1320 the transit-time frequency limit. The same two series and shunt equations are the attenuation of a PIN attenuator set to the resistance RS: 50 Ω in a 50 Ω line is 3.52 dB either way. The drawing is the two switches in a line.
  • Varactor: the capacitance at 0 V (pF), the contact potential Φ (V) and γ; a low and a high reverse voltage (V) and the series resistance RS (Ω); the frequency (MHz), the tuning inductor (nH) and the package capacitance (pF). The picker in the Output heading chooses the doping (abrupt γ 0.47, ideal abrupt 0.5, hyperabrupt about 2, or a typed γ, which typing γ selects). The big result is the tuning ratio C(low) / C(high); cells: the two capacitances and the Q at the high voltage; rows: Q at both, the highest frequency of a VCO and of a tunable filter, the drift of the capacitance with temperature, and the resonance of the tuning inductor with the junction and package capacitance at the two voltages. The drawing is the package model.

  • Schottky: a detector diode. The saturation current IS (nA), the bias current IB (µA), the load RL (kΩ), the junction capacitance Cj (pF), the series resistance RS (Ω), the frequency (GHz) and the input power (µW). The picker fills the numbers of the HP 5082-2755 of Application Note 988. The big result is the video resistance RV; cells: the voltage sensitivity with the load, without it, and the frequency; rows: the share of the voltage the load takes, the output for the input power, and the matching bandwidth for |ρ| = 0.5. The drawing is the video source: the diode with RS and Cj, RV, the load.

  • Units: fixed (MHz, GHz, Ω, kΩ, pF, nH, V, mA, µA, nA, µW, W); the pickers are the family, the part, the doping and the Schottky part.

  • Remembered: the pill and the family.

Examples: the SMP1320 at 1 mA and at 10 mA, a PIN as a 3.52 dB attenuator, the 1969 article's C4 / C60 of 3, a hyperabrupt varactor, the 5082-2755 at zero bias at 10 GHz and with 20 µA and 100 kΩ, the PIN limiter and the step-recovery diode.

Terms

  • PIN diode, I region: a P layer, an N layer and between them a thick intrinsic (undoped, in practice lightly doped) layer of width W. Forward current stores charge in it, which lowers its resistance to RS; at zero or reverse bias it is a capacitor CT. Carrier lifetime τ: how long the stored charge lives. Transit-time frequency: about 1300 / W² MHz (W in µm); below it the diode acts as an ordinary junction diode.
  • Series, shunt switch; loss, isolation: the diode in the line, or across it to ground. Loss is what the switch costs when it passes the signal, isolation how much it blocks when it should not. Reflective: the diode reflects the blocked signal instead of absorbing it.
  • System impedance Z0: the impedance of the line, usually 50 Ω. PAV: the power available from the source, V² / (4 Z0).
  • Varactor (varicap), tuning ratio, Φ, γ: a reverse-biased junction used as a voltage-controlled capacitor; the ratio of its capacitance at a low voltage to that at a high one; the contact potential of the junction (0.7 V silicon, 1.3 V GaAs); the slope of log C against log (V + Φ). Abrupt, hyperabrupt: the doping profiles, γ near 0.5 and about 2.
  • Q, Tcc: the quality factor 1 / (2π f RS C) of a capacitor with a series resistance; the temperature coefficient of the capacitance in ppm per °C.
  • Schottky diode, saturation current IS, video resistance RV: a metal-semiconductor diode; the current at the knee of its I-V law; the resistance the detected (video) voltage sees, 0.026 V / (IS + IB), 0.026 V being kT / q. Square-law: a small-signal detector's output is proportional to the input power.
  • Step-recovery diode (SRD): stores charge when forward biased and gives it back as a very fast edge when the voltage reverses (the snap), so it makes harmonics. Gunn, IMPATT, TRAPATT, tunnel, point-contact: microwave sources and detectors without a formula here.

Sources

  • Skyworks Application Note 200312D, "Design With PIN Diodes" (October 2012; the PDF, all 19 pages read as text; pages 2 to 7 rendered and read as printed): the PIN diode as a current-controlled resistor; RS = W² / ((µn + µp) Q) with Q = IF τ (equation 2), valid above the transit-time frequency f > 1300 / W² (MHz, µm) (3); CT = ε A / W (4); the series switch, loss 20 log(1 + RS / 2Z0) (9) and isolation 10 log(1 + (4π f CT Z0)⁻²) (10); the shunt switch, loss 10 log(1 + (π f CT Z0)²) (18) and isolation 20 log(1 + Z0 / 2RS) (19); 6 dB more isolation for a multi-throw switch; the on-state dissipation 4 RS Z0 / (2 Z0 + RS)² PAV for a series diode (11) and 4 RS Z0 / (Z0 + 2 RS)² PAV for a shunt one (20), for a perfectly matched line; the attenuation of series and shunt PIN attenuators (31, 32), the same equations; more than 40 dB from one diode is hard.
  • Skyworks SMP1320 data sheet (200047 Rev. E, February 2006; read): 0.3 pF typical at 30 V; 2 Ω typical at 1 mA and 0.9 Ω at 10 mA at 100 MHz; I region 8 µm; carrier lifetime 0.4 µs; and the table of RS against current and temperature at 500 MHz, whose 25 °C column the tool uses.
  • Skyworks Application Note 200480 Rev. C, "PIN Limiter Diodes in Receiver Protectors" (read): RS = k IF^−α + RSAT with 0.84 < α < 0.9; the limiter as a power-controlled resistor (under 0.5 dB of loss at small signal), 20 to 30 dB a stage, thresholds of 7 to 10 dBm (1 µm I layer) to 20 to 23 dBm (7 to 10 µm); gold doping for a short lifetime.
  • Skyworks Application Note 200824 Rev. A, "Varactor Diodes" (read; pages 3 and 5 rendered): C = C0 / (V / Φ + 1)^0.47 with γ 0.5 for an ideal abrupt junction and 0.47 for a practical one, Φ 0.7 V (Si) and 1.3 V (GaAs), hyperabrupt junctions not fitted by one γ (a curve-fit model is advised); Tcc = K γ / (V + Φ) ppm per °C with K = 2300 (abrupt) and 1700 (hyperabrupt); Q = 1 / (2π f RS C), Q(f1) = Q(f2) f2 / f1, and the limits fmax = Qref fref / 10 for a VCO and / 100 for a tunable filter; Q varying as T^−3/2; the package model with CP and LP.
  • Irwin Carroll, "Variable-Capacitance Diodes", Electronics World, July 1969 (the RF Cafe copy, read): the same law with Φ about 0.6 V and γ about 0.45 for an abrupt junction and γ about 2 for a hyperabrupt one; the rating C4 / C60 = 3; tuning ratios of 4:1 (diffused), 5:1 (alloy) and 20:1 and more (hyperabrupt); Φ changing by 1.5 to 2.7 mV per °C; step-recovery diodes up to the 25th harmonic, about 30 % efficient at ×8 and 10 % at ×25.
  • Hewlett-Packard Application Note 988, "All Schottky Diodes are Zero Bias Detectors" (1982; the PDF from a copy on hpmemoryproject.org, read; equations rendered) and Application Note 956-5, "Dynamic Range Extension of Schottky Detectors" (1975; read): the detector as a video source RV feeding RL, RV = 0.026 / (IS + IB); the basic voltage sensitivity 0.020 RV, degraded to 0.02 RV / (1 + ω² C² RS RV) by the parasitics and by RL / (RL + RV); the matching bandwidth Δf = 1 / (2 R C ln(1 / |ρ|)); the 5082-2755: IS about 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ A, 42 MΩ at zero bias and 1300 Ω with 20 µA, RS 16 Ω, C 0.1 pF; small-signal detectors are square-law, a bias current lowers the sensitivity but widens the square-law range.
  • Electronics Notes, "Diode Types" (read): the families without a formula here: Gunn, IMPATT (about 3 to 100 GHz and more, ten watts and more), TRAPATT, tunnel, point-contact, backward and BARITT diodes, and the Schottky forward drop of 0.15 to 0.4 V against 0.6 V for silicon. HP Application Note 920, "Harmonic Generation Using Step Recovery Diodes" (a poor scan; read in part): the step-recovery diode as a charge-controlled switch, for multipliers and combs.
  • Not read: the data sheets of any varactor or Schottky part, HP Application Notes 969 and 923 (scans), Skyworks' notes APN1003, APN1011 and APN1014 (not found in a form I could download), and the Gunn and IMPATT literature. A first copy of AN 988 at mikrocontroller.net and the dtsheet.com copy of APN1014 were refused (403), and an HSMS-286x data sheet page at elcodis.com failed its certificate check; all were left alone.

Why the formulas are these

The PIN switch. A source and a load of Z0 each, with a resistance RS in series, give the load Z0 / (2 Z0 + RS) of the source voltage instead of 1/2: the loss is 20 log(1 + RS / 2Z0) (Skyworks 9; the divider is derived here and reproduces it). Off, the diode is the capacitor CT whose reactance 1 / (2π f CT) takes the place of RS: the isolation is 10 log(1 + (1 / (4π f CT Z0))²) (10). Across the line the roles swap: the capacitance in parallel with the line costs 10 log(1 + (π f CT Z0)²) (18) and the forward resistance shorts it, 20 log(1 + Z0 / 2RS) (19). A series diode and a shunt diode of the same RS = 50 Ω in 50 Ω both give 20 log(1.5) = 3.52 dB, which is why the attenuator equations (31, 32) are the same ones. The dissipation of the diode in the on state is the share of the available power the diode's resistance takes, 4 RS Z0 / (2 Z0 + RS)² for a series diode (and the shunt equivalent); both are for a matched line, as the note says.

RS from the SMP1320 table. The data sheet gives RS at 500 MHz for eight currents from 0.02 to 100 mA at 25 °C. Between two rows the tool draws a straight line on log-log paper (derived; RS falls roughly as a power of the current, the α of the limiter note, 0.84 to 0.9 for its diodes; the table's own slope goes from 0.8 at the lowest currents to 0.2 at the highest as the bulk resistance takes over), so 1 mA gives 1.9 Ω and 10 mA 0.76 Ω as printed. The headline figures are for 100 MHz (2 Ω and 0.9 Ω max): RS depends a little on frequency, which the tool ignores.

The varactor. C = C0 / (V / Φ + 1)^γ is the junction capacitance of a depletion layer that widens with the reverse voltage; γ 0.5 is the ideal abrupt junction (Skyworks) and 0.45 is the 1969 article's typical value. The tuning ratio is C(V1) / C(V2). Q = 1 / (2π f RS C) (Skyworks, Carroll's equation 2); the highest frequencies are the manufacturer's empirical rules, Q f / 10 and Q f / 100. The drift Tcc = K γ / (V + Φ) is C's dependence on Φ: from C ∝ (V + Φ)^−γ and a Φ that falls about 2.3 mV per °C, (1 / C) dC/dT = γ · 2.3 mV / (V + Φ), which is the note's K = 2300 (ppm V per °C) and agrees with the article's 1.5 to 2.7 mV per °C. The resonance is 1 / (2π √(L (CJ + CP))).

The detector. The diode equation I = IS (e^((V − I RS) / 0.026) − 1) has the small-signal resistance 0.026 / (IS + IB) at the operating point (AN 988), the video resistance, and a current sensitivity of about 20 A/W, so the voltage sensitivity 0.02 RV in mV per µW. Its parasitics divide it by 1 + ω² C² RS RV and the load by RL / (RL + RV). The output for a small power is the sensitivity times the power. The bandwidth 1 / (2 RV C ln 2) is the note's Bode formula with |ρ| = 0.5 and the video resistance as R.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal diodes in a perfect line. The PIN equations are for a purely resistive RS and a purely capacitive CT, without the package inductance (under about 1 nH, which limits the isolation of a shunt diode at higher frequencies) or the board; the note says more than 40 dB is hard from one diode and that a faulty switch is usually the circuit, not the diode. The 6 dB for a multi-throw switch is stated in the tool's text, not added. CT is the data sheet's at 30 V; at zero bias it is higher. RS is the 500 MHz table's at any frequency, and the 25 °C column.
  • Switching speed, distortion and the large-signal conditions (the note's equations 1, 5, 6, the speed table, the thermal model) are not computed.
  • The varactor's γ is one number. For hyperabrupt junctions the slope changes with the bias (Skyworks), so the ratio and the capacitances are approximate; the manufacturer's C-V curve is better. RS is one value for both voltages though it falls as the bias rises, so Q at the low voltage is pessimistic. The empirical frequency limits and K are the rules of the notes. Leakage and breakdown (the reverse voltage should stay at least 5 V under breakdown) are not checked.
  • The detector is small-signal and matched. The sensitivity assumes the diode is matched to the source (AN 988 says matching its high impedance to 50 Ω is the limit of bandwidth), the thermal constant is 0.026 V for an ideality factor of 1, the temperature dependence (RS proportional to T, IS exponential) is not in it, and the output stops being proportional to the power at the compression point (AN 956-5). The 5082-2755 is discontinued.
  • The Types texts are summaries of the notes above; the ranges quoted (3 to 100 GHz, thresholds, harmonic limits) are theirs and vary with the part.
  • Display. Three figures; dB, W, mW or µW as the size asks.

How it was checked

125 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the formulas above (every figure and every label of the drawings; the types table and the notes read out of the tool; the SMP1320 table and the doping choices compared with a second typing): - Types: all ten families, the opening pill, the picker and the remembered family; - PIN: the default, the SMP1320 at 14 currents from 0.02 to 100 mA, 15 other settings (frequencies from 10 MHz to 2 GHz, 25 and 75 Ω, powers from 1 mW to 25 W, RS and CT other values), the return to typed values, the picker, eight refusals; - Varactor: the default, the four dopings, γ typed, 16 other settings (the 1969 C4 / C60, equal and reversed voltages, GaAs, other frequencies and tank inductances), nine refusals; - Schottky: the default, the 5082-2755 picker, zero bias into 10 GΩ, 17 other settings, the return to typed values, the picker, seven refusals and the remembered pill; - the nine examples and the formula-search card.

540 more cases (three batches of 180: random currents, frequencies, impedances, powers, capacitances, voltages, potentials, γ, inductances, saturation and bias currents, loads) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

RF & microwave › Reference

Microwave bands

What it computes

A frequency has several names. The ITU numbers the radio bands; the IEEE has radar letters (L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, V, W); NATO has letters of its own (A to M, and N and O for the US military); some bands are set aside for industrial, scientific and medical equipment (ISM); and a standard rectangular waveguide, WR-90 for instance, carries only a limited range. The tool gives all of these for one frequency. Three pills:

  • Find: the frequency, in MHz, GHz or THz (one picker). The big result is the IEEE letter band, with its range and what the letters stand for. In three cells: the ITU band, the NATO letter and the ISM band, if there is one. Under them: the free-space wavelength; the standard waveguides whose nominal range holds the frequency, each a button that opens it in the Waveguide pill; and, for an IEEE band, a note of what it is typically used for. An edge belongs to both bands it separates: exactly 2 GHz is "L / S" to the IEEE and "D / E" to NATO. The ITU's own rule is kept for its numbers: a band's lower limit is out and its upper limit in, so 3 GHz is in band 9.
  • Bands: the same as lists. A picker in the Output heading chooses IEEE letters, NATO letters, ITU numbers or ISM bands; the row that holds the frequency is tinted, and tapping a row sets the frequency to the middle of that band (the geometric mean of its edges; the centre frequency for an ISM band; half the top for NATO's A, which starts at 0 Hz). The big result and three cells give the band's edges and the ratio of the two (for ISM bands: the centre, the type, and where it applies).
  • Waveguide: one of the 34 standard sizes, WR-2300 to WR-3, picked from the list or, left on "Best fit", chosen from the frequency. The big result is its name, with its IEC and UK names and its inner size in millimetres under it. In three cells: the cut-off frequency, the nominal range, and your frequency as a multiple of the cut-off. Under them: what that means (below the cut-off nothing propagates; above it but under the nominal range; inside it; over it but under twice the cut-off, still one mode; over twice the cut-off, where other modes can exist); the inner size in inches; where the next mode starts; the EIA recommended band where it is known; the letters the maker's table gives it; and the other sizes that hold your frequency.

The drawing of Find and Bands puts the ITU bands, the IEEE letters and NATO's on one logarithmic scale from 0.3 to 300 GHz, the three decades of the ITU's UHF, SHF and EHF. The bands that hold the frequency are green and the frequency is a blue stem (an arrow at the edge of the scale when it is off it). The Waveguide drawing is the guide's opening to scale, its wide side a, its short side b, and the TE10 field in green, pointing along b and strongest in the middle of a.

  • Units: MHz, GHz or THz for the frequency.
  • Remembered: the pill, the unit, the system picker and the waveguide.

Examples: a microwave oven's 2.45 GHz, satellite TV at 11.7 GHz, GPS L1, Wi-Fi at 5.8 GHz, a 77 GHz car radar, and WR-90 at 10 GHz.

Terms

  • ITU band: the radio spectrum divided into bands numbered 4 to 12, each a decade of frequency; band N runs from 0.3 × 10ᴺ to 3 × 10ᴺ Hz. Band 9 is UHF, 10 SHF, 11 EHF and 12 has no symbol. They are the only names the ITU wants used in dealings with it.
  • IEEE letter band: L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, V, W and mm (with HF, VHF and UHF), the names of IEEE Std 521 for radar frequency bands. The letters began in the Second World War and are used well beyond radar, where their edges move.
  • NATO letter band: the A to M letters (and N, O of the US military) used for military and electronic-warfare work. They are not the IEEE letters: NATO's J is 10 to 20 GHz, IEEE's X is 8 to 12.
  • ISM band: a band designated for "industrial, scientific and medical applications (of radio frequency energy)": equipment that makes and uses radio-frequency energy locally, for heating for instance, and not for telecommunications (RR 1.15). Type A (RR 5.138): use is subject to the administration's special authorization. Type B (RR 5.150): the other services in the band must accept the interference ISM equipment may cause. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth use the 2.4 GHz one without being ISM equipment.
  • Region: the ITU's three regions: 1 is Europe, Africa and Russia, 2 the Americas, 3 Asia outside Russia, Australia and New Zealand.
  • Waveguide: a hollow metal pipe that carries a signal; above a few gigahertz it loses less than a cable. WR stands for "waveguide rectangular" and the number is the inner width in hundredths of an inch: WR-90 is 0.900 in wide.
  • TE10 mode, cut-off: the first mode a rectangular guide can carry; the electric field points along the short side b and is strongest in the middle of the wide side a. Below its cut-off frequency, c / (2 a), nothing propagates.
  • Nominal range: the frequencies a size is meant for, from about 1.25 to 1.9 times its cut-off, where only the TE10 mode propagates.
  • EIA, IEC, UK (RCSC) names: the same guide under three standards: WR-90, R 100 and WG 16.

Sources

  • ITU, Radio Regulations, edition of 2020, volume 1 (the 443-page PDF; text extracted and read): Article 2.1, bands 4 to 12 with their symbols and metric subdivisions, "lower limit exclusive, upper limit inclusive", band N from 0.3 × 10ᴺ to 3 × 10ᴺ Hz; 2.2, that in communications with the ITU no names, symbols or abbreviations should be used for the bands other than those of 2.1; 1.15, the definition of ISM applications; and the footnotes 5.138 (6765 to 6795 kHz, 433.05 to 434.79 MHz in Region 1 except in the countries of 5.280, 61 to 61.5 GHz, 122 to 123 GHz, 244 to 246 GHz), 5.150 (13 553 to 13 567 kHz, 26 957 to 27 283 kHz, 40.66 to 40.70 MHz, 902 to 928 MHz in Region 2, 2400 to 2500 MHz, 5725 to 5875 MHz, 24 to 24.25 GHz) and 5.280 (eleven European countries for which 433.05 to 434.79 MHz is an ISM band with type B's terms), each with the centre frequency it gives.
  • Wikipedia, "Radio spectrum" (the wikitext, downloaded and read): the IEEE radar band table, credited to IEEE Std 521-2002, and the ITU table.
  • David Kelley, "Radar Band Letter Designations (from IEEE Standard 521-2002)" (Bucknell University handout; PDF text read), and radioing.com's page on the IEEE radar bands (read): the same letter edges: L 1 to 2 GHz, S 2 to 4, C 4 to 8, X 8 to 12, Ku 12 to 18, K 18 to 27, Ka 27 to 40, V 40 to 75, W 75 to 110, mm 110 to 300 GHz; and HF 3 to 30 MHz, VHF 30 to 300 MHz, UHF 300 to 1000 MHz. Both say that the IEEE standard gives 110 to 300 GHz to the millimetre band although in popular usage it is often 30 to 300 GHz; radioing.com adds that the standard relates the letters in common use to the frequencies they stand for, that they are not a substitute for specific frequency limits and that they are meant for radar.
  • Wikipedia, the "NATO radio band table" template (wikitext): NATO's letters, A 0 to 250 MHz, B 250 to 500 MHz, C 500 MHz to 1 GHz, D 1 to 2, E 2 to 3, F 3 to 4, G 4 to 6, H 6 to 8, I 8 to 10, J 10 to 20, K 20 to 40, L 40 to 60, M 60 to 100 GHz, and the US military's N 100 to 200 and O 200 to 300 GHz, 1978 to the present. The template cites the NATO ARFA handbook, the 1978 US ECM instruction (AFR 55-44 and its twins) and Belov, Smolskiy and Kochemasov's handbook; none of those was read (the server of the instruction refused the download).
  • Spinner GmbH, TD-00036 issue V, "Cross reference for hollow metallic waveguides" (H.-U. Nickel, 2025; PDF text read): the inner dimensions (in inches and millimetres), the IEC nominal ranges, the IEC, EIA and UK designations and the letters of each size, from IEC 60153-2:2016, EIA-261-C, MIL-DTL-85 and IEEE Std 1785.1-2012; the rule that a nominal range runs from about 1.25 to 1.9 times the TE10 cut-off, and that the cut-off is c₀ / (2 a) with c₀ = 299 792 458 m/s.
  • Wikipedia, "Waveguide (radio frequency)" (the wikitext, read): the table of standard sizes with the EIA recommended bands and the cut-offs; that the WR number is the inner width in hundredths of an inch; the usual design rules (the band's lower edge about 25 % above the cut-off and its upper edge about 5 % below the cut-off of the next mode, the height half the width); and f = c / 2W for the lowest frequency.
  • Precision mmW, "Waveguide Frequency Bands with Interior Dimensions" (PDF text read): an independent chart of the sizes with their recommended bands.
  • Wikipedia, the articles on the L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, V and W bands, and on the ISM band (wikitext, read): the examples of use, given as examples and not as allocations.
  • Not read: IEEE Std 521 itself, in any edition (it is sold; the 2019 revision may differ from the 2002 table used here); the NATO documents above; EIA-261-C and IEC 60153-2 themselves (only through Spinner and Wikipedia); national rules (FCC Parts 15 and 18, ISED, ETSI), and Article 5's table of allocations. Two servers refused downloads (apps.dtic.mil and the Marine Corps' publications site) and were left alone.

Why the formulas are these

The ITU band. Band N holds the frequencies f with 0.3 × 10ᴺ < f ≤ 3 × 10ᴺ Hz (RR 2.1, Note 1, and "lower limit exclusive, upper limit inclusive"), so 3 GHz is the top of band 9 and 30 GHz the top of band 10. The letter bands have no such rule in the sources, so an edge here belongs to both bands.

The wavelength. λ = c / f in free space, with c = 299 792 458 m/s: 12.2 cm at 2.45 GHz.

The cut-off. The longest wave a rectangular guide of inner width a carries is 2 a, so its lowest frequency is

fc = c / (2 a)

for the nominal width of the table: WR-90, a = 0.900 in = 22.86 mm, gives 6.557 GHz. The tool takes a in inches from the EIA name (Spinner's imperial column) and the millimetres as 25.4 mm to the inch.

The next mode, the nominal range, the verdict. In all 34 sizes the height is at most half the width, so the next modes (TE20, and TE01 when b = a / 2) start at 2 fc; that is the "next mode" column of Wikipedia's table for every size (WR-90: 13.114 GHz). The nominal range runs from about 1.25 fc, which keeps away from the strong dispersion and the loss near the cut-off, to about 5 % under 2 fc, 1.9 fc. The tool says "below the cut-off" at or under fc, "under the nominal range" up to its lower edge, "inside" up to its upper edge, "still one mode" up to 2 fc and "other modes" from there.

The best fit. Among the sizes whose nominal range holds the frequency, the one whose range is centred nearest it on a log scale (the geometric mean of its edges); with none, the nearest of all.

Assumptions and limits

  • Letters are for radar. IEEE Std 521's letters are radar designations, and radioing.com's summary of the standard says they are not meant for other uses; satellite and test-equipment makers use the same letters with edges of their own. 11.7 GHz is Ku band to a satellite receiver and X band to the IEEE (whose Ku starts at 12 GHz); C-band satellites use 3.7 to 4.2 GHz, partly in IEEE's S. The ITU asks that only its own band names be used with it.
  • Waveguide letters differ again. The waveguide world's K is 18 to 26.5 GHz and Ka 26.5 to 40, against IEEE's 18 to 27 and 27 to 40; Spinner's letter column (L, S, C, X, Ku, K, Ka, Q, U, V, E, W, F, D, G, Y, H, J, and Ls, R, Xn, Xb, M, P, N for some sizes) is shown as it is, for the size.
  • Two sources for the letters, one date. The IEEE table is the 2002 one, from three copies and not from the standard; NATO's letters come from a Wikipedia template whose own sources were not read.
  • ISM bands of the Radio Regulations only. National rules (the FCC's Parts 15 and 18, ETSI's short-range-device bands) are not here, and the bands under 433 MHz are listed but do not matter to a microwave user.
  • Examples of use, not allocations. The uses come from encyclopaedia articles. An allocation depends on the country and the service (RR Article 5 holds them).
  • Waveguide: ordinary rectangular sizes only. No reduced-height, square, circular or ridged guide, no WM sizes under WR-3, no tolerances, no loss, impedance, power rating or guide wavelength: those belong to a waveguide calculator of their own.
  • The cut-off is for the nominal width. Spinner's table prints the IEC sizes' cut-offs 0.2 to 0.6 % lower (WR-90: 6.54 GHz) while its millimetre table, from IEEE 1785.1, equals c / (2 a) (WR-10: 59.014 GHz). Its own footnote says c / (2 a); I could not tell why the IEC figures are lower and did not read IEC 60153-2.
  • Two kinds of range. The nominal range shown is IEC 60153-2's (through Spinner), which every size has. The EIA recommended band (WR-90: 8.2 to 12.4 GHz, the IEC giving 8.20 to 12.5) is shown only for the 23 sizes WR-340 to WR-4, where Wikipedia and Precision mmW agree; for the others the sources differ (WR-430: 1.72 or 1.70 GHz at the bottom; WR-650; WR-770; WR-3: 330 or 325 GHz at the top) or only Wikipedia gives one, and none is shown.
  • Typographical errors in a source. Wikipedia's table prints the height of WR-284 as 34.94 mm and of WR-1150 as 146.5 mm; Spinner's 34.04 and 146.05, which are 1.340 in and 5.750 in, are the ones used. Precision mmW prints 1.150 in for the height of WR-229 against 1.145 in in Spinner and Wikipedia.
  • Range. The IEEE letters cover 3 MHz to 300 GHz, the ITU numbers 3 kHz to 3 THz, NATO's letters up to 300 GHz, the waveguides 0.32 to 330 GHz; outside, the tool says so.
  • Display. Frequencies to four figures, wavelengths and ratios to three.

How it was checked

100 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation written from the sources (every figure and every label of the drawing): - Find: the five examples (2.45 GHz, 11.7 GHz, GPS L1, 5.8 GHz, 77 GHz) and the edges (2, 3, 8, 30 and 300 GHz), 0.4 GHz, 7 MHz, 2 MHz, 400 GHz, 2 THz and 5 THz, the ISM bands (6.78 MHz, 433.92 MHz, 915 MHz, 2.4 and 2.5 GHz, 24.125, 61.25 and 245 GHz), the unit picker, the refusals, the waveguide chip and the remembered choices; - Bands: each of the four lists at 2.45 GHz, every row; an edge, HF, mm, NATO's A, the ISM bands, ITU band 12 and the frequency below band 4; tapping a row; the picker; - Waveguide: all 34 sizes, each at the middle of its range (name, names, size, cut-off, nominal range, inches, next mode, EIA band, letters, drawing labels); WR-90 at 5, 7, 10, 12.45, 13 and 14 GHz; the best fit at 1000 and 0.1 GHz; the picker's 35 entries; - the six examples and the formula-search card.

About 1 100 more cases (every edge of every table typed exactly, 117 frequencies in three views each, and 260 random frequencies from 300 kHz to 5 THz in three views, with random systems and sizes) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept. The cut-offs of the 34 sizes, worked as c / (2 a), agree with Wikipedia's printed ones to its rounding (at worst 0.16 %), and the 34 IEC nominal ranges come out at 1.21 to 1.27 and 1.86 to 1.91 times the cut-off.

RF & microwave › Reference

Amateur radio bands

What it computes

The amateur service is the radio service for people who use radio for self-training and experiment without pay. Which slices of spectrum they may use, how wide a signal may be and on what terms differs from one country to the next. The tool takes one frequency and says which amateur band it is in and what five systems allow there: Canada, the United States, and the three ITU Regions (1 Europe, Africa and Russia; 2 the Americas; 3 Asia outside Russia, and Oceania). Two pills:

  • Find: the frequency, in kHz, MHz or GHz (one picker), and, in the Output heading, the system to read it in (Canada, the default). The big result is the band's name (40 m) with where that system puts it ("7 to 7.3 MHz in Canada"), or, if the system does not allow the frequency, why: "not allowed in Region 1: 40 m is 7 to 7.2 MHz there". In three cells: the free-space wavelength; the maximum bandwidth (RBR-4's column II; the United States has none in its band table); and the provision. Under them: for Canada and the Regions, the operator qualifications; what the provision means; and a note on where the system's figures come from. When the frequency sits exactly on the edge of two segments (24.05 GHz in Canada) a row says what the other segment gives.
  • Bands: the same head, then three cells (the lower edge, the upper edge and the width of the stretch that holds the frequency) and the list of the system's bands, each with its range and, where RBR-4 gives one, its maximum bandwidth. The row of the band that holds the frequency is tinted; tapping a row puts the frequency in the middle of that band's widest segment. A band made of several pieces says so ("5.332 to 5.405 MHz in 5 parts" for Canada's 60 m); touching pieces count as one stretch, so Canada's 1.25 m reads 219 to 225 MHz although 220 to 222 MHz is for exceptional circumstances only (Find says so).

The drawing, in both pills, is the band holding the frequency (or, between bands, the nearest) in the five systems: one bar per segment on a single linear scale, the one holding the frequency green, the others grey; the range written beside each system in green where the frequency is inside it and in amber where it is not; a blue stem at the frequency (with an arrow at the edge when the frequency is outside the band). The selected system's row is tinted, and a tap on a row picks that system, as the picker does.

  • Units: kHz, MHz or GHz for the frequency.
  • Remembered: the pill, the unit and the system.

Examples: 7.25 MHz on 40 m, a 60 m channel at 5.332 MHz, 221 MHz in Canada, 445 MHz on 70 cm, 77.8 GHz on 4 mm, and 100 MHz, which is in no amateur band.

Terms

  • Band name (40 m, 70 cm): a wavelength, rounded: 40 m is the band around 7 MHz, where λ = c / f = 300 / 7.15 = 42 m. The names are the FCC's (47 CFR 97.301's first column) and common usage; 9 cm for 3.3 to 3.5 GHz is common usage, the FCC's table no longer lists that band.
  • Primary and secondary: a primary service is protected from the others; a secondary one must not cause harmful interference to a primary one and cannot claim protection from it (ITU Radio Regulations 5.28 to 5.31). In the Radio Regulations' table a primary service is printed in capitals (AMATEUR) and a secondary one in lower case (Amateur) (RR 5.24 to 5.26).
  • The star and the dash (RBR-4, column III): RBR-4 defines the star as: the transmissions must not cause interference to, and are not protected from, the stations of the other services in that band, that is, secondary. A dash means RBR-4 lists no operating provision. The tool says "secondary" and "none" and nothing more.
  • Footnote codes: a code without a prefix (5.142) is a footnote of the ITU's table; one with a "C" (C21) is from the Canadian Table of Frequency Allocations. RBR-4 prints their text and the tool shows a short form of it.
  • Maximum bandwidth: how wide the signal may be. RBR-4 section 4 measures a signal's bandwidth as the width of frequency it occupies at 26 dB below its peak.
  • Channel: a centre frequency and a width around it. Canada's and the United States' 60 m channels are 5332, 5348, 5373 and 5405 kHz, 2.8 kHz wide: the channel spans the centre frequency plus and minus half of that.
  • Operator qualifications (RBR-4, column IV): B is the Amateur Radio Operator Certificate with Basic Qualification; 5 that with Morse Code (5 words per minute) Qualification; B/H a Basic with Honours (a score of 80 % or more); A the Advanced Qualification. "B and 5, B/H, B and A" (every band under 30 MHz) is written out as "Basic + Morse 5, Basic with Honours, or Basic + Advanced"; "B" (50 MHz and up) is "Basic".
  • ITU Regions: 1, 2 and 3, bounded by lines A, B and C (RR 5.3 to 5.9).
  • e.i.r.p.: the power radiated in the antenna's strongest direction, as if from an isotropic antenna (transmitter power times antenna gain). PEP: peak envelope power, the most a transmitter delivers at the crest of its modulation. RTTY: radioteletype. w.p.m.: words per minute.
  • The services the footnotes name (fixed, mobile, maritime mobile, radiolocation, radionavigation, radio astronomy, inter-satellite, and so on) are the ITU's radiocommunication services (RR 1). AMTS is the US Automated Maritime Telecommunications System, UTC the Utilities Telecom Council, PLC power-line carrier, Line A a line defined in 47 CFR 97.3(a) (not read), ISM industrial, scientific and medical equipment (see Microwave bands).

Sources

  • ISED Canada, RBR-4, "Standards for the Operation of Radio Stations in the Amateur Radio Service", Issue 3, July 2022 (the PDF from the University of New Brunswick's amateur radio files, www.ece.unb.ca/petersen/amateur-radio-files/RBR04e-Operating-Standards-2022-Jul.pdf; text extracted and read): the definitions; section 3, the frequency bands and the qualifications; section 4, the bandwidths (the 26 dB rule); section 7, operation outside Canada (Schedules II to IV are for a Canadian-registered ship or aircraft in international waters or airspace, "subject to the requirements for operator qualifications"); section 8, interference; and the four schedules with their notes: Schedule I, Canada, 40 items; Schedules II, III and IV, Regions 1, 2 and 3, 31, 34 and 32 items; each with the band, the maximum bandwidth, the operating provision and the operator qualifications, and the text of the footnotes 5.67A, 5.80A, 5.133B, 5.142, 5.561A, C6, C11 and C21. Not used: the sections on station identification and the rest.
  • 47 CFR 97.301 and 97.303 (the eCFR's XML for 2026-11-13, read): 97.301 (a) and (b), the Region 2 column: the bands of a station whose control operator holds an Amateur Extra class licence (the widest; (c) to (e) give the other classes' narrower ones), each with its wavelength-band name and the paragraphs of 97.303 that apply; 97.303 (a) to (t), the sharing requirements, and (h)(3), the four 60 m channels, their centre frequencies and the 2.8 kHz.
  • ITU, Radio Regulations, edition of 2020, volume 1 (the PDF, text read): 1.56, the amateur service; 5.3 to 5.9, the Regions; 5.24 to 5.31, primary and secondary; and the amateur entries of Article 5's table of allocations, which a script read for part of the rows and I looked at by eye for the five rows it flagged, on pages 169, 186 and 192 of the PDF (see "How it was checked").
  • Not read: ISED's Canadian Table of Frequency Allocations (the C footnotes are known only as RBR-4 prints them), RIC-3 and the certification rules (so whether the Morse 5 qualification is still awarded was not checked); the rest of 47 CFR Part 97 (97.305, which emissions in which band; 97.307, emission standards; 97.313, power; the licence classes' details; 97.3's definitions) and 47 CFR 2.106, the US Table of Allocations, which says whether each US amateur band is primary or secondary; the band plans of the ARRL, the IARU and the national societies; every other country's rules.

Why the numbers are what they are

The wavelength. λ = c / f in free space with c = 299 792 458 m/s: 41.4 m at 7.25 MHz. The band's name is a rounded wavelength of its middle, not the exact one.

In the band, on the edge. A frequency is in a segment when the lower edge ≤ f ≤ the upper edge, to within a relative 10⁻¹², so that a typed 5.3515 MHz is on the edge it names. The sources print ranges with both ends and do not say that an end is out, so both ends count as in; a frequency on the edge of two segments is in both, and the second is shown ("Also, on the edge"). A channel is in when f is within its centre plus or minus half its bandwidth. The band's name is found from a nominal range (40 m: 7.0 to 7.3 MHz, the widest of the systems' versions), so a frequency can be in a band's name and in none of a system's segments of it; that system is then said not to allow it, with the nearest segment.

The drawing. One linear scale from the lowest to the highest edge of the band over the five systems, widened to hold the frequency when that is in the band's nominal range; frequencies outside every band show the nearest band in log frequency.

The tap on a band. The middle of the widest segment, not the middle of the whole band, so the frequency is not put on a boundary between two segments.

Assumptions and limits

  • Schedules II to IV are not the Regions' own rules. RBR-4 gives them for a Canadian-registered ship or aircraft in international waters or airspace of that Region; they follow the ITU's table of allocations, which was cross-checked only in part (below). A person in a country of Region 1 is bound by that country's rules.
  • The United States is the Amateur Extra class's. The other classes have narrower segments (97.301 (c) to (e)); 97.305, 97.307 and 97.313 (emissions, standards, power) and the band plans are not shown, so the US cells have no maximum bandwidth. The row "Above 275 GHz" of 97.301 has no upper limit and is not listed. The Region 2 column is used (the United States, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands are in Region 2, 97.303's last paragraph); other insular areas are in Region 2 or 3 (appendix 1 to Part 97, not read).
  • The US 60 m channels are the four centre frequencies and the block 5351.5 to 5366.5 kHz, 2.8 kHz at most everywhere on 60 m (97.303(h)(3)). Phone, data and RTTY may set the carrier 1.5 kHz below the centre; the tool takes the frequency typed as the centre.
  • Primary or secondary. Canada and the Regions: RBR-4's star is "secondary" by its own definition; its dash is shown as "none". In the ITU table I could read, the dash rows are the capitals (primary) and the star rows lower case, but that was not read everywhere. The United States' status is in the Table of Allocations (not read), so the tool shows 97.303's paragraphs instead.
  • The paragraph and footnote texts are short paraphrases, mine, of RBR-4's reproduction of the Radio Regulations' footnotes and of 97.303; the country lists (5.80A, 5.133B) and the places and conditions are cut. Read the original before operating.
  • Qualifications as RBR-4 prints them, written out with RBR-4's own definitions; the Regions' schedules carry them too.
  • Canada's 220 to 222 MHz is listed as a segment, with the note "Exceptional circumstances only" (item 20), because RBR-4 lists it; C11 says it is for disaster relief.
  • A signal's width is not checked against the edges. The maximum bandwidth is shown; a signal that wide centred within half of it of an edge reaches over the edge, and no source read says what the rule is there.
  • Currency. RBR-4 is Issue 3 (July 2022); the eCFR text is of 2026-11-13. Both change as rules do. A reference, not legal advice: check with ISED, the FCC or the country's authority.
  • Display. Frequencies to seven figures at most, wavelengths to three.

How it was checked

309 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation of the lookups and the wording (every label of the drawing too), the long texts read out of the tool's own source: - Find: 7.25 MHz in each of the five systems; the 60 m channels, their edges (5.3305, 5.3306, 5.4064 and 5.4065 MHz) and a frequency between them; 1.25 m (219.5, 220, 221, 222, 223, 225, 226 MHz) in Canada, the US and Region 2; the 24.05 GHz, 77.5, 78 and 81 GHz edges; 135 kHz, 100 MHz and 1000 GHz (no band); the edges and the gaps of Canada's and Region 1's bands (7, 7.2, 7.3 and 7.301 MHz; 1.8, 1.85 and 1.86 MHz; 137.8 kHz; 29.7 and 30 MHz; and so on); every one of the 170 segments of the five systems at its middle; the units and the refusals; a tap on a row of the drawing; the remembered choices; - Bands: each system's whole list; eleven frequencies and systems for the three cells; taps on a band; - the six examples and the formula-search card.

About 1 300 more cases (660 random frequencies and systems in both pills, 644 at the exact edges of every segment) compared every figure and label with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept.

The tables themselves were checked with code that does not share the generator's parser: every row of the four RBR-4 schedules (items 1 to 40, 1 to 31, 1 to 34 and 1 to 32) agrees, field by field, with the shipped segments (frequencies, bandwidth, provision, qualification, note); the union of 97.301's Region 2 rows in (a) and (b) equals the shipped US segments, and the four 60 m centre frequencies equal 97.303(h)(3)'s. Against the ITU's table of allocations the check is partial: a script read the amateur entries of Article 5 and confirmed the edges and the primary or secondary status of 18 of Region 1's 31 segments, 17 of Region 2's 34 and 4 of Region 3's 32; five more of Region 2's (24.05 to 24.25, 76 to 77.5, 78 to 81, 122.25 to 123 and 136 to 141 GHz) the script flagged, and by eye on pages 169, 186 and 192 they are consistent (the entries of neighbouring rows are merged on those pages); the rest could not be read by script (rows that span the three Regions) and were not checked against the table. No disagreement was found.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Linear regulator

(formerly Linear regulator (LDO))

What it computes

A linear regulator, picked from the common ones, in two groups: - Variable (adjustable with two resistors): LM317, LM1117-ADJ, AMS1117-ADJ, LM1086-ADJ, the negative LM337, or a custom part with your own Vref and dropout. - Fixed: 7805, 7812, 7815, AMS1117-3.3, AP2112-3.3, MCP1700-3.3.

Three ways, by pill:

Pill Inputs Output
Vout R1 (OUT to ADJ) and R2 (ADJ to ground) the output voltage
R2 the wanted output and R1 R2, and the nearest 1 % value with the output it gives
Heat Vin, Vout, the load current, the package or RθJA, the ambient the heat in it, the junction temperature
  • Vout also gives the spread over Vref's tolerance and the share of the adjust-pin current.
  • Vout and R2 say whether the current through R1 is above the datasheet's minimum load.
  • Heat also gives:
  • the efficiency;
  • whether there is enough voltage across the regulator (the LM317's 3 V, the LM337's 2.5 V, the 78xx's input for regulation, the others' dropout);
  • the most current before the junction reaches 125 °C, or the part's rating if that is lower;
  • a warning past the rated current, the input voltage or the voltage it takes across it.
  • A fixed part has no divider to set, so Vout and R2 are greyed out and Heat takes its output from the part. It also shows the output's tolerance and its own current to ground, Iq, which adds Vin × Iq to the heat: 8 mA in a 7805, 1.6 µA in an MCP1700, which matters on a battery.
  • The LM337 works with negative voltages; they are shown with their minus, and can be typed with or without it.
  • Drawing: the regulator with its IN, OUT and ADJ pins and the two resistors, R2 green when it is the answer; a fixed part with its GND pin to ground and its output voltage.
  • Remembered: the regulator, the pill and the units.

Examples: an LM317 at 5 V, R2 for 12 V, an LM1117 from 5 V to 3.3 V at 500 mA, an LM317 from 12 V to 5 V at 1 A, an LM1117 then an MCP1700 from a 3.7 V cell, a 7805 from 12 V at 500 mA, and an LM337 at −5 V.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; on the R2 pill, it sets the series R2 is rounded to (E96 by default).

Source

Read in review, each from the maker's datasheet: - TI LM317 (SLVS044Z, April 2025): - VO = VREF (1 + R2 / R1) + (IADJ × R2), equation 2, "IADJ is typically 50 µA and negligible in most applications"; the typical application uses R1 = 240 Ω; - VREF 1.25 V, from 1.2 to 1.3 V; - adjustment pin current 50 µA, 100 µA max; - minimum load current 3.5 mA, 10 mA max; - recommended: VO 1.25 to 37 V, VI − VO 3 to 40 V, IO 0.01 to 1.5 A, TJ 0 to 125 °C; - RθJA 66.8 °C/W (SOT-223), 23.5 (TO-220, KCS), 38.0 (TO-263). - TI LM1117 (SNOS412Q, January 2023): - VREF 1.25 V, from 1.238 to 1.262 V at 25 °C; - dropout 1.1 V at 100 mA, 1.15 V at 500 mA, 1.2 V at 800 mA (typical, 25 °C); - adjust pin current 60 µA, 120 µA max; - minimum load current 1.7 mA, 5 mA max; - 800 mA, input to 15 V, TJ 0 to 125 °C; - RθJA 61.6 °C/W (SOT-223), 45.1 (TO-252), 23.8 (TO-220), 41.3 (TO-263); - "PD = (TJ(max) – TA) / RθJA". - Advanced Monolithic Systems AMS1117 (ds1117): - reference 1.250 V, 1.232 to 1.268 V at 25 °C; the -3.3 gives 3.251 to 3.349 V; - adjust pin current 55 µA, 120 µA max; minimum load 5 mA, 10 mA max; - dropout 1.1 V typical, 1.3 V max, at 0.8 A, "decreasing at lower load currents"; - quiescent current of the fixed versions 5 mA, 11 mA max; - up to 1 A, input to 15 V, junction to 125 °C; - θJA 90 °C/W (SOT-223, from 46 to over 90 with the copper area), 80 (TO-252), 160 (SO-8). - TI LM1086 (SNVS039J, April 2015): - VREF 1.25 V, 1.238 to 1.262 V at 25 °C; - adjust pin current 55 µA, 120 µA max; minimum load 5 mA, 10 mA max; - dropout 1.3 V typical, 1.5 V max, at 1.5 A; - 1.5 A, 29 V maximum between input and output (ADJ); - RθJA 23.0 °C/W (TO-220), 40.8 (TO-263), 35.9 (WSON-8). - TI LM337 (SLVS047L, January 2015): - reference −1.25 V, from −1.2 to −1.3 V over load and temperature; - adjustment current 65 µA, 100 µA max; - minimum output current 2.5 mA, 10 mA max (up to 40 V across it); - recommended VI − VO −2.5 to −37 V, 1.5 A, TJ 0 to 125 °C; - RθJA 24.8 °C/W (TO-220, KCS), 25.3 (TO-263), 30.3 (TO-252). - TI LM340 / LM7805 family (SNOSBT0L, September 2016): - output 4.8 to 5.2 V, 11.5 to 12.5 V, 14.4 to 15.6 V at 25 °C; - "input voltage required to maintain line regulation" 7.5 V, 14.6 V, 17.7 V; dropout 2 V at 1 A; - quiescent current 8 mA (the only figure, a maximum); - 1.5 A, DC input to 35 V; - RθJA 23.9 °C/W (TO-220), 44.8 (TO-263), 62.1 (SOT-223), from its thermal information table. A footnote in the same datasheet gives older figures (54 °C/W TO-220, 174 SOT-223); the table is used. - Diodes AP2112 (DS39724 Rev. 2-2, June 2017): - the -3.3 gives 3.251 to 3.350 V (± 1.5 %); - dropout 5 mV at 10 mA, 125 mV at 300 mA, 250 mV at 600 mA (typical); - quiescent current 55 µA, 80 µA max; - 600 mA, input 2.5 to 6.0 V; - θJA 184 °C/W (SOT-23-5, the AP2112K), 120 (SOT-89-5), 114 (SO-8). - Microchip MCP1700 (DS20001826E): - output within ± 2 % at 25 °C (± 3 % over temperature); - dropout 178 mV typical, 350 mV max, at 250 mA; - quiescent current 1.6 µA, 4 µA max; - 250 mA, input 2.3 to 6.0 V, junction to 125 °C; - θJA 212 °C/W (SOT-23), 104 (SOT-89), 92 (TO-92), 91 (2×2 DFN).

Why the formulas are these

Vout = Vref (1 + R2/R1) + Iadj × R2
R2 = (Vout − Vref) / (Vref / R1 + Iadj)
P = (Vin − Vout) × I + Vin × Iq,   Tj = Ta + P × RθJA
Imax = ((125 °C − Ta) / RθJA − Vin × Iq) / (Vin − Vout)

The regulator holds Vref across R1, so R1 sets a current of Vref / R1. That current and the adjust current flow on through R2, whose voltage adds to Vref to make the output. A fixed regulator has the same divider inside, and its own working current flows from the input to ground. The regulator drops the rest of the input as heat, and the junction runs RθJA degrees per watt above the air.

Assumptions and limits

  • RθJA is the datasheet's, measured on the board it names. A real board, smaller copper or still air can make it worse; a heatsink makes it better. Type your own figure if you have one.
  • The dropout is the typical figure at 25 °C. Between the LM1117's and the AP2112's listed currents it is interpolated. For the AMS1117, LM1086 and MCP1700 only the full-load figure is given, so it is used at every current: their real dropout is lower at light loads. It is a little higher over temperature.
  • An adjustable part's own current goes to the output through R1 and R2, so it is not added to the heat; the minimum-load line covers it.
  • 125 °C is the junction limit used for every part: the recommended maximum of most of them. Some allow 150 °C.
  • Other fixed voltages (1.8 V, 2.5 V, 5 V versions…) work with the Custom part in Heat, without the Iq term.

How it was checked

17 cases: - the LM317 with 240 and 720 Ω gives 5.036 V, 36 mV from the adjust current, and 4.836 to 5.236 V over Vref's tolerance; - 240 Ω carries 5.208 mA, above the typical minimum load only; - R2 for 12 V is 2.044 kΩ, and 2.05 kΩ gives 12.03 V; - the LM1117 from 5 to 3.3 V at 500 mA: 850 mW, 77 °C; - the LM317 from 12 to 5 V at 1 A: 190 °C, over the limit; - the LM1117 with 0.4 V across it is under its dropout, and its current is capped at its 800 mA rating; - the MCP1700 with the same 0.4 V is above its 178 mV dropout: 40 mW, 33 °C, 1.6 µA to ground (5.92 µW); - a 7805 from 12 V at 500 mA: 3.5 W plus 96 mW from its 8 mA, 111 °C in a TO-220, 584 mA before 125 °C; - the LM337 with 240 and 720 Ω gives −5.047 V, and its −12 V input shows with its minus; - the AP2112 at 300 mA needs 125 mV, so 100 mV will not regulate; - the LM1086 with 30 V across it is over its 29 V; - a fixed part keeps only Heat; - a custom 0.8 V reference gives 3.2 V; - an input below the output is refused; - picking a package fills in its RθJA; - the remembered regulator and pill.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Zener regulation

(also found as Zener voltage stabilization)

What it computes

The series resistor for a zener shunt regulator, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the zener (a 1N4728A–1N4761A, 1.3 W, or a BZX55, 500 mW, each with its datasheet figures, or a custom Vz and power rating), the least zener current, the supply's lowest and highest voltage, the load's least and most current, and the resistor you use.
  • The big result: the largest E24 value inside the window that works, with the window itself: under (Vin min − Vz max) / (IL max + Iz min) so the zener still gets its least current at the lowest supply and the heaviest load, and over (Vin max − Vz min) / (Iz max + IL min) so it stays within its current at the highest supply and the lightest load. The largest wastes the least. When the window is empty it says so, and why.
  • The resistor you use follows that value until you type your own. For it, the tool gives:
  • the zener current at the two extremes, flagged under the least current (the zener drops out) or over Iz max;
  • the most load it can feed while keeping the least zener current, as a current and as the smallest load resistance;
  • the zener's and the resistor's heat at the worst case;
  • the output: the zener's tolerance band, plus ZZT times the current range.
  • The least zener current starts at the part's knee test current, IZT2 (1, 0.5 or 0.25 mA on the 1N47xxA, 1 or 0.5 mA on the BZX55); it can be raised for better regulation.
  • Units: currents in µA, mA or A (one unit for all three), the resistor in Ω, kΩ or MΩ.
  • Drawing: the supply, Rs, the reverse-biased zener and the load.
  • Remembered: the part and the units.

Examples: Kuphaldt's 12.6 V from 45 V through 1 kΩ, the same with a 500 Ω load, 5.1 V at 20 mA from 9–12 V with a 1N4733A, and a BZX55C5V1 for 5 mA.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; it sets the series the series resistor is chosen from (E24 by default).

Source

  • Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 3, "Zener diodes" (read, ibiblio HTML): the zener is reverse-biased; "zener diodes regulate voltage by acting as complementary loads"; worked example 12.6 V, 45 V, 1 kΩ: 32.4 mA, the zener 408 mW, the resistor 1.05 W; with a 500 Ω load "this leaves 7.2 mA of current through the zener diode"; with 100 kΩ the regulator only works down to a 38.889 kΩ load; Vz "may be anywhere from 5 percent to 10 percent in error".
  • Vishay 1N4728A to 1N4761A, document 85816 rev. 2.7, 7 Nov 2024 (read): Vz 3.3 to 75 V, ± 5 %; Ptot 1300 mW "provided that leads at a distance of 4 mm from case are kept at ambient temperature"; per part IZT1, IZT2, ZZT at IZT1, ZZK at IZT2 and the regulator current IZM (e.g. 1N4733A: 5.1 V, 49 mA, 1 mA, 7 Ω, 550 Ω, 178 mA). IZM × Vz comes to about 0.9 W, under the 1.3 W Ptot: the tool checks the current against IZM and the heat against Ptot, so a design can pass one and not the other, as the sheet's own figures do.
  • Vishay BZX55, document 85604 rev. 2.0, 7 Nov 2024 (read): Vz 2.4 to 75 V with min / nom / max per part, IZT1 5 mA (2.5 mA from 39 V), IZT2 1 mA (0.5 mA), ZZ, ZZK, Ptot 500 mW (4 mm leads at 25 °C); Iz max is taken as Ptot / Vz.

Why the formulas are these

Rs ≤ (Vin min − Vz max) / (IL max + Iz min)
Rs ≥ (Vin max − Vz min) / (Iz max + IL min)
Iz = (Vin − Vz) / Rs − IL,   Pz = Vz × Iz,   PR = (Vin − Vz)² / Rs

The resistor carries the load's current and the zener's together, and drops what the supply has over Vz. At the lowest supply and the heaviest load the least current reaches the zener: the resistor must be small enough that it is still above the knee. At the highest supply and the lightest load the most reaches it: the resistor must be large enough to keep it within its rating. Taking Vz at the edge of its tolerance that makes each case worst keeps the window honest.

Assumptions and limits

  • ZZT is the zener's dynamic resistance at its test current; near the knee it is ZZK, much higher, so the output moves more there than the tool's figure.
  • The power ratings assume the leads held at ambient 4 mm from the body; on a board, a zener runs hotter and must be derated (Vishay's figure 1).
  • The supply's ripple is part of its range: enter the lowest valley and the highest peak.
  • For more current, a zener feeding a transistor (Zener + transistor stabilization, planned) or a linear regulator is the better circuit.

How it was checked

15 cases: - 1N4733A, 9–12 V, 0–20 mA: 40.2 to 173.6 Ω, E24 160 Ω; 2.78 to 44.7 mA, 239 mW in the zener, 320 mW in the resistor; - its output: 4.84 to 5.35 V, plus about 294 mV over that range; - Kuphaldt's 1 kΩ: 32.4 mA, 408 mW, 1.05 W, 12.6 V; - Kuphaldt's 500 Ω load: 7.2 mA left for the zener; - 1 kΩ from 45 V feeds 31.4 mA keeping 1 mA: a load of 401.3 Ω or more; - Kuphaldt's 100 kΩ: 324 µA, too little for a 1 mA knee; - BZX55C5V1 from 11–13 V at 0–5 mA: 910 Ω, 48.7 mW; - too large a resistor starves the zener; too small passes IZM (while under Ptot); a BZX55 at 22 Ω goes over 500 mW; - a supply range too wide leaves no resistor; - a supply under the zener voltage is refused; - picking a part brings its knee current (1N4740A: 0.25 mA); - the remembered part.
