DC/DC buck converter

What it computes

The power stage of a buck (step-down) converter in continuous conduction, the way TI's application note lays it out, on one screen:

  • Shared inputs: the highest input voltage, the output voltage, the most output current, the switching frequency and the efficiency η (90 % by default).
  • Four pills:
  • Inductor: the ripple you allow (a share of the output current) gives the smallest inductor, and the box proposes the next standard value up (E6: 1, 1.5, 2.2, 3.3, 4.7, 6.8). It follows the inputs until you type your own. Then the duty cycle, the ripple with that inductor, the peak current (the inductor's saturation rating and the switch's), and, with the switch's minimum current limit, the most the IC can deliver, flagged when under the output current. A limit of 0 skips that row.
  • Diode: its average current, the power at its forward voltage VF, the reverse voltage and peak current it must stand. A synchronous converter has a second switch instead, and no diode loss.
  • Output cap: the least capacitance for the output ripple allowed, the ripple its ESR adds, and the capacitance a load step needs to stay within an overshoot. The larger of the two is the result.
  • Feedback: from the IC's feedback voltage VFB and R2, R1 exact and as the nearest E96 resistor, the output it gives, and the divider current against 100 × the FB pin's bias current IFB.
  • Units: the currents in mA or A (one picker moves them all), the frequency in kHz or MHz, the inductor in nH or µH, IFB in nA or µA, R2 in Ω or kΩ; ripple and overshoot in mV, ESR in mΩ.
  • Drawing: the power stage as TI draws it, with the feedback divider: the IC with its SW and FB pins, the input capacitor, the diode, the inductor, R1 and R2 with their middle wired back to the FB pin (the wire crosses the diode's lead above the diode, without a junction), and the output capacitor last, by the output. The part the pill works out is green.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: TI's TPS54331 design (its inductor, its feedback divider, its output capacitor), a 12 V to 5 V Schottky diode, and a 2 MHz 5 V to 1.2 V.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; on the Feedback pill, it sets the series R1 is rounded to (E96 by default).

Terms

  • Buck converter: a switching regulator that steps a voltage down. A switch connects the inductor to the input for part of each cycle; the rest of the time a diode (or a second switch) lets the inductor's current keep flowing to the output.
  • Duty cycle (D): the fraction of each cycle the switch is on. Ideally Vout / Vin; the losses make it a little more.
  • Efficiency (η): output power over input power.
  • Inductor ripple (ΔIL): how far the inductor's current rises and falls each cycle, peak to peak.
  • Continuous conduction: the inductor's current never falls to zero; the formulas assume it.
  • Saturation current: above it the inductor's core saturates and its inductance collapses; it must exceed the peak current.
  • ESR: the capacitor's equivalent series resistance.
  • VFB, IFB: the voltage the IC regulates its FB pin to, and the small current that pin draws.
  • Synchronous converter: one with a second switch in place of the diode.

Source

  • TI SLVA477C, "Basic Calculation of a Buck Converter's Power Stage", Brigitte Hauke, December 2011, revised September 2026 (read, all 9 pages): D = Vout / (Vin(max) × η) (eq. 1; η "e.g., estimated 90%" in section 2, 85 % in its appendix); ΔIL = (Vin(max) − Vout) × D / (fs × L) (eq. 2); IMAXOUT = ILIM(min) − ΔIL / 2 (eq. 3); ISW(max) = ΔIL / 2 + IOUT(max), "the peak current, the inductor, the integrated switch(es), and the external diode have to withstand" (eq. 4); L = Vout (Vin − Vout) / (ΔIL fs Vin) (eq. 5) with ΔIL "20% to 40% of the output current" (eq. 6); IF = IOUT(max) (1 − D), PD = IF × VF (eqs. 7, 8); the divider current at least 100 × IFB, R2 = VFB / IR1/2, R1 = R2 (VOUT / VFB − 1) (eqs. 9 to 11); COUT(min) = ΔIL / (8 fs ΔVOUT) (eq. 12); ΔVOUT(ESR) = ESR × ΔIL (eq. 13); COUT(min),OS = ΔIOUT² L / (2 VOUT VOS) (eq. 14). It has no worked numbers.
  • TI TPS54331 datasheet, SLVS839H, October 2023, section 8.2 (read): its design is 7 to 28 V in, 3.3 V, 3 A, 570 kHz, 30 mV of output ripple; LMIN = VOUT (VIN(max) − VOUT) / (VIN(max) × KIND × IOUT × FSW) (eq. 8), KIND = 0.3, "calculated as 5.7 μH", and "a large value was selected: 6.8 μH"; the divider R5 = 10.2 kΩ over R6 = 3.24 kΩ on its 0.8 V reference, "resulting in a 3.31-V output voltage"; two 47 µF ceramics at the output.

Why the formulas are these

D = Vout / (Vin × η)
L = Vout (Vin − Vout) / (ΔIL × fs × Vin)
ΔIL = (Vin − Vout) × D / (fs × L),   Ipeak = Iout + ΔIL / 2
IF = Iout (1 − D),   PD = IF × VF
Cout = ΔIL / (8 fs ΔV),   Cout = ΔI² L / (2 Vout Vos)
R1 = R2 (Vout / VFB − 1)

While the switch is on, the inductor sees Vin − Vout and its current rises at (Vin − Vout) / L for D / fs seconds: that rise is the ripple. The inductor's current averages the output current, so its peak is half the ripple above it. While the switch is off the diode carries it, a fraction 1 − D of the time. The ripple current flows into the output capacitor, whose charge swings by ΔIL / (8 fs) each cycle, hence the capacitance for a ripple voltage. When the load jumps, the energy ½ L ΔI² the inductor must gain comes from the capacitor first, ½ C ((Vout + Vos)² − Vout²) ≈ C Vout Vos, hence the load-step capacitance.

Which input voltage. SLVA477 puts the typical input in the inductor formula; the TPS54331 datasheet puts the highest, where the ripple is the largest, and so does this tool, so the ripple stays within what you allow over the whole input range. With 28 V in, it gives the datasheet's 5.7 µH.

The datasheet's ripple. TPS54331's ripple formula (its eq. 9) divides by a further 0.8 and leaves out η: it gives 0.939 A of ripple and 3.47 A of peak with 6.8 µH, where SLVA477's formulas, which this tool uses, give 0.835 A and 3.42 A.

Assumptions and limits

  • Continuous conduction only: at light load the inductor's current reaches zero and the formulas no longer hold.
  • The IC decides much: use the inductor and capacitor ranges its datasheet gives, above all when its compensation is internal (SLVA477 section 7); the switching frequency, the current limit, VFB and IFB come from it too.
  • Ceramic capacitors lose capacitance with DC bias and temperature: X5R or better (SLVA477), and check the value at the working voltage.
  • The input capacitor is the datasheet's minimum, raised when the input is noisy (SLVA477 section 6); it is not computed here.
  • No losses beyond η and the diode: the switch's and the inductor's losses, and the inductor's RMS current, are not computed.

How it was checked

11 cases: - TPS54331's design, 28 V to 3.3 V at 3 A, 570 kHz, 30 %: 5.67 µH at least (its 5.7 µH), the next E6 value 6.8 µH (its choice); - the same at 90 %: D 13.1 %, 835 mA of ripple, 3.42 A peak, a 3.5 A limit delivering 3.08 A; - its divider: R1 for 3.3 V over 3.24 kΩ on 0.8 V is 10.13 kΩ, E96 10.2 kΩ (its R5) gives 3.319 V (its 3.31 V); - its output capacitor: 6.1 µF for 30 mV of ripple, 10.3 µF for a 1 A step within 100 mV; - 12 V to 5 V at 2 A: the diode carries 1.07 A and burns 537 mW at 0.5 V; - 5 V to 1.2 V at 2 MHz: 760 nH at least, so 1 µH; - the proposed inductor follows the output current (1 A: 22 µH) until one is typed, and a typed one stays while its ripple follows; - a switch limit too low is flagged; - the current pickers move together; - a step-up is refused.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

DC/DC boost converter

What it computes

The power stage of a boost (step-up) converter in continuous conduction, as TI's application note lays it out, on one screen, the twin of DC/DC buck converter:

  • Shared inputs: the lowest input voltage (the worst case for a boost), the output voltage, the most output current, the switching frequency and the efficiency η (80 % by default).
  • Four pills:
  • Inductor: the ripple you allow, as a share of the average inductor current, gives the smallest inductor, and the box proposes the next standard value up (E6). It follows the inputs until you type your own. Then the duty cycle, the average inductor current (what the input draws), the ripple with that inductor, the peak current (the inductor's saturation rating and the switch's), and, with the switch's minimum current limit, the most the IC can deliver, flagged when under the output current. A limit of 0 skips that row.
  • Diode: it carries the whole output current; its power at VF, the reverse voltage (the output) and the peak current it must stand.
  • Output cap: the least capacitance for the output ripple allowed, the ripple its ESR adds, the total, and the peak current into it.
  • Feedback: as in the buck: R1 exact and as the nearest E96 resistor, the output it gives, and the divider current against 100 × IFB.
  • Units: the currents in mA or A (one picker moves them all), the frequency in kHz or MHz, the inductor in nH or µH, IFB in nA or µA, R2 in Ω or kΩ; ripple in mV, ESR in mΩ.
  • Drawing: the power stage as TI draws it: the inductor from the input to the switch node, the IC's switch below it, the diode on to the output, R1 and R2 with their middle wired to the FB pin, the output capacitor last. The part the pill works out is green.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: TI's TPS61030 design (its inductor and its output capacitor), TPS61023's feedback divider, and a 5 V to 12 V Schottky diode.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; on the Feedback pill, it sets the series R1 is rounded to (E96 by default).

Terms

  • Boost converter: a switching regulator that steps a voltage up. The switch charges the inductor from the input; when it opens, the inductor pushes its current through the diode into the output.
  • Duty cycle (D): the fraction of each cycle the switch is on; ideally 1 − Vin / Vout.
  • Inductor current (IL): in a boost it is the input current, larger than the output current by Vout / Vin (and the losses).
  • The other terms (efficiency, ripple, continuous conduction, saturation current, ESR, VFB, IFB, synchronous) are as in DC/DC buck converter.

Source

  • TI SLVA372D, "Basic Calculation of a Boost Converter's Power Stage", Brigitte Hauke, November 2009, revised November 2022 (read, all 10 pages): D = 1 − VIN(min) × η / VOUT (eq. 1; η "e.g. estimated 80%" in section 2, 85 % in section 8); ΔIL = VIN(min) × D / (fS × L) (eq. 2); IMAXOUT = (ILIM(min) − ΔIL / 2) × (1 − D) (eq. 3); ISW(max) = ΔIL / 2 + IOUT(max) / (1 − D) (eq. 4); L = VIN (VOUT − VIN) / (ΔIL fS VOUT) (eq. 5) with ΔIL = (0.2 to 0.4) × IOUT(max) × VOUT / VIN (eq. 6); IF = IOUT(max), PD = IF × VF (eqs. 7, 8); the divider as in SLVA477 (eqs. 9 to 11); COUT(min) = IOUT(max) × D / (fS × ΔVOUT) (eq. 12); ΔVOUT(ESR) = ESR × (IOUT(max) / (1 − D) + ΔIL / 2) (eq. 13). It has no load-step formula and no worked numbers.
  • TI TPS61030 datasheet, SLUS534G, March 2015, section 11.2 (read): 1.8 to 5.5 V in, 5 V out, 600 kHz; "for an output current of 1000 mA at 5 V, at least 3500 mA of average current flows through the inductor at a minimum input voltage of 1.8 V" (its eq. 4, with 0.8 for the losses); L = VBAT (VOUT − VBAT) / (ΔIL f VOUT) with ΔIL "10% × IL": "the desired inductor has the value of 5.5 µH. In typical applications a 6.8 µH inductance is recommended"; the switch's current limit 4500 mA at 5 V; "with a chosen ripple voltage of 10 mV, a minimum capacitance of 100 µF is needed"; 80 mΩ of ESR adds 80 mV.
  • TI TPS61023 datasheet, SLVSF14B, August 2020, section 8.2 (read): 2.7 to 4.35 V to 5 V at 1.5 A; VREF 0.595 V typical, FB leakage 4 nA typical, 20 nA maximum; R1 732 kΩ, R2 100 kΩ; the ripple best under 40 % of the average inductor current; η "use 90% for most applications"; its current limit is a valley limit, not the peak limit SLVA372 assumes.

Why the formulas are these

D = 1 − Vin × η / Vout,   IL = Iout / (1 − D)
L = Vin (Vout − Vin) / (ΔIL × fs × Vout)
ΔIL = Vin × D / (fs × L),   Ipeak = IL + ΔIL / 2
IF = Iout,   PD = IF × VF
Cout = Iout × D / (fs × ΔV)
R1 = R2 (Vout / VFB − 1)

While the switch is on, the inductor sees the input and its current rises at Vin / L for D / fs seconds: that rise is the ripple. The output gets the inductor's current only while the switch is off, a fraction 1 − D of the time, so the inductor carries Iout / (1 − D) on average, which is Iout × Vout / (Vin × η). While the switch is on, the capacitor alone feeds the load for D / fs seconds, losing Iout × D / fs of charge: hence its size. The diode passes every bit of the output current. The ESR sees the full inductor current at the instant the switch opens.

Which input voltage. The lowest input gives the largest duty cycle, the largest inductor current and the largest switch current, so the tool uses it everywhere, as the TPS61030 and TPS61023 datasheets do; SLVA372 puts the typical input in its inductor formula.

The ripple's base. SLVA372 takes the ripple as a share of Iout × Vout / Vin; both datasheets take it as a share of the average inductor current, which includes the losses, and so does this tool: that is how TPS61030's 10 % gives its 5.5 µH.

Where TPS61030 differs. Its capacitor formula, Iout (Vout − Vin) / (f ΔV Vout), is SLVA372's with η left out, so it asks 107 µF ("100 µF") where SLVA372's asks 119 µF. Its ESR ripple is Iout × ESR, 80 mV; SLVA372 counts the inductor's peak current, as the ESR really sees it, and gets 290 mV.

Assumptions and limits

  • Continuous conduction only.
  • The IC decides much: use its datasheet's inductor and capacitor ranges, above all with internal compensation (SLVA372 section 7); its frequency, current limit, VFB and IFB come from it too.
  • Peak current limits only: the IC row assumes the switch limit is a peak limit, as SLVA372 does; an IC with a valley limit (TPS61023) can deliver more, by its own datasheet's formula.
  • Ceramic capacitors lose capacitance with DC bias: X5R or better, and check the value at the working voltage.
  • The input capacitor is the datasheet's minimum; not computed here.

How it was checked

8 cases: - TPS61030's design, 1.8 V to 5 V at 1 A, 80 %, 600 kHz, 10 %: 3.47 A in the inductor (its "at least 3500 mA"), 5.53 µH at least (its 5.5 µH), the next E6 value 6.8 µH (its recommendation); - the same: D 71.2 %, 314 mA of ripple, 3.63 A peak, its 4.5 A limit delivering 1.25 A; - its output capacitor: 119 µF for 10 mV, and its 80 mΩ ESR adds 290 mV; - TPS61023's divider: R1 for 5 V over 100 kΩ on 0.595 V is 740.3 kΩ, E96 732 kΩ (its R1) gives 4.95 V, 298 × its 20 nA maximum leakage; - 5 V to 12 V at 0.5 A: the diode carries 500 mA, 200 mW at 0.4 V, and blocks 12 V; - the proposed inductor follows the output current (0.5 A: 4.7 µH); - a switch limit too low is flagged; - a step-down is refused.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Zener + transistor

(formerly Zener + transistor stabilization)

What it computes

A zener holding the base of an NPN emitter follower, which passes the load current: on one screen,

  • Inputs: the zener (the same 1N4728A–1N4761A and BZX55 parts as Zener regulation, or custom), the transistor (BD139, TIP31C, 2N3055, or custom with its least hFE), the supply's lowest and highest voltage, the most load current, the zener's least current, the base-emitter drop (0.7 V by default), and the zener's resistor you use.
  • The big result: the output, Vz less the base-emitter drop, over the zener's tolerance; under it, the zener's resistor: the largest E24 value in its window, or why none works.
  • For the resistor you use:
  • the base current at full load, IL / (hFE + 1), with the hFE used;
  • the zener current at the two extremes, flagged under its least current or over its maximum;
  • the zener's and the resistor's heat at worst;
  • the transistor's heat at worst, (Vin max − Vout) × IL, compared with its free-air rating and its rating with the case at 25 °C, pointing to Heat sink sizing when it needs one;
  • its current and VCEO ratings;
  • the base-emitter drop the datasheet gives at a high current.
  • The resistor box follows the suggestion until you type your own.
  • Units: currents in µA, mA or A, the resistor in Ω, kΩ or MΩ.
  • Drawing: the supply on the collector, the resistor to the base, the reverse-biased zener to ground, the emitter feeding the load.
  • Remembered: the zener, the transistor and the units.

Examples: 5 V at 500 mA from 12–18 V with a 1N4734A and a BD139; 12 V at 0.5 A from 16–20 V with a 1N4743A and a TIP31C; a 2N3055 at 4 A, where no resistor works.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; it sets the series the zener's resistor is chosen from (E24 by default).

Source

  • Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, vol. III, ch. 4 (read, ibiblio HTML), "common collector application: voltage regulator": a common-collector transistor amplifies the current "so that the zener diode circuit only has to handle the amount of current necessary to drive the base of the transistor"; "the load voltage will be approximately 0.7 volts less than the zener diode voltage"; when one transistor's gain is not enough, several can be combined (a Darlington). His ch. 9 shows the zener alone at 5.1 V and 500 mA from 12–18 V would dissipate "close to 5W".
  • ST BD135/BD139, September 2001 (read, a copy on MIT's wiki): IC 1.5 A, VCEO 80 V, Ptot 12.5 W at Tcase ≤ 25 °C and 1.25 W at Tamb ≤ 25 °C, VBE 1 V at IC 0.5 A, hFE 25 min at 0.5 A (40 at 150 mA), Rth j-case 10 °C/W.
  • Fairchild TIP31 series, rev. A, February 2000 (read): TIP31C VCEO 100 V, IC 3 A, PC 40 W at TC 25 °C and 2 W at Ta 25 °C, hFE 25 min at 1 A and 10 to 50 at 3 A, VBE(sat) 1.8 V at 3 A. θJC is taken as (150 − 25) / 40 = 3.125 °C/W from the derating, which the sheet does not print.
  • 2N3055, a two-page sheet whose maker is not printed (read): VCEO 60 V, IC 15 A, 115 W at TC 25 °C, RthJC 1.52 °C/W, hFE 20 to 70 at 4 A, VBE(on) 1.5 V at 4 A. onsemi's own sheet could not be downloaded.
  • The zeners: Vishay's sheets, as in Zener regulation.

Why the formulas are these

Vout = Vz − VBE
IB = IL / (hFE + 1)
Rs ≤ (Vin min − Vz max) / (IB + Iz min)
Rs ≥ (Vin max − Vz min) / Iz max
P transistor = (Vin max − Vout min) × IL

The emitter follows the base less one diode drop, so the output is set by the zener. The emitter carries the load; the base needs that divided by the gain plus one, and that is all the zener's resistor has to supply on top of the zener's own least current. With no load the base takes nothing, so the whole resistor current goes through the zener: that sets the other end of the window. The transistor drops everything between the supply and the output, at the full load current.

Assumptions and limits

  • hFE is the datasheet's minimum at the current it names; it falls at higher currents (the TIP31C's 25 at 1 A is 10 at 3 A). For a load near the transistor's rating, type the lower figure as a custom part.
  • VBE is 0.7 V by default, Kuphaldt's figure at modest current; the datasheets give up to 1 to 1.8 V at amps, so the output falls a little as the load grows.
  • No current limit: a short on the output puts the whole supply across the transistor; this circuit has no protection.
  • A base needing more than the zener can give needs a driver transistor (a Darlington), not drawn here.

How it was checked

9 cases: - 1N4734A and BD139, 12–18 V, 500 mA: base 19.2 mA, a 78.27–302.5 Ω window, 300 Ω, output 4.62–5.18 V; - with 300 Ω: 1.17 to 42.3 mA in the zener, 249 mW, 536 mW in the resistor; - the BD139 at 6.69 W: over free air, under its case rating; - 1N4743A and TIP31C, 16–20 V, 0.5 A: a 110.9–120.6 Ω window, 120 Ω, 353 µA left at worst, 4.17 W; - a 2N3055 at 4 A needs 190 mA of base: no resistor works; - a 50 mA load stays within the BD139's free-air rating (669 mW); - 2 A is flagged over the BD139's 1.5 A; - a custom hFE of 100 needs 4.95 mA; - the remembered transistor and zener.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Constant current

(formerly Constant current source/driver)

What it computes

An adjustable regulator made into a current source with one resistor, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the regulator (LM317, LM1117-ADJ, AMS1117-ADJ, LM1086-ADJ, with the figures read for Linear regulator, or a custom Vref and dropout), the current wanted, the supply's lowest and highest voltage, the load's least and most voltage (an LED string, a battery), and the resistor you use.
  • The big result: the resistor, Vref / (I − Iadj), and the E24 values either side of it with the current each gives.
  • The resistor you use follows the nearest E24 value until you type your own; a new current wanted brings it back. When the nearest would pass the part's rating, it takes the larger one instead (Pierre: an LM1086 at 1450 mA picked 820 mΩ, 1.52 A, over its 1.5 A; now 910 mΩ, 1.37 A). For it:
  • the current, with its spread over the reference's tolerance;
  • the resistor's heat, Vref × I;
  • the most load voltage it can drive at the lowest supply (supply less Vref and the part's headroom or dropout at that current), flagged when the load needs more;
  • the regulator's heat at the highest supply and the lowest load voltage;
  • warnings under the part's minimum load current (typical, then guaranteed) and over its current rating, naming the resistor.
  • Units: the current in µA, mA or A, the resistor in Ω, kΩ or MΩ.
  • Drawing: the regulator with IN, OUT and ADJ, R from OUT, ADJ tied to the load side of R, the load to ground.
  • Remembered: the regulator and the units.

Examples: TI's 50 mA charger (24 Ω), 350 mA for a power LED, 20 mA for an LED string, and 5 mA, too little for an LM317.

Standard values. The resistors' tolerance, with its E series, is picked in the "Your inputs" heading above the inputs, as in the Passive components tools: ±0.1 % to ±20 %, ±5 % being E24 and ±1 % E96; it sets the series the resistor is chosen from (E24 by default).

Source

  • TI LM317, SLVS044Z, April 2025 (read): "By connecting a fixed resistor between the adjustment pin and output, the LM317 is also able to be used as a precision current regulator"; §8.3.3, a precision current limiter, Ilimit = 1.2 V / R1; §8.3.7, a 50 mA constant-current battery charger, "ICHG = 1.25V ÷ 24 Ω. Make sure VI is greater than VBAT + 4.25V. (1.25V [VREF] + 3V [headroom])". The tool takes the reference at its worst, 1.3 V, so it asks for 4.3 V over the battery.
  • The parts' figures: as in Linear regulator (TI LM317 and LM1117, AMS AMS1117, TI LM1086): Vref and its spread, the adjust-pin current, the minimum load current, the headroom or dropout, the current rating.

Why the formulas are these

I = Vref / R + Iadj
R = Vref / (I − Iadj)
Vload max = Vin min − Vref − headroom
P resistor = Vref × (I − Iadj),   P regulator = (Vin max − Vload min − Vref) × I

The regulator holds Vref between OUT and ADJ. With only R between them, the current through R is Vref / R whatever the load; it flows on into the load, joined by the adjust-pin current. The regulator keeps this up as long as it has its headroom: the supply must cover the load's voltage, Vref and that headroom. Whatever the load does not use, the regulator drops as heat.

Assumptions and limits

  • The minimum load current is the least the regulator needs to regulate at all (LM317: 3.5 mA typical, 10 mA guaranteed); a current source below it is not assured.
  • The LM1117's dropout is interpolated between its listed currents; the others' is their full-load figure, as in Linear regulator.
  • Vref's tolerance moves the current by the same proportion (the LM317's 1.2 to 1.3 V is ± 4 %); a 1 % resistor adds its own 1 %.
  • The regulator's heat needs a heatsink past a watt or two; see Heat sink sizing.

How it was checked

13 cases: - TI's 24 Ω: 52.1 mA (50 to 54.2 mA over Vref), 65.1 mW in R; - that charger from 12 V: 7.7 V left for the battery, 248 mW in the regulator; - 350 mA: 3.572 Ω, 3.6 Ω (E24) gives 347 mA, 434 mW; - 20 mA: 62 Ω gives 20.2 mA, three LEDs at 9.6 V fit under 9.7 V; - 5 mA is under the LM317's guaranteed 10 mA, 2 mA under even its typical 3.5 mA; - a load needing more than the supply leaves is flagged; - the LM1117 needs only its 1.13 V dropout at 347 mA: 9.61 V left; - a typed resistor holds (4.7 Ω gives 266 mA); - over 1.5 A is over the LM317's rating; - an LM1086 at 1450 mA picks 910 mΩ (1.37 A), not the nearer 820 mΩ (1.52 A), which is flagged when typed; - the remembered regulator.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Inrush limiter (NTC)

(formerly Inrush current limiter (NTC))

What it computes

An NTC thermistor in series with a supply, to hold down the surge that charging its capacitor draws at turn-on, on one screen:

  • AC mains or DC (pills): the line voltage (or the DC supply), how far it can run high (%), the highest inrush current allowed, the load capacitance, and the running current.
  • The big result: the least cold resistance, the peak voltage over the inrush allowed; the peak is √2 × the highest line voltage on AC.
  • Below it:
  • the energy the thermistor must absorb, ½ C Vpeak²;
  • the Vishay Ametherm SL10 parts that fit on all counts (the low end of their R25 tolerance still over the least resistance, their energy rating over the need, their current rating over the running current, 265 Vac at most), the coolest first, each with its resistance, energy and current ratings, its running resistance, the voltage it loses (and that share of the supply) and the heat;
  • over 2 % of the supply lost (Pierre's threshold), a flag: a bypass relay after start-up, or an active (MOSFET) soft-start, loses less;
  • when none fits, why, and that a larger series is needed.

Why an NTC rather than a resistor (Pierre asked): cold, it holds the surge down; warmed by its own current, it falls 10 to 50 times (TDK), so it loses little while running. At 230 V and 1 A an SL1025002 is about 1 Ω hot, 1 V lost (0.4 %) and 1 W; a fixed 18 Ω limiting the same surge would lose 18 V and 18 W for good. It is not free: some volts remain, and a hot NTC barely limits a quick restart. It need not be big: the energy (½ C V²) and the running current set its size, and it should run at 30 to 100 % of its rating (TDK) to heat up. It suits mains supplies (about 100 to 265 Vac) and higher DC rails, where its drop is under 1 %; on a 12 V rail at 3 A the same parts lose 4.5 to 7 %, and an active soft-start is the better choice. - Drawing: the supply, the NTC (the calculated part, green), the bridge on AC, the capacitor, and the peak voltage. - Units: both currents in mA or A, the capacitance in µF or mF, each with its own picker. - Remembered: AC or DC, and the units.

Examples: Eaton's 110 Vac + 10 %, Ametherm's 265 Vac and 100 A, a 230 V supply with 220 µF, a 48 V DC rail, and a 12 V rail at 3 A.

Source

  • Eaton, "Understanding the current limiting capabilities of power NTC thermistors", technical note ELX1247, July 2022 (read): the minimum zero-power resistance is the application's voltage divided by "the maximum desired peak surge current" (equation 2); the peak voltage from the maximum line voltage (equation 3): "a 110 VAC power supply with line voltage fluctuations that can inflate that value by 10% would yield a Vmax voltage of 121 V. Then, maximum peak voltage (Vpeak) would be 171 V"; the energy of the load capacitance must be known to select the part; the running current must not exceed its rating. Its equations are images in the PDF; the text gives them in words.
  • TDK Electronics, "NTC Inrush Current Limiters, application notes", July 2019, and EPCOS application note 2013 (read): the thermistor is connected in series, never in parallel; it drops by a factor of 10 to 50 when hot; its maximum permissible capacitance is tested per IEC 60539-1; it needs one to two minutes to cool before limiting fully again; the running resistance can be fitted as R = k·Iⁿ between 30 and 100 % of Imax.
  • Vishay Ametherm SL10, document 24503, revision 13 Aug 2026 (read): per part R25 and tolerance, the maximum steady current up to 65 °C, the maximum recommended energy (J), 265 Vac maximum, the maximum capacitance at 120 Vac, the resistance at 100 % and 50 % of the maximum current. Its own figures follow ½ C Vpeak²: 2000 µF at 120 Vac (170 V peak) is 28.8 J against the part's 30 J; 1300 µF is 18.7 J against 20 J. SL1050001 is left out: its table gives a lower resistance at 50 % than at 100 % current.
  • Ametherm's inrush page (read): its example, 265 Vac (375 V peak) and 100 A, "select a thermistor that can handle 13 A of current and has a capacity of at least 126 Joules"; 1800 µF reproduces 126 J, though the page does not print the capacitance.

Why the formulas are these

Vpeak = √2 × V line × (1 + high-line %)     (DC: V × (1 + %))
R cold ≥ Vpeak / I inrush
E = ½ × C × Vpeak²
P running = I² × R hot

At turn-on the capacitor is empty: the surge is the peak voltage over whatever resistance is in the way, so that resistance sets the surge. Charging a capacitor through a resistance costs as much energy in the resistance as ends up in the capacitor, ½ C V², and the cold NTC must take it without cracking. Once running, the current heats it until its resistance is small.

Assumptions and limits

  • Running resistance: the datasheet's points at 100 % and 50 % of the part's current, interpolated between; under half its current it is higher than the 50 % figure, and the tool says only that.
  • Ambient: the SL10's currents hold up to 65 °C; above that, derate (the datasheet's curve).
  • Restarting: a hot thermistor barely limits; it needs one to two minutes off to cool (TDK).
  • The wiring and the capacitor's ESR also limit the surge; the tool leaves them out, which is on the safe side.
  • One series: the SL10 (10 mm discs, up to 5 A and 30 J); bigger supplies need a larger series.

How it was checked

12 cases: - Eaton's 110 Vac + 10 %: 171 V peak, 8.56 Ω for 20 A, 6.88 J; - six SL10 parts fit, coolest first (SL1050002, 440 mΩ, 880 mV lost, 0.8 %, 1.76 W); - at 230 V and 1 A the hot NTC loses under 1 % (SL1025002: 0.46 %); - a 12 V rail at 3 A: every part loses over 2 % (SL102R005: 4.5 %), flagged; - Ametherm's 265 Vac, 100 A: 3.75 Ω, 126 J, no SL10 fits; - 230 V + 10 %, 220 µF, 30 A: 11.9 Ω, 14.1 J, six fit; - a part under half its current is over its light-load resistance; - a 48 V DC rail: 5.04 Ω, 1.27 J, three parts carry 3 A; - over 265 Vac and over 5 A are flagged; - the remembered AC or DC; - capacitance in mF and running current in mA: 220 µF reads 0.22, 1 A reads 1000.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

SMPS flyback basics

What it computes

The power stage of an isolated flyback converter in continuous conduction (CCM), the way TI's John Betten designs one, on one screen:

  • Shared inputs: the input range (lowest and highest), the output voltage and current, the switching frequency and the output diode's drop.
  • Three pills:
  • Transformer: from the maximum duty cycle you choose at the lowest input, the turns ratio Np : Ns, proposed until you type your own (Betten rounds his 4.08 to 4); the duty cycle over the input range with it; the primary inductance that keeps the converter in CCM down to a share of full load you set, proposed (two figures, rounded up) until you type your own, flagged when yours is lower; the peak primary current.
  • Switch & diode: the MOSFET's flat-top drain voltage and the 25 to 50 % more to allow for ringing, the peak primary current, the diode's reverse voltage, its current while it conducts and its loss.
  • Capacitors: the least output capacitance for the ripple allowed, its RMS current, and the input capacitance for the input ripple.
  • Units: the current in mA or A, the frequency in kHz or MHz, the inductance in µH or mH, each ripple in mV or V with its own picker.
  • Drawing: the input capacitor, the primary winding and the n-channel MOSFET Q (gate plate, three-dash channel, body arrow tied to the source, as in the MOSFET tools) on the primary ground; the secondary wound the other way (the dots), the diode, and the output capacitor last on the isolated secondary ground. The pill's parts are green.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: TI's 60 W design (its turns ratio and inductance as calculated, then rounded to its 4 : 1 and 80 µH), its MOSFET and diode, and its capacitors.

Terms

  • Flyback converter: a switching supply that stores energy in a transformer's core while its switch is on, and releases it to the output through the diode while the switch is off. The two windings are wound the opposite way (the dots) and isolate the output from the input.
  • MOSFET (the switch, Q): an n-channel enhancement MOSFET. FET (field-effect transistor) is the family it belongs to, with the JFET; Betten's article just says "FET".
  • Turns ratio (Np : Ns): primary turns over secondary turns.
  • The dots (winding sense): each dot marks the end of a winding that goes positive at the same moment as the other dotted end. In a flyback the dots sit at opposite ends, primary at the input end, secondary at the ground end: the windings are wound (or connected) the opposite way. While the MOSFET is on, the input drives the primary's dotted end positive, so the secondary's dotted (ground) end is positive too and its other end, the diode's anode, is negative: the diode blocks, no current flows to the output, and the energy builds up in the core (in its magnetizing inductance, the primary L). When the MOSFET turns off, the core's field keeps the current going and every winding's voltage reverses: the diode's anode goes positive, the diode conducts and the stored energy "flies back" to the output capacitor and the load (Betten, Power Tips #98: during the on-time the diode "is reverse-biased because of T1's secondary winding polarity"; at turn-off the "secondary voltage polarity reverses"). That is why a flyback's transformer works as two coupled inductors, and why the primary inductance matters. Both windings' turns face the core in the drawing, as in any transformer symbol; only the dots show the sense.
  • Reflected voltage: while the diode conducts, the output plus the diode drop appear across the primary multiplied by Np/Ns; the MOSFET sees the input plus that.
  • Flat-top voltage: the MOSFET's drain voltage while off, before the ringing that the transformer's leakage inductance adds.
  • CCM / DCM: in continuous conduction the transformer's current never falls to zero within a cycle; below a certain load it does (discontinuous conduction, DCM).
  • Primary inductance (L): the inductance of the primary winding; it sets the load at which the converter leaves CCM.
  • RMS current: the heating value of a current; capacitors are rated for it.

Source

  • John Betten, "Designing a CCM flyback converter", TI technical article SSZTCY0, February 2024 (read): a 60 W, 53 V to 12 V at 5 A flyback at 250 kHz, 51 to 57 V in, 50 % maximum duty cycle at 51 V. Eq. 1, the volt-second balance; eqs. 2, 3: Nps = Vinmin × dmax / ((Vout + Vd)(1 − dmax)), 51 V × 0.5 / (12.5 V × 0.5), "4:1 step-down"; eq. 4: d = Nps (Vout + Vd) / (Vin + Nps (Vout + Vd)), 0.47 at 57 V; eq. 5: Vdsmax = Vinmax + Nps (Vout + Vd) = 107 V, "derate the FET voltage an additional 25-50%, selecting a 200V FET"; eq. 6: the diode's reverse voltage Vout + Vinmax / Nps, 26 V; eq. 7: ID1 = Ioutmax / (1 − dmax), 10 A; eq. 8: PD1 = Ioutmax × Vd, 1.7 W at the 0.33 V of the diode chosen; eq. 9: Lmin = Vinmin² dmax² η / (2 fsw Poutmin), 80 µH at 0.91 and 15 W, Poutmin "typically 20-30% of POUTMAX"; eq. 10: Ipripk = Ioutmax / ((1 − dmax) Nps) + Vinmin dmax / (2 Lpri fsw), 3.14 A; eq. 14: Coutmin = Ioutmax dmax / (fsw Vripout), 83 µF for 0.12 V; eq. 15, the output RMS current, 5 A; eq. 16: Cinmin = Ipripk dmax / (2 fsw Vinrip), 2 µF for 1.5 V. The PDF's text lost the square root in eq. 15; at 50 % both readings give 5 A, and the tool uses Iout √(d / (1 − d)).
  • John Betten, "Power Tips #98: Designing a DCM flyback converter", TI (read): the same converter in discontinuous conduction, its equations for the turns ratio with an idle time, the inductance and the peak current. The tool does not compute DCM; this is for further reading.
  • Not used: Unitrode's "60 Watt Flyback Regulator" (TI SLUP072, read): its primary inductance is derived in appendices missing from TI's PDF; Fairchild's AN-4137 could not be downloaded.

Why the formulas are these

Np/Ns = Vin(min) × dmax / ((Vout + Vd)(1 − dmax))
d = N (Vout + Vd) / (Vin + N (Vout + Vd))
Vds = Vin(max) + N (Vout + Vd),   Vdiode = Vout + Vin(max) / N
L = Vin(min)² d² η / (2 fs Pout(min))
Ipk = Iout / ((1 − d) N) + Vin(min) d / (2 L fs)
Cout = Iout d / (fs ΔVout),   Cin = Ipk d / (2 fs ΔVin)

The core must end each cycle where it started: the input across the primary for the on-time d must equal the reflected output, (Vout + Vd) × N, for the off-time 1 − d. That gives the turns ratio for the duty cycle chosen, and the duty cycle at any input once the ratio is set. The output gets current only during 1 − d, so the diode carries Iout / (1 − d) while it conducts, and the primary that times 1/N, plus half the ripple: the peak. While the switch is on the output capacitor alone feeds the load, hence its size.

Which duty cycle. Betten works his currents and capacitors at dmax = 0.5 although his rounded 4 : 1 gives 0.495 at 51 V. The tool works everything at the duty cycle the turns ratio in use gives at the lowest input, so with 4 : 1 it shows 3.11 A of peak current where he gives 3.14 A, 77.3 µH where he gives 80 µH, 82.5 µF where he gives 83 µF and 2.05 µF where he gives 2 µF. With his exact 4.08 : 1 they agree.

Assumptions and limits

  • CCM at full load only: below Pout(min) the converter enters DCM, the duty cycle falls and these formulas no longer hold.
  • The diode drop is one figure for both the turns ratio and the loss; Betten assumes 0.5 V for the ratio and uses his diode's 0.33 V for the loss.
  • Ringing: the flat-top voltages leave out the leakage-inductance spike; the 25 to 50 % allowance is Betten's, and a snubber or clamp is usually needed.
  • Not computed: the transformer's core, turns and wire, the leakage inductance, the current-sense resistor, the MOSFET's losses, the control loop and any second output.

How it was checked

7 cases: - TI's design: 51 V at 50 %, 12 V + 0.5 V, gives 4.08 : 1, and 78.9 µH at 91 % keeps CCM down to 15 W (its 80 µH); 50 % to 47.2 % over the input; - rounded to its 4 : 1: 49.5 % to 46.7 % (its 0.47 at 57 V), 3.11 A peak with its 80 µH; - 107 V flat-top on the MOSFET (its 107 V), 26.3 V on the diode (its 26 V), 9.9 A while it conducts, 2.5 W at 0.5 V; - 82.5 µF for 120 mV, 2.05 µF for 1.5 V, 4.95 A RMS in the output capacitor; - the proposed turns ratio follows the input (40 V: 3.2 : 1); - a typed inductance under the minimum is flagged; - a 100 % maximum duty is refused.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

Power factor

What it computes

A load's power factor and the capacitor that raises it to a target: single phase, or three phase with the capacitors in delta or in star. The drawing, single phase, is the supply, the capacitor (green, the answer) and the load (R and L) across it. Three phase, it shows how the bank is wired (Pierre): the lines L1, L2, L3 from the supply to the motor (M 3~), and the three capacitors tapped off them, in delta one between each pair of lines (L1–L2, L2–L3, L1–L3), in star one from each line to a common star point. A tap that crosses another line without joining it hops over it; a dot is a connection.

  • Pills: Single phase, Three phase (the voltage then the line voltage U between phases; 230 V becomes 400 V and back, unless typed). In three phase the Your inputs heading picks Capacitors in delta or in star.
  • Inputs: the voltage and frequency, the active power P (W or kW), cos φ now, the target cos φ, and the current's THDi in % (0 for a sine).
  • Big result: the capacitor, per phase in three phase, with the reactive power Qc it supplies; "none" when cos φ is already at or over the target.
  • Cells: Qc and the line current before and after. Rows: S and Q before and after, tan φ − tan φ′ (the var per W of the guide's table), the capacitor's current (the bank's line current Q / (√3 U) in three phase), the true power factor λ before and after, and, with THDi, the most a capacitor can reach.
  • Remembered: the pill, the connection and the power unit.

Examples: the guide's 100 kW motor (48.7 kvar), the guide's table from 0.7 to 0.95 (59.1 kvar), a 1 kW motor on 230 V (33.3 µF), a rectifier input with THDi 120 % (λ 0.63).

Terms

  • Active power P (W): the power that does work. Reactive power Q (var): the power that flows back and forth each cycle in an inductance or capacitance. Apparent power S (VA): what the wiring carries, V I; with sine waves S = √(P² + Q²).
  • cos φ (displacement power factor): φ is the current's lag behind the voltage, for the fundamental; tan φ = Q / P.
  • Power factor λ: P / S, which counts the harmonics too; with a sine current it is cos φ.
  • THDi: the r.m.s. of the current's harmonics over its fundamental, in %.
  • Delta, star: a three-phase bank's three capacitors each across two lines (delta, the line voltage U), or each from a line to a common point (star, U / √3).

Sources

  • Schneider Electric, "Electrical Installation Guide" (electrical-installation.org wiki, read in the browser pane; the site refuses automated fetches): "Theoretical principles to improve power factor" (chapter L), Qc = P (tan φ − tan φ′) and its example, 100 kW at 0.75 (tan φ 0.88) to 0.93 (0.4): 48 kvar; "How to determine the optimum level of compensation", 0.691 × 85.4 = 59 kvar from 0.7 to 0.95 (seen in the search extract); "Implementation of capacitor banks", a three-phase bank's rated current IN = Q / (√3 U), 50 kvar at 400 V: 72 A; "Harmonic distortion indicators – Power factor" (chapter M), λ = P / S, not to be mixed up with cos φ, and with a sinusoidal voltage λ ≈ cos φ / √(1 + THDi²).

Why the formulas are these

The capacitor's reactive power Qc = P (tan φ − tan φ′), from the guide: P stays, Q falls from P tan φ to P tan φ′. The tool gives 48.7 kvar for the guide's motor (48 with the guide's rounded tangents), 0.692 var per W and 59.1 kvar for its table's case (0.691 and 59).

The capacitance (derived): a capacitor C across a voltage V takes Q = 2π f C V². Single phase C = Qc / (2π f V²). Three phase, three capacitors share Qc: in delta each is across U, C = Qc / (3 · 2π f U²); in star each is across U / √3, C = Qc / (2π f U²), three times as much.

The currents (derived): the line current is S / V (single phase) or S / (√3 U). The fundamental current is P / (V cos φ); the harmonic currents, I1 THDi, are left as they are by the capacitor, so the current after is √(I1′² + Ih²) and λ after is P over the new S. Corrected fully (cos φ′ = 1), λ reaches at most 1 / √(1 + (THDi / cos φ)²).

Assumptions and limits

  • A lagging (inductive) load and a sinusoidal voltage; a balanced three-phase load.
  • Harmonics: a capacitor corrects only the displacement; with harmonics it can also resonate with the supply (the guide warns of it), which the tool does not check.
  • Display. Three figures.

How it was checked

35 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps and typing, itself checked against the guide's three examples. The cases: the opening screen and the picker; three phase in delta and star, the voltage carried over and kept when typed; targets, starting factors, frequencies, voltages, powers and THDi single phase and three phase; the target under cos φ now; W and kW; remembered choices; eight refusals; the four examples.

Power electronics › Supply & regulation

PoE classes

What it computes

The Power over Ethernet class a device needs, and what a real cable does to it: the current, the power the PSE (the switch or injector) must source, the cable's loss and the voltage left at the device. The drawing shows the PSE, the cable and the device, the answers (current, loss, voltage at the device) in green, the voltage red when it falls under what the device may need.

  • Inputs: the device's power, the cable's length (m or ft) and the PSE voltage, which follows the class's minimum (44, 50 or 52 V) until typed. The Your inputs heading picks the wire gauge (AWG 22, 23, 24 or 26) and the pairs (2 or 4; Classes 5 to 8 always use 4).
  • Big result: the class, the smallest whose device power covers the one entered, with its standard and Type and the power the PSE sources; or, in its place, why it fails: the PSE over its class's power, or the device's voltage under its minimum.
  • Cells: the voltage at the device, the current, the cable's loss. Rows: the class's PSE power and minimum voltage, the power the device may draw at 100 m, the cable's loop resistance against the standard's maximum, the voltage the device may need.
  • Remembered: the length unit, the gauge and the pairs.

Examples: a 25.5 W device at 100 m (Class 4, 45.3 V at the device), the white paper's 65 W Class 8 device (66.2 W sourced; 66.5 W measured), a 13 W camera at 100 m (Class 3, 41.4 V), 25 W over 200 m (too far).

Terms

  • PSE, PD: the power sourcing equipment (a PoE switch or injector) and the powered device (a camera, an access point).
  • Class: the power level a device asks for at start-up, 1 to 8; Type: the generation (Type 1 802.3af, Type 2 802.3at, Types 3 and 4 802.3bt).
  • Pairs: an Ethernet cable has four twisted pairs; PoE sends the current out on one pair and back on another (2 pairs), or on all four, which halves the loop resistance.
  • Loop resistance: the resistance the current meets going to the device and back.

Sources

  • L. Yseboodt (Philips Lighting) and D. Abramson (Texas Instruments), "Overview of 802.3bt – Power over Ethernet standard" (Ethernet Alliance white paper, April 2018, based on P802.3bt Draft 3.3; PDF read as text): the classes' PSE output 4, 7, 15.4, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90 W and device power 3.84, 6.49, 13, 25.5, 40, 51, 62 and 71.3 W (p. 2); the Types and their pairs (pp. 10–11); the maximum pairset loop resistance RCh 12.5 Ω, 6.25 Ω on four pairs, RChan = RPair1 + RPair2 (p. 12); equation (5), the PSE power that delivers PClass_PD at the device over RChan from VPSE, PClass = VPSE (VPSE − √(VPSE² − 4 RChan PClass_PD)) / (2 RChan) (p. 37); the Autoclass example, a 65 W Class 8 device on a 25 m AWG 23 patch cord from 55 V, 66.5 W measured at the PSE (p. 29).
  • Texas Instruments, TPS2372 data sheet, table 6 "Comparison of Operational Limits" (PDF read as text): Type 1 20 Ω, 15.4 W, 44 V, 13 W, device 37–57 V; Type 2 and Type 3 on two pairs 12.5 Ω, 30 W, 50 V, 25.5 W; Type 3 on four pairs 6.25 Ω, 60 W, 50 V, 51 W; Type 4 6.25 Ω, 90 W, 52 V, 71.3 W; the device's static input voltage 37–57 V up to 13 W, 42.5–57 V above, 41.2–57 V for Type 4.
  • Not read: IEEE 802.3 itself (paywalled); Microchip's PoE pages (down for maintenance) and Analog Devices' article (the site refuses access).

Why the formulas are these

The class table follows from the two sources together: each class's PSE power, at its Type's lowest voltage, over its maximum loop, leaves the device power, P_device = P_PSE − (P_PSE / Vmin)² R; all eight classes within 0.4 % (the tables round: 12.95 W is printed 13 W).

The real cable. Equation (5) is the root of R I² − V I + P = 0: the current that leaves P at the device after a loop resistance R. The PSE sources V I, the cable burns I² R, the device sees V − I R. When V² < 4 R P no current can deliver P: the most that can reach the device is V² / 4R. The white paper's example comes out 66.2 W against its 66.5 W measured (−0.4 %), as the copper alone should (connectors and a warm cable add a little).

The wire. Copper at 20 °C, 1/58 Ω·mm²/m, on the AWG diameter (as in Wire sizing); a pair is two wires in parallel, so the loop of one wire's length on two pairs, half that on four. 100 m of AWG 24 is 8.42 Ω, inside the 12.5 Ω the standard allows for 100 m with patch cords, connectors and heat.

Assumptions and limits

  • Single-signature devices, powered on 2 or 4 pairs as a whole; dual-signature devices (each pairset its own class) are not covered.
  • The cable at 20 °C: a warm bundle has more resistance (copper +0.39 %/°C); patch cords and connectors add to the loop.
  • Class 0 (an alias of Class 3 in 802.3af, deprecated in 802.3bt) is shown as Class 3. Autoclass and power demotion are not modelled.
  • Display. Three figures.

How it was checked

43 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's typing and picks, itself checked against the class table and the white paper's example. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; fifteen powers across the class edges (3.84 / 3.85 W, 13 / 13.1 W, 71.3 W); lengths from 5 m to 400 m, two over the class and one that cannot deliver; three gauges; four pairs, and Class 5 fixing them; a typed PSE voltage kept when the class changes; 57 V; feet; remembered choices; five refusals; the four examples.

Power electronics › Battery

Battery runtime

(formerly Runtime / capacity estimation)

What it computes

Any one of runtime, load current and battery capacity from the other two, one pill each, with a "usable" share of the capacity (100% by default). The answer is the large result; under a runtime of more than two days the same span is given in days, and past two years in years. The pill, the usable share and the units are remembered.

Examples: a CR2032 at the load its datasheet rates it at, a sensor averaging 20 µA on one, an 18650 at 500 mA, the current that lasts a day, and the capacity a 1 A load needs for 8 hours.

Source

  • Energizer CR2032 datasheet: typical capacity 235 mAh to 2.0 V, rated at 15 kΩ (a drain of 0.19 mA at 2.9 V), 1245 hours to 2.0 V in that test, and about 1% a year self-discharge.
  • Panasonic NCR18650B datasheet: rated capacity at least 3200 mAh (typical 3350 mAh), discharged to 2.5 V.
  • Energizer E91 (AA alkaline) datasheet: it gives capacity as a graph against continuous discharge current, 25 to 500 mA, not as one number — which is why the tool leaves the usable share to you rather than inventing one figure.

Why the formulas are these

Runtime = Capacity × Usable / Current
Current = Capacity × Usable / Runtime
Capacity = Current × Runtime / Usable

Capacity in ampere-hours is a charge: a current times a time. A battery that delivers 2000 mA for one hour holds 2000 mAh, and in this model gives 20 mA for 100 hours. The CR2032 checks it: 235 mAh at 0.19 mA is 1237 hours, and Energizer measured 1245.

Assumptions and limits

  • Constant current. Real loads pulse; use the average current, and know that heavy pulses cost more than their average on small cells.
  • Capacity depends on the load. Datasheets rate capacity at one drain, which they state; at higher currents a cell generally delivers less, most markedly lead-acid (Peukert's effect). The usable share is where that goes, and no single figure fits every cell and load.
  • Cutoff voltage. The rated capacity is to a stated end voltage (2.0 V for the CR2032, 2.5 V for the NCR18650B); a circuit that quits earlier gets less.
  • Self-discharge and temperature are not modelled: over a year and more, the CR2032's 1% a year starts to count, and cold cuts capacity.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Cell capacities are in Battery types & sizes and Button cell sizes.
  • C-rate, the current as a multiple of capacity, has its own tool.

How it was checked

2000 mAh at 500 mA gives 4 h; at 80% usable, 3 h 12 min. 235 mAh at 0.19 mA gives 1237 h, about 51.54 days; at 20 µA, 11750 h, about 489.6 days. 3200 mAh at 500 mA gives 6 h 24 min. 2000 mAh over 24 h allows 83.3 mA. 1 A for 8 h at 85% usable needs 9.41 Ah.

The review made these changes: - The answer gained a line in days or years for long runtimes. - Values are kept in Ah, A and h, so a remembered unit only changes how a field shows them; the pill, the usable share and the units are remembered. - The drawing gained the cell's + plate, its designator BT1 and the current arrow its comment had promised. - It added five examples from the CR2032 and NCR18650B datasheets, the first cases (10) and this section.

Power electronics › Battery

Battery C-rate

(formerly C-rate)

What it computes

Any one of current, C-rate and capacity from the other two, one pill each, with the time a full charge or discharge takes at that rate, and a table of common C-rates and their times. The pill and the units are remembered.

Examples: a Panasonic 18650's standard charge, the same cell at 1C, a CR2032 at the load its datasheet rates it at, and the capacity a 2 A load needs to stay at 0.5C.

Source

  • Panasonic NCR18650B datasheet: standard charge CC-CV at 1625 mA to 4.20 V; capacity at least 3250 mAh at 25 °C, rated capacity at least 3200 mAh at 20 °C; its cycle-life and temperature curves discharge at 1C.
  • Energizer CR2032 datasheet: 235 mAh rated at 15 kΩ, a drain of 0.19 mA.

Why the formulas are these

Current = C-rate × Capacity
Time = 1 / C-rate

1C is the current that would move the battery's rated capacity in one hour: a 2000 mAh cell at 1C draws 2 A, at 0.5C 1 A for two hours. The C is the capacity, not the coulomb, though capacity in Ah is itself a charge (1 Ah = 3600 C). The 18650's standard charge checks it: 1625 mA into 3250 mAh is exactly 0.5C.

Assumptions and limits

  • A notation, not a permission. A cell's allowed charge and discharge C-rates are in its datasheet; this tool converts, it does not judge.
  • The time is nominal. A real charge slows in its constant-voltage phase, and a real discharge stops at the cutoff voltage, both before 1 / C-rate.
  • Capacity is the rated one. Which figure a datasheet's C refers to — the rated or the typical capacity — is its own; the NCR18650B quotes both.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Runtime from a real load is Battery runtime, with a usable share.
  • Peukert's effect and temperature are not modelled.

How it was checked

2000 mAh at 1C gives 2 A and 1 h; at 0.2C, 400 mA and 5 h. 1625 mA into 3250 mAh gives 0.5C and 2 h. 1C on 3200 mAh gives 3.2 A. 0.19 mA from 235 mAh gives 0.0008085C, 1237 h. 2 A at 0.5C needs 4 Ah.

The review made these changes: - Values are kept in Ah and A, so a remembered unit only changes how a field shows them; the pill and the units are remembered. - It added four examples from the NCR18650B and CR2032 datasheets, the first cases (9) and this section.

Power electronics › Battery

Internal resistance

(formerly Battery internal resistance)

What it computes

A battery's internal resistance, and the voltage it costs under load, three ways, by pill:

Pill Inputs Output
Two loads the voltage at a light and at a heavy current R, and the open-circuit voltage extrapolated
Resistor the voltage open, then across a known resistor R, and the current drawn
Drop the open-circuit voltage, R and a load current the voltage at the terminals
  • Measured modes also give:
  • the short-circuit current, Voc / R, in theory;
  • the most power the cell can deliver, into a load equal to R.
  • Drop mode also gives:
  • the power lost inside the cell, I²R;
  • the power delivered;
  • the current that would pull the cell down to a cutoff voltage you set.
  • Units: currents in µA, mA or A, resistance in mΩ or Ω, the test resistor in Ω or kΩ.
  • Drawing: the cell as an ideal source behind its resistance, in a dashed box, feeding the load.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: Energizer's dual pulse and voltage-drop examples, a 9 V battery with a 100 Ω resistor, a lithium-ion cell at two loads, and that cell at 10 A.

Source

Energizer, "Battery Internal Resistance", technical bulletin, version 1.1.0, December 2005 (data.energizer.com), read in review: - The definition: internal resistance is "the opposition to the flow of current within the battery", electronic plus ionic. - The dual pulse: a low stabilising drain, then a heavier pulse of about 100 ms; the resistance is "the change in voltage by the change in current". Its example: 5 mA then 505 mA, 1.485 V to 1.378 V, 0.107 V / 500 mA = 0.214 Ω. Fresh alkaline cylindrical cells run "approximately 150 to 300 milliohms". - Voltage under load: "multiplying the total effective resistance by the current". Its example: 1 A on 0.1 Ω from 1.6 V leaves 1.5 V. - Its cautions: - a 1000 Hz impedance test reads less than this total effective resistance; - the resistance rises as the cell discharges and as the temperature drops; - results depend on the technique, and are "a general guideline and not a precise value".

Why the formulas are these

two loads:  R = (V1 − V2) / (I2 − I1),  Voc = V1 + I1 × R
resistor:   I = V / RL,  R = (Voc − V) / I
under load: V = Voc − I × R,  loss = I² × R
Isc = Voc / R,  Pmax = Voc² / (4R)

A cell is modelled as a perfect source of its open-circuit voltage behind its resistance. The voltage falls in step with the current, so two readings give the slope, R. The most power comes out when the load equals R, and half of it then heats the cell.

Assumptions and limits

  • One resistance: a real cell's resistance has a fast electronic part and a slower ionic part, and changes with charge, age and temperature. The figure is for the conditions it was measured in.
  • The open-circuit voltage in Two loads is extrapolated along the straight line; it may differ from a cell left at rest.
  • The short-circuit current is a limit, not a test: shorting a cell, a lithium one above all, can burn it.

How it was checked

11 cases: - Energizer's dual pulse is 214 mΩ, extrapolating to 1.486 V open; - Energizer's drop leaves 1.5 V and loses 100 mW; - a 9 V battery at 8.6 V across 100 Ω has 6.977 Ω inside, at 86 mA; - a lithium-ion cell at two loads is 50 mΩ; - that cell at 10 A keeps 3.5 V, loses 5 W, and reaches 3.0 V at 20 A; - equal currents, readings the wrong way round, and a loaded voltage above the open one are refused; - a unit change keeps the value; - the remembered choices; - the test resistor in kΩ: 15 Ω reads 0.015.

Power electronics › Battery

Battery types & sizes

What it computes

A searchable list of cylindrical cells — AAAA to D, 9V, the lithium AA and AAA, CR2, CR123A and the Li-ion 14500, 18650, 21700 and 26650 — each with its IEC and ANSI designations where they exist, dimensions, a capacity, and its chemistry and voltage. A filter splits alkaline/NiMH from lithium, and is remembered; the search matches the size, either designation or the text.

Source

Energizer's datasheets, one per size, read in review:

  • Designations: AAAA IEC LR61 (also LR8D425), ANSI 25A; AAA LR03, 24A; N LR1, 910A; AA LR6, 15A; C LR14, 14A; D LR20, 13A; 9V 6LR61 (also 6LF22), 1604A; lithium AAA (L92) FR03, 24-LF; lithium AA (L91) FR6 (FR14505), 15-LF; CR123A CR17345, 5018LC.
  • Lithium iron disulfide against alkaline: the L91 AA weighs 15 g against the E91 alkaline AA's 23 g, the L92 AAA 7.6 g against the E92's 11.5 g; both lithium cells run from −40 to 60 °C and keep 25 years on the shelf, against 10 years for the alkaline AA; the L91 allows 2.5 A continuous.
  • CR123A: 1500 mAh to 2.0 V, rated at 100 Ω; 1.5 A continuous.

Not from those sheets: the dimensions are the industry-standard maxima the sheets draw but whose figures could not be read as text, the CR2's sheet was not found, and the "≈" capacity ranges are typical market figures, because Energizer gives alkaline capacity only as a graph against the load.

Why the formulas are these

There is no formula: it is a reference. Two conventions are worth knowing. The IEC designation encodes the chemistry in its letters (L alkaline, F lithium iron disulfide, C lithium manganese dioxide, R round) and the size after them; the Li-ion names encode their dimensions, the first two digits the diameter in mm and the next two the length, so a 21700 is 21 × 70 mm.

Assumptions and limits

  • Capacity depends on the load. A capacity is meaningful only with the drain it was measured at; the ranges here are orientation, not a spec. For a real design, read the cell's datasheet graph at your current.
  • NiMH cells in the same sizes are 1.2 V and have their own capacities.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Button and coin cells are their own tool, Button cell sizes.
  • Runtime from a capacity is Battery runtime.

How it was checked

Searching "fr6" finds the lithium AA, "1604" the 9V, "17345" the CR123A with 1500 mAh and ANSI 5018LC; the Lithium filter starts with the lithium AAA and is remembered.

The review made these changes: - The lithium AA and AAA showed Energizer's model numbers L91 and L92 where the IEC designation belongs; they now read FR6 and FR03. The CR123A gained its IEC CR17345, and every cell with one its ANSI code. - The lithium cells' claimed advantages — a third lighter, below freezing, long shelf life — now carry Energizer's figures; the CR123A's capacity is Energizer's 1500 mAh rather than an approximation. - The search covers the ANSI codes; the filter is remembered. - It added the first cases (5) and this section.

Power electronics › Battery

Button cell sizes

(formerly Button cells)

What it computes

A searchable list of coin and button cells — alkaline, silver oxide, lithium and zinc-air — each with its IEC and ANSI designations where known, dimensions, a capacity with the end voltage it is measured to, its chemistry and voltage, and a note on uses and substitutes. A filter by chemistry is remembered; the search matches the common name, either designation or the chemistry.

Source

Energizer's datasheets, read in review, give each cell's typical capacity and designations:

  • Alkaline: LR44 (Energizer A76) 150 mAh to 0.9 V at 7.5 kΩ, IEC LR44, ANSI 1166A; LR1130 (189) 80 mAh to 0.9 V, IEC LR54.
  • Silver oxide, to 1.2 V: SR44 (357) 150 mAh at 6.8 kΩ, IEC SR44, ANSI 1131SO; SR621 (364) 23 mAh at 68 kΩ, IEC SR60, ANSI 1175SO; SR626 (377) 27 mAh at 45 kΩ, IEC SR66, ANSI 1176SO; SR920 (371) 35 mAh at 30 kΩ, IEC SR69.
  • Lithium, to 2.0 V: CR1220 37 mAh (ANSI 5012LC), CR1616 60 mAh, CR1632 130 mAh, CR2016 100 mAh (5000LC), CR2025 170 mAh (5003LC), CR2032 235 mAh at 15 kΩ (5004LC), CR2450 620 mAh (5029LC).

Not from those sheets: the dimensions, which the sheets draw but could not be read as text, and the zinc-air capacities, which remain typical market ranges.

Why the formulas are these

There is no formula: it is a reference. A lithium coin's name gives its size: the first two digits are the diameter in mm and the last two the thickness in tenths of a mm, so a CR2032 is 20 × 3.2 mm. The IEC numbers of alkaline and silver-oxide cells (LR54, SR66) are size codes, not dimensions, which is why trade names like LR1130 and SR626 stay in use.

Assumptions and limits

  • Capacity is to an end voltage at one load, given with each figure; a heavier load or a higher cutoff gets less.
  • Same size, different chemistry: LR44 and SR44 share a case at 1.5 V and 1.55 V; silver oxide's flatter curve suits watches, so the substitution works one way only.
  • Zinc-air cells start their life when the tab is peeled.

What it deliberately does not do

  • Cylindrical cells are Battery types & sizes.
  • Runtime is Battery runtime.

How it was checked

Searching "lr54" finds the LR1130 with 80 mAh to 0.9 V; "cr2016" shows 100 mAh to 2.0 V and ANSI 5000LC; "sr66" finds the SR626; the Zinc-air filter is remembered.

The review made these changes: - Capacities are Energizer's typical figures with their end voltage, where the table had ranges — three of which (CR1616, CR2016, CR2025) sat below Energizer's figure. - IEC and ANSI designations were added; LR1130's IEC name is LR54, and the silver-oxide cells' are SR44, SR60, SR66 and SR69. The search covers them. - The filter is remembered; it added the first cases (4) and this section.

Power electronics › Thermal management

Heat sink sizing

(also takes in the planned Thermal resistance (θJA / θJC))

What it computes

The thermal chain from a part's junction to the air, three ways, by pill:

Pill Inputs Output
Sink needed power, junction limit, ambient, θJC, θCS the heatsink θSA to buy, at most
Junction power, ambient, θJC, θCS, θSA the junction temperature
Max power junction limit, ambient, θJC, θCS, θSA the most power the part can dissipate
  • The terms, each a thermal resistance in °C per watt:
  • θJC, junction to case: the part's datasheet, the figure through the tab or the bottom of the package (often written RθJC(bot));
  • θCS, case to sink: the interface, grease, a pad or mica;
  • θSA, sink to air: the heatsink's rating, usually in still air.
  • Sink needed says how to find a heatsink: search a distributor's heatsinks for the part's package, rated at the answer or less in still air. It then checks five real heatsinks, small to large (19.7 to 7 °C/W), each with its maker and order code and what it fits (package, clip or channel, solder pins, size), and gives the junction temperature each one would reach. When θJC and the interface alone use up the whole budget, it says no heatsink is enough and gives the most power an ideal one (0 °C/W) would allow.
  • Junction also gives the case (tab) and heatsink temperatures, which is what a finger or a thermocouple meets.
  • Max power also gives the heatsink temperature at that power.
  • A picked heatsink is named, with what it fits, in Junction and Max power.
  • Pickers: the interface fills θCS with a TO-220 figure (grease, dry, mica with grease, dry mica); the heatsink fills θSA. Any value can be typed instead, and the picker then reads Custom.
  • Drawing: the chain as a circuit, the power as a source driving into the junction, θJC, θCS and θSA in series to the ambient, with the temperature of each node; the unknown in green.
  • Units: power in mW or W. Remembered: the pill and the unit.

Examples: a 7805 dissipating 3.6 W (from the Linear regulator tool's 12 V to 5 V at 500 mA) in a TO-220 with grease, the same insulated with mica in a 50 °C box, 7 W on an SK 104, the most power on an SK 104 with dry mica, and 50 W in a TO-220.

Source

  • Fairchild (onsemi) AN-4166, "Heat Sink Mounting Guide", rev. 1.0.0, 2014 (read): the junction-to-ambient resistance "is the sum of" junction-case, case-heat sink, heat sink and heat sink-ambient resistances (figure 1); the contact resistance between case and sink depends on surface roughness and contact pressure, and grease or a pad fills the air gap. Its table 1 gives interface materials per area (°C·in²/W), not per package, so it is not used for the figures.
  • Motorola AN-778, "Mounting Considerations for Power Semiconductors" (read, a scanned copy; its successor is onsemi AN1040, which onsemi's site refused to serve), table 1, TO-220AB on a 6-32 screw at 8 in-lb: metal to metal 1.2 °C/W dry, 1.0 lubed (grease); with a 2 mil mica insulator 3.4 dry, 1.6 lubed. "Dry interface values are subject to wide variation." Its text: grease typically reduces the interface resistance 2 to 1 to 3 to 1 with an insulator.
  • θJC in the examples: TI LM340/LM7805 family (SNOSBT0L, September 2016), thermal information table, TO-220 RθJC(bot) 1.7 °C/W.
  • Heatsinks, each from its maker's own sheet (copies hosted by distributors), in still air; the makers rate them at different points, as noted:
  • Wakefield-Vette 268-85CTE: "channel style TO-220 heat sink featuring integrated mounting clip", 21.55 × 13.21 × 13.08 mm, 19.73 (the sheet prints no unit or condition; taken as °C/W in still air, like the others);
  • Aavid (Boyd) 530614B00000G: TO-220, "channel style heat sink with wide mounting surface", 29.97 × 11.68 × 12.70 mm, 16.70 °C/W "based on a 75 °C rise in natural convection";
  • Fischer Elektronik SK 104 38,1 STC: TO-220 drilling, "transistor clip mounting", solder pins, 34.9 × 12.7 mm, 38.1 mm long, Rth 11 K/W (Fischer's product page, a copy downloaded from Arrow);
  • Aavid (Boyd) 563202B00000G: TO-220, "space saving staggered fin heat sink", board-mounted, 9.40 °C/W at a 75 °C rise;
  • Ohmite WA-DT2-101E: "heat sink for TO-247 & TO-220", integral spring clip, solderable feet, vertical through-hole, Rs-a 7 °C/W in natural convection at 10 W.

An Aavid 577202B00000G (24.4 °C/W) was in the first version; it was dropped because only distributor listings of it were read.

Why the formulas are these

Tj = Ta + P × (θJC + θCS + θSA)
θSA = (Tj − Ta) / P − θJC − θCS
Pmax = (Tj − Ta) / (θJC + θCS + θSA)
Tc = Ta + P × (θCS + θSA),   Ts = Ta + P × θSA

Heat flowing through a thermal resistance raises the temperature across it by θ × P, as a current through a resistor raises a voltage. The three steps are in series, so their resistances add, and each node sits above the ambient by the power times everything between it and the air. The heatsink you need is what is left of the allowed total, (Tj − Ta) / P, once the part and the interface have taken theirs; a smaller θSA is a bigger heatsink.

Assumptions and limits

  • All the heat goes through the heatsink. A part also loses a little through its leads and the board, so the real junction runs slightly cooler.
  • θSA is not constant. Makers rate a heatsink at one temperature rise, in still air, mounted a given way; it improves as the sink gets hotter and with any airflow, and gets worse in a closed box or mounted flat.
  • The interface figures are for a TO-220 on a screw. Other packages, clips, thermal pads and torques differ; type the pad maker's figure.
  • The ambient is the air around the heatsink, which inside a box is above room temperature.
  • 125 °C is the default junction limit, the recommended maximum of most regulators; type the part's own.

How it was checked

11 cases: - 3.6 W, 125 °C from 25 °C, θJC 1.7 and grease 1.0: 25.1 °C/W or better, out of 27.8 in all; the Wakefield gives 106 °C, the SK 104 74 °C, and the hint names 25.1 °C/W; - mica and grease in a 50 °C box: 17.5 °C/W, the Wakefield too weak at 133 °C, the Aavid 530614 at 122 °C, the SK 104 at 101 °C; - a picked heatsink is named with what it fits; - 7 W through 1.7 + 1.0 + 11 °C/W: junction 121 °C, tab 109 °C, sink 102 °C; - from 50 °C through 16.1 °C/W in all: 4.66 W at most, the sink at 101 °C; - 50 W in a TO-220: no heatsink is enough, 37 W with an ideal one; - the interface picker fills 3.4 °C/W, and a typed value reads Custom; - a unit change keeps the power (3.6 W reads 3600 mW); - a junction limit under the ambient is refused; - the remembered pill.

Power electronics › Motors

Torque & power conversion

What it computes

A shaft's mechanical power from its torque and speed, or the torque from the power, in the usual units, and what the motor then draws from its supply. The drawing shows the supply and its current, the motor and its shaft turning, the torque and speed; what the tool finds is green.

  • Inputs: the speed (rpm, rad/s or rev/s), the torque (N·m, mN·m, kgf·cm, oz·in, lb·in, lb·ft) or the power (W, kW, hp, PS), the supply voltage and the motor's efficiency. The Output heading picks Given: torque (the power found) or Given: power (the torque found); switching carries the shaft over, to three figures.
  • Big result: the power or the torque, in its box's unit; under it the shaft it describes and the current it takes from the supply (the supply voltage changes only the current: the shaft's power and torque do not depend on it).
  • Cells: ω, the electrical input power and the current from the supply. Rows: the torque in metric and imperial units, the power in W, hp and PS, the speed in rpm, rad/s and rev/s, and the heat in the motor.
  • Remembered: what is given and the three units.

Examples: one horsepower at 1000 rpm (7.12 N·m), 100 oz·in at 1000 rpm (73.9 W), a drill at 10 N·m and 400 rpm (419 W, 31 A from 18 V), a small fan at 5 W and 3000 rpm (15.9 mN·m).

Terms

  • Torque τ: a turning force, a force at a lever arm: N·m (newton metres), or a weight at a distance, kgf·cm (a kilogram's weight at a centimetre), oz·in, lb·in, lb·ft.
  • Angular speed ω: radians per second; one turn is 2π radians, so ω = 2π n / 60 with n in rpm.
  • Horsepower: 550 foot-pounds-force per second, 745.7 W; the metric horsepower (PS, CV, ch) is 75 kilogram-force metres per second, 735.5 W.
  • Efficiency η: the mechanical power out over the electrical power in; the rest heats the motor.

Sources

  • NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), "Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI)", appendix B (PDF read as text): ounce (avoirdupois)-force inch 7.061 552 × 10⁻³ N·m, pound-force inch 1.129 848 × 10⁻¹ N·m, pound-force foot 1.355 818 N·m, kilogram-force meter 9.806 65 N·m, horsepower (550 ft·lbf/s) 745.699 9 W, horsepower (metric) 735.498 8 W, revolution per minute 1.047 198 × 10⁻¹ rad/s.

Why the formulas are these

P = τ ω is the definition of mechanical power for a rotating shaft (derived: the work of a torque through an angle). The units are computed from their definitions (the pound-force 4.448 221 615 260 5 N, the inch 0.0254 m, standard gravity 9.806 65 m/s²); each rounds to SP 811's seven figures (the metric horsepower is 735.498 75 W exactly, which SP 811 prints 735.498 8). The supply: the electrical input is P / η, the current P / (η V) for a DC supply (derived).

Assumptions and limits

  • A DC supply: for an AC motor the current also depends on its power factor (see Power factor).
  • One operating point: a motor's torque, speed and efficiency vary together along its curve; the tool converts the point given, it does not model the motor.
  • Display. Three figures.

How it was checked

35 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's typing and picks, its factors checked against SP 811. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; torques, speeds, efficiencies and voltages; every torque, power and speed unit; the unit linking; power given, the carry-over both ways; remembered choices; six refusals; the four examples.

Power electronics › Motors

Back-EMF / Lenz's law

What it computes

A brushed DC motor under a load, from its circuit: the supply, the winding's resistance and the back-EMF the turning rotor makes. The drawing is that circuit: the supply on the left, R on top, the back-EMF source E on the right, the current around the loop; what the tool finds is green.

  • Inputs: the supply voltage, the winding's resistance, the motor constant in the form the datasheet gives it (Kv in rpm/V, Ke in V/krpm, or Kt in N·m/A or mN·m/A; changing the form keeps the motor, its constant shown in the new form to three figures) and the load torque (mN·m, N·m, oz·in, kgf·cm; 0 for none).
  • Big result: the speed under the load, with the back-EMF and the power at the shaft under it.
  • Cells: the current, the back-EMF, the efficiency. Rows: the no-load speed, the stall current and torque, the electrical input and the copper loss, the constant as Kv, Ke and Kt together, the motor constant KM.
  • Remembered: the constant's form and the torque unit.

Examples: Wikipedia's 5700 rpm/V motor on 11.1 V (63 270 rpm), its 3600 rpm/V motor at 2 A (5.31 mN·m, 7200 rpm, 4 W), a 12 V motor under 20 mN·m, a datasheet in V/krpm.

Terms

  • Back-EMF E: the voltage a turning motor generates against its supply, in proportion to its speed (Lenz's law: the induced voltage opposes the change that makes it).
  • Kv: the speed per volt of supply with no load, rpm/V. Ke: the back-EMF per speed, V·s/rad or V/krpm, the inverse of Kv. Kt: the torque per ampere, N·m/A; in SI units Kt and Ke are the same number.
  • Stall: the rotor held still: no back-EMF, the current limited by R alone.
  • KM: the motor constant Kt / √R, the torque per square root of the copper loss; it depends on the motor's size, not its winding.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, "Motor constants" (the article's wikitext, read as text): Kv = ω_no-load / V; Ke = Kb = 1 / Kv; Kt = τ / Ia = 60 / (2π Kv(rpm)) = 1 / Kv(SI), the same unit as Ke; "by Lenz's law, a running motor generates a back-EMF proportional to the speed", the limit speed being where it equals the supply; KM = Kt / √R; its examples, Kv 5700 rpm/V on 11.1 V giving 63 270 rpm, Kv 3600 rpm/V giving 0.00265 N·m/A, and 2 A with 2 V of back-EMF giving 7200 rpm and 4 W.
  • Not used: Microchip AN905 "Brushed DC Motor Fundamentals" (read as text) describes back-EMF and the linear speed–torque line in words, without the constants.

Why the formulas are these

The circuit (derived from the source's relations): in steady state the supply is shared between the winding's resistance and the back-EMF, V = I R + E; the load torque sets the current, I = τ / Kt, and the back-EMF the speed, ω = E / Ke = (V − I R) / Ke. Unloaded, ω = V / Ke (the source's Kv × V); stalled, I = V / R and τ = Kt V / R. The power at the shaft is τ ω, the electrical input V I, the copper loss I² R; the efficiency their ratio. The tool reproduces the source's three examples exactly.

Assumptions and limits

  • No friction or iron loss: a real motor draws a no-load current, so it runs a little slower and less efficiently than this; datasheets give it.
  • Steady state and DC: the winding's inductance matters only while the current changes (start-up, PWM); brushless motors follow the same constants per phase.
  • The winding warms: copper's resistance rises about 0.4 % per °C, which lowers the speed under load and the stall current.
  • Display. Three figures (63 270 rpm shows as 63 300 rpm).

How it was checked

30 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's typing and picks, itself checked against the source's three examples. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; loads, supplies, resistances and constants; the constant typed in each form and each form picked; loads in each torque unit, the unit linking; remembered choices; five refusals (the load past stall among them); the four examples.
