Power electronics › Motors

RPM ↔ frequency conversion

What it computes

A shaft's speed and the frequency that goes with it, both ways. AC motor: the speed from the supply frequency and the poles, less an induction motor's slip, or the frequency a drive must give for a wanted speed. Pulses: the pulse rate of an encoder, a tachometer or a stepper's steps for a speed, or the speed for a pulse rate. The drawing shows the supply and motor, or the slotted disc and its pulse train; what is found is green.

  • Pills: AC motor and Pulses, each with its own frequency and speed (50 Hz is a supply, not a pulse rate).
  • Inputs: the frequency (Hz or kHz) or the speed (rpm, rad/s, rev/s), as the Output heading's Given: frequency or Given: speed picks; the slip (AC) or the pulses a turn (Pulses). The Your inputs heading picks the poles (2 to 12) or the edges counted: × 1, × 2 (both edges) or × 4 (quadrature).
  • Big result: the speed or the frequency; under it the synchronous speed and slip, or the edges a turn.
  • Cells: AC, the synchronous speed, the slip in rpm and ω; Pulses, the period between edges, the edges a turn and ω. Rows: AC, the synchronous speed three other pole counts give; Pulses, the counts in 100 ms and the speed resolution they give; both, the speed in rpm, rad/s and rev/s.
  • Remembered: the pill, what is given, the poles, the edges counted and the units.

Examples: a 4-pole motor on 50 Hz with 3 % slip, a drive set for 1000 rpm (34.4 Hz), a stepper at 600 rpm in 1/16 steps (32 kHz), a 1000-line encoder × 4 at 3000 rpm (200 kHz).

Terms

  • Poles: the magnetic poles of the stator per phase; 2 poles turn the field once per cycle, 4 poles half as fast.
  • Synchronous speed: the speed of the stator's turning field; a synchronous motor turns at it, an induction motor a little slower.
  • Slip: how far an induction motor's rotor lags the field, as a fraction of the synchronous speed; a few percent at full load.
  • Pulses a turn (PPR): an encoder's lines, a tachometer's teeth or marks, a stepper's steps a turn times its microsteps (200 × 16 = 3200).
  • Quadrature: an encoder's two channels A and B, a quarter cycle apart; counting both edges of both gives four counts a line.

Sources

  • Wikipedia, "Induction motor" (the article's wikitext, read as text): "Synchronous speed", n_s = 120 f / p rpm, p the number of poles per phase; its example, a 4-pole motor at 1500 rpm on 50 Hz and 1800 rpm on 60 Hz; "Slip", s = (n_s − n_r) / n_s.

Why the formulas are these

AC. The synchronous speed and slip as the source gives them; the speed n = n_s (1 − s), and for a wanted speed f = n p / (120 (1 − s)). Pulses (derived): a shaft turning at n rpm passes n / 60 turns a second, each with PPR × k counted edges, so f = n PPR k / 60. Resolution (derived): a count over a gate time T is uncertain by one edge, so the speed is known to 60 / (PPR k T) rpm; the tool shows it for T = 100 ms.

Assumptions and limits

  • Slip is an input: it depends on the load, so the tool does not predict it.
  • Steppers: the step rate gives the speed only if no step is missed (the motor's torque must suffice at that rate).
  • Display. Three figures (1455 rpm shows as 1460 rpm).

How it was checked

37 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps, typing and picks, itself checked against the source's 1500 and 1800 rpm. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; 2 to 12 poles; 60 and 400 Hz, slip; the speed given; rad/s; the pulses with their own values, and back; 1 to 1024 pulses a turn, × 2 and × 4; the speed given; kHz; remembered choices; five refusals; the four examples.

PCB & interconnect › Trace current, resistance & inductance

Trace width

(replaces PCB trace width / resistance, Trace current capacity (ampacity) and Trace current — IPC-2152 method)

What it computes

How hot a copper trace on a PCB runs for its current, by IPC-2152, three ways, by pill:

Pill Inputs Output
Width the current and the temperature rise allowed the width needed
Current the width and the temperature rise the current it carries
Rise the width and the current how far above the ambient it runs
  • The trace: an outer layer (in air) or an inner one (inside the board), in 0.5, 1, 2 or 3 oz copper, the width in mm or mil.
  • Along its length: the resistance at the temperature it runs at, the voltage drop and the power lost, for a length in mm, cm or in and an ambient temperature.
  • Also shown: the width in the other unit and the current density, in A/mm².
  • Switching pills keeps the answer: a width just solved is the width the Rise pill then heats.
  • Remembered: the pill, the layer, the copper and the units (the current in mA or A).

Examples: 2 A at a 10 °C rise, Brooks and Adam's 10 A on 100 mil of 2 oz, what a 10 mil trace carries, 3 A on an inner layer, and the drop along a 5 cm power trace.

Source

IPC-2152 (2009), Standard for Determining Current Carrying Capacity in Printed Board Design, through Brooks and Adam, "Trace Currents and Temperatures Revisited", UltraCAD Design, 2015, read in review. The standard itself is sold by IPC and was not read; the paper digitised its curves and fitted equations to them.

  • Table 3-1 and appendix 6: ΔT = K · I^c · W^w · Th^t, with W the width and Th the thickness in mils and I in amperes:
Trace K c w t
outer, any copper 215.3 2 −1.15 −1.0
inner, 0.5 oz 130 to 110 (by width) 2 −1.10 −1.52
inner, 1 oz 200 1.9 −1.10 −1.52
inner, 2 oz 300.3 2 −1.15 −1.52
inner, 3 oz 200 to 300 (by width) 1.9 −1.15 −1.52

For 0.5 and 3 oz the appendix lists the constant at a few widths; the tool interpolates between them. One appendix row prints the 0.5 oz thickness exponent as +1.52; taken as −1.52 like its neighbours. - The paper's example checks the units: a 100 mil, 2 oz trace at 10 A rises "just under 40 °C" outside and "only 33 °C" inside. The tool gives 39.38 °C and 32.52 °C. - Its findings: IPC-2152 allows "approximately 25 % lower" current than the older IPC-2221 curves on outer layers, and inner traces "cool almost as well or better" than outer ones, through the board.

IPC-2221 is not used, as Pierre chose: IPC-2152 is the newer standard.

Why the formulas are these

ΔT = K · I^c · W^w · Th^t                    IPC-2152, as fitted
R = ρ · L / (W · Th) · (1 + 0.00393 (T − 20 °C)),  ρ = 1/58 Ω·mm²/m
T = Tambient + ΔT,  drop = I · R,  loss = I² · R

A trace heats as I²R and sheds the heat into the board and the air; it settles where the two balance. The width and the thickness do not count alike (−1.15 against −1.0), so the shape of the trace matters, not only its cross-section. Copper weight is the mass per area: 1 oz/ft² is taken as 1.37 mil, 34.8 µm, the figure with which the paper's example comes out. The resistance uses the same copper as Wire sizing: 1/58 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C, rising 0.393 % per °C, at the temperature the trace runs at.

Assumptions and limits

  • The fits follow IPC-2152's test conditions: a trace alone on a board, without the planes and pours that cool real ones further. A real board usually runs cooler.
  • Copper weights: 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 oz, the ones the paper fits.
  • Not here: vias, which carry their own current limit, and traces in a vacuum, which the paper fits separately.

How it was checked

11 cases: - 2 A at a 10 °C rise needs 0.93 mm, 36.6 mil; - the paper's 10 A on 100 mil of 2 oz: 39.38 °C outside, 32.52 °C inside; - 10 mil of 1 oz carries 948 mA at a 10 °C rise; - 3 A on an inner 1 oz layer at 20 °C needs 0.889 mm; - 5 cm of 0.5 mm at 2 A: 54.5 mΩ, 109 mV, 218 mW; - a width solved and heated again gives back its 10 °C; - a unit change keeps the width; - a zero current is refused; - the remembered choices; - the current in mA: 2 A reads 2000, the width unchanged.

PCB & interconnect › Trace current, resistance & inductance

Via current capacity

What it computes

How many vias a current needs, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the drill, the plating in the hole, the board thickness, the trace feeding the via (width and copper weight), the current, the temperature rise you allow (a picker, 5 to 60 °C), and the number of vias you use.
  • The current sets the copper: IPC-2152, through the same Brooks & Adam fit as Trace width (outer layer), gives the trace width the current needs for that rise. The vias match the larger of that and your trace. The first version used your trace alone, so the current changed nothing: Pierre put in 100 A and still got 2 vias.
  • The big result: that many vias, IPC-2152's area rule: together at least the copper cross-section of the trace.
  • The vias you use follow that count until you type your own.
  • Below it:
  • how hot your trace runs at that current, flagged when over the rise allowed ("it would burn" past 1000 °C);
  • each via's current, resistance, voltage drop and heat;
  • the trace's area over your vias' area;
  • Brooks & Adam's nearest simulated case to that ratio, quoted as they give it, or "none close" outside their 0.64× to 8×;
  • the finished hole, the drill less twice the plating.
  • Units: metric (mm, plating in µm, areas in mm²) or mil for everything (areas in mil², the simulated cases' widths too); every length has a picker, and changing any one changes them all. Copper in oz, 1 oz = 34.8 µm as in Trace width.
  • Drawing: a trace on each side of the board joined by the via, the current going through it.
  • Remembered: the units, the copper weight and the rise. The current has its own mA/A picker.

Examples: Brooks & Adam's via beside a 1.2 mm trace at 4 A (30 °C rise), the same via with a 0.66 mm trace, 10 A on a 2.5 mm 2 oz trace with two vias, 20 A through a 30 mm 2 oz pour, and a 0.3 mm drill with 25 µm plating.

Source

Douglas G. Brooks and Johannes Adam, "Via Currents and Temperatures", July 2015 (read; UltraCAD paper, from a copy shared on the KiCad forum): - IPC-2152's rule, as they quote it from page 26 of the standard: "The cross-sectional area of a via should have at least the same cross-sectional area as the conductor or be larger than the conductor coming into it. If the via has less cross-sectional area than the conductor, then multiple vias can be used". IPC-2152 itself was not read. - The via's area, π(r² − (r − th)²), r the via's radius, th the plating; their via, 0.26 mm drill and 0.030 mm plating, is 0.0217 mm², "approximately equivalent to a 1 Oz. 26 mil (.66 mm) wide trace". - Their model: two 60 mm traces on either side of 1.6 mm FR-4, joined by that via, simulated with TRM (Thermal Risk Management). - Their tables (trace at the thermocouple, via at its midpoint): - 0.4 mm, 1 oz, 2 A: trace 91.4, via 82.4 °C; - 0.66 mm, 3 A: 86.9, 80.9 °C; - 1.2 mm, 4 A: 74.1, 75.8 °C; - 1.8 mm, 5 A: 70.8, 76.8 °C; - 2.5 mm, 6 A: 68.1, 77.6 °C; - 2.5 mm, 2 oz, 10 A: 93.5, 117.9 °C; - two vias, 2.5 mm 1 oz, 7 A: 88.6, 92.4 °C; 2 oz, 10 A: 89.6, 97.3 °C. - Their conclusion: the rule is "extremely conservative"; "It is not the current that determines the via temperature. The trace itself has much more influence over the via temperature." A filled hole changes little with solder, more with copper. - Resistance: IACS copper, 1/58 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C (NBS Handbook 100), as in Wire sizing.

Why the formulas are these

A via = π (r² − (r − b)²)
A trace = w × t,   w needed: IPC-2152 for I and the rise
vias = ⌈max(A trace, A needed) / A via⌉
R via = ρ × l / A via,   per via: I / N, drop I R / N, heat (I/N)² R

Current flows in the via's plated wall, a copper ring; the rule asks for as much copper in the vias as in the trace, so they heat no more than it. The current decides how much copper the trace needs to stay within the rise, so it decides the vias too. Brooks and Adam show the trace and the board cool the via, so it runs near the trace's temperature well past that point; the nearest case is there to show how far.

Assumptions and limits

  • The width the current needs is for an outer-layer trace, as in their via model (traces on both faces); an inner trace runs a little cooler (see Trace width).
  • The nearest case is a pointer, not a prediction. Their cases are for a 1.6 mm board and 60 mm traces at one current each; nothing is interpolated or scaled from them.
  • The ratio uses 34.8 µm per oz for the trace and their via's own area for their cases, so their 0.66 mm trace comes to 1.06×, not exactly 1.
  • Plating is assumed even; they note it often is not.
  • The resistance is at 20 °C; a hot via is a little higher (0.393 % per °C).
  • Heat from the part itself is not included: for vias carrying heat rather than current, see Thermal vias.

How it was checked

15 cases: - 4 A at a 10 °C rise needs a 3.11 mm, 1 oz trace: 5 of their 0.0217 mm² vias, 0.8 A each; the 1.2 mm trace rises 30 °C, over the 10 allowed; - five vias against the 1.2 mm trace (0.385×) are outside their cases; - 100 A needs an 838 mm trace for 10 °C, 1346 vias, and the 1.2 mm trace would burn; - a 30 °C rise lets 4 A use the 1.2 mm trace, so its own area sets 2; - one via at 4 A is their 1.2 mm case, 1.7 °C hotter than the trace; - the 0.66 mm trace at 3 A rises 33 °C, one via is their case, 6 °C cooler; - 10 A on a 2.5 mm 2 oz trace rises 40.1 °C (not flagged over 40); 9 vias; with two, their case is 7.7 °C over the trace; - 20 A through a 30 mm 2 oz pour rises 9 °C; 97 vias match its copper; - a 0.3 mm drill with 25 µm plating: 0.0216 mm², 1.28 mΩ; - a typed via count stays when the trace changes; - plating as thick as the hole's radius is refused; - mil turns every length and area to mil (122 mil, 168 mil²); - every length's picker switches them all; - the remembered copper weight and rise; - the current in mA: 4 A reads 4000.

PCB & interconnect › Trace current, resistance & inductance

Trace inductance

What it computes

The inductance of a PCB trace, with its return path: over a plane, between two planes, or with no plane near it. The drawing is a cross-section of the trace with the plane or planes it returns through, its length above.

  • Pills: Over a plane (a surface trace, or any trace with one solid plane under it), Between planes (an inner trace centred between two planes), No plane.
  • Inputs: the length l, the width w, the height h over the plane (the dielectric under the trace) or the distance b between the planes, and a frequency. The Your inputs heading picks the copper: ½, 1, 1½ or 2 oz.
  • Big result: the inductance L, with a line saying what loop it is. Over and between planes, a badge says the field solver answered (Solving… for a moment after typing; Formula if the solver cannot run, the formula then standing in).
  • Cells: the inductance per mm (per inch in mil), the reactance 2πfL at the frequency, the skin depth there. Rows: over and between planes, Wadell's or Wheeler's formula with its difference from the solver, and the same trace with no plane; with no plane, the high-frequency value and Terman's form; for all, the voltage a current step of 1 A in 1 ns makes across the trace.
  • Units: one length unit for every length, mm or mil; kHz, MHz or GHz. Remembered: the pill, the copper and the units.

Examples: an inch of 10 mil trace over its plane (9.89 nH), the same inch with no plane (28.8 nH), an inner trace between planes (7 nH), a 2 mm power trace (4.76 nH).

Terms

  • Loop inductance: a current always comes back to where it started; the inductance belongs to the whole loop, and the closer the return runs to the trace, the smaller it is. Over a plane, the return flows in the plane right under the trace.
  • Partial inductance: one conductor's own share of a loop's inductance (Grover's formula for a flat bar); the loop's total adds the return conductor's share and subtracts what the two share, which grows as they come closer.
  • Skin depth: at high frequency the current keeps to the copper's surface, within about a skin depth; when it is under the copper's thickness, the inductance inside the copper drops away (the trace's high-frequency value).

Sources

  • B. C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook" (Artech House, 1991; Pierre's scanned copy, the pages read as images): §6.2.2 (pp. 382–383), the flat wire: Greenhouse's form of Grover's L = 0.002 l [ln(2l / (w + t)) + 0.25049 + (w + t) / (3l) + μ T(x) / 4] µH (l, w, t in cm), T = 1 at DC, so 0.50049 in all (Grover's flat bar), T → 0 when the current keeps to the surface; Terman's form 0.002 l [ln(2l / (w + t)) + 0.5 + 0.2235 (w + t) / l], whose 0.2235 varies from 0.22313 (t = 0) to 0.22352 (t = w). The page labels Terman's form "(nH)": with l in cm it gives µH (a 1 cm trace comes to about 9.5 nH only so), read here as a misprint. §3.5.1 (Wadell's microstrip) as in the Microstrip tool.
  • Wheeler's stripline formula (IEEE MTT-26, 1978) as D. Hafner, M. Dressel and M. Scheffler give it (Rev. Sci. Instrum. 85, 014702, 2014, appendix A), as in the Stripline tool.

Why the formulas are these

Over and between planes. The trace and the plane form a transmission line, whose inductance per length is that of the same line in air (derived: the dielectric changes the capacitance, not the inductance), L′ = Z0(air) / c. The app's field solver gives Z0 for the cross-section in air (js/fieldsolver.js, microstrip with εr = 1, the box 80 h out; stripline), the same solver as the impedance tools. Wadell's microstrip formula stays within 1 % of it (−0.3 % for the opening trace, +1.1 % for a strip 100 times wider than its height); Wheeler's stripline formula within 0.02 %. As a trace widens, L′ approaches the parallel-plate value μ0 h / w (0.77 of it at w / h = 10, 0.97 at 200: the fringing field keeps it under).

No plane. Grover's partial inductance of a flat bar at DC, the current spread through the copper; at high frequency, the current on the surface, 0.25 less inside the brackets. Terman's form agrees with it within 0.2 % for traces long against their width; for a short square piece it reads 8 % low.

Voltage. V = L di/dt (derived): 1 A in 1 ns across 10 nH is 10 V, the ground bounce a fast edge makes across a shared connection.

Assumptions and limits

  • Long traces: the length is taken as long against the height (over and between planes, the ends are not counted) and against the width (Grover's formula is for a long bar).
  • A solid plane under the whole trace: a gap or slot in the plane forces the return around it and adds inductance the tool does not see.
  • High frequency over planes: the solver gives the inductance outside the copper; at low frequencies (the skin depth over the copper's thickness) the current inside the trace and plane adds a little. Between planes: the trace is centred.
  • Display. Three figures.

How it was checked

38 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps and typing, the inductance per length from tools/fd_lines.py (direct sparse solves of the same grids). The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; the three pills; widths, heights, lengths and a wide strip over a plane; three traces between planes; three with no plane (a short square piece among them); ½ and 2 oz; mils and kHz to GHz, the unit linking; remembered choices; six refusals; the four examples.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Microstrip

(formerly Microstrip impedance)

What it computes

The characteristic impedance of a trace on an outer layer over a ground plane, or the width that gives an impedance, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the trace width, the dielectric's thickness h (to the ground plane), the copper weight (its thickness t, ½ to 3 oz), the material (FR-4, polyimide or PTFE at AN-905's round figures, a maker's laminate from Laminate materials, or custom) and its dielectric constant εr.
  • Width and impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Z0; type the impedance you need and the width box shows the width that gives it (shown again when you leave the box).
  • The big result: Z0 from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), or the width for the impedance typed, with the width in the other unit and w/h. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and Wadell's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • Wadell's equations' Z0, the big result until 2026-11-07, and how far it is from the solver's;
  • the older, simpler IPC-2141 formula's Z0, and how far it is; flagged when w > 2h, outside its range;
  • the effective dielectric constant, from the solver;
  • the delay per length, per cm in mm and per inch in mil;
  • the capacitance and inductance per length.
  • Units: mm or mil for the width, the thickness and the solder mask; any of their pickers switches them all.
  • Drawing: the board in cross-section, the trace with its w and t, the dielectric with its h and εr, the ground plane; w, h and t in both mm and mil (Pierre), the unit in use first. The trace is green when its width is the answer.
  • Solder mask (pill): "No mask" (the default) or "Solder mask", with the mask on the board, on the copper and its εr; see Solder mask below.
  • Remembered: the unit, the copper weight, the mask pill and its unit.

Examples: AN-905's three slide-rule examples (25 mil on 20 mil, the same in metric, the width for 93 Ω on 30 mil), 50 Ω on a 1.6 mm two-layer board and on the 0.2 mm prepreg of a four-layer board, and the same under solder mask (the examples without one set "No mask").

Terms

  • Microstrip: a trace on the outer layer of a board with a ground plane under it, separated by the dielectric (the board's insulating material).
  • Characteristic impedance (Z0): the ratio of voltage to current a fast signal sees as it travels along the trace, set by its geometry and the dielectric, not by its length. A line driven and ended in its Z0 carries a signal without reflections.
  • Dielectric constant (εr): how much the material slows the field compared with vacuum; FR-4 about 4.3.
  • Effective dielectric constant (εeff): part of the field runs in the air above the trace, so the signal sees less than εr.
  • Effective width (w'): the trace's thickness widens it electrically; Wadell's equations replace w by w'.
  • Delay (Td): the time a signal takes per length of trace.
  • C0, L0: the trace's capacitance and inductance per length.
  • oz: copper weight in ounces per square foot; 1 oz is 34.8 µm thick (as in Trace width).

Source

  • Zachariah Peterson, "High Speed Design Basics", Altium, 3 May 2022 (read; Pierre's copy, slide 23 rendered, its equations being images):
  • IPC-2141: Z0 = 87 / (εr + 1.41)^0.5 × ln(5.98h / (0.8w + t)), marked "Only accurate for 50 Ohm traces";
  • Wadell's equations, marked "Highly accurate": Z0 = 60 / (2εr + 2)^0.5 × ln(1 + 4h/w' × [(14 + 8/εr)/11 × 4h/w' + √(((14 + 8/εr)/11)² (4h/w')²
    • π² (1 + 1/εr)/2)]), where w' = w + ((1 + 1/εr)/2)(t/π) ln(4e / √((t/h)² + ((1/π)/(w/t + 1.1))²)); and εeff = (εr + 1)/2 + (εr − 1)/2 × ((1 + 12h/w)^−0.5 + 0.04 (1 − w/h)²) if w < h, (εr + 1)/2 + (εr − 1)/2 × (1 + 12h/w)^−0.5 if w > h;
  • slide 25 ranks IPC-2141 lowest in accuracy, Wadell's equations moderate, field solvers high.
  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §3.5.1, pages 93–95 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): the slide's equations, Wheeler's Z0 with Schneider's εeff as improved by Hammerstad and Bekkadal, as Bogatin recommends after comparing them with measurements. Wadell writes the factor η0 / (2√2 π √(εr + 1)), where the slide has 60 / √(2εr + 2): the same with η0 taken as 120π, 0.07 % above η0 = 376.73 Ω; the tool keeps the slide's 60. The thickness correction is Wheeler's, "the most accurate" by Owens and Potok's comparison; "Error in Z0 is less than 2% for any εr, w"; the εeff equations are "accurate to within 1%" for εr ≤ 16 and 0.05 ≤ w/h ≤ 20, for a paper-thin trace (the copper's thickness is not in them).
  • National Semiconductor AN-905, "Transmission Line RAPIDESIGNER Operation and Applications Guide", James A. Mears, May 1996, TI SNLA035 (read, appendix A rendered): the same formula as IPC-2141, written Z0 = 60 / √(0.475 εr + 0.67) × ln[4h / (0.67 (0.8w + t))] "if w ≤ 2h (maximum error ≅ 3%)"; its slide-rule examples: a 25 mil trace on 20 mil of εr 4.3 with 1 oz copper, 63 Ω; 0.127 cm on 0.102 cm, 64 Ω; 93 Ω on 30 mil of εr 3.8 with ½ oz, 18 mil (0.051 cm). Appendix D: FR-4 and G-10 4.3, polyimide 4.2, PTFE 2.4.
  • Walt Kester, ADI tutorial MT-094, "Microstrip and Stripline Design", Rev. 0, January 2009 (read, Pierre's copy): its eq. 3, quoted from IPC-2141A, is the same IPC formula, in mils; its example: a 20 mil, 1 oz (T 1.4 mil) trace on 10 mil of FR-4 at εr 4.0 is "about 50 Ω" by the W/H = 2 rule of thumb, while eq. 3 "predicts Zo to be about 46 Ω"; "The IPC microstrip equation is most accurate between 50 and 100 Ω, but is substantially less so for lower (or higher) impedances"; 75 Ω takes "about 8.3 mils". The tool gives 46.2 Ω by IPC-2141A and 48.9 Ω by Wadell for that trace, and 8.35 mil for 75 Ω by IPC-2141A (8.56 by Wadell).
  • IPC-2141A, "Design Guide for High-Speed Controlled Impedance Circuit Boards", March 2004, §4.2.2 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): its surface microstrip formulas [4-4]–[4-6] are Wadell's above, the same εeff, but with εr,eff written where Wadell has εr in the Z0 formula; read that way they come out 12 to 14 % high, so the tool keeps Wadell's. The 87/√(εr + 1.41) formula, which Peterson's slide labels IPC-2141 and MT-094 quotes from IPC-2141A, is in neither the 2004 text nor its errata; AN-905 (1996) already uses it, so it is presumably the first IPC-2141's (not read). The tool shows it as the "older IPC formula".
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, checked against Polar's boundary-element microstrip table to 0.02 % (Edge-coupled embedded's section); tools/fd_lines.py, a separate implementation, gives the values in every case below.
  • Not read: IPC-2141 (1996) itself, and the papers Wadell draws on (Wheeler's, Schneider's, Hammerstad and Bekkadal's).

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result:

∇·(ε ∇φ) = 0 between the trace (1 V) and the plane (0 V)
S = C / ε0 = Σ ε (Δφ)², once with the board, once in air (S_air)
Z0 = η0 / √(S × S_air),   εeff = S / S_air
Td = 33.36 √εeff ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Z0,   L0 = Z0 × Td

Wadell's equations, the first comparison:

d = √((t/h)² + (1/π / (w/t + 1.1))²)
w' = w + (1 + 1/εr)/2 × t/π × ln(4e / d)
x = 4h / w',   a = (14 + 8/εr) / 11
b = √(a² x² + π² (1 + 1/εr) / 2)
Z0 = 60 / √(2εr + 2) × ln(1 + x (a x + b))
εeff = (εr+1)/2 + (εr−1)/2 / √(1 + 12h/w)   (+ (εr−1)/2 × 0.04 (1 − w/h)² for w < h)
Td = 33.36 √εeff ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Z0,   L0 = Z0 × Td

A wider trace, or a ground plane closer under it, adds capacitance per length and so lowers the impedance. Wadell's formula follows the field over the whole range of w/h, where IPC-2141's logarithm is a fit good near 50 Ω and for w ≤ 2h. The signal travels at the speed of light divided by √εeff (33.36 ps/cm is 1 cm at the speed of light), and Z0 = √(L0 / C0) with Td = √(L0 C0) gives C0 and L0. The width for an impedance has no closed form here: Z0 falls steadily as the width grows, so the tool halves the range of widths until it lands on it.

How the formulas compare with the solver (1 oz copper):

Case Solver Wadell IPC-2141 εeff, solver (Wadell)
25 mil on 20 mil, εr 4.3 62.27 Ω +0.20 % +0.70 % 3.08 (3.16)
1.27 mm on 1.02 mm, εr 4.3 63.20 Ω +0.11 % +1.31 % 3.11 (3.16)
3.07 mm on 1.6 mm, εr 4.3 50.00 Ω −0.12 % −2.00 % 3.24 (3.26)
0.36 mm on 0.2 mm, εr 4.3 50.00 Ω +0.10 % −4.54 % 3.13 (3.25)
4 mm on 1.6 mm, εr 4.3 42.43 Ω −0.28 % −6.95 % 3.32 (3.34)
20 mil on 10 mil, εr 4.0 48.93 Ω −0.02 % −5.49 % 2.99 (3.07)

Wadell's equations stay within 0.3 % of the solver for the impedance. The older IPC formula is within 2 % on the thick boards, but 4.5 to 5.5 % low on thin dielectric (0.2 mm, 10 mil) and 7 % low beyond w = 2h. Wadell's effective εr leaves out the copper's thickness, whose sides put more of the field in the air: it reads 0.35 to 3.7 % high with 1 oz copper, while for a paper-thin trace it is within 0.2 % of the solver's (four of the cases computed again at t = 0). The delay the tool gives therefore comes from the solver's εeff.

Solder mask

The "Solder mask" pill coats the board and the trace with a solder mask of its own εr, as on almost every outer layer: c1 thick on the bare board, c2 over the copper's top and sides (a conformal coat; mask thins over copper, so c2 is usually less than c1), in the lengths' unit, mm or mil, their pickers moving with the others'. The solver puts the mask's εr in those cells and solves as before; a second solve without the mask gives the row "Without the mask"; the formula rows, which know no mask, say "no mask".

  • Defaults: Sanwa Chemical's SPSR-950 C-20 LPI mask (Florida CirTech technical bulletin, revision 072511, read): "a dried thickness of 15-20 microns"; dielectric constant at 1 MHz 2.8 as received and 3.5 after 96 hours at 55 °C and 95 % RH. The tool takes 20 µm on the board, 15 µm over the copper and εr 3.5, the sheet's damp value; the sheet gives one thickness only, so enter the board maker's c1 and c2 for a real board. (Taiyo's PSR-4000 sheet, the most common mask, could not be opened.)
  • Checked: a mask of εr 1 gives the bare trace's impedance (49.955 against 49.963 Ω, 0.36 mm on 0.2 mm, 1 oz); a mask of the board's εr, c1 = c2 + t, makes a uniform cover and gives Embedded microstrip's solver value to 0.001 % (46.865 Ω, cover to h + 64.8 µm).
  • What it does: on 0.36 mm over 0.2 mm FR-4 the default mask lowers Z0 2.7 %, so 50 Ω needs 0.342 mm instead of 0.36; on 3 mm over 1.6 mm, 0.5 %. A pair is hit harder (Edge-coupled microstrip).

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static field solution: dispersion, losses and copper roughness are left out; the trace is a rectangle. The board maker's stack-up calculation decides.
  • The mask's shape: a uniform coat c1 on the board and c2 around the trace; real mask is thicker in the corners at the trace's foot.
  • εr changes with frequency and between laminates: FR-4's 4.3 is a nominal figure; use the maker's value at your frequency.
  • No losses: the copper's resistance and the dielectric's loss are left out.

How it was checked

13 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip: - AN-905's 25 mil on 20 mil, εr 4.3, 1 oz: 62.3 Ω (62.27); Wadell 62.4 Ω (+0.2 %), IPC-2141 62.7 Ω (+0.7 %), its slide rule 63 Ω; 149 ps/in; - the same in metric, 1.27 mm on 1.02 mm: 63.2 Ω (IPC-2141 64 Ω, its slide rule 64 Ω), εeff 3.11; - 93 Ω on 30 mil, εr 3.8, ½ oz: 17.9 mil (17.906; its slide rule's 18 mil); - 50 Ω on 1.6 mm FR-4: 3.07 mm (3.070), where IPC-2141 gives 49.0 Ω; - 50 Ω on 0.2 mm: 0.36 mm (0.3595), IPC-2141 4.5 % low; - 75 Ω at εr 3.8: 0.739 pF/cm and 4.16 nH/cm, the material becoming custom; - beyond w = 2h the IPC-2141 comparison is flagged (4 mm on 1.6 mm, 42.4 Ω); - the length pickers move together; - PTFE sets εr to 2.4; - MT-094's 20 mil on 10 mil at εr 4.0: 48.9 Ω (48.93), its IPC-2141A eq. 3 46.2 Ω (its "about 46 Ω"); - 50 Ω under the default mask on 0.2 mm, 1 oz: 0.342 mm (0.34169), 51.4 Ω without the mask (+2.8 %); - the default trace under the mask: 50.4 Ω (50.421), 50.7 Ω without it; - a mask εr under 1 is refused.

The first version used AN-905's (IPC-2141's) formula; Pierre chose Wadell's equations once his copy of Peterson's slides showed both; since 2026-11-07 the big result is the field solver's (Pierre: the most accurate value first).

Embedded microstrip

(formerly Embedded microstrip impedance)

What it computes

The impedance of a microstrip covered by more dielectric (solder mask over an outer-layer trace, or prepreg over an inner trace with no plane above), or the width that gives an impedance under that cover:

  • Inputs: the trace width w, the dielectric under it h1, H2 from the ground plane to the top of the cover, the copper weight, the material and εr (the cover taken as the same εr).
  • Width and impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows the covered Z0; type the impedance you need and the width box shows the width that gives it covered.
  • The big result: the covered Z0 from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with the uncovered one, solved too, and how much the cover takes off; or the width, with the Z0 it would have uncovered. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and IPC-2141A's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • IPC-2141A's formula, the big result until 2026-11-07, and how far it is from the solver's;
  • the cover b = H2 − h1 and how much of it is over the copper's top, flagged when it is thinner than the copper;
  • the deep limit, the impedance once the cover is thick enough that all the field is in the dielectric;
  • the effective εr uncovered and covered, from the solver;
  • the delay per length, covered.
  • Units: mm or mil for the lengths, moving together; oz for the copper.
  • Drawing: the ground plane, the dielectric with the trace on h1, the cover up to H2, in mm and mil. The trace is green when its width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper weight.

Examples: solder mask over a 50 Ω trace on 0.2 mm, the width for 50 Ω under that mask, no cover (the surface microstrip), and 0.2 mm of prepreg over the trace.

Terms

  • Embedded microstrip: a microstrip with dielectric over the trace as well as under it, but no plane above (a plane above makes it a stripline).
  • h1, H2, b: h1 is the dielectric between the plane and the bottom of the trace; H2 runs from the plane to the top of the cover; b = H2 − h1 is the cover measured from the bottom of the trace (IPC-2141A figure 4-3(b)).
  • Solder mask: the thin coating over the outer layers; its thickness over the copper comes from the board maker.
  • Deep limit: under a thick enough cover, the trace sees εr all round; Z0 falls to the uncovered value × √(εeff / εr) and goes no lower.
  • Z0, εr, εeff, oz: as in Microstrip.

Source

  • IPC-2141A, "Design Guide for High-Speed Controlled Impedance Circuit Boards", March 2004, §4.2.3 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): embedded microstrip Z0,embed = Z0,surf / √(e^(−2b/h) + (εr/εr,eff)(1 − e^(−2b/h))) [4-7], with b = h2 − h1 [4-8]; its figure 4-3(b) draws h1 from the plane to the trace and h2 from the plane to the top of the cover; Z0,surf and εr,eff are its surface microstrip's [4-4]–[4-6].
  • IPC-2141A errata (read, a Wayback Machine copy): writes [4-7]'s exponent with h1, the dielectric under the trace, as the tool does.
  • Uncovered Z0 and εeff in the formula: Wadell's equations, as in Microstrip (IPC-2141A's [4-6] εeff is the same; for its [4-4] see there).
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, as in Microstrip, with the cover from the board up to H2 and air above it; tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip, a separate implementation, gives the values below.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, solved twice, with the cover and without:

∇·(ε ∇φ) = 0, the board and the cover up to H2, air above
S = C / ε0 = Σ ε (Δφ)², once with the dielectric, once in air (S_air)
Z0 = η0 / √(S × S_air),   εeff = S / S_air,   Td = 33.36 √εeff ps/cm
deep limit = η0 / (√εr × S_air) = Z0 √(εeff / εr)

The deep limit needs no third solve: with dielectric all round, the capacitance is εr times the one in air, which the covered solve already has.

IPC-2141A's formula, the comparison:

b = H2 − h1,   k = e^(−2b/h1)
Z0,emb = Z0 / √(k + (εr / εeff)(1 − k))
εeff,emb = εeff k + εr (1 − k),   Td = 33.36 √εeff,emb ps/cm
deep limit = Z0 √(εeff / εr)

Uncovered, part of the field runs in the air over the trace and the line sees εeff. A cover puts dielectric where that air was: the line sees more of εr, its capacitance rises and Z0 falls. The exponential blends the two cases, k = 1 with no cover, k → 0 under a cover a few h1 thick. With b = 0 the formula gives the surface microstrip back. The width for an impedance starts from the formula's, then the solver's answer corrects it.

Assumptions and limits

  • One εr for the board and the cover, as IPC-2141A's formula has; a solder mask's own εr, from its maker, may differ.
  • No plane above the cover.
  • Uniform cover: real solder mask is thinner over the copper's edges and thicker between traces.
  • Quasi-static field solution: the trace a rectangle, no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How IPC-2141A's formula compares with the solver (1 oz copper, FR-4):

Case Solver IPC-2141A [4-7]
0.36 mm on 0.2 mm, 10 µm of mask over the copper 47.52 Ω −0.44 %
the same, 20 µm of mask 47.17 Ω −0.57 %
the same, 30 µm of mask 46.87 Ω −0.70 %
dielectric only beside the trace, up to its top 47.96 Ω −0.37 %
cover b 0.1 mm (H2 0.3 mm) 46.05 Ω −1.07 %
cover b 0.2 mm (H2 0.4 mm) 44.70 Ω −1.13 %
cover b 1 mm (H2 1.2 mm) 42.88 Ω +1.33 %
0.15 mm on 0.1 mm, 20 µm of mask 48.45 Ω −0.39 %
3 mm on 1.6 mm, filled to the copper's top 50.26 Ω +0.06 %

The formula stays within −1.1 to +1.3 % for the impedance; its deep limit misses more, 43.45 Ω against the solver's 42.63 Ω for the 0.36 mm trace (+1.9 %) and 46.1 Ω against 44.5 Ω for 0.15 mm on 0.1 mm (+3.7 %), since Wadell's εeff, on which it rests, leaves out the copper's thickness.

How it was checked

5 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip: - 0.36 mm on 0.2 mm of FR-4 under 20 µm of mask: 47.2 Ω (47.168; 50.0 Ω uncovered, the cover takes 5.6 %), IPC-2141A 46.9 Ω (−0.6 %), εeff 3.13 → 3.51, 62.5 ps/cm; - 50 Ω under that mask: 0.321 mm (0.32116); - no cover, 3 mm on 1.6 mm: 50.7 Ω, Microstrip's value; - 0.2 mm of prepreg over the 0.36 mm trace: 44.7 Ω (44.696), deep limit 42.6 Ω, IPC-2141A 44.2 Ω (−1.1 %); - the default: 47.2 Ω (47.162).

Until 2026-11-07 [4-7] was the big result, being within 1.6 % of fd_lines' first embedded() check; Pierre chose the field solver for every impedance tool (the most accurate value first).

Edge-coupled microstrip

(formerly Differential microstrip impedance, then Differential microstrip)

What it computes

The differential impedance of two edge-coupled traces on an outer layer over a ground plane, or the trace width that gives it at a spacing:

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the gap between them s, the dielectric h, the copper weight, the material and εr.
  • Width and differential impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Zdiff; type the Zdiff you need (90 Ω for USB, 100 Ω for Ethernet or LVDS) and the width box shows the width at your spacing.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with each trace's impedance alone and the coupling (Zdiff over twice that); or the width for the Zdiff typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and IPC-2141A's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • the odd-mode impedance, each trace's share of the pair, Zdiff / 2;
  • the even-mode impedance, both traces driven alike, and the common-mode impedance, half of it;
  • one trace alone, from the solver as in Microstrip;
  • Zdiff by IPC-2141A's pair formula, the big result from 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-07, and by AN-905's simpler factor, each with its difference from the solver's;
  • s/h against AN-905's range, 0.2 to 3, flagged outside.
  • Units: mm or mil for the three lengths and the solder mask; any of their pickers switches them all.
  • Drawing: the pair on the dielectric over the ground plane, w and s as a chain dimension, h and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Solder mask (pill): as in Microstrip; with it, a fourth solve, the pair without the mask, and the formula rows say "no mask".
  • Remembered: the unit, the copper weight, the mask pill and its unit.

Examples: AN-905's two slide-rule examples, USB's 90 Ω and Ethernet's or LVDS's 100 Ω on a 0.2 mm layer.

Terms

  • Differential pair: two traces carrying a signal as equal and opposite voltages; the receiver reads the difference, so noise common to both cancels.
  • Differential impedance (Zdiff): the impedance the driver sees between the two traces.
  • Odd-mode impedance: the impedance of one trace while the other carries the opposite signal, half of Zdiff.
  • Even-mode and common-mode impedance: the impedance of one trace while the other carries the same signal; the two in parallel, half of it, is what a common-mode signal (noise on both) sees.
  • Coupling: brought close, each trace's field reaches the other; Zdiff falls below twice one trace's impedance.
  • Edge-coupled: side by side on the same layer (AN-905's only case).
  • Z0, εr, oz: as in Microstrip.

Source

  • National Semiconductor AN-905, TI SNLA035 (read, appendix A rendered): for microstrip, Zdiff ≅ 2 Z0 (1 − 0.48 e^(−0.96 s/h)) ohms; "These functions were derived from empirical data … Various sources cite possible errors of up to ±10%. The practical ranges for Z0 and Zdiff are from 20Ω to about 150Ω"; the slide rule's range "0.20 ≤ s/h ≤ 3.0"; "Both conductors of the pair must have the same physical cross sectional dimensions"; its examples: two 75 Ω microstrips 0.10 cm apart on a 0.076 cm substrate, factor 0.86, 128 Ω; 10 mils apart on 20 mils, factor 0.702, 105 Ω.
  • Single-trace Z0 in the formulas: Wadell's equations, as in Microstrip.
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, as in Microstrip, the pair solved with the traces at +1 V and −1 V (odd mode) and both at +1 V (even mode); tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip, a separate implementation, gives the values below.
  • IPC-2141A, March 2004, §4.4.1 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): its edge-coupled surface microstrip is not AN-905's exponential: [4-24]–[4-41] give the odd-mode impedance Z0,o = Z0 √(εeff/εeff,o) / (1 − Z0/η0 √εeff Q10), with εeff,o and ten fitted terms Q1 to Q10 in u = w/h and g = s/h, citing its references 2 and 6. §4.4 warns that the balanced-line formulas "exist in various forms, some of which are not in agreement". It was the big result from 2026-11-05 (Pierre: the most accurate value first) until the field solver took over on 2026-11-07; AN-905's factor, the first version's, is shown for comparison too.

IPC-2141A's pair formula, and how it was checked. Its terms [4-25]–[4-41] are, in full:

u = w/h,  g = s/h,  Z0 and εeff one paper-thin trace alone
a0 = 0.7287 (εeff − (εr+1)/2)(1 − e^(−0.179u))
b0 = 0.747 εr / (0.15 + εr),  c0 = b0 − (b0 − 0.207) e^(−0.414u)
d0 = 0.593 + 0.694 e^(−0.562u)
εeff,o = ((εr+1)/2 + a0 − εeff) e^(−c0 g^d0) + εeff
Q1 = 0.8695 u^0.194,  Q2 = 1 + 0.7519g + 0.189g^2.31
Q3 = 0.1975 + (16.6 + (8.4/g)^6)^−0.387 + ln(g^10 / (1 + (g/3.4)^10)) / 241
Q4 = 2Q1 / (Q2 (e^−g u^Q3 + (2 − e^−g) u^−Q3))
Q5 = 1.794 + 1.14 ln(1 + 0.638 / (g + 0.517g^2.43))
Q6 = 0.2305 + ln(g^10 / (1 + (g/5.8)^10)) / 281.3 + ln(1 + 0.598g^1.154) / 5.1
Q7 = (10 + 190g²) / (1 + 82.3g³),  Q8 = e^(−6.5 − 0.95 ln g − (g/0.15)^5)
Q9 = ln(Q7) (Q8 + 1/16.5),  Q10 = (Q2Q4 − Q5 e^(ln(u) Q6 u^−Q9)) / Q2
Z0,o = Z0 √(εeff/εeff,o) / (1 − Z0/η0 √εeff Q10),  Zdiff = 2 Z0,o

It is printed correctly: against tools/fd_lines.py (the field solver of Edge-coupled stripline, with the board and the air above it, checked against Polar's microstrip table to 0.3 %) it is within 0.3 % for paper-thin traces (0.1 to 0.5 mm wide, 0.05 to 0.5 mm apart, on 0.2 mm of εr 4.3). Its terms carry no copper thickness, and with 1 oz copper it reads 2 to 18 % high. The tool widens each trace to Wadell's w' and narrows the gap by as much: then it is within −0.4 to +2.8 % of the solver, where AN-905's factor is within −2.1 to +11.1 % (worst for a 0.05 mm gap).

How the formulas compare with the solver (1 oz copper, εr 4.3):

Case Solver Zdiff IPC-2141A AN-905
AN-905's 75 Ω traces 1 mm apart on 0.76 mm 131.72 Ω +0.51 % −1.58 %
10 mil apart on 20 mil 106.88 Ω +1.01 % −1.34 %
USB: 0.315 mm, 0.2 mm apart on 0.2 mm 90.00 Ω +1.69 % −2.38 %
100 Ω: 0.251 mm, 0.2 mm apart on 0.2 mm 100.00 Ω +1.94 % −1.16 %
the default, 0.15 mm, 0.15 mm apart on 0.2 mm 114.40 Ω +2.54 % +1.66 %

For USB, IPC-2141A's 0.326 mm would give 88.5 Ω, 1.6 % under the 90 Ω wanted; the solver's width is 0.315 mm.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, solved three times:

odd mode: the traces at +1 V and −1 V,  Zodd = η0 / √(S × S_air)
Zdiff = 2 Zodd
even mode: both at +1 V,  common mode = Zeven / 2
one trace alone, as in Microstrip

IPC-2141A's pair formula, the first comparison:

w' = w + (1 + 1/εr)/2 × t/π × ln(4e / √((t/h)² + (1/π / (w/t + 1.1))²))
u = w'/h,   g = (s − (w' − w))/h
the terms above, with Z0 and εeff of a paper-thin trace w' wide
Zdiff = 2 Z0,o
AN-905, for comparison: Zdiff = 2 Z0 × (1 − 0.48 e^(−0.96 s/h))

Far apart, the two traces are independent and the pair is two lines in series: Zdiff = 2 Z0. Brought closer, their mutual capacitance and inductance lower it. IPC's terms fit that fall for paper-thin traces, through the odd mode's own effective εr and the coupling term Q10; the copper's thickness makes each trace act wider (w', as in Microstrip) and so the gap narrower. AN-905 fits the fall with a single exponential in s/h. The width for a Zdiff starts from IPC-2141A's, the spacing kept, then the solver's answer corrects it.

Solder mask

As in Microstrip (its section has the mask's model, defaults and source). On a pair the mask fills part of the gap between the traces, where the odd mode's field is strongest, so it lowers Zdiff more than one trace's Z0: 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart on 0.2 mm FR-4 read 114.4 Ω bare and 107.0 Ω under the default mask (−6.5 %); USB's 90 Ω on 0.2 mm, 0.2 mm apart, needs 0.287 mm under the mask instead of 0.315 mm.

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces rectangles, no losses; the board maker's calculation decides for a controlled-impedance board.
  • Equal traces, edge-coupled; the mask, when used, a uniform coat.
  • IPC's pair formula with copper: the w' widening and narrower gap are the tool's, checked against the field solver, not IPC's.
  • AN-905's row: its factor was fitted with AN-905's own Z0 (the older IPC-2141 formula); here it multiplies Wadell's.
  • Spacing to other traces: AN-905 asks for more than 2s to the next pair, to keep crosstalk and the impedance in hand.

How it was checked

10 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip: - AN-905's 75 Ω traces (75 Ω by Wadell's equations, 74.8 Ω by the solver) 1 mm apart on 0.76 mm: 132 Ω (131.72), coupling 0.881; IPC-2141A 132 Ω (+0.5 %), AN-905 130 Ω (−1.6 %; its slide rule 128 Ω); even mode 83.3 Ω, common mode 41.6 Ω; - 10 mil apart on 20 mil: 107 Ω (106.88), 53.4 Ω odd mode; IPC-2141A 108 Ω (+1.0 %), AN-905 105 Ω (−1.3 %), s/h 0.5; - USB 90 Ω on 0.2 mm, 0.2 mm apart: 0.315 mm (0.31510), 53.7 Ω alone; - 100 Ω on the same layer: 0.251 mm (0.25055), 50 Ω odd mode; - the default pair: 114 Ω (114.40); IPC-2141A 117 Ω (+2.5 %), AN-905 116 Ω (+1.7 %); common mode 45.8 Ω; - USB 90 Ω under the default mask: 0.287 mm (0.28684), 94.1 Ω without it (+4.5 %); - the default pair under the mask: 107 Ω (106.958), 114 Ω without it (+7.0 %), IPC-2141A (no mask) 117 Ω; - a spacing beyond 3 h is flagged; - a gap the copper closes is refused; - the three length pickers move together.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Edge-coupled embedded

What it computes

The differential impedance of two edge-coupled traces buried in the board: on h1 of dielectric over a ground plane, covered by the same dielectric up to H2 above the plane, with no plane on top (Saturn PCB Toolkit's "Edge Cpld Embed"); or the trace width that gives a differential impedance at a gap. It is the first tool computed by the app's field solver (below):

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the gap s, the dielectric under the traces h1, the height of the cover's top above the plane H2, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and differential impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Zdiff; type the Zdiff you need and the width box shows the width that gives it at your gap.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver, with the cover over the copper; or the width for the Zdiff typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and the formula estimate stands in.
  • Below it:
  • the odd-mode impedance and its effective εr;
  • the even-mode impedance and the common-mode impedance, half of it;
  • the formula estimate (below), and how far it is from the solver;
  • the delay per length in the odd mode.
  • Units: mm or mil for the four lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the plane, the dielectric under the traces, the cover over them up to H2, w and s as a chain dimension, h1, H2, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: 100 Ω under 0.1 mm of prepreg, the default pair under solder mask only, the same pair bare (no cover), and buried under 1 mm.

Terms

  • Embedded (buried) pair: a differential pair with dielectric over it as well as under it, and no plane above (a plane above makes it a stripline).
  • Odd mode: the two traces at equal and opposite voltages, as a differential signal drives them. Zdiff = 2 Zodd.
  • Even mode: both traces at the same voltage, as noise picked up by both drives them. The common-mode impedance, the two traces in parallel against the plane, is Zeven / 2.
  • Effective εr (εeff): the permittivity the signal sees, between that of the air and that of the board, since part of the field runs in each; under a thick cover it reaches εr.
  • Field solver: a program that finds the impedance from the cross- section itself, by solving for the electric field, rather than from a formula fitted to some shapes.
  • h1, H2, εr, oz: as in Embedded microstrip.

The field solver

The app lays the cross-section on a grid of points, finer near the copper's edges, where the field changes fastest, and coarser far away. Each trace is held at 1 V (−1 V for the second trace in the odd mode, so the plane midway between them is at 0 V), the plane at 0 V, and the potential at every other point is found so that each one balances its neighbours (Laplace's equation). The energy of that field gives the capacitance per length, once with the dielectric and once with air everywhere; the two give the impedance and the effective εr:

∇·(ε ∇φ) = 0
S = C / ε0 = Σ over the grid's edges of ε (Δφ)²
Z0 = η0 / √(S × S_air),   εeff = S / S_air,   η0 = 376.73 Ω

Each case is solved on three grids, every cell halved from one to the next, and the three results are extrapolated to an infinitely fine grid (Z = (4R2 − R1)/3, R1 = 2Z1 − Z0, R2 = 2Z2 − Z1). The air above the board is closed by a grounded box 80 h1 away; nearer, at 20 h1, it read 0.1 to 0.3 % low. The equations are solved by conjugate gradients with a modified incomplete-Cholesky preconditioner, in a background thread (a Web Worker), so typing never waits: about 0.1 s per solve on an iPhone 15 Pro Max, and a width for a typed Zdiff in two or three solves.

How the solver was checked: - Cohn's exact stripline (zero thickness, centred between two planes; the single strip and the odd mode of a pair, as Burkhardt et al. quote them): within 0.005 %. Cohn's 30π takes η0 as 120π, which is 0.069 % high; with that taken out the solver agrees to the third decimal. - Polar Instruments' boundary-element table (Burkhardt et al., table 1: 1.5, 0.45 and 3.3 mm on 0.794 mm, εr 4.2, 35 µm copper): 50.635, 89.648 and 30.090 Ω against 50.63, 89.63 and 30.09 Ω, within 0.02 %. - tools/fd_lines.py, a separate implementation in Python (a direct sparse solver, scipy), with the same grids: it gives the app's values in every case below. - tools/fs_bench.html runs nine reference cases in the browser and times them: 1.16 s in all on Pierre's iPhone 15 Pro Max, before the solver was made three times faster.

Source

  • No published formula for this structure was found: IPC-2141A (March 2004) has the bare pair (§4.4.1) and one covered trace (§4.2.3); Wadell's "Transmission Line Design Handbook" (1991), §4.5.3, is a pair under a metal lid with air between; a web search found calculators that name the structure without giving their equations. Saturn PCB Toolkit lists it; its online help does not say how it computes it (read).
  • A. J. Burkhardt, C. S. Gregg and J. A. Staniforth, "Calculation of PCB Track Impedance", Polar Instruments, IPC Printed Circuits Expo 1999 (read): Cohn's exact expressions (their equations 4–8) and their table 1, computed by their boundary-element method and checked against 1500 measured boards; the numerical principle, the capacitance found from the potential.
  • The estimate: IPC-2141A §4.4.1 [4-24]–[4-41] and §4.2.3 [4-7], as in Edge-coupled microstrip and Embedded microstrip.

Why the formulas are these

The estimate shown at once, and kept for comparison: the bare pair's odd mode by IPC-2141A's pair formula with the copper allowed for, as Edge-coupled microstrip computes it, once in the board (Zbare) and once in air (Zair), then IPC-2141A [4-7]'s cover blend applied to the odd mode's effective εr:

k = e^(−2b/h1),   b = H2 − h1
εbare = (Zair / Zbare)²
Zodd ≈ Zair / √(εbare k + εr (1 − k))

It gives the bare pair with no cover and the right limit under a deep one; in between it reads 1 to 4 % high in the examples. No formula of it is needed for the answer, which is the solver's.

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static: the field solved is the one at low frequency; the frequency dependence (dispersion), the losses and copper roughness are left out.
  • Rectangular traces of equal width; an etched trace's trapezoid is not modelled. The cover has the board's εr.
  • One plane, nothing else nearby: the next pair or a plane above would change the answer; the grounded box is 80 h1 away.
  • The model is exact to about 0.05 %; a real board is not: εr's tolerance, the etching and the copper's thickness move the impedance more. The board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

8 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip: - the default pair, 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart on 0.2 mm, H2 0.3 mm: 93.3 Ω (93.30), odd mode 46.7 Ω with εeff 3.72, even mode 84.1 Ω, common mode 42.1 Ω, estimate 95.9 Ω (+2.7 %), 64.3 ps/cm; - 100 Ω typed: 0.115 mm traces (0.1154), odd mode 50 Ω, common mode 46.3 Ω; - 100 Ω under 0.1 mm of prepreg, 0.2 mm gap: 0.146 mm (0.14596); - under 20 µm of solder mask only: 99 Ω (98.99), estimate +2.7 %; - no cover: 114 Ω (114.40), where Edge-coupled microstrip's formula reads 117 Ω; - under 1 mm: 86.8 Ω (86.76), εeff 4.3; - H2 below h1 is refused; - the four length pickers move together.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Stripline

(formerly Stripline impedance)

What it computes

The characteristic impedance of a trace on an inner layer, centred between two ground planes, or the width that gives an impedance, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the trace width, the spacing between the planes b, the copper's thickness t (in oz, µm or mil, its own picker), the material (FR-4, polyimide or PTFE at AN-905's round figures, a maker's laminate from Laminate materials, or custom) and its dielectric constant εr.
  • Width and impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Z0; type the impedance you need and the width box shows the width that gives it.
  • The big result: Z0 from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), or the width for the impedance typed, with w/b and the dielectric on each side, h = (b − t)/2. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and Wheeler's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • Wheeler's formula, the big result until 2026-11-07, and how far it is from the solver's;
  • IPC-2141A's simpler formula set: its wide-strip formula for w/b of 0.35 and over, its narrow-strip one below; the narrow one's limits (t/b ≤ 0.25, t/w ≤ 0.11) are named when the trace is outside them, as 1 oz copper on a 0.2 mm trace is;
  • AN-905's formula (MT-094's eq. 7), flagged outside b − t > 2w and b > 4t; each with its difference from the solver's;
  • the delay per length, the signal seeing the full εr;
  • the capacitance and inductance per length.
  • Units: mm or mil for the width and the spacing; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the two ground planes, the dielectric between them with b and εr, the trace centred with its w and t, lengths in mm and mil. The trace is green when its width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: the two stripline resonators of Hafner et al. (their table I), 50 Ω between planes 0.6 mm apart in FR-4, and AN-905's 35 Ω stripline at εr 2.4.

Terms

  • Stripline: a trace on an inner layer with a ground plane above and below, the dielectric filling the space between.
  • b, h: b is the spacing between the planes; h = (b − t)/2 is the dielectric between the trace and each plane.
  • Characteristic impedance (Z0), εr, C0, L0, oz: as in Microstrip.
  • Delay: all the field runs in the dielectric, so a stripline is slower than a microstrip on the same material: Td depends on εr only.

Source

  • D. Hafner, M. Dressel and M. Scheffler, "Surface-resistance measurements using superconducting stripline resonators", Rev. Sci. Instrum. 85, 014702 (2014), arXiv 1309.5331, appendix A (read): Wheeler's approximate impedance of a stripline (H. A. Wheeler, IEEE Trans. MTT-26, 866, 1978), Zc = 30/√ε × ln[1 + ½ (16h/πw')(16h/πw' + √((16h/πw')² + 6.27))], with the equivalent zero-thickness width w' = w + (t/π) ln(e / √((t/(4h + t))² + ((1/4π)/(w/t + 1.10))^(6/(3 + t/h)))); its table I, computed with it: t 1 µm, w 155 µm, εr 10, h 430 µm, 50.06 Ω; w 45 µm, h 127 µm, 49.79 Ω. The tool reproduces both to the hundredth. The text extraction of the PDF garbled the first term of w'; the form t/(4h + t), as on Peterson's slide, is the one that reproduces the table.
  • Zachariah Peterson, "High Speed Design Basics", Altium, May 2022, slide 24 (read, Pierre's copy, rendered):
  • IPC-2141: Z0 = 94.15 / (√εr (W/(B − T) + Cf/π)) "when W/B > 0.35", Cf = 2B/(B − T) ln(B/(B − T) + 1) − (T/(B − T)) ln(1/(1 − T/B)² − 1), marked "Only accurate for 50 Ohm traces";
  • Wadell's equations, "Highly accurate": the same equation as Wheeler's above, but printed with 60/√εr where Hafner et al. have 30/√εr, εr where they have e, and πT/4(W + 1.1T) where they have (1/4π)/(W/T + 1.1). Their table rules out the slide's version (its 60 alone would double the impedance), so the tool follows Hafner et al.
  • National Semiconductor AN-905, TI SNLA035, appendix A (read): stripline Z0 = 60/√εr × ln[4b / (0.67π (0.8w + t))], best "if b − t > 2w and b > 4t"; its stripline scales: delay 56 ps/cm at εr 2.8; a 35 Ω stripline at εr 2.4, 1.47 pF/cm and 1.8 nH/cm.
  • Walt Kester, ADI MT-094, "Microstrip and Stripline Design", January 2009 (read, Pierre's copy): IPC-2141A's symmetric stripline Z0 = 60/√εr × ln(1.9B / (0.8W + T)) (eq. 7), B = 2H + T, "accuracy … typically on the order of 6%" (Bogatin); this is AN-905's formula (4 / (0.67π) = 1.900).
  • IPC-2141A, March 2004, §4.2.4 (read, Pierre's scanned copy):
  • formula set 1 [4-9]–[4-11] is slide 24's "Wadell" equation exactly, with its 60 and πt/4(w + 1.1t): the slide copied IPC's misprints, and Hafner et al.'s table rules them out as above;
  • formula set 2: for w/b < 0.35, t/b ≤ 0.25 and t/w ≤ 0.11, Z0 = 60/√εr × ln(4b/(πD)), D = w/2 × (1 + t/(πw) (1 + ln(4πw/t)) + 0.551 (t/w)²) [4-12], [4-14], the strip treated as a round wire of diameter D; for w/b ≥ 0.35, Z0 = 94.15 / ((w/b)/(1 − t/b) + θ/π) [4-15], θ = 2b/(b − t) ln((2b − t)/(b − t)) − t/(b − t) ln((2bt − t²)/(b − t)²) [4-16]. [4-15] is printed without √εr; slide 24's version, with it, is the one that gives ohms in a dielectric, and the tool uses it;
  • the 60 ln(1.9B/(0.8W + T)) formula MT-094 attributes to IPC-2141A is not in the 2004 text; the tool labels it AN-905's.
  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §3.6.2 "Centered Stripline, Triplate or Sandwich Line", pages 126–127 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): Wheeler's formula with the same w′ as Hafner et al.'s, "stated error … less than 1.5%", and the side walls negligible beyond 1.5 b (the solver's are 5 b away). Two things in its printing:
  • its factor η0 / (2π √εr) is twice Hafner et al.'s 30/√εr = η0 / (4π √εr) with η0 = 120π: the 60 that IPC-2141A [4-9] and slide 24 carry;
  • its b must be read as b − t, twice the dielectric between the trace and each plane (its eq. 3.6.2.2, "2.0 h = b"): read that way its three b terms are Hafner et al.'s exactly; read as the spacing between the planes, as its figure 3.6.2.1 draws b, Z0 comes out 3 to 4 % above the solver with 1 oz copper on 0.6 mm (+3.0 % at the default trace, +4.1 % at 35 Ω).
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, checked against Cohn's exact zero-thickness stripline to 0.005 % (Edge-coupled embedded's section); tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline, a separate implementation, gives the values below.
  • Not read: Wheeler's 1978 paper itself.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, as in Microstrip but all in one dielectric:

S_air = C_air / ε0, the trace at 1 V, both planes at 0 V
Z0 = η0 / (√εr × S_air)
Td = 33.36 √εr ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Z0,   L0 = Z0 × Td

Wheeler's formula, the first comparison:

h = (b − t) / 2,   m = 6 / (3 + t/h)
d = √((t/(4h + t))² + (1/4π / (w/t + 1.1))^m)
w' = w + t/π × ln(e / d)
x = 16h / (π w'),   y = x (x + √(x² + 6.27)) / 2
Z0 = 30 / √εr × ln(1 + y)

Wheeler's formula fits the exact solution for a zero-thickness strip between two planes, and replaces the real strip by a slightly wider one of zero thickness, w', to account for its copper. All the field is in the dielectric, so the wave travels at c / √εr. The width for an impedance starts from Wheeler's, then the solver's answer corrects it.

How the formulas compare with the solver:

Case Solver Wheeler IPC-2141A AN-905
Hafner et al.'s 155 µm, 1 µm thick, h 430 µm, εr 10 50.05 Ω +0.00 % −0.2 % −2.5 %
0.2 mm, 1 oz, b 0.6 mm, εr 4.3 51.82 Ω +0.00 % out of range −1.3 %
0.217 mm, 1 oz, b 0.6 mm, εr 4.3 50.00 Ω −0.00 % −0.6 % −1.7 %
0.683 mm, 1 oz, b 0.6 mm, εr 2.4 35.00 Ω −0.34 % −0.05 % −25 %, out of range

Wheeler's formula is within 0.01 % of the solver in the first three cases, and 0.3 % low for the strip wider than the spacing, where IPC-2141A's wide-strip formula does better. For the single stripline the solver mostly confirms Wheeler's formula; it is the same engine as for the stripline pairs, where the formulas part further.

Core and prepreg

The "Core + prepreg" pill gives the stripline two dielectrics, as a real stack-up has: the core the trace is etched on, under it, and the prepreg pressed over it, which fills around the copper and up to the other plane (boxes "Core εr" and "Prepreg εr"; the material picker sets both). The solver takes the two layers (εr under the trace's bottom face, the prepreg's from there up) and gives the impedance and an effective εr, from which the delay; the comparison formulas, which know one εr, take the mean weighted by the dielectric's thickness on each side, as the manual used to ask the user to do by hand. With one εr (the default) the tool is as before.

  • Checked: a paper-thin trace centred between the planes has a field symmetric about its plane, so its εeff is exactly the mean of the two: core 3 and prepreg 5 give εeff 4.00000 and the same impedance as one εr of 4 (61.617 Ω, 0.2 mm in 0.6 mm); two equal εr give the one-εr value.
  • What it does: the default 0.2 mm trace with 1 oz copper, core 3.8 and prepreg 4.6: 52.2 Ω and εeff 4.233, where the thickness-weighted mean is 4.223: the prepreg around the copper's sides counts a little more than its thickness.

Assumptions and limits

  • Symmetric stripline: the trace centred between the planes; an off-centre trace is Asymmetric stripline's case.
  • One dielectric or core and prepreg: with the pill, two layers split at the trace's bottom face (see Core and prepreg); more layers are averaged by the user.
  • Quasi-static field solution: the trace a rectangle, the planes wide (the solver's side walls 5 b away), no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

9 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline: - Hafner et al.'s two resonators: 50.05 Ω (50.054; their table I's Wheeler value 50.06) and 49.79 Ω (49.792); IPC-2141A's narrow-strip formula 49.9 Ω for the first; - 50 Ω between planes 0.6 mm apart, FR-4, 1 oz: 0.217 mm (0.21735), IPC-2141A's wide-strip formula −0.6 %, AN-905 −1.7 %; - 35 Ω at εr 2.4: 1.48 pF/cm and 1.81 nH/cm (AN-905's 1.47 and 1.8), 51.7 ps/cm; - the same 35 Ω, a strip wider than the spacing: 0.683 mm (0.68273), Wheeler's formula 0.3 % low; - the default 0.2 mm trace between planes 0.6 mm apart: 51.8 Ω (51.819), Wheeler +0.0 %, AN-905 51.1 Ω, outside IPC-2141A's narrow-strip limit (t/w 0.17); - the copper's own picker (1 oz is 34.8 µm); - copper as thick as half the spacing is refused; - the length pickers move together.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Asymmetric stripline

(formerly Dual stripline impedance, then Dual stripline)

What it computes

The impedance of a trace between two ground planes but nearer one of them (the asymmetric, offset or off-centre stripline, as each trace is on a board with two signal layers between the same pair of planes), or the width that gives an impedance:

  • Inputs: the trace width w, the dielectric under it h1 and over it h2, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Z0; type the impedance you need and the width box shows the width that gives it.
  • The big result: Z0 from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with the spacing between the planes and how far the trace is off centre; or the width for the impedance typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and an estimate stands in.
  • Below it, each with its difference from the solver:
  • Robrish's formula, flagged outside its ±2 % range;
  • Hogan's formula, the one IPC-2141A reprints;
  • the two dual-stripline formulas, the trace seen as one of two signal layers between the planes: IPC-2251's, and the older IPC one that other calculators still use ("Older IPC formula"); each flagged outside its range (W/(H − T) < 0.35, T/H < 0.25), and absent when the far side leaves no room for a second layer;
  • the same trace centred between the same planes;
  • the delay per length, the signal seeing the full εr;
  • the capacitance and inductance per length.
  • Units: mm or mil for the three lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the two planes, the trace drawn nearer the closer one, h1, h2, t and εr, lengths in mm and mil. The trace is green when its width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: a 0.2 mm trace 0.2 and 0.4 mm from the planes, the width for 50 Ω on those layers, a centred trace (Stripline's case), a narrow trace close to one plane, and two dual striplines: LearnEMC's case with a 2 mil trace, and a 0.43 mm trace well outside the dual formulas' range.

Terms

  • Asymmetric (offset) stripline: a stripline whose trace is not centred: h1 ≠ h2. A board with two signal layers between the same planes (a dual stripline) has each layer's traces offset like this; the tool leaves out the other layer's traces.
  • Name: IPC-2141A's. The tool was first called Dual stripline; Pierre renamed it on 2026-11-05, since that name is used for the two-layer stack-up, not for one offset trace. Saturn PCB Toolkit calls it "Stripline Asym", Polar "offset stripline", Wadell "off-center stripline".
  • h1, h2, B: the dielectric between the trace and the lower and the upper plane; B = h1 + h2 + t is the spacing between the planes.
  • Z0, εr, C0, L0, oz: as in Microstrip and Stripline.

Source

  • The field solver (js/fieldsolver.js; how it works and how it was checked are in Edge-coupled embedded's section). For this case it reproduces tools/fd_lines.py, a separate implementation, in every case below.
  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §3.6.3 "Off-Center Stripline" (read, Pierre's scanned copy). It gives three methods:
  • Robrish's, extending Cohn's (3.6.3.1–3.6.3.13): for a narrow strip, w/(b − t) < 0.35, a round wire of diameter d0 = w (0.5008 + 1.0235x − 1.0230x² + 1.1564x³ − 0.4749x⁴), x = t/w, and Z0 = η0/(2π√εr) × cosh⁻¹(sin(πc/b) coth(πd0/2b)), c the strip's centre above the lower plane; for a wide one, the parallel plates on either side and the edges' fringing (3.6.3.6–3.6.3.10). "Agreement with exact analytic solutions is better than 0.5 %", and ±2 % against numerical solutions for 0.2 < c/b < 0.8, w > t, t/b < 0.2;
  • Howe's parallel plates and fringing (3.6.3.14–3.6.3.20), which Wadell says differ substantially from the centred equations when the strip is centred; not used here;
  • Hogan's (3.6.3.21–3.6.3.23, from Sean Hogan's 1988 note "Closed Form Transmission Line Equation"): Z0 = (1/√εr)[Z0,ctr(1, w, b, t) − ΔZ0,air], Z0,air = 2 Z0,ctr(1, w, h1, t) Z0,ctr(1, w, h2, t) / (their sum), ΔZ0,air = (0.26π/8) Z0,air² (0.5 − (h1 + t/2)/(h1 + h2 + t))^2.2 ((t + w)/(h1 + h2 + t))^2.9, Z0,ctr the centred stripline (3.6.2.1). No range or accuracy is given.
  • IPC-2141A, March 2004, §4.2.5, [4-17]–[4-19] (read, Pierre's scanned copy): Hogan's formula, citing its reference 2, with 1/εr where Wadell has 1/√εr. That 1/εr is a misprint: a uniform dielectric divides the impedance in air by √εr, and with 1/εr a centred FR-4 stripline would come out at half its value.
  • The dual-stripline formulas. For two signal layers between the planes, H is the dielectric between a trace and its nearer plane and C (D in the book below) the dielectric between the two signal layers; for the tool's trace, H = the smaller of h1 and h2, and C = the larger − t − H, the room left for the other layer.
  • IPC-2251, "Design Guide for Electronic Packaging Utilizing High-Speed Techniques", 4th working draft, February 2001, as the LearnEMC dual stripline calculator (learnemc.com, also on the Missouri S&T EMC Laboratory's site) publishes it, in its code and its equation image (read; the IPC document itself not read): Z0 = ½ [60/√εr × ln(8H / (0.67π (0.8W + T))) + 60/√εr × ln(8(H + C) / (0.67π (0.8W + T)))], valid for W/(H − T) < 0.35, T/H < 0.25; the calculator's notes give it within 1 % of a 2D field solver for 0.08 < W/H < 0.35 at εr 4, H 15 mil, C 10 mil, T 1.37 mil. It is the mean of two AN-905 striplines (Stripline's section), planes 2H and 2(H + C) apart.
  • The older IPC dual stripline formula, as Mark I. Montrose, "Printed Circuit Board Design Techniques for EMC Compliance — A Handbook for Designers", 2nd edition, prints it (§4.2.4 "Dual or Asymmetric Stripline Topology", eq. 4.10, page 117 of Pierre's PDF; that page read, the rest of the book not): Z0 = (80/√εr) ln[1.9 (2H + T) / (0.8W + T)] [1 − H / (4 (H + D + T))], the same range, "approximate"; the page adds that both layers should be routed at right angles to each other. Other calculators still use it: it reproduces one's 32.689 Ω for W 0.4318, H 0.254, C 0.2032 mm, T 18 µm, εr 4.6. Its IPC source (IPC-D-317A, 1995, or the first IPC-2141, 1996) was not read.
  • Which is the latest: IPC-2251 followed IPC-D-317A; IPC-2141A (2004, read) gives Hogan's formula for the offset trace instead, and no IPC-2141B was found (2026-11-07).
  • A correction: this manual first called the full-B first term and the Z0,SS(b = h1) arguments of [4-17] and [4-19] misprints too. Wadell prints them the same way: they are Hogan's formula as published, and it is that formula which is inaccurate off centre.

Why the formulas are these

∇·(ε ∇φ) = 0 between the trace (1 V) and the planes (0 V)
S = C / ε0 = Σ ε (Δφ)² over the grid
Z0 = η0 / (√εr × S),   η0 = 376.73 Ω
Td = 33.36 √εr ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Z0,   L0 = Z0 × Td

Between two planes all the field runs in one dielectric, so one solve, in air, gives the impedance for any εr. The nearer plane takes more of the trace's field, its capacitance rises and Z0 falls below the centred value.

How the formulas compare with the solver (FR-4, 1 oz):

Case Solver Robrish Hogan Centred
0.2 mm, h1 0.2, h2 0.4 mm 49.87 Ω −1.7 % +6.7 % +7.0 %
0.5 mm, h1 0.2, h2 0.4 mm 30.64 Ω −1.5 % +7.1 % +8.9 %
0.1 mm, h1 0.1, h2 0.5 mm 50.81 Ω −1.8 % (c/b 0.19) +33 % +34 %
0.2 mm centred, b 0.6 mm 51.82 Ω −2.8 % (wide form) 0.0 % 0.0 %

The dual-stripline formulas against the solver (one trace, the other layer left out):

Case Solver IPC-2251 Older IPC dual
εr 4, H 15, C 10, T 1.37 mil, W 1 mil 107.13 Ω −1.3 % +6.1 %
the same, W 2 mil 96.63 Ω −0.3 % +6.5 %
the same, W 3 mil 89.21 Ω −0.1 % +6.2 %
the same, W 4 mil 83.42 Ω −0.0 % +5.6 %
εr 4.6, H 0.254, C 0.2032 mm, T 18 µm, W 0.4318 mm (W/(H − T) 1.83) 38.27 Ω −7.1 % −14.6 %

Within their range IPC-2251's mean of two striplines is within 0.3 % of the solver above W = 2 mil, the older formula 5 to 6.5 % high; outside it both read low, the older one by 15 % on the wide trace.

Robrish's stays within 3 %; Hogan's is barely below the centred value, its offset term being a fraction of an ohm, so it reads 7 to 33 % high off centre. Wadell's centred stripline (3.6.2.1), which Hogan's uses, is printed with η0/(2π√εr), twice Wheeler's η0/(4π√εr) (Stripline's section); the tool uses Wheeler's. The estimate shown while the solver works is the tool's earlier formula: the two halves (planes 2h1 + t and 2h2 + t apart) in parallel, minus Hogan's term; it is within 0.3 % in the first case but −6.2 % for the wide trace and +4.9 % near a plane.

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static, no losses: dispersion, losses and roughness are left out.
  • One dielectric or core and prepreg: with the pill, the core under the trace (h1) and the prepreg from its bottom face up, as in Stripline's Core and prepreg; more layers are averaged by the user.
  • One trace: traces on the other signal layer are left out.
  • Rectangular trace; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

8 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline: - 0.2 mm trace 0.2 and 0.4 mm from the planes, FR-4, 1 oz: 49.9 Ω (49.87); Robrish 49 Ω (−1.7 %), Hogan 53.2 Ω (+6.7 %), centred 53.4 Ω (+7.0 %); 69.2 ps/cm; 1.39 pF/cm and 3.45 nH/cm; - 50 Ω on those layers: 0.199 mm (0.19881); - centred, planes 0.6 mm apart: 51.8 Ω (51.82); Hogan's equals the centred value there, Robrish's wide form 2.8 % low; - 0.1 mm trace 0.1 and 0.5 mm from the planes: 50.8 Ω (50.81); Hogan +33.4 %; Robrish's flagged outside its range; - h1 and h2 swapped: the same impedance; - the three length pickers move together; - dual stripline, LearnEMC's case with a 2 mil trace: 96.6 Ω (96.631); IPC-2251 96.3 Ω (−0.3 %), the older formula 103 Ω (+6.5 %); - dual stripline, the 0.4318 mm trace: 38.3 Ω (38.269); IPC-2251 35.6 Ω (−7.1 %) and the older formula 32.7 Ω (−14.6 %), both flagged outside their range.
