PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Edge-coupled stripline

(formerly Edge-coupled stripline)

What it computes

The differential impedance of two edge-coupled traces centred between two ground planes (a differential pair on an inner layer), or the trace width that gives it at a gap:

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the gap between them s, the spacing between the planes b, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and differential impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Zdiff; type the Zdiff you need (90 Ω for USB, 100 Ω for Ethernet or LVDS) and the width box shows the width at your gap.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with each trace's impedance alone and the coupling (odd mode over one trace alone); or the width for the Zdiff typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and IPC-2141A's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • the odd-mode impedance, each trace's share of the pair, Zdiff / 2;
  • the even-mode and common-mode impedance, as in Edge-coupled microstrip;
  • one trace alone, from the solver as in Stripline;
  • Zdiff by IPC-2141A's form, the big result until 2026-11-07, and its difference from the solver's;
  • which of IPC-2141A's two forms applies, by s/t;
  • the delay per length, the signal seeing the full εr.
  • Units: mm or mil for the three lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the two planes, the pair centred between them, w and s as a chain dimension, b, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: 100 Ω and 90 Ω between planes 0.6 mm apart with a 0.2 mm gap, a close pair (IPC's narrow-gap form), and a pair far enough apart that it no longer couples.

Terms

  • Differential pair, differential impedance (Zdiff), odd mode, coupling: as in Edge-coupled microstrip.
  • Edge-coupled: side by side on the same layer; a pair one above the other is broadside-coupled.
  • Fringing capacitance (Cf): the capacitance from a strip's edge to the planes, beyond the part directly under and over it. A thicker strip has more.
  • Paper-thin strip: a strip of zero thickness, for which Cohn found the impedance exactly; the thick strip is worked out from it.
  • b, t, εr, oz: as in Stripline.

Source

  • IPC-2141A, "Design Guide for High-Speed Controlled Impedance Circuit Boards", March 2004, §4.4.2, figure 4-6(b) (read, Pierre's scanned copy), citing its references 2 and 7:
  • [4-42] for s/t ≥ 5: Z0,o(w/b, t/b, s/b) = {1/Z0(w/b, t/b) − (C'f(t/b)/C'f(0)) [1/Z0,o(w/b, 0, s/b) − 1/Z0(w/b, 0)]}^−1;
  • [4-43] for s/t ≤ 5: Z0,o = {1/Z0(w/b, t/b) + [1/Z0,o(w/b, 0, s/b) − 1/Z0(w/b, 0)] − (2/(377ε)) (C'f(t/b) − C'f(0) − ε/s)}^−1;
  • Z0(w/b, t/b) its stripline [4-9]; Z0(w/b, 0) and Z0,o(w/b, 0, s/b) the zero-thickness impedances of its references 2 and 7;
  • [4-44] C'f(t/b) = (0.0885 εr/π) {2b/(b − t) ln((2b − t)/(b − t)) − ((2b − t)/(b − t)) ln(b²/(b − t)² − 1)}; [4-45] C'f(0) = (0.0885 εr/π) 2 ln 2.
  • A. J. Burkhardt, C. S. Gregg and J. A. Staniforth, "Calculation of PCB Track Impedance", Polar Instruments, IPC Printed Circuits Expo 1999 (read): Cohn's exact zero-thickness stripline, Z0 = η0/(4√εr) × K(k)/K(k'), k = sech(πw/2b), k' = tanh(πw/2b), and the coupled pair's odd mode with k0 = tanh(πw/2b) coth(π(w + s)/2b) (their equations 4, 5, 7, 8); their table 1, a surface microstrip computed by their boundary-element solver: 30.09, 50.63 and 89.63 Ω for 3.3, 1.5 and 0.45 mm on 0.794 mm, εr 4.2, 35 µm copper.
  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §4.6.5, pages 234–235 (read, Pierre's scanned copy): its C′f(t/b) has 1/(1 − t/b) − 1 = t/(b − t) as the second coefficient, and its odd mode's fringing term C′f,o = C′f(0, s/b) + εt/s (4.6.5.9): two of the three corrections below.
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, checked against Cohn's exact zero-thickness pair to 0.005 % (Edge-coupled embedded's section); tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline, a separate implementation, gives the values below.
  • Not read: Cohn's papers themselves, and IPC's references 2 and 7.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, solved three times, all in one dielectric:

odd mode: the traces at +1 V and −1 V,  Zodd = η0 / (√εr × S_air)
Zdiff = 2 Zodd,   even mode: both at +1 V,  common mode = Zeven / 2
one trace alone, as in Stripline

IPC-2141A's form, the comparison:

In air:   Z0, Zo,0 = 30π K(k)/K(k'), Cohn's paper-thin strip alone and in the pair
          Z(t): Wheeler's strip alone, with its copper
          ΔY = 1/Zo,0 − 1/Z0
s/t ≥ 5:  1/Zo = 1/Z(t) + (Cf(t)/Cf(0)) ΔY
s/t < 5:  1/Zo = 1/Z(t) + ΔY − (2/η0)(Cf(t) − Cf(0) − t/s)
Zdiff = 2 Zo / √εr

The odd-mode admittance of a paper-thin strip in a pair is known exactly; so is one strip alone. Their difference ΔY is what the neighbour adds. For a strip with copper, IPC starts from that strip alone, Z(t), and adds ΔY, scaled by how much the copper raises the edge's fringing capacitance when the gap is wide. Across a narrow gap the two copper walls face each other: for the odd mode the plane midway between them is at 0 V, adding a parallel-plate capacitance t/(s/2) per wall in units of ε. In one dielectric everything scales as 1/√εr, so the tool works in air (IPC's ε becomes ε0) and divides at the end. K is computed by the arithmetic-geometric mean, K(k) = π / (2 agm(1, k')).

Three misprints corrected. - [4-42] subtracts the scaled ΔY: a strip would then have a higher impedance next to its odd-mode partner than alone, which the field contradicts (13 to 50 % off). With the sign that [4-43] and the physics give, it adds it. - [4-43] ends in ε/s, which is not a capacitance per length; the copper walls' parallel-plate term is εt/s, and the field solver agrees with that within 1.4 %. - [4-44]'s second coefficient (2b − t)/(b − t) multiplies ln 0 as t goes to zero, where [4-45] says C'f(0) = 2 ln 2 (in units of ε0 εr, over π). With t/(b − t), as in IPC's own θ [4-16] (b²/(b − t)² − 1 = (2bt − t²)/ (b − t)²), it does.

How IPC-2141A's form compares with the solver (1 oz copper, planes 0.6 mm apart, εr 4.3):

Case Solver Zdiff IPC-2141A
100 Ω: 0.125 mm, 0.2 mm gap ([4-42]) 100.00 Ω +3.6 %
90 Ω: 0.175 mm, 0.2 mm gap ([4-42]) 90.00 Ω +2.9 %
0.15 mm, 0.2 mm gap, the default ([4-42]) 94.60 Ω +3.2 %
0.15 mm, 0.1 mm gap ([4-43]) 76.82 Ω +1.0 %
0.15 mm, 2 mm apart 116.03 Ω +0.0 %

Corrected, the form is 1 to 3.6 % high with 1 oz copper; it was the big result until 2026-11-07, when the solver took over. At 100 Ω the difference is in the width: IPC-2141A's 0.14 mm gives 96.7 Ω, the solver's 0.125 mm gives 100 Ω.

Core and prepreg

As in Stripline: the "Core + prepreg" pill puts the core's εr under the traces and the prepreg's from their bottom faces up; the solver takes the two layers, the formulas the thickness-weighted mean. The default pair with core 3.8 and prepreg 4.6: 95.1 Ω (95.080), 68.8 ps/cm.

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces rectangles, no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides. For the formula, §4.4 itself warns that the balanced-line formulas "exist in various forms, some of which are not in agreement".
  • Centred between the planes, equal traces, one dielectric, no losses.
  • The jump at s/t = 5: IPC's two forms differ there by about 2 %; the solver has no such jump.

How it was checked

6 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline: - 100 Ω, planes 0.6 mm apart, FR-4, 1 oz, 0.2 mm gap: 0.125 mm traces (0.12513), 61.8 Ω alone, [4-42]; - 90 Ω, same planes and gap: 0.175 mm (0.17450); - 0.15 mm traces 0.1 mm apart: 76.8 Ω (76.815), coupling 0.662, IPC's [4-43] 77.6 Ω (+1.0 %); even mode 74.5 Ω, common mode 37.2 Ω; - 2 mm apart: 116 Ω (116.03), twice one trace's 58 Ω; - the default pair: 94.6 Ω (94.596), IPC-2141A 97.6 Ω (+3.2 %), 69.2 ps/cm; - the three length pickers move together.

Edge-coupled asym stripline

What it computes

The differential impedance of two edge-coupled traces between two ground planes but nearer one of them (the asymmetric, offset or off-centre edge-coupled stripline, Saturn's "Edge Cpld Int Asym"), as a pair is on a board with two signal layers between the same planes, or the trace width that gives it at a gap:

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the gap s, the dielectric under the traces h1 and over them h2, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and differential impedance are two live boxes, as in Edge-coupled stripline.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with the spacing between the planes, b = h1 + t + h2, and how far the pair is off centre; or the width for the Zdiff typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and the estimate stands in.
  • Below it:
  • the odd-mode impedance, each trace's share, Zdiff / 2;
  • the even-mode and common-mode impedance, as in Edge-coupled microstrip;
  • one trace alone, from the solver, and the coupling (odd mode over it);
  • the estimate, and how far it is from the solver's;
  • the delay per length, the signal seeing the full εr.
  • Units: mm or mil for the four lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the two planes, the pair drawn nearer the closer one, w and s as a chain dimension, h1, h2, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: 100 Ω and 90 Ω with 0.2 mm under and 0.4 mm over the pair, a pair close to one plane, and the centred pair, Edge-coupled stripline's.

Terms

  • Differential pair, Zdiff, odd mode, even mode, common mode, coupling: as in Edge-coupled microstrip.
  • h1, h2, b, t, εr, oz: as in Asymmetric stripline.

Source

  • No published formula read covers this pair. Wadell's §4.6.7 "Asymmetric Edge-Coupled Striplines" (Transmission Line Design Handbook, 1991, pages 239–240, read, Pierre's scanned copy) is a different structure: a centred pair of unequal widths, worked from each line's capacitances (Cristal's method). IPC-2141A (March 2004, read) has the centred pair only (§4.4.2).
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, its stripline cross-section with the pair's gap, the odd or even mode and h1; tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline, a separate implementation with the same settings, gives the values below.
  • The estimate: the tool's, built from IPC-2141A's centred pair as Edge-coupled stripline corrects it.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, solved three times, all in one dielectric:

odd mode: the traces at +1 V and −1 V,  Zodd = η0 / (√εr × S_air)
Zdiff = 2 Zodd,   even mode: both at +1 V,  common mode = Zeven / 2
one trace alone, as in Asymmetric stripline

The estimate, the comparison and the width search's start:

Zo,a = IPC-2141A's centred pair between planes 2h1 + t apart
Zo,b = the same between planes 2h2 + t apart
1/Zo = (1/Zo,a + 1/Zo,b) / 2,   Zdiff = 2 Zo

The pair's field divides between the two planes: the part going down sees the pair as if it were centred between planes 2h1 + t apart, the part going up as if centred between planes 2h2 + t apart, each with half the capacitance; the two halves add, as in Asymmetric stripline's and Broadside-coupled stripline's copper term. It leaves out how the field of one half spills into the other, so it reads high:

Case (1 oz, εr 4.3) Solver Zdiff Estimate
0.15 mm, gap 0.2, h1 0.2, h2 0.4 mm 92.39 Ω +3.7 %
0.1 mm, gap 0.15, h1 0.15, h2 0.3 mm 91.80 Ω +1.7 %
0.15 mm, gap 0.2, h1 0.15, h2 0.6 mm 87.66 Ω +4.9 %
0.1 mm, gap 0.1, h1 0.1, h2 0.4 mm 76.41 Ω +2.1 %
0.25 mm, gap 0.3, h1 0.3, h2 0.5 mm 92.30 Ω +2.1 %
0.2 mm, gap 0.2, centred, h1 = h2 = 0.2 mm 77.18 Ω +1.5 %

Centred, the estimate is IPC-2141A's own pair, whose error it carries (up to +3.6 % in Edge-coupled stripline).

Assumptions and limits

  • Traces on the other signal layer left out: a trace under or over the pair changes its impedance; the tool takes the space between the planes as plain dielectric.
  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces rectangles, one dielectric (or core and prepreg with the pill, as in Stripline), no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

7 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_stripline: - the default: 0.15 mm traces, 0.2 mm gap, 0.2 mm under and 0.4 mm over, FR-4, 1 oz: 92.4 Ω (92.386), odd mode 46.2 Ω, even mode 65 Ω, common mode 32.5 Ω, 56 Ω alone, coupling 0.825, estimate 95.8 Ω (+3.7 %), 69.2 ps/cm; - 100 Ω on the same layers: 0.117 mm (0.11662); - USB 90 Ω: 0.162 mm (0.16208); - close to one plane, 0.1 mm traces 0.1 mm apart, 0.1 and 0.4 mm away: 76.4 Ω (76.413), estimate +2.1 %; - centred, h1 = h2: 94.6 Ω, Edge-coupled stripline's value, the estimate IPC-2141A's 97.6 Ω; - the four length pickers move together; - a zero gap is refused.

The pair placed nearer the upper plane (h1 and h2 swapped) gives the same 92.4 Ω, as its mirror image must.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Broadside-coupled stripline

(formerly Broadside stripline)

What it computes

The differential impedance of two traces one above the other on two inner layers (a broadside-coupled pair), centred between two ground planes, or the trace width that gives it:

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the dielectric between the two traces s, the spacing between the planes b, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and differential impedance are two live boxes, as in Edge-coupled stripline.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), with the odd-mode impedance; or the width for the Zdiff typed. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and the copper method's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • the even-mode and common-mode impedance, as in Edge-coupled microstrip;
  • Zdiff by the tool's copper method, the big result until 2026-11-07, and its difference from the solver's;
  • IPC-2141A's paper-thin Zdiff, and how much higher it reads;
  • w/s against IPC's range, 0.35 or more, flagged below;
  • the delay per length, the signal seeing the full εr.
  • Units: mm or mil for the three lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the two planes, the pair stacked between them with w and s, b, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: 100 Ω between planes 0.8 mm apart, a 0.15 mm pair 0.15 mm apart, wide traces close together, and narrow traces flagged, all with 1 oz copper.

Terms

  • Broadside-coupled: the two traces of a pair face each other across the dielectric between two layers, instead of side by side.
  • Paper-thin: copper of zero thickness. Here the traces face each other with their full width, so their thickness matters more than for a side-by-side pair.
  • Odd mode, even mode, common mode, Zdiff: as in Edge-coupled microstrip.

Source

  • IPC-2141A, "Design Guide for High-Speed Controlled Impedance Circuit Boards", March 2004, §4.4.3, figure 4-6(c) (read, Pierre's scanned copy), citing its references 2, 8 and 9: Z0,o = (293.9/√εr) (s/b) / tanh⁻¹(k) [4-46], k the solution of w/b = (1/π)[ln((1 + R)/(1 − R)) − (s/b) ln((k + R)/(k − R))] [4-47], R = √(k(kb − s)/(b − ks)) [4-48]; "nearly exact for w/s ≥ 0.35, and is more accurate for substrates with large values of εr". No copper thickness.
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, as in Edge-coupled embedded, on the lower half of the cross-section: the mid-plane between the traces at 0 V for the odd mode, a mirror for the even mode; tools/fd_lines.py's app_broadside, a separate implementation with the same settings, gives the values below.
  • Not read: IPC's references 2, 8 and 9.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result, solved twice on the lower half:

odd mode: the mid-plane at 0 V,  Zodd = η0 / (√εr × S_air),  Zdiff = 2 Zodd
even mode: the mid-plane a mirror (both traces at +1 V),  common mode = Zeven / 2

The even mode was checked against its limit: as the traces close up, two paper-thin strips in contact are one strip, each carrying half its charge, so Zeven tends to twice Cohn's single stripline: 4.1, 2.4, 1.3, 0.8 and 0.45 % under it for gaps of 8, 4, 2, 1 and 0.5 µm (0.15 mm strips, planes 0.6 mm apart), the gap's own thickness closing as it shrinks.

IPC-2141A's paper-thin formula, a comparison:

R = √(k (kb − s) / (b − ks))
w/b = (ln((1+R)/(1−R)) − (s/b) ln((k+R)/(k−R))) / π,  solved for k
Zo = 295.9/√εr × (s/b) / tanh⁻¹(k),   Zdiff = 2 Zo

For the odd mode the plane midway between the two traces is at 0 V, so each trace is a strip between its ground plane and that mid-plane; the formula is the exact (conformal-mapping) solution for a paper-thin strip there. k has no closed form: the tool halves the range from s/b to 1 until w/b comes out. The width for a Zdiff is found the same way.

The constant. Against the field solver (tools/fd_lines.py, as in Edge-coupled stripline) the printed formula's ratio is 0.9934 for every geometry tried: its shape is exact, and the constant that matches is η0π/4 = 295.9, not 293.9. With 295.9 the tool is within 0.1 % of the solver for paper-thin traces at w/s ≥ 0.35 (80.0 against 79.97 Ω for 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart, planes 0.6 mm apart), 1.2 % low at w/s 0.25.

The copper method. 1 oz copper lowers Zdiff by 6 to 25 % against the solver: each trace's outer face moves 35 µm closer to its plane, and its edges add fringing. From 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-07 the big result allowed for it by the tool's own method, not IPC's, now a comparison row:

h1 = (b − s)/2 − t,  the copper's outer face to its plane
Zpar(t) = halves in parallel: Z(2h1 + t) ∥ Z(s + t), Wheeler's striplines, ×2 / √εr
1/Zo,cu = 1/Zo,thin(planes b − 2t apart) + 1/Zpar(t) − 1/Zpar(0)

The paper-thin pair with the planes 2t closer, plus the admittance the copper adds to one strip between its plane and the mid-plane, from the two half-striplines of Asymmetric stripline (without its offset term, which fails this close to a plane). Against the solver, for w 0.1 to 0.5 mm, s 0.1 to 0.2 mm, b 0.4 to 0.8 mm, εr 4.3: −1.4 to −0.1 % for ½, 1 and 2 oz.

How the formulas compare with the solver (1 oz copper, εr 4.3):

Case Solver Zdiff Copper method IPC paper-thin
100 Ω: 0.0917 mm, s 0.2 mm, b 0.8 mm 100.00 Ω −0.32 % +20.4 %
0.15 mm, s 0.15 mm, b 0.6 mm 68.04 Ω −0.43 % +17.5 %
0.3 mm, s 0.1 mm, b 0.6 mm 35.62 Ω −0.61 % +10.2 %
0.05 mm, s 0.2 mm, b 0.6 mm (w/s 0.25) 114.45 Ω −1.03 % +29.3 %

Assumptions and limits

  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces rectangles, no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.
  • The copper method is the tool's, checked against the solver over the range above only.
  • Centred pair, equal traces, one dielectric: core and prepreg are averaged by the user, or core and prepreg with the pill (the core between the traces, the prepreg outside, as in Stripline's Core and prepreg).

How it was checked

7 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_broadside: - 100 Ω with 1 oz, planes 0.8 mm apart, 0.2 mm between: 0.0917 mm traces (0.09173); paper-thin they would read 120 Ω (+20.4 %); - 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart, planes 0.6 mm, 1 oz: 68 Ω (68.044), odd mode 34 Ω, even mode 73.9 Ω, common mode 36.9 Ω; copper method 67.8 Ω (−0.4 %), paper-thin 80 Ω (+17.5 %); 69.2 ps/cm; - 0.3 mm traces 0.1 mm apart: 35.6 Ω (35.615), copper method −0.6 %, paper-thin 39.2 Ω; - 0.05 mm traces 0.2 mm apart: 114 Ω (114.45), copper method −1.0 %, w/s 0.25 flagged; - no copper: 80 Ω, IPC's paper-thin formula (with 295.9) within 0.01 %; - copper reaching the planes is refused; - traces as far apart as the planes are refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Broadside-coupled, no plane

What it computes

The differential impedance of two traces facing each other on the two faces of a dielectric sheet, with no ground plane anywhere (a double-sided flex pair: the parallel-strip line, Wadell's "paired strips"), or the trace width that gives it:

  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the sheet between them h, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and Zdiff are two live boxes: type a width and the Zdiff box shows Zdiff; type the Zdiff you need and the width box shows the width.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver, with the odd-mode impedance; or the width for the Zdiff typed, with w/h. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and Wheeler's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • Wheeler's paper-thin formula, and how far it is from the solver's;
  • the common mode: none, with no plane to return through;
  • the effective εr, from the solver;
  • the delay per length;
  • the capacitance and inductance per length between the two traces.
  • Units: mm or mil for the two lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the sheet with a trace on each face, w, h, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: 100 Ω on a 0.1 mm polyimide flex, wide traces on a thin sheet with 1 oz and paper-thin, and narrow paper-thin strips.

Terms

  • Paired strips (parallel-strip line): two flat conductors facing each other across a dielectric sheet; the field runs between them, partly in the sheet and partly in the air around it.
  • No plane, no common mode: with no ground plane, a signal on both traces at once has nothing to return through; only the differential (odd) mode is a transmission line.
  • Differential pair, Zdiff, odd mode: as in Edge-coupled microstrip.
  • εr, εeff, Td, C0, L0, oz: as in Microstrip.

Source

  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §3.3.5 "Paired Strips", pages 71–72 (read, Pierre's scanned copy), a = w/2, b = h/2 (3.3.5.3, 3.3.5.4), paper-thin:
  • wide strips, a/b > 1: Z0 = η0/√εr × {a/b + (1/π) ln 4 + (εr + 1)/(2π εr) ln[π e (a/b + 0.94)/2] + (εr − 1)/(2π εr²) ln(e π²/16)}^−1 (3.3.5.1), "Stated error is less than 1% for wide strips";
  • narrow strips, a/b < 1: Z0 = η0/(π√εr) × [ln(4b/a) + (1/8)(a/b)² − (εr − 1)/(2(εr + 1)) (ln(π/2) + ln(4/π)/εr)] (3.3.5.2), "less than 1% for narrow strips".
  • A misprint corrected: as printed, 3.3.5.2 reads 20 % below the solver for εr 3.5 (126.0 against 156.8 Ω for 0.1 mm strips on 0.2 mm). With η0/(π√((εr + 1)/2)) it comes within 0.3 % (157.2 Ω), and that factor is Wheeler's narrow microstrip formula's, η0/(π√(2(εr + 1))), doubled with h → b: the pair is two microstrips on the sheet's mid-plane. In air (εr 1) the two factors agree.
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js's microstrip on h/2, as in Microstrip; tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip, a separate implementation, gives the values below.

Why the formulas are these

odd mode: the sheet's mid-plane at 0 V
each half: a microstrip w wide, t thick, on h/2 of the sheet
Zdiff = 2 × Z0,ms(w, t, h/2),   εeff the half's
Td = 33.36 √εeff ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Zdiff,   L0 = Zdiff × Td

The two traces carry equal and opposite voltages, so by symmetry the plane midway through the sheet is at 0 V: each trace with its half of the sheet is a microstrip over a ground plane, and the two are in series between the traces. Wheeler's formulas, from conformal mapping, cover the paper-thin strips; the copper's thickness adds capacitance at the edges and lowers Zdiff:

Case Solver Wheeler
0.5 mm on 0.1 mm, εr 3.5, paper-thin 32.90 Ω +0.01 %
0.1 mm on 0.2 mm, εr 3.5, paper-thin 156.80 Ω +0.24 % (corrected)
0.3 mm on 0.2 mm, εr 4.3, paper-thin 75.68 Ω −0.63 %
0.5 mm on 0.1 mm, εr 3.5, 1 oz 31.87 Ω +3.3 %
0.3 mm on 0.2 mm, εr 4.3, 1 oz 71.75 Ω +4.8 %
0.0863 mm on 0.1 mm, εr 4.2, 18 µm 100.00 Ω +9.3 %

The width for a Zdiff starts from Wheeler's, then the solver's answer corrects it.

Assumptions and limits

  • Air on both sides, nothing nearby: a ground plane, a metal case or a cover layer near the pair changes Zdiff (with planes it is Broadside-coupled stripline).
  • Equal traces facing each other exactly; a sideways offset between the layers raises Zdiff.
  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces rectangles, no losses; the flex maker's calculation decides.

How it was checked

7 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_microstrip: - the default, 0.3 mm traces on 0.2 mm of FR-4, 1 oz: 71.7 Ω (71.748), odd mode 35.9 Ω, Wheeler 75.2 Ω (+4.8 %), εeff 3.26, 60.2 ps/cm, 0.839 pF/cm and 4.32 nH/cm; - 100 Ω on 0.1 mm polyimide, 18 µm: 0.0863 mm (0.08632); - 0.5 mm on 0.1 mm, εr 3.5, 1 oz: 31.9 Ω (31.867), Wheeler +3.3 %; - the same paper-thin: 32.9 Ω (32.901), Wheeler +0.0 %; - 0.1 mm on 0.2 mm, εr 3.5, paper-thin: 157 Ω (156.80), Wheeler's narrow form, corrected, +0.2 %; - the two length pickers move together; - a zero sheet is refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Coplanar waveguide

What it computes

The characteristic impedance of a trace with ground copper on both sides of it on the same layer, with or without a ground plane under the board, or the trace width that gives an impedance at a gap:

  • Two pills: "Ground plane below", the grounded coplanar waveguide (GCPW), the default; "No plane below", the coplanar waveguide (CPW) on its own, air under the board.
  • Inputs: the trace width w, the gap s between the trace and each ground, the dielectric h, the copper's thickness t (in oz, µm or mil, its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and impedance are two live boxes: type a width and the impedance box shows Z0; type the impedance you need and the width box shows the width that gives it, the gap kept.
  • The big result: Z0 from the field solver (as in Edge-coupled embedded), or the width for the impedance typed, with b = w + 2s, the distance between the grounds' edges, and w/b. For the moment the solver takes, the badge reads "Solving…" and Wadell's value stands in.
  • Below it:
  • Wadell's formula for the mode, and how far it is from the solver's (for the grounded mode it is the paper-thin one, so the row says so);
  • the effective εr, from the solver;
  • the delay per length, per cm in mm and per inch in mil;
  • the capacitance and inductance per length;
  • how wide the ground copper beside the trace should be, each side: 5 b or more with no plane (Wadell §3.4.1), b or more with a plane below (§3.4.3's notes, which also tie the two sides together).
  • Units: mm or mil for the three lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the trace between its two grounds on the substrate, the plane under it in the grounded mode, w and s as a chain dimension, h, t and εr, in mm and mil. The trace is green when its width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the mode, the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: Wadell's 50 Ω probe on alumina, 50 Ω with a plane below on a 0.2 mm layer and on a 1.6 mm board, and a CPW with no plane below.

Terms

  • Coplanar waveguide (CPW): a trace with ground copper on both sides of it on the same layer; the field runs mostly across the two gaps.
  • Grounded coplanar waveguide (GCPW): the same with a ground plane under the board as well (also called conductor-backed, CBCPW), the usual form on RF boards; the side grounds are tied to the plane by rows of vias.
  • s, b: s is the gap between the trace's edge and the ground's edge; b = w + 2s is the distance between the two grounds' edges (Wadell's a and b are the trace's width and that distance).
  • Z0, εr, εeff, Td, C0, L0, oz: as in Microstrip.
  • K(k): the complete elliptic integral of the first kind; Wadell's formulas are conformal mappings, which turn the cross-section into a parallel-plate one whose capacitance is a ratio of two such integrals.

Source

  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991 (read, Pierre's scanned copy):
  • §3.4.1, "Coplanar Waveguide", pages 73–76: Z0 = 30π/√εeff,t × K(kt′)/K(kt) (3.4.1.1); εeff,t = εeff − (εeff − 1)/((b − a)/2 / 0.7t × K(k)/K′(k) + 1) (3.4.1.2); εeff = 1 + (εr − 1)/2 × K(k′)K(k1)/(K(k) K(k1′)) (3.4.1.3); k = a/b, kt = at/bt; k1 = sinh(πat/4h)/sinh(πbt/4h) (3.4.1.6); at = a + 1.25t/π (1 + ln(4πa/t)), bt = b − the same (3.4.1.8, 3.4.1.9); "The ground plane should extend greater than 5b on each side of the gap"; its example 3.4.1.1, a 50 Ω probe, a = 10 mil, t = 1 mil, h = 25.2 mil of 96 % alumina (εr 10): b = 0.0234 in (it prints "= 0.615 cm" for 0.0594 cm);
  • §3.4.3, "Coplanar Waveguide with Ground", page 79: Z0 = 60π/√εeff / (K(k)/K(k′) + K(k1)/K(k1′)) (3.4.3.1), k = a/b, k1 = tanh(πa/4h)/ tanh(πb/4h) (3.4.3.5), εeff = (1 + εr r)/(1 + r), r = K(k′)K(k1)/ (K(k)K(k1′)) (3.4.3.6), no copper thickness; page 80: to avoid microstrip-like modes, the side ground should extend more than b from the trace on each side, and jumpers can tie its two halves together.
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, its coplanar cross-section; tools/fd_lines.py's app_coplanar, a separate implementation with the same settings, gives the values below (the two agree to the last digit shown: 49.218 and 66.165 Ω for the first cases below).
  • Not read: the papers Wadell draws on (Ghione and Naldi, Gupta et al.).

Why the formulas are these

The solver, the big result:

∇·(ε ∇φ) = 0: the trace at 1 V, the side grounds (and the plane) at 0 V
S = C / ε0 = Σ ε (Δφ)², once with the board, once in air (S_air)
Z0 = η0 / √(S × S_air),   εeff = S / S_air
Td = 33.36 √εeff ps/cm,   C0 = Td / Z0,   L0 = Z0 × Td

The side grounds run to the solver's side wall, 20 b past the gap, and its box is 40 b above the copper and, with no plane, 40 b below the board: a paper-thin CPW in air then comes within 0.001 % of its exact impedance, η0/4 × K(k′)/K(k) (120.48 Ω for w/b 0.5). A box at 10 b, the side wall 5 b past the gap, read 0.15 % low.

Wadell's formulas, the comparison, grounded and paper-thin:

k = a/b,   k1 = tanh(πa/4h) / tanh(πb/4h),   k′ = √(1 − k²)
r = K(k′) K(k1) / (K(k) K(k1′)),   εeff = (1 + εr r) / (1 + r)
Z0 = 60π / √εeff / (K(k)/K(k′) + K(k1)/K(k1′))

and with no plane, with the copper:

at, bt = a ± 1.25t/π (1 + ln(4πa/t)),   kt = at/bt
k1 = sinh(πa/4h) / sinh(πb/4h)
εeff = 1 + (εr − 1)/2 × K(k′) K(k1) / (K(k) K(k1′))
εeff,t = εeff − (εeff − 1) / ((b − a)/2 / (0.7t) × K(k)/K(k′) + 1)
Z0 = 30π / √εeff,t × K(kt′) / K(kt)

One reading corrected. Eq. 3.4.1.6 prints k1 with at and bt; with them Wadell's example needs b = 25.9 mil for 50 Ω. With a and b, as in the εeff equation that uses k1, it needs 23.43 mil, his 23.4 mil: the tool reads it that way. K(k)/K(k′) is computed by the arithmetic-geometric mean, and k′ from √((b − a)(b + a))/b, which keeps its precision for wide traces.

How Wadell's formulas compare with the solver (εr 4.3 unless noted):

Case Solver Wadell
No plane, paper-thin, 0.3 mm, s 0.15 mm, h 1.6 mm 74.14 Ω +0.09 %
No plane, 1 oz, 0.3 mm, s 0.15 mm, h 1.6 mm 66.17 Ω −9.6 %
No plane, 1 oz, 1 mm, s 0.2 mm, h 1.6 mm 53.97 Ω −7.9 %
No plane, 1 oz, 0.5 mm, s 0.25 mm, h 0.2 mm 77.69 Ω −3.8 %
No plane, Wadell's probe, εr 10 52.64 Ω −5.1 %
Plane below, paper-thin, 0.3 mm, s 0.15 mm, h 0.2 mm 53.91 Ω +0.53 %
Plane below, paper-thin, 0.3 mm, s 0.15 mm, h 1.6 mm 73.42 Ω +0.06 %
Plane below, paper-thin, 1 mm, s 0.2 mm, h 1.6 mm 54.86 Ω +0.07 %
Plane below, 1 oz, 0.3 mm, s 0.15 mm, h 0.2 mm 49.22 Ω +10.1 %
Plane below, 1 oz, 1 mm, s 0.2 mm, h 1.6 mm 51.33 Ω +7.0 %

Paper-thin, both formulas meet the solver within 0.5 %: the conformal mappings are sound. The copper is what they handle badly. Its walls face each other across the gap and add capacitance, about t/s per wall on top of the gap's own field, so 1 oz on 0.15 mm gaps lowers Z0 by 9 to 11 % in the solver. §3.4.3 has no copper term and reads 7 to 10 % high; §3.4.1's correction overshoots and reads 4 to 10 % low. On Wadell's own probe, 52.6 Ω where he designed for 50 Ω.

Assumptions and limits

  • Wide side grounds: the solver takes them out to 20 b; narrower ground copper raises Z0 (Wadell's 5 b, or b with a plane below, keeps it close).
  • Grounds tied together: in the grounded mode, the side grounds and the plane are at the same potential, as stitching vias make them; a CPW without them can carry other modes (Wadell p80).
  • Quasi-static field solution: the trace and the grounds rectangles, one dielectric, no solder mask, no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

10 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_coplanar: - the default, plane below: 0.3 mm trace, 0.15 mm gaps on 0.2 mm FR-4, 1 oz: 49.2 Ω (49.219), εeff 2.77, 55.5 ps/cm, 1.13 pF/cm and 2.73 nH/cm; Wadell paper-thin 54.2 Ω (+10.1 %); - Wadell's example 3.4.1.1: 10 mil probe, b 23.4 mil, 1 mil copper, 25.2 mil of εr 10, no plane: 52.6 Ω (52.639); his formula 50.0 Ω (−5.1 %), the 50 Ω he solved for; - 50 Ω with a plane below on 0.2 mm, 0.15 mm gaps: 0.29 mm (0.29035); - 50 Ω with a plane below on 1.6 mm, 0.2 mm gaps: 1.09 mm (1.08937); - no plane, 0.3 mm on 1.6 mm, 0.15 mm gaps: 66.2 Ω (66.166), Wadell 59.8 Ω (−9.6 %), side grounds 3 mm (5 b); - the default without the plane: 70.5 Ω (70.530), Wadell 64.3 Ω (−8.8 %); - paper-thin copper: 53.9 Ω (53.909), Wadell +0.5 %; - the copper's own picker (1 oz is 34.8 µm); - the three length pickers move together; - a zero gap is refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Edge-coupled coplanar

What it computes

The differential impedance of an edge-coupled pair with ground copper beside it on the same layer (the differential or edge-coupled coplanar waveguide), with or without a ground plane under the board, or the trace width that gives it at given gaps:

  • Two pills, as in Coplanar waveguide: "Ground plane below" (the edge-coupled CPWG, the default) and "No plane below".
  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the gap s between the two traces, the gap g from each trace to its ground, the dielectric h, the copper's thickness t (its own picker), the material and εr.
  • Width and Zdiff are two live boxes; a Zdiff typed sets the width, the gaps kept.
  • The big result: Zdiff from the field solver, with the odd-mode impedance; or the width for the Zdiff typed.
  • Below it:
  • the even-mode and common-mode impedance;
  • the same pair without the side grounds (moved 50 times the cross-section away), the comparison: how much the grounds lower Zdiff;
  • the odd mode's effective εr and the delay per length.
  • Units: mm or mil for the four lengths; oz, µm or mil for the copper. Any picker switches them all: mil anywhere makes every length mil, mm or µm makes them metric; oz, a copper weight, stays oz.
  • Drawing: the pair between its two grounds on the substrate, the plane under it in the grounded mode, w, s and g, h, t and εr, in mm and mil. The traces are green when their width is the answer.
  • Remembered: the mode, the length unit and the copper unit.

Examples: USB's 90 Ω and 100 Ω with a plane below on a 0.2 mm layer, the grounds moved far away (Edge-coupled microstrip's case), and the default pair with no plane below.

Terms

  • Edge-coupled coplanar waveguide: a differential pair whose outer edges each face a ground on the same layer, g away; with a plane below as well, the side grounds are tied to it by rows of vias.
  • Differential pair, Zdiff, odd mode, even mode, common mode: as in Edge-coupled microstrip.
  • s, g: s the gap between the two traces, g between each trace and its ground. (Wadell writes s for the first and d for the second.)
  • εr, εeff, t, oz: as in Coplanar waveguide.

Source

  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, its coplanar cross-section extended to a pair (half the cross-section, the pair's centre line at 0 V for the odd mode, a mirror for the even); tools/fd_lines.py's app_coplanar, a separate implementation with the same settings, gives the values below. Checked against two limits: with the grounds 5 mm away and a plane below it gives Edge-coupled microstrip's solver value to 0.003 % (114.401 against 114.397 Ω for 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart on 0.2 mm); with the traces 3 mm apart the odd and even modes meet within 0.3 %. The single Coplanar waveguide is unchanged (49.219 Ω).
  • Brian C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook", Artech House, 1991, §4.4.2 "Edge-Coupled CPW" and §4.4.3 "Edge-Coupled CPWG", pages 194–198 (read, Pierre's scanned copy). Neither is usable as a comparison: §4.4.3's odd and even impedances (4.4.3.1–4.4.3.12, after Hanna) use K(β1)/K′(β1) and K(β1k1)/K′(β1k1) for the plane below, with β1 and k1 defined nowhere on those pages; §4.4.2's (4.4.2.1–4.4.2.7) needs incomplete elliptic integrals solved for k5 and k7 and "assume[s] … that the substrate is infinitely thick". The tool shows no formula rather than guess the missing terms.
  • Not read: Hanna's 1985 paper and the others Wadell cites.

Why the formulas are these

The solver, three times:

odd mode: the traces at +1 V and −1 V, the grounds (and plane) at 0 V
Zodd = η0 / √(S × S_air),   Zdiff = 2 Zodd,   εeff = S / S_air
even mode: both traces at +1 V,  common mode = Zeven / 2
without the side grounds: the odd mode with g = 50 (w + s + h)

The grounds beside the pair add capacitance to each trace and lower Zdiff, and keep the field, and so the crosstalk to other traces, close to the pair. A typed Zdiff sets the width: the search starts from a rough estimate (Wadell's single CPW or CPWG, as Coplanar waveguide computes it, with s/2 and g combined harmonically; −30 to +36 %) and the solver's answers correct it.

Case (1 oz, FR-4) Zdiff Without the side grounds
0.15 mm, s 0.15, g 0.15 mm, h 0.2 mm, plane below 109.82 Ω 114.40 Ω, +4.2 %
the same, no plane below 118.82 Ω 135.40 Ω, +14.0 %

With a plane below, the plane already holds most of the field and the side grounds take 4 %; with none, they take 14 %.

Assumptions and limits

  • Wide side grounds, tied to the plane in the grounded mode, as stitching vias make them.
  • Equal traces, the two gaps to ground equal.
  • Quasi-static field solution: the traces and grounds rectangles, one dielectric, no solder mask, no losses; the board maker's stack-up calculation decides.

How it was checked

8 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's app_coplanar: - the default, plane below, 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart, 0.15 mm to the grounds, 0.2 mm FR-4, 1 oz: 110 Ω (109.823), odd mode 54.9 Ω, even mode 82.9 Ω, common mode 41.5 Ω, without the side grounds 114 Ω (+4.2 %), εeff 2.41, 51.8 ps/cm; - USB 90 Ω: 0.254 mm (0.25427); - 100 Ω: 0.195 mm (0.19481); - the grounds 5 mm away: 114 Ω (114.401), the same without them; - no plane below: 119 Ω (118.819), common mode 65.9 Ω, without the side grounds 135 Ω (+14.0 %); - the pill switches to no plane; - the four length pickers move together; - a zero gap to the ground is refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Propagation delay

What it computes

The time a signal takes along a trace, and what follows from it. It takes the place of the planned "Effective dielectric constant" and "Signal propagation delay" tools (Pierre, 2026-11-08), as every impedance tool already shows both for its own structure:

  • Three pills: Microstrip (the trace on an outer layer: εeff from the field solver for its width, dielectric and copper), Stripline (between two planes in one dielectric: εeff is εr exactly, whatever the trace) and Known εeff (typed, for any other line: coplanar, embedded, a maker's figure).
  • Inputs: the trace's width w, the dielectric h and the copper (microstrip), the material and εr (or εeff), the trace's length l, a length mismatch Δl, and the rise time.
  • The big result: the delay along the trace; below it εeff and the speed as a share of the speed of light.
  • Below it: the delay per length (ps/cm and ps/in), the speed (cm/ns and in/ns), the skew of the mismatch, the length of the rising edge on the board (tr × v), and the length beyond which the trace is electrically long, orange when this trace is.
  • Units: mm or mil for the cross-section and the mismatch, oz, µm or mil for the copper, mm, cm or in for the length, linked (in switches the others to mil); ps or ns for the rise time.
  • Drawing: the trace seen from above, driver to receiver, its delay in green, the length in mm and in.
  • Remembered: the pill and the units.

Examples: a 50 Ω microstrip, length matching in a stripline, a known εeff in inches.

Terms

  • Effective dielectric constant, εeff: the εr of a uniform material that would give the line's speed; between 1 and εr when part of the field is in air (microstrip), εr when all of it is in the dielectric (stripline).
  • Propagation delay: the time for an edge to travel the trace, l √εeff / c; per length it is √εeff / c, 33.356 ps/cm × √εeff.
  • Skew: the difference in arrival time of two signals, here from a length mismatch Δl.
  • Rising edge on the board: how much of the trace the edge spans while it rises, tr × v; a trace much shorter than it behaves as a lumped load.
  • Electrically long: a trace whose delay is a large enough share of the rise time that its reflections matter, and that should be terminated.

Sources

  • The delay: the speed of a TEM wave, c/√εr, c = 299 792 458 m/s exactly (SI); for a microstrip's quasi-TEM wave, εeff from the app's field solver (as in Microstrip), Hammerstad's formula while it works.
  • Electrically long: Barry Olney, "Beyond Design: High-speed Rules of Thumb", I-Connect007 (Design007 Magazine), 21 November 2024 (read): drivers need "provision for termination" when the "length (in inches) is equal to or greater than the rise and fall time (in ns)", and "the propagation speed of a signal is ~6 in/ns in FR-4"; together, a delay of a sixth of the rise time. The tool takes tr/6 with the trace's own speed: 24.1 mm (0.949 in) for a stripline in FR-4 at 1 ns, his 1 in.
  • The caution: Howard Johnson, "Resonance in Short Transmission Line", High-Speed Digital Design Online Newsletter vol. 6 issue 06, 2003 (read): the delay-to-rise-time ratio "doesn't actually determine whether a termination is needed"; a short line with a low-impedance driver and a capacitive load can still ring.

Assumptions and limits

  • Lossless, no dispersion: εeff at the frequencies of the edge; a real laminate's εr falls slowly with frequency, and a microstrip's εeff rises toward εr at high frequency.
  • Stripline: one dielectric all round; with core and prepreg of different εr, use Known εeff with the Stripline tool's value.
  • The rule of thumb: tr/6 is a guide (see Johnson above); other authors use tr/4 or tr/2.

How it was checked

7 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's microstrip and the formulas above: - the default microstrip, 0.36 mm on 0.2 mm FR-4, 1 oz, 100 mm: εeff 3.13 (3.13056), 59.0 ps/cm, 150 ps/in, 16.9 cm/ns, 590 ps, 5.9 ps for 1 mm, the edge 169 mm at 1 ns, long beyond 28.2 mm; - the stripline length-matching example: 346 ps for 50 mm, 3.46 ps for 0.5 mm, long beyond 12.0 mm at 0.5 ns; - a known εeff of 3, 6 in: 880 ps, 147 ps/in, long beyond 1.14 in; - Olney's rule: a stripline in FR-4 at 1 ns is long beyond 24.1 mm; - 20 mm at 1 ns is not long; - inches on the length switch the cross-section to mil; - a zero rise time is refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Crosstalk

What it computes

The crosstalk a step or a sine on one trace (the aggressor) induces on its neighbour (the victim), two equal traces side by side, as a share of the aggressor's signal:

  • Two pairs of pills, side by side: Microstrip (the pair on an outer layer over a plane) or Stripline (the pair centred between two planes); Step edge (a logic edge with a rise time, below) or Sine wave (a sine at one frequency, see Sine wave).
  • Inputs: each trace's width w, the spacing s between them, the dielectric h (microstrip) or the spacing between the planes b (stripline), the copper's thickness t, the material and εr, the length the traces run side by side, the aggressor's rise time, and its voltage swing on the line (3.3 V unless typed).
  • The big result: the near-end noise on the victim (NEXT) in volts, the coefficient times the aggressor's swing; below it the coefficient in %, how long the plateau lasts (the round trip 2T), and whether the coupled length saturates it.
  • Below it:
  • the far-end noise (FEXT) on the victim in volts, with its share in %, negative in microstrip (an inverted pulse about as long as the rise time), zero in stripline, shown as "0 V: the two couplings cancel" (in one dielectric the capacitive and inductive parts are equal and opposite, Lm/L = Cm/C); flagged as an upper bound when the even and odd modes' edges arrive further apart than the rise time;
  • the pair's even- and odd-mode impedances, from the solver;
  • each trace's impedance with its neighbour present, ζ = √(L/C);
  • the coupling ratios Lm/L and Cm/C;
  • in microstrip, how far apart the even and odd edges reach the far end.
  • Units: mm or mil for the cross-section; oz, µm or mil for the copper; mm, cm or in for the coupled length: any of them switches the others, mil or in to imperial, mm, µm or cm to metric (oz stays oz); ps or ns for the rise time; MHz or GHz for the sine's frequency.
  • Drawing: the aggressor (blue) and the victim (green) over the plane or between the planes, w and s as a chain dimension, h or b, εr, in mm and mil.
  • Remembered: the pills and the units.

Examples: the 3w rule (spacing three trace widths), a short run with a slow edge (below saturation), a stripline pair (no FEXT), and a 100 MHz clock (Sine wave).

Sine wave

With "Sine wave" the rise time box becomes Frequency (MHz or GHz), and the tool gives the victim's noise for a sine on the aggressor:

  • The big result: the near-end noise in dB, 20 log of its share of the aggressor's amplitude (−30 dB is 3.2 %), as RF crosstalk is quoted and whatever the swing (Pierre); below it the same in volts (the share times the aggressor's swing; a peak-to-peak swing gives peak-to-peak noise) and in %.
  • Below it: the far-end noise in dB and volts ("0 V: the two couplings cancel" in stripline); the quarter-wave frequency, where the coupled run is a quarter wavelength long, with the run's length in wavelengths at the chosen frequency; the even and odd modes, ζ, Lm/L and Cm/C as for the step.
  • Drawing: in place of the cross-section, the near-end (green) and far-end (blue) noise in dB against frequency, on a log scale over a few decades around the quarter wave and the chosen frequency, which is marked.

How: the pair splits exactly into its even mode (both traces at the same voltage) and odd mode (opposite voltages), each an ordinary line with its own impedance Z and speed v from the field solver. Each end of each trace is taken to have a resistor R = ζ, the trace's impedance; the aggressor's source is 2 × the swing behind R, so a matched line carries the swing. Each mode is then one line of electrical length θ = 2π f l / v, with half the source and R at both ends; from the standard line equations (A = D = cos θ, B = j Z sin θ, C = j sin θ / Z):

V_end = swing × R / (2R cos θ + j sin θ (Z + R²/Z))
V_in  = V_end × (cos θ + j (Z/R) sin θ)
near = V_in,even − V_in,odd,   far = V_end,even − V_end,odd

This is worked out here from those equations, not taken from a paper; it is exact for lossless lines with all four ends in R, at any frequency and any coupling, microstrip included.

  • What it shows: the near-end noise grows with frequency, 6 dB per octave at first, peaks near the quarter wave at twice the step's plateau, falls to a null at the half wave and repeats; Shlepnev's remark that a real signal's crosstalk can reach twice the step's is this peak. The far-end noise grows with frequency in microstrip and is zero in stripline.
  • Checked: at the quarter wave (cos θ = 0) the near end is exactly Ze²/(Ze² + R²) − Zo²/(Zo² + R²); in stripline, R² = Ze Zo, that is (Ze − Zo)/(Ze + Zo) = Cm/C, twice the step's ¼ (Lm/L + Cm/C) = ½ Cm/C: 17.82 % against 2 × 8.915 %. At low frequency the far end is the step's FEXT times 2π f tr: 16.00 % × 2π × 100 MHz × 100 ps = 1.005 %, against 1.004 %. The scratchpad script xt_sine.py, on tools/fd_lines.py's modes, gives the values.
Sine, FR-4, 1 oz, 50 mm, 3.3 V near end far end
microstrip, 0.15 mm, s 0.15, h 0.2 mm, 100 MHz 4.12 %, −27.7 dB 1.00 %, −40.0 dB
the same at 1 GHz 22.5 %, −12.9 dB 9.85 %, −20.1 dB
stripline, 0.15 mm, s 0.2, b 0.6 mm, 711.28 MHz (quarter wave) 17.8 %, −15.0 dB 0

Terms

  • Crosstalk: a signal one trace induces on another through their mutual capacitance Cm and mutual inductance Lm.
  • Near end, far end: the victim's end next to the aggressor's driver, and its end next to the aggressor's receiver.
  • NEXT (near-end, backward): a plateau at the near end that grows with the coupled length until the length's round trip, 2T, reaches the rise time, then stays: the length saturates it.
  • FEXT (far-end, forward): a pulse at the far end, as long as the rise time, growing with the coupled length and with faster edges; the capacitive and inductive parts cancel when both modes travel at one speed, as in a stripline.
  • Even and odd modes: the pair driven alike and driven opposite; any signal on one trace is half of each.
  • Aggressor swing: the voltage step the aggressor's driver puts on the line: about the logic swing for a stiff CMOS driver, half the open-circuit voltage for a driver matched to the line. The victim's noise is the coefficient times it.
  • Saturation length: the coupled length whose round trip equals the rise time, tr × v / 2.
  • 3w rule: a common rule of thumb, traces three widths apart to keep crosstalk low; the example takes the edge-to-edge spacing s = 3w.

Source

  • Yuriy Shlepnev, "How Interconnects Work: Crosstalk Quantification", Signal Integrity Journal, 10 March 2025 (read; its formulas as an equation image on the page): the step-response coefficients of a coupled segment of length l, rise time tr, K_B = l/(2(T1 + T2)) (L21/ζ1 − ζ2 C21) min(1, (T1 + T2)/tr) at the near end, K_F = −l/(2 max(|T1 − T2|, tr)) (L21/ζ1 + ζ2 C21) at the far end, T1, T2 the traces' flight times, ζ1, ζ2 their impedances, L21 and C21 the mutual inductance and capacitance; "relatively accurate for lossless or low loss cases", "an estimate of the maximal possible step crosstalk", and the step "may underestimate the actual peak-to-peak crosstalk for short links by up to 2x". It cites Bracken's DesignCon 2016 paper "Improved Formulas for Crosstalk Coefficients" (not read).
  • The field solver: js/fieldsolver.js, the microstrip and stripline pairs' odd and even modes, as in Edge-coupled microstrip and Edge-coupled stripline; tools/fd_lines.py gives the values below.

Why the formulas are these

From the two modes, per length, with ve, vo = c/√εeff,e, c/√εeff,o:

Ce = 1/(Ze ve),  Le = Ze/ve,  Co = 1/(Zo vo),  Lo = Zo/vo
C = (Ce + Co)/2,  Cm = (Co − Ce)/2,  L = (Le + Lo)/2,  Lm = (Le − Lo)/2
ζ = √(L/C),   v = 1/√(L C),   T = l / v

and, for two equal traces (T1 = T2 = T, ζ1 = ζ2 = ζ, C21 = −Cm, as the capacitance matrix's off-diagonal term is negative):

NEXT = l/(4T) (Lm/ζ + ζ Cm) × min(1, 2T/tr) = ¼ (Lm/L + Cm/C) × min(1, 2T/tr)
FEXT = −l/(2 tr) (Lm/ζ − ζ Cm)
saturation length = tr v / 2

The even mode sees the pair's capacitance less its mutual part and its inductance plus its mutual part, the odd mode the reverse, so the four mode values give L, Lm, C and Cm exactly. In a stripline, one dielectric all round, Lm/L = Cm/C and FEXT cancels; in a microstrip part of the field is in air, Cm/C is smaller than Lm/L and FEXT is negative.

Checked: the stripline's FEXT comes out 0 (Lm/L = Cm/C = 0.1783); the saturated NEXT agrees within 2 % with the near-end voltage the two modes give a matched driver, Ze/(Ze + Z0) − Zo/(Zo + Z0), Z0 = √(Ze Zo) (11.72 against 11.52 %, 3.41 against 3.40 %).

Case (FR-4, 1 oz, 100 ps) NEXT FEXT
microstrip, 0.15 mm, s 0.15, h 0.2 mm, 50 mm 11.52 % −16.00 %
the same, s 0.45 mm (3w) 3.40 % −9.19 %
the same as the first, 10 mm, 1 ns 1.32 % −0.32 %
stripline, 0.15 mm, s 0.2, b 0.6 mm, 50 mm 8.92 % 0

Assumptions and limits

  • A step on matched, lossless lines: the coefficients are the plateau and the pulse a step gives, the victim terminated in its impedance at both ends; other terminations reflect the noise and change the voltages; with losses, long lines or reflections the real waveform differs, and for short links the peak-to-peak crosstalk of a real signal can be up to twice the step's (Shlepnev).
  • FEXT's growth: it is linear in the length; once the even and odd edges reach the far end further apart than the rise time, the pulse stops growing, and the tool flags the value as an upper bound.
  • The sine's terminations: every end in R = ζ; a victim left open or shorted at one end, or a driver of another impedance, changes the standing waves and the voltages.
  • Two equal traces, no other neighbours; the cross-sections and their limits as in Edge-coupled microstrip and Edge-coupled stripline (no solder mask here).

How it was checked

10 cases, the expected values from tools/fd_lines.py's modes and the formulas above, the swing 3.3 V unless said: - the default microstrip pair, 0.15 mm traces 0.15 mm apart on 0.2 mm FR-4, 1 oz, 50 mm side by side, 100 ps: NEXT 11.5 % (11.519), FEXT −16 % (−16.003), saturated beyond 8.73 mm, even and odd modes 91.6 and 57.2 Ω, ζ 73.4 Ω, Lm/L 0.286 and Cm/C 0.175, the edges 32.9 ps apart; 380 mV at the near end for 573 ps, −528 mV at the far end; - the same with a 1.8 V aggressor: 207 mV and −288 mV; - the 3w rule, 0.45 mm apart: NEXT 3.4 % (3.397), 112 mV, FEXT −9.19 %, −303 mV; - 10 mm at 1 ns: below saturation (reached at 87.3 mm), NEXT 1.32 %, FEXT −0.32 %; - the stripline pair: NEXT 8.9 % (8.915), FEXT 0; - a zero coupled length is refused; - sine, the 100 MHz clock example: −27.7 dB (136 mV, 4.12 %) at the near end, −40.0 dB (33.1 mV) at the far end, quarter wave at 873 MHz, the run 0.0286 λ; - sine at 1 GHz: −12.9 dB (744 mV, 22.5 %), far end −20.1 dB (325 mV); - sine on the stripline pair at its quarter wave, 711.28 MHz: −15.0 dB (588 mV, 17.8 %), twice the step's 8.9 %, far end 0; - a zero frequency is refused.

PCB & interconnect › Impedance

Laminate materials

What it computes

A reference of real PCB laminates from their makers' data sheets, and the list behind every impedance tool's Material picker (Pierre, 2026-11-08). It takes the place of the planned "Laminate material reference (Dk/Df) — IPC-4101":

  • Cards: maker and name, the kind (FR-4, low loss, RF, flex), Dk and Df at the frequency the sheet gives, Tg; then how Dk and Df move with frequency, a note, the slash sheet the maker states, and the sheet read.
  • Filters and search: All, FR-4, Low loss, RF, Flex; search any maker, name or word.
  • In the impedance tools: each Material picker lists FR-4, polyimide and PTFE at AN-905's round figures (4.3, 4.2, 2.4), then these laminates grouped by maker, then Custom; picking one sets εr to the Dk on its card. Typing εr sets the picker to the laminate with that value, or to Custom.
  • Remembered: the filter.
Laminate Kind Dk the pickers take Df Tg
Isola 370HR FR-4 4.17 at 1 GHz 0.0161 180 °C
Isola FR408HR FR-4, lower loss 3.69 at 1 GHz 0.0091 190 °C
Shengyi S1000-2M FR-4 4.6 at 1 GHz 0.018 180 °C
Panasonic MEGTRON 6 Low loss 3.40 at 1 GHz 0.002 185 °C
Rogers RO4003C RF 3.55 design (8–40 GHz) 0.0027 at 10 GHz > 280 °C
Rogers RO4350B RF 3.66 design (8–40 GHz) 0.0037 at 10 GHz > 280 °C
Rogers RT/duroid 5880 RF, PTFE 2.20 design (8–40 GHz) 0.0009 at 10 GHz —
DuPont Pyralux AP Flex 3.2 at 10 GHz 0.003 220 °C

Terms

  • Dk (dielectric constant, εr, relative permittivity): how much the material slows a signal and raises a trace's capacitance; it sets the impedance and the delay.
  • Df (dissipation factor, loss tangent, tan δ): the share of the field's energy the material turns into heat per cycle; it sets the dielectric loss, which grows with frequency.
  • Design Dk: Rogers' value for circuit design, "an average number from several different tested lots of material", measured on circuits from 8 to 40 GHz (differential phase length); the process Dk (clamped stripline, IPC-TM-650 2.5.5.5) is the one for quality acceptance, and Rogers warns it "may be incorrect for design purposes, especially microstrip designs".
  • Tg (glass transition temperature): where the resin softens and its expansion rises sharply; DSC and DMA give different figures (both shown where the sheet gives both).
  • Resin content, glass style: a laminate is woven glass in resin; glass has a higher Dk than the resin, so thin, resin-rich layers (106, 1080) read lower than thick, glass-rich ones (7628). Makers give Dk per construction; the cards give one typical figure.
  • Slash sheet: the IPC specification sheet a material is qualified to: IPC-4101 for rigid FR-4-type laminates, IPC-4103 for high-frequency ones, IPC-4204 for flexible ones. The cards give the slash sheets the makers state; IPC-4101 itself was not read.
  • Core, prepreg: the cured, copper-clad laminate, and the uncured sheets that bond the cores; the same resin system usually has both.

Sources

All typical values, read from the makers' sheets: - Isola 370HR data sheet, revision C, last updated 15 April 2021: Tg 180 °C (DSC), Dk 4.24, 4.17, 4.04, 3.92, 3.92 and Df 0.0150, 0.0161, 0.0210, 0.0250, 0.0250 at 100 MHz, 1, 2, 5 and 10 GHz; IPC-4101 /98 /99 /101 /126. - Isola FR408HR data sheet, revision E, last updated 15 April 2021 (a copy hosted by Michigan State University; Isola's server refused): Tg 190 °C (DSC), 230 °C (DMA); Dk 3.72, 3.69, 3.68, 3.64, 3.65 and Df 0.0072, 0.0091, 0.0092, 0.0098, 0.0095 at the same frequencies; IPC-4101 /98 /99 /101 /126. - Shengyi S1000-2M typical data sheet CN-TDS-1911-03: Tg 180 °C (DSC), 185 °C (DMA), permittivity 4.6 and loss tangent 0.018 at 1 GHz (IPC-TM-650 2.5.5.9) on 1.6 mm of 8 × 7628, IPC-4101/126 "for your reference only"; an older S1000-2M/S1000-2MB sheet: 4.9 and 0.009 at 1 MHz, its spec column ≤ 5.4 and ≤ 0.035. - Panasonic MEGTRON 6 laminate R-5775(N), prepreg R-5670(N), data sheet No. 17061630, June 2017, low-Dk glass cloth version: Tg 185 °C (DSC), 210 °C (DMA); Dk 3.40, Df 0.002 at 1 GHz and 3.35, 0.004 at 12 GHz on a 0.75 mm core; Dk 3.18 to 3.40 at 1 GHz across its cores. - Rogers RO4000 series data sheet, PUB 92-004, 2022: RO4003C process Dk 3.38 ± 0.05 and RO4350B 3.48 ± 0.05 at 10 GHz, design Dk 3.55 and 3.66; Df 0.0027 and 0.0037 at 10 GHz, 0.0021 and 0.0031 at 2.5 GHz; Tg

280 °C; IPC-4103 /10 (RO4003C), /11 and /240 (RO4350B); the design Dk "decreases by about 0.1 as the core thickness decreases from 0.020” to 0.004”". - Rogers RT/duroid 5870/5880 data sheet, Publication 92-101, 2022: 5880 Dk 2.20 ± 0.02 at 10 GHz, design Dk 2.20 (8 to 40 GHz), Df 0.0004 at 1 MHz and 0.0009 at 10 GHz. - DuPont Pyralux AP data sheet EI-10124 (2/25): AP9121 Dk 3.4 and 3.2, Df 0.002 and 0.003 at 1 MHz and 10 GHz; Tg 220 °C (TMA); IPC-4204/11. - The round figures: AN-905's Appendix D (see Microstrip): FR-4 and G-10 4.3, polyimide 4.2, PTFE 2.4.

Assumptions and limits

  • Typical, not guaranteed: every sheet says so; a stack-up's real Dk comes from the board maker, for the glass styles and resin contents it uses.
  • One Dk per laminate: the pickers take one figure; Dk changes with frequency (a few % per decade for FR-4, less for the RF laminates) and with the construction.
  • Not every laminate: a short list of widely used ones; Custom takes any other value.

How it was checked

5 cases: - RF shows the three Rogers laminates and hides the FR-4s; - searching "megtron" finds MEGTRON 6 alone; - RO4350B's card reads Dk 3.66 · Df 0.0037 at 10 GHz, Tg > 280 °C; - in Microstrip, RO4350B sets εr 3.66: 3 mm on 1.6 mm with 1 oz, 54.4 Ω (tools/fd_lines.py 54.430); - in Microstrip, typing εr 4.17 picks 370HR: 51.4 Ω (51.387).

PCB & interconnect › Vias & layout

Thermal vias

What it computes

The thermal resistance of plated vias carrying heat from a hot part's pad (an exposed-pad QFN, a regulator's tab, a MOSFET's drain) through the board to the copper on the other side. One screen, from the board thickness, the finished hole, the plating and the fill:

  • Vias and θ are two live boxes: type the number of vias and the θ box shows their resistance; type the θ you need and the vias box shows the fewest that reach it (rounded up, so the real θ is a little lower, shown when you leave the box). The first version had them on two pills, and the vias box of one had nothing to do with the target of the other; Pierre asked why 9 vias became 20, and the boxes are now linked.
  • The big result is the temperature difference across the board at the power you give, or the vias' θ when the power is 0.
  • The terms: l is the board thickness, d the finished hole (after plating), b the copper plating in the hole; the drill is d + 2b.
  • With and without filling: the hole can be empty (air), filled with solder, or filled with copper; whichever is picked, a row gives the same vias empty, solder-filled and copper-filled side by side.
  • Also: one via's sleeve and hole resistances, and the temperature difference across the board at a power you give.
  • The drill (d + 2b), in mil too, against Pierre's rule: a 13 mil drill (0.33 mm, the size AN-1520 recommends), down to 10 mil for a smaller IC; under 10 mil it is flagged with AN-1520's finding below.
  • The pad (optional): the exposed pad's width and height. A row gives how many vias fit whole on it at AN-1520's 1.2 mm (47 mil) pitch, as columns × rows; it is flagged when you ask for more, and asks for the vias near the pad's edge when you use fewer. Past 16 vias a row says AN-1520 saw little more gain.
  • Units: metric (board, hole and pad in mm, plating in µm) or mil for all of them; every length has a picker, the pad's two included, and changing any one changes them all.
  • Drawing: the board in cross-section, the plated sleeve and its pads, the hole shaded when filled, the heat going through; beside it the pad from above, every place a via fits, the vias in use filled green, the outer ones first.
  • Remembered: the fill and the units.

The result is a θ in °C/W like any other in the thermal chain: it sits between the part's pad and the copper below, as θCS does in Heat sink sizing.

Examples: Fineline's single via, nine of them under a 2 W pad, the same filled with solder, the vias needed for 10 °C/W, a 0.8 mm board, and AN-1520's 7 × 7 mm pad with 0.33 mm vias.

Source

  • Fineline, "Temperature Management for Printed Circuit Boards", Albert Schweitzer, November 2021 (read): θ = l / (λ × A) with A = π (d + b) b; with b = 25 µm, d = 250 µm, l = 1.6 mm and λCu = 384 W/m·K, "a single thermal via has a thermal resistance of 193 K/W"; the air in the hole (λ 0.026 W/m·K) in parallel gives 192.98 K/W, "negligible"; a via array is the single via's value divided by the number of vias; counting the FR-4 between vias lowers it by "2-3 K/W per via". Its table of conductivities gives copper ≈ 400, solder (SnCuNi) ≈ 64, FR-4 ≈ 0.2 to 0.9 W/m·K.
  • TTM Technologies ANN-8804 rev B, "Power Handling Considerations for SMD Terminations, Attenuators and Resistors" (read): the board's thermal resistance is the reciprocal sum of the dielectric, the via plating and the via fill, each θ = L / (kA); "typical SAC solder has a thermal conductivity of 57 W/m-K"; copper fill lowers it "by a large factor", most via-fill pastes barely help. Its table 3 (one 0.035" via, 1 mil plating, in 0.1" × 0.1" of board: 27.8 °C/W empty, 13.8 solder, 3.5 copper) does not print the board thickness or the conductivities, so it is not a check case; with a 0.032" board the same model lands within a few percent of it.
  • TI AN-1520, "A Guide to Board Layout for Best Thermal Resistance for Exposed Packages", SNVA183B, September 2006, revised April 2013 (read, with its figures): for the via-diameter study "the maximum number of vias is determined based on the pad size and 1.2 mm distance between vias"; its figure 13 (36-lead LLP, 7 × 7 mm pad, 0.2 mm vias, 4-layer JEDEC board) draws that maximum as a 6 × 6 grid, 36 vias, which is the count of vias whole on the pad at a 1.2 mm pitch; "make the thermal vias near the periphery of the exposed DAP if the maximum number of vias is not applicable"; "use 0.33 mm diameter of vias if possible": 0.2 mm "may increase the θJA by about 15∼25%" on a pad holding 4 vias or fewer, "generally less than 10%" with 9 or more. Read off figure 13 (6.4 mm die): θJA about 26.7 °C/W with no vias, 22.5 with 4, 20.6 with 8, 19.0 with 16, 17.8 with 36; the 2.1 mm die runs about 33.6, 29.8, 28.0, 26.2, 24.7. In this revision figure 12's panels (b) and (c), the via diameter and distribution, are a copy of figure 11(b); only the text gives the diameter figures. Its "diameter" is not said to be the drill or the finished hole; the tool compares it with the drill.
  • Pierre's rule: a 13 mil drill for thermal vias, down to 10 mil for a smaller IC.
  • Not read: the Micron study of thermal via size and spacing Pierre mentioned (AN-1520 covers the same question); TI SPRADB7, whose via formula did not survive text extraction.

Why the formulas are these

θsleeve = l / (λCu × π (d + b) b)
θhole = l / (λfill × π (d/2)²)
θvia = θsleeve ∥ θhole,   θN = θvia / N,   ΔT = P × θN

Heat conducts straight down the copper sleeve, a tube of wall b around the hole; its cross-section is the ring π (d + b) b. A filled hole is a second column of material beside it, so the two are in parallel. Vias side by side share the heat, so N of them in parallel divide θ by N.

Assumptions and limits

  • Straight conduction only: the heat is assumed to reach every via evenly and to leave the far side freely. Spreading in the pads and planes, and the solder joint above, add resistance not counted here.
  • The FR-4 between vias is left out, which slightly overstates θ (Fineline: 2-3 K/W per via).
  • Solder fill assumes the hole is completely filled; voids and wicking during reflow are why many datasheets ask for filled or tented vias.
  • Copper at 384 W/m·K, Fineline's figure; plated copper can be a little lower.
  • Size and spacing follow AN-1520 (1.2 mm pitch, 0.33 mm) and Pierre's 13/10 mil rule; a fab's own minimum drill and annular ring come first.
  • The pad's vias and θJA: the vias' θ here keeps falling as 1/N, but AN-1520's whole-package θJA does not: from 16 to 36 vias it fell only about 1.2 °C/W, because the spreading in the board and the air beyond then dominate. The vias' θ is one link in that chain.

How it was checked

20 cases: - Fineline's via: 193 °C/W, air negligible, drill 0.3 mm (11.8 mil, fine for a smaller IC); - nine in parallel: 21.4 °C/W in the θ box, 42.9 °C across the board at 2 W; - the nine empty, solder-filled and copper-filled: 21.4, 16 and 6.55 °C/W; - solder in the hole: 572 °C/W beside the 193 °C/W sleeve, 32.1 °C at 2 W; - 0.3 mm holes are 163 °C/W each, so 17 reach 10 °C/W (9.6); - typing 10 °C/W in the θ box sets the vias to 20 (9.64 °C/W, 19.3 °C); - typing 4 vias sets the θ box to 48.2 °C/W; - a 0.8 mm board halves it, 96.4 °C/W; - mil turns every length to mil (1.6 mm reads 62.99 mil, 25 µm 0.9843 mil), and µm plating brings them back to mm; - a fraction of a via is refused; - the remembered fill; - AN-1520's fit: a 3 × 3 mm pad holds 3 × 3 = 9 vias, a 5 × 2.5 mm pad 4 × 2 = 8, in mil 118 × 118 mil at 47 mil; - AN-1520's 7 × 7 mm pad: 6 × 6 = 36 vias of 0.33 mm (13 mil, the size it recommends), 4.83 °C/W, with the past-16 note; - 4 vias on the 3 × 3 mm pad go near its edge, 12 are too many; - a 0.2 mm drill (7.87 mil) is flagged under 10 mil; - the pad's own picker turns every length to mil; - with the pad emptied the vias still compute.

Via impedance (R, L, C)

What it computes

The inductance, capacitance and resistance of a plated through via, and what they do to a signal. The drawing is a cross-section through the via: the board, the planes with their clearance holes, the plated barrel and its pads, to scale in height.

  • Inputs: the via's length T (the board's thickness), the drill, the pad and clearance diameters, the gap from the outer copper to the first plane, εr, a frequency and the distance to a return via, centre to centre. The Your inputs heading picks the copper layers and planes (“4 layers · 2 planes”: the two outer layers plus the planes), the outer copper (the pads, as finished after plating), the inner copper (the planes) and the plating thickness.
  • Big result: the via's impedance √(L / C), with a line saying how it looks on a 50 Ω line (under 50 Ω a small capacitor, over it a small inductor, within 2 % nearly invisible) and a badge saying the solver answered (Solving… for a moment after typing; Formula if the solver cannot run, Johnson's coaxial estimate then standing in for C).
  • Given: impedance (the Output heading's picker): an impedance replaces the clearance among the inputs, and the big result becomes the clearance diameter that gives it, with the drill, pad, board and planes as entered (the line under it repeats the impedance and how it looks on a 50 Ω line). Switching keeps the screen's state: going to impedance takes the current impedance to three figures, going back takes the found clearance. An impedance out of reach says so, with the most (or least) this drill and pad can give.
  • Cells: R (the plating's DC resistance), L (Grover's tube), C (the field solver) and the delay √(L C). Rows: the reactances of L and C at the frequency, the resistance there (with the skin effect), the loop inductance with a return via (two planes or more), how much the capacitance slows an edge on a 50 Ω line, the frequency up to which the lumped model holds, Johnson's coaxial estimate of C with its difference from the solver.
  • Units: one length unit for every length, the plating included: mm, mil or µm; MHz or GHz. Remembered: the planes, the outer and inner copper, the plating, what is given and the units.

Examples: Johnson's measured via, LaMeres's 18 mil blind via, a 1.6 mm 4-layer board, a 50 Ω via in 1.6 mm (the clearance found: 1.27 mm).

Terms

  • Plane: a solid copper layer the via passes through a clearance hole in: ground, power, or a pour around the via on an inner layer. Inner layers with traces only are not planes (the via has no pad there, as non-functional pads are usually removed); 2 planes is the usual 4-layer board, and a 6-layer board with two inner signal layers is still 2 planes. The planes are placed evenly between the two outer gaps.
  • Pad, clearance (antipad): the copper ring around the via on the outer layers; the hole cut in each plane around it.
  • Via impedance √(L / C): how the via looks to a line; under the line's impedance it acts as a small capacitor (the usual case), over it as a small inductor.
  • Loop inductance: the inductance of the whole path, the via and the return current's path; the via's own (partial) inductance is what Grover's formula gives.

Sources

  • B. C. Wadell, "Transmission Line Design Handbook" (Artech House, 1991; Pierre's scanned copy, the pages read as images): §5.9.1 (pp. 370–375), the via as a round wire or tube (Chapter 6) and Kasten's measured via; §6.2.1 (p. 380), Grover's round wire; §6.2.3 (p. 384–385), Grover's tube L = 0.002 l [ln(2l / ρ1) + ln ζ − 1] µH (l, ρ1 in cm) with the fit ln ζ = 0.25009128 − 0.0017049618 q − 0.51598981 q² + 0.37420782 q³ − 0.10669571 q⁴, q = ρ2 / ρ1, within 0.3 % of Grover's table.
  • Howard Johnson's newsletters (sigcon.com, read as text): vol. 6 issue 04 and 08, the loop inductance of a signal via between planes with a return via s away and his measured values (scale model, 4 layers): 0.46 to 1.41 nH, and 0.37 to 0.40 pF; the formula itself is an image there, but his predicted column is reproduced by L = (μ0 h / π) ln(s / r) to 0.01 nH; vol. 5 issue 09, his book's coaxial capacitance formula is "a crude approximation". The excerpt of "High-Speed Signal Propagation" (sigcon.com PDF, read as text): LaMeres's blind vias (capacitance and inductance against drill, pad and clearance), Teradyne's back-drilled vias, √(L / C) as the via's impedance, and "use a three-dimensional field solver".
  • J. E. Rayas-Sánchez, ITESO lecture "Interconnect models 3" (read as text): Johnson and Graham's C = 1.41 εr T D1 / (D2 − D1) pF (inches), as quoted from their book (not read here), and the lumped model's limit.
  • Z. Peterson, "Why Most Via Impedance Calculators Are Inaccurate" (Altium resources, read as text): a lumped L-C model holds only while the via is electrically short.
  • Not used: Goldfarb and Pucel's via-inductance formula (the lecture's copy did not survive text extraction, the paper is paywalled); Johnson and Graham's "+1" inductance formula (5.08 h [ln(4h/d) + 1] nH, as quoted), 2.4 times LaMeres's values.

Why the formulas are these

Inductance. Grover's tube, the barrel's own inductance, with the plating's inner radius. Against LaMeres's simulated vias it is −2 %, +8 % and +12 % for drills of 18, 12 and 8 mil (25 µm plating); his values include the return path through the clearance hole, which he enlarged with the drill, so they fall off more slowly than the barrel's own.

Capacitance by an axisymmetric field solver (js/fieldsolver.js, via): the via as a body of revolution in (r, z), the barrel and its outer pads at 1 V, the planes with their clearance holes at 0 V, the dielectric between the outer copper and air above and below, the box's outer faces mirrors. Laplace's equation by finite volumes (the radial weights carry 2πr, the axial ones the annuli), C = ε0 times the field's energy sum; two grids, the second twice as fine, extrapolated as h². Checks: inside a solid grounded wall the capacitance per length is within 0.00002 % of the exact 2π ε / ln(ra / rv); against three grids twice as fine within 0.2 %; LaMeres's 20 mil pads −1.6 %, −2.4 %, +2.7 %; Johnson's measured via −3.2 % (his conductor thickness read as 0.00062 in, ½ oz: the page prints 0.0062, ten times ½ oz). LaMeres's larger pads (30 and 40 mil) come out 15–29 % low: they imply a plane closer to the pads than the 18.9 mil the excerpt gives, so his setup is not fully known. Johnson's coaxial formula is shown for comparison: +60 % to +290 % against the same data.

The clearance for an impedance. L does not depend on the clearance, so the impedance wanted fixes the capacitance needed, C = L / Z². The clearance is found by solving for it: the unknown is u = ln(ra / rv) (ra the clearance's radius, rv the via's outer radius), the first guess the coaxial one (C ≈ 2π ε0 εr T / u), then secant steps on 1 / C, each step a full field solve, until the capacitance is within 0.002 % of the target (at most twelve steps). The clearance is kept between 1.02 times the via and the larger of ten pads or five board thicknesses; if the target lies beyond either end the tool says so, with the impedance at that end.

Loop inductance with a return via: Johnson's two parallel conductors across the cavity between the outermost planes, h from the first plane's lower face to the last plane's upper face. Resistance (derived): ρCu T / (π (ρ1² − ρ2²)) at DC; at a frequency, ρ T / (2π ρ1 δ) once the skin depth δ is under the plating. Edge (derived): a shunt C on a matched line sees Z0 / 2, a time constant C Z0 / 2, a 10–90 % time 2.2 times that. Lumped limit: a tenth of a wavelength in the board.

Assumptions and limits

  • Short vias only: the lumped model fails as the via nears a tenth of a wavelength; above that it resonates (stitching vias, stubs), a 3D solver's job.
  • Through vias with pads on the outer layers; no non-functional pads on inner layers, no outer-layer pour around the pad, planes evenly spaced between the outer gaps; traces and their own capacitance are not included.
  • One via, not a pair: a differential impedance (USB's 90 Ω, for example) is between the two vias of a pair; each via alone is roughly half of it (about 45 Ω for USB, a little more when the pair is tightly coupled). The coupling between the two vias is not modelled.
  • Display. Three figures.

How it was checked

58 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps and typing, the capacitance from tools/fd_lines.py (direct sparse solves of the same grids; the app's iterative solve, stopped once the residual is 10⁻⁵ of its start, agrees within 0.2 parts per million) and the clearance search repeated there step for step. The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; 1 to 8 planes; drills, pads, clearances, boards, εr, frequencies and return vias; copper and plating; mils and MHz, the unit linking with the plating; remembered choices; ten refusals; the given impedance (45 to 70 Ω, other drills, boards and εr, in mils, out of reach above and below, zero refused, the carry-over both ways, remembered); the four examples.
