Planar (PCB) inductor

What it computes

The inductance of a flat spiral of copper on a PCB (or a chip): four pills, Square, Hexagonal, Octagonal and Circular. The drawing shows the spiral to scale with the via at its inner end and the return on the other layer (dashed), the outer size, the trace, the gap and the inner diameter.

  • Given: turns (the Output heading's picker): the turns n, the outer size dout (flat to flat), the trace width w, the spacing s and the copper thickness; the big result is the inductance by Mohan's current-sheet expression. Given: inductance: the big result is the turns needed, with the inductance of the spiral as built.
  • Turns are built in whole sides (¼ turn for a square, ⅙ for a hexagon, ⅛ for an octagon); a round spiral takes any fraction.
  • Cells: the inner diameter, the fill ratio ρ and the DC resistance. Rows: the segment sum, the modified Wheeler and the monomial expressions, each with its difference from the big result; the trace length, the DC resistance at 20 °C and the average diameter; a note when the gap is over 3 trace widths (where the current-sheet expression can be 8 % off) or the spiral is nearly full or very hollow.
  • Units: one length unit for the whole tool, mm, mil or µm, picked on any size or thickness box (the thickness also takes ounces of copper, 1 oz = 1.37 mil); the inductance in nH or µH. A box changed to a new unit shows three figures. Switching what is given carries the coil over.
  • Remembered: the shape, what is given and the units.

Examples: two of Mohan's measured on-chip spirals, a 10 mm square on a PCB, 1 µH in 15 mm, a round 30 mm coil.

Terms

  • dout, din: the outer and inner sizes across the spiral (flat to flat for a polygon). din = dout − 2n w − 2(n − 1) s.
  • davg: the average diameter, (dout + din) / 2. Fill ratio ρ: (dout − din) / (dout + din): near 0 for a hollow coil, near 1 for a full one. A full coil has less inductance for its davg: its inner turns are small and their field partly opposes the outer ones.
  • Current-sheet expression: treats each side of the spiral as a sheet of current. Modified Wheeler: Wheeler's 1928 coil formula with new coefficients. Monomial: a power law fitted to 19 000 on-chip spirals. Segment sum: every straight piece of trace with its own inductance, plus the mutual inductance of every pair (positive when their currents run the same way, negative when opposite).
  • Via and return: the inner end has to come out on another layer; that piece is not in the formulas (it adds a little).

Sources

  • S. S. Mohan, M. del Mar Hershenson, S. P. Boyd and T. H. Lee, "Simple Accurate Expressions for Planar Spiral Inductances", IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits 34 (10), October 1999, pp. 1419–1424 (the Stanford copy). Its text was read, and its equations (1) to (3), Tables I to III (the coefficients) and Table IV (61 measured inductors, with the field solver ASITIC's error and each expression's error) on the rendered pages 2 to 4. Used: the three expressions and their coefficients, the definitions of din, davg and ρ, the 8 % limit of the current-sheet expression when s > 3w, and Table IV for the checks. Its Fig. 1 caption swaps the hexagon and the octagon (the drawing labelled hexagonal has eight sides).
  • A. Faria et al., "A Fast and Precise Tool for Multi-Layer Planar Coil Self-Inductance Calculation", Sensors 21 (2021) 4864 (the PubMed Central copy, read as text): at PCB sizes (traces of 0.10–0.15 mm) the current-sheet expression was 0.04–6.7 % from a finite-element model, the modified Wheeler up to 36 %, the monomial up to 11 %; the segment method, the coil as straight conductors with Grover's self-inductance of a rectangular bar 0.002 l (ln(2l / (w + t)) + 0.50049 + (w + t) / 3l) µH (l, w, t in cm) and the mutual inductances of every pair.
  • Not used: a review in MDPI's Bioengineering (the server answered "Access Denied"; left alone).

Why the formulas are these

The big result. Against ASITIC's values for Mohan's 61 inductors (Table IV), the current-sheet expression is 1.35 % off on average (4.8 % at worst), the segment sum here 1.45 % (6.1 %), the modified Wheeler 1.63 % (5.7 %), the monomial 2.53 % (9.5 %); at PCB sizes Faria found the current-sheet expression the steadiest of the three. So it is the big result, and the segment sum, which follows any geometry, is the independent check: when the two disagree by more than a few percent the coil is outside what the expressions were fitted to.

The segment sum (derived here from the sources' pieces). The spiral is built as Mohan draws it: each side lies on its own turn's polygon and the trace steps in once a turn (for a square this is the usual layout, sides d, d, d, d − p, d − p, d − 2p …); a round spiral is summed as the 16-sided polygon of the same area, and drawn round. The trace is three filaments across its width. Each filament piece has Grover's self-inductance (with a third of the width); every pair of pieces has the mutual inductance of two straight filaments, Neumann's double integral of cos(angle) / r, the inner integral in closed form (asinh) and the outer one by tanh-sinh quadrature for pieces closer than half a length, 8- or 4-point Gauss farther. Pieces more than 3 pitches and 8 trace widths apart are summed as their centrelines (the difference is of order (w / distance)², under 0.2 % in the checks). The total is divided by 9 (three equal currents). A spiral of more than 400 straight pieces is not summed (too slow on a phone).

Resistance: copper at 1.7241 µΩ·cm (IACS, as in Wire sizing) over the trace's centreline length, w wide and t thick, at DC.

Assumptions and limits

  • Air around the coil. Copper planes nearby lower the inductance; a ferrite sheet raises it. The board's dielectric does not change it.
  • One layer, no via or return piece in the formulas, DC (at high frequency the current crowds to the edges and the self-capacitance makes it resonate).
  • The monomial was fitted to on-chip spirals 100–480 µm across; its result at PCB sizes is shown for comparison only.
  • Display. Three figures; the differences to one decimal.

How it was checked

72 cases, the expected values from a Python implementation that replays each case's taps and typing. In every case the turns found for an inductance give it back to 1 part in 10⁹, the square spiral matches the Manhattan construction, and (for up to 32 pieces) the segment sum matches the same sum done with every filament pair everywhere and a quadrature twice as fine, to 0.2 %. Mohan's own error columns in Table IV are reproduced from the inputs within 0.61 points (his coefficients are printed to three figures). The cases: the opening screen and the pickers; the unit linking; eight geometries on each shape; three designs on each; micrometres, mils and ounces, nanohenries; the rounding of the turns; the 400-piece limit; the carry-over; nine refusals; the five examples and the formula-search card.

540 more cases (three batches of 180: random shapes, sizes from 100 µm to 50 mm, traces, gaps, copper and turns, a tenth of them refused) compared every figure with the Python implementation; they were run and not kept. Building them found that the quadrature for neighbouring filaments needed a finer step, and that the first way of summing distant pieces was too slow for a phone.

Published answers reproduced (Mohan's Table IV, measured):

Inductor Measured ASITIC Tool (current sheet) Segment sum
#7, square, 9.5 turns, 153 µm, w 1.8 µm, s 1.9 µm 18.2 nH 17.7 nH 17.8 nH 17.6 nH
#56, octagon, 5 turns, 346 µm, w 18 µm, s 2 µm 7.50 nH 7.30 nH 7.45 nH 7.26 nH

Decoupling capacitor

What it computes

The target-impedance method for a supply's decoupling, with mixed values, on one screen:

  • Inputs: the supply voltage, the ripple allowed (%), the current step, the regulator's response time and the fastest current edge; then up to three kinds of capacitor, each a row of C (µF), ESR (mΩ), ESL (nH) and how many, added with "+ add" (a decade larger than the largest) and removed with ×. Boards mix values (Pierre), so the tool does.
  • The big result: the target impedance, the ripple allowed over the current step.
  • Below it:
  • the band where all the capacitors together stay under the target, around their lowest point;
  • with more than one kind, the highest anti-resonance peak between the first and last resonances, flagged when over the target;
  • each kind's resonant frequency;
  • the total capacitance against the bulk the regulator's delay needs;
  • the total ESL (all in parallel) against the most inductance the fastest edge allows.
  • Drawing: the impedance of all the capacitors together from 1 kHz to 10 GHz, log-log, each kind alone faint behind it, the target dashed.
  • Units: as engineers quote them: V, %, µs, ns, µF, mΩ, nH; the current step in mA or A, its picker remembered.

Choosing the capacitors, after AVX: a bulk capacitance for the low frequencies (the bulk row), a value that resonates where coverage is needed with enough in parallel that their ESRs reach the target, and low ESL for the fast edges (the inductance row); then the curve must stay under the line with no peak above it.

The rows start as a suggestion and follow the supply's figures (Pierre changed the ripple from 5 % to 1 % and expected the capacitors to change): the heading says "suggested". Editing a row, adding or removing a kind makes them "yours", and they stay; Suggest gives them back. The suggestion follows those rules: the smallest of 1, 2.2, 4.7, 10, 22, 47, 100 µF that covers the bulk (several 100 µF past that); 100 nF parts, as many as ESR / Ztarget; and, only when the total ESL is still over the edge's limit, enough 0612 LICC parts (0.1 µF, 550 pH, AVX's figure 7) to bring it under. ESR is the illustrative 10 mΩ and ESL a 1206's 1.25 nH until replaced. The rules do not promise a flat curve: a peak can remain between the bulk part and the 100 nF, and the tool flags it; an in-between value fills it.

Examples: AVX's 20 A step at 1.8 V, a small MCU at 3.3 V, 10 µF + 100 nF + 1 nF, and an FPGA core at 1 V.

Source

  • Yun Chase, Kyocera AVX, "Introduction to Choosing MLC Capacitors for Bypass/Decoupling Applications" (read; no date printed):
  • |Z| = √(ESR² + (ωESL − 1/ωC)²) (eq. 4), resonance at 1 / (2π √(ESL·C)) (eq. 8), where the impedance is the ESR;
  • "Ztarget = Allowed Ripple Voltage / I" (eq. 13), ripple a small percentage of the supply, "i.e. 5%";
  • bulk: C = I dt / dV (eq. 14); "a 20 amp current transient, the VRM responds in 15 µSec, and the PDS must remain within 5% of a 1.8V power supply": 3333 µF (eq. 15);
  • inductance: L = V dt / dI (eq. 16); the same with a 1 ns rise: 4.5 pH (eq. 17);
  • n identical capacitors in parallel: nC, ESL/n, ESR/n, the resonance unchanged (eq. 18 to 22);
  • "a capacitance value is chosen so that when mounted on the PCB, it will resonate at the desired frequency"; different values in parallel "produce an unwanted anti-resonance";
  • measured ESL: 1206 about 1250 pH, 0612 LICC about 550 pH, 0612 IDC about 175 pH, 0508 IDC about 110 pH.
  • ROHM, "Impedance Characteristics of Bypass Capacitor", application note 63AN091E rev. 001 (read): use a capacitor below its self-resonance; low ESL for high frequencies; capacitors of very different self-resonance in parallel can make an anti-resonance.

Why the formulas are these

Ztarget = ΔV / ΔI,   ΔV = V × ripple
C bulk = ΔI × t regulator / ΔV
L max = ΔV × t edge / ΔI
Z kind = (ESR + jωESL + 1/(jωC)) / n,   Y = Σ 1 / Z kind,   |Z| = 1 / |Y|

The supply may sag by ΔV when the load steps by ΔI, so its impedance must stay under ΔV / ΔI at every frequency in the step. Until the regulator catches up, capacitors carry the step; their charge sets the bulk. During the fastest edge, inductance limits how fast current can come out of them. Each capacitor is lowest at its resonance; in parallel their complex admittances add, so between one kind's resonance (already inductive) and the next (still capacitive) the two can resonate together: the anti-resonance peak.

Assumptions and limits

  • The ESR in the rows is illustrative (10 mΩ by default); neither paper gives one. Type your parts' from their datasheets.
  • ESL is the capacitor's own; the pads and vias add more (AVX: "this is a mounted inductance").
  • The board's planes are not modelled; they matter above about 1 GHz (AVX figure 5).
  • MLCC capacitance falls with DC bias and temperature; type the capacitance at your voltage.

How it was checked

15 cases: - the rows start as the suggestion; 1 % ripple instead of 5 % moves the bulk part from 1 µF to 4.7 µF; an edited row stays when the ripple changes; - AVX's example: 4.5 mΩ, 3333 µF, 4.5 pH; three 100 nF (417 pH) far over; - Suggest: for the MCU, 1 µF and one 100 nF (89.1 kHz to 414 MHz); for AVX's 20 A, 34 × 100 µF, 3 × 100 nF and 106 low-ESL parts (4.5 pH); for the FPGA core, a 93.9 mΩ peak left at 4.14 MHz, flagged; - those three get under 4.5 mΩ only around 14.2 MHz (14.1 to 14.7 MHz); - a small MCU: 1.65 Ω from 962 kHz to 207 MHz, 606 nF of bulk needed; - 10 µF + 2 × 100 nF + 2 × 1 nF: 48.2 kHz to 85.8 MHz, a 4.36 Ω anti-resonance at 136 MHz; - an FPGA core: 50 mΩ, 175 pH over 50 pH; - "+ add" puts 10 µF beside 1 µF: the band widens, its peak stays under; - × removes a kind; - a zero current step is refused; - the current step in mA: 0.1 A reads 100.

PCB & interconnect › Cabling

Wire sizing

(formerly Wire gauge (AWG/SWG); Cable resistance / voltage drop and the planned Cable current capacity are merged into it)

What it computes

One copper wire on one run, on one screen:

  • Its size on every scale: an AWG gauge, an SWG gauge and a size in mm² or mm are linked boxes, and setting any one updates the others. A gauge picked by hand is exact; the others show their nearest gauge, the one on the other side and how much more or less copper each has. The line under Output gives the diameter, the cross-section, the circular mils and the resistance per metre (or foot) at 20 °C.
  • Its voltage drop over the run, large: in volts, as a share of the supply, the power turned to heat in the wire, and the temperature the wire runs at.
  • Its current limit, large: the most current it can carry before it reaches its insulation's rating, alone in free air or in a bundle, and how much of that the current uses.
  • The smallest wire that passes both, on the scale in use, and which check decided it.

The inputs are the gauge, the insulation's temperature rating (60 to 260 °C), the number of wires in the bundle, the one-way length, the current, the supply, the largest drop allowed and the ambient temperature. The mm²/mm, m/ft and mA/A choices and the insulation rating are remembered.

Examples: a 12 V LED strip 5 m away (the drop decides), 5 V at 3 A over 1 m, a short 20 A motor lead (the current decides), a harness of 12 wires, 200 °C silicone wire for a drone, and 1.5 mm² cable.

Sources

NBS Handbook 100, Copper Wire Tables (US National Bureau of Standards, 1966), public domain, read in review:

  • AWG: "the diameter of No. 0000 is defined as 0.4600 inch and of No. 36 as 0.0050 inch", with 38 sizes between in geometric progression.
  • SWG: table 15, every size from 7/0 (500 mils) to 50 (1 mil), held here in mils and converted exactly.
  • Copper: the International Annealed Copper Standard is "1/58 = 0.017241 … ohm square millimetre per metre" at 20 °C, and the best temperature coefficient to assume for commercial annealed copper wire is α20 = 0.003 93 per °C (the IEC values of 1913).

FAA AC 43.13-1B, Change 1 (2001), chapter 11, section 5, "Electrical wire rating", public domain, read in review:

  • Figures 11-4a and 11-4b, "Single copper wire in free air": current against the temperature difference "wire rating minus the ambient", one straight line per size on log-log paper, sizes 26 to 4/0.
  • Figure 11-5, "Bundle derating curves": the factor on each wire's free-air current, for 1 to 41 wires, by the share of the bundle's capacity in use (20 to 100 %).
  • Paragraph 11-66d(6): the wire's temperature, T2 = T1 + (TR − T1)(I2 / Imax)², and (4) the copper resistance correction (234.5 °C + T).
  • Table 11-9: in-harness ratings at 70 °C, 33 wires, 20 % load and 60,000 ft, used here only as a cross-check.

MIL-W-5088L (1991, inactive; superseded by SAE AS50881), the military wiring specification the FAA charts come from, read in review: figure 3 is the same free-air chart (its large-size half was read from here, its scan being cleaner), figure 4 the bundle curves; 3.8.8.1.1 states that table I was derived from these figures, and 3.8.8.1.2 that connector contacts, relays, breakers and switches carry their own, often lower, ratings.

How the charts were read

The figures are scanned images, so each line was traced off the scan and located against the chart's own labelled gridlines, tracked across the page so a skewed or unevenly stretched scan does not shift the values. Each wire line is straight on the log-log paper, so it is kept as its two ends, the current at a 30 °C and at a 240 °C margin; the stored pairs match the traced lines within 0.2 %. For the bundle, the lowest curve (100 % loading) was traced and smoothed, moving no point by more than 0.8 %.

Checked against every figure the documents quote: 22 AWG at a 140 °C margin reads 16.2 A (FAA and MIL: 16.2), 20 AWG 21.4 (21.5), 12 AWG at 175 °C 67.3 (68) and at 140 °C 60.5 (61), 14 AWG at 150 °C 46.9 (47); the bundle factor for 12 wires at full load reads 0.425 (0.43). MIL-W-5088L's table I, built from free air × bundle × altitude, implies the same bundle factor for all nine sizes from 8 AWG to 4/0 to within 1 %, which checks the large sizes.

Why the formulas are these

AWG:  d(mm) = 0.127 × 92^((36 − n) / 39)
R20 = 2L × (1/58 Ω·mm²/m) / A
R   = R20 × (1 + 0.00393 (T − 20 °C))
Drop = I × R        Loss = I² × R
Limit = free-air current at (Tr − Ta) × bundle factor
T = Ta + (Tr − Ta) × (I / Limit)²
  • 2L: the current goes out on one wire and back on the other, so the run's resistance counts twice its one-way length.
  • 1/58 Ω·mm²/m: the standard copper of wire tables. The textbook figure for pure copper, 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m, which the old cable tool used, is 2.6 % lower than the wire you buy, so it under-stated every drop.
  • The limit is the current that heats the wire to its insulation's rating Tr when the air is at Ta: the chart is read at that margin. A size between two chart sizes (an odd AWG, an SWG, a metric size) is read between them, by cross-section on a log scale.
  • The temperature: heating grows as the square of the current, reaching Tr at the limit; copper's resistance rises with it, so the drop is worked out at the temperature the wire really runs at. The FAA calls the estimate "quite conservative": it errs warm.
  • Smallest wire: a thicker wire passes whatever a thinner one passes, so the answer is the thicker of the thinnest passing the drop and the thinnest passing the current.

Assumptions and limits

  • Copper only. The charts are for copper, and electronics wire is copper; aluminium was dropped in the merge.
  • 26 AWG to 4/0 (0.129 to 107 mm²). Outside, no current limit is shown, and the smallest-wire search stops at 26 AWG, saying so, with the size the drop alone would allow.
  • A 30 to 245 °C margin, where the chart's lines run; outside it the line is extended, and the screen says so.
  • Every wire in the bundle carries current (the 100 % curve, the lowest). If only some do, the chart allows more; count every wire in the bundle, loaded or not, for a safe figure. Past 41 wires, the chart's last factor.
  • Free air at sea level. Wire in conduit, against a hot surface, or at altitude (the FAA's figure 11-6: 0.91 at 20,000 ft) carries less.
  • Aircraft wire. The charts were drawn for MIL wire with thin PTFE or polyimide insulation; PVC hookup wire's thicker insulation changes the figures somewhat. Treat the limit as an engineering estimate, not a rating.
  • The wire, not its ends. Connectors, terminals, switches and fuses usually limit the current first.
  • Solid round wire sizes. A stranded conductor is sized by its copper's total cross-section.

How it was checked

18 AWG with 3 A over 5 m at 12 V: 644 mV, 5.37 %, wire at 26 °C, limit 18.6 A in 25 °C air with 80 °C insulation, smallest AWG 15 by the 3 % drop. The chart values above; 12 bundled wires ×0.425; 30 AWG has no limit; a 100 mA load stops at 26 AWG (drop alone: 30 AWG); an ambient at the rating gives no safe current; a 20 °C margin and 50 wires are flagged. Sizes: SWG 2/0 is 8.839 mm and 121,104 CM, nearest AWG 2/0; 4/0 AWG is 11.68 mm and 211,600 CM; 1.5 mm² sits at AWG 15.41; a 1 mm diameter is AWG 18 and SWG 19.

The review made these changes: - Wire gauge, Cable resistance / voltage drop and the planned Cable current capacity became one tool, on Pierre's choice, named Wire sizing. - The current limit is new, from the FAA and MIL charts; the wire's temperature now sets its resistance. - Copper's resistivity is the IACS 1/58 Ω·mm²/m, not 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m. - Lengths can be in feet; aluminium was dropped. - It added six run examples, 17 cases and this section.

Wire & cable colors

What it shows

A searchable list of what each wire colour means, grouped by system:

  • IEC / HD 308 (international, EU): low-voltage AC, single- and three-phase.
  • NEC (US): single-phase 120/240 V, and three-phase by voltage system: 120/208 V wye, 277/480 V wye and 120/240 V high-leg delta.
  • Canada (CSA C22.1).
  • DC: positive, negative, a grounded conductor, and −48 V telecom.
  • DIN 47100: how the cores of a multi-core cable are numbered by colour, cores 1 to 60.

Each row says whether a colour is required by the code or only a convention. Filter chips jump to one group (remembered); the search box matches a colour, a function or a standard.

Sources, and what was actually read

  • DIN 47100 and HD 308: Lapp's selection table T9 (appendix of its catalogue), read in review. Its harmonised-core table for VDE 0293-308 / HD 308 S2 gives the cores of a multi-core power cable as GNYE/BN/BU, GNYE/BN/BK/GY and GNYE/BU/BN/BK/GY: green-and-yellow earth, brown, black and grey lines, blue neutral. Its DIN 47100 table lists cores 1 to 60. All 44 of the standard's colours match the tool's. Lapp notes that its 45 to 60 are "in contrast to DIN: without colour repetition after the 44th core": DIN 47100 itself (January 1988, withdrawn 1998 but still widely used) starts again at 1 from core 45. The tool now says that 45 to 60 are a makers' extension.
  • IEC 60445: the standard itself could not be read; only the contents pages of its previews were available. Per a reader quoting BS EN IEC 60445:2021 on the IET's Engineering Exchange, clause 6.2.3 lists BLACK, BROWN and GREY for AC line conductors in alphabetical order, and this "does not indicate any preferred phasing". The order L1 brown, L2 black, L3 grey comes from HD 308 S2 (and BS 7671's table 51), so the tool now attributes it there.
  • NEC (NFPA 70): the code text could not be read. The rows rest on the sections as trade sources quote them: 200.6 (a grounded conductor is white or grey, or three white stripes), 250.119 (an equipment grounding conductor is green, green with yellow stripes, or bare), 110.15 (the high leg is "durably and permanently marked by an outer finish that is orange in color" or by other effective means), and Southwire's technical note that white and green may not be used on ungrounded conductors.
  • CSA C22.1: the code could not be read. Rule 4-038, "Identification of insulated conductors", is named in Electrical Industry News' guide to the code; the colours (red, black, blue phases; white or grey neutral) are as a forum post quotes the rule.

Assumptions and limits

  • Not a substitute for the code in force. Local amendments differ: San Francisco, for one, asks for purple on the high leg. Old installations use older colours (the UK's red, yellow and blue before 2004).
  • Always test. A colour says what a wire should be, not what it is.
  • DC is mostly convention. IEC 60445 has had colours for DC line conductors since 2017, but they could not be read, so they are not listed.

How it was checked

7 cases: the list opens on IEC/HD 308 with L1 brown; the US hot's note; the DC filter; the high leg's NEC 110.15 note; DIN core 45 as an extension; a search with no match; the remembered filter.

The review made these changes: - The NEC rows had said "required by NEC" for things the code does not require. A white-only neutral, a grey 277/480 V neutral and an orange-only high leg were all marked as required. They now give what the code allows and say where a colour is convention. - The IEC phase order is attributed to HD 308, not to IEC 60445. - DIN 47100's cores 45 to 60 are labelled a makers' extension. - A DC filter chip (DC rows had no filter), the remembered filter, a new subtitle, the first cases and this section.

PCB & interconnect › Electrical safety

IP ratings

What it shows

The meaning of an IEC 60529 ingress protection code, both ways. You can type a code (IP67, IPX4, IP20C, IP54W), or build one with four pickers:

  • the first digit, solids;
  • the second digit, water;
  • the optional additional letter;
  • the optional supplementary letter.

The code shows large, with a two-part summary. Each part's meaning follows, water with its test conditions. Notes flag the cases people get wrong.

Examples: IP20 terminal blocks, an IP65 outdoor box, IP67 against IP66, an IP68 phone, an IP54 enclosure, and IP69K washdown.

The code

IP 6 5 C S
   │ │ │ └ supplementary letter, optional: H, M, S or W
   │ │ └── additional letter, optional: A, B, C or D
   │ └──── water, 0–9
   └────── people and solid objects, 0–6
  • First digit: two meanings at once. One is how well people are kept from hazardous parts: the back of a hand at 1, a finger at 2, a tool at 3, a wire at 4 and above. The other is how small an object stays out: 50, 12.5, 2.5 and 1 mm, then dust protected at 5 and dust-tight at 6.
  • Second digit: water, from vertical drips (1) to powerful jets (6). Then come immersion up to 1 m (7), immersion beyond that on the maker's terms (8), and close-range hot high-pressure jets (9).
  • X in either place means not tested, which is not the same as 0.
  • Additional letter: people are kept from hazardous parts better than the first digit says. It is used when the first digit is low or X.
  • Supplementary letter:
  • H: high-voltage equipment;
  • M: water-tested with moving parts running;
  • S: water-tested with them at rest;
  • W: for stated weather conditions.

Sources, and what was actually read

IEC 60529:1989 + A1:1999 + A2:2013, consolidated edition 2.2. Its preview (VDE Verlag) was read in review, but it stops after the definitions. It confirms the structure:

  • separate tables for people and for objects under the first digit;
  • the additional letter (table 4) and the supplementary letters (clause 8);
  • test 14.2.7, temporary immersion between 0.15 and 1 m;
  • test 14.2.9 for second digit 9 with a spray nozzle, and its IPX9 test device. Digit 9 is IEC's own since amendment 2.

The tables themselves could not be read. The wording and test figures follow Wikipedia's IP code article, which reproduces them from the standard:

  • 1 mm of rain a minute for 1;
  • 3 mm a minute, 2.5 minutes each way for 2;
  • 10 L a minute for 3;
  • a 6.3 mm nozzle at 12.5 L a minute for 5;
  • a 12.5 mm nozzle at 100 L a minute for 6;
  • 30 minutes at 1 m for 7;
  • 80 °C water at 8–10 MPa and 14–16 L a minute for 9.

The same article is the source for the point that water ratings are "not cumulative beyond IPX6" and are dual-coded, as in IPX5/IPX7. NEMA's complimentary copy of ANSI/IEC 60529 now redirects to a store, and two other manufacturer guides could not be fetched.

Assumptions and limits

  • K codes are not IEC. IP69K and IP6K9K come from ISO 20653 (formerly DIN 40050-9), for road vehicles. The tool reads them and says so, rather than putting K on IEC's scale.
  • One supplementary letter. The standard allows several, in alphabetical order; codes with more than one are rare.
  • A rating is for the enclosure as tested. Cable glands, seals and covers must be fitted as the maker says, and ageing seals lose it.
  • Not NEMA types. The US NEMA 250 enclosure types (1, 3R, 4X…) test more than IP (corrosion, icing) and don't map one-to-one.

How it was checked

9 cases: - IP65 by default, with its jet test; - typing ipx7 sets X and 7, with the warning that immersion excludes jets; - IP69K explained as ISO 20653; - digit 9 as IEC's hot jet test; - IP20C's additional letter; - IP40A's letter adds nothing; - W from its picker; - a malformed code; - the IP20 example.

The review made these changes: - A code box: type the code instead of picking its digits. It also reads the K codes, so they can be explained. - The additional and supplementary letters, which the tool lacked. - Test conditions in each water description. - The warning that 7 and 8 don't include 5 and 6. - The first digit's two meanings, people and objects. - "Heavy seas" dropped from 6: it is the old wording, not the current standard's. - Six examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Calculators

Calculator

(formerly Standard & Scientific Calculators)

What it does

A calculator with three keypads, chosen by pills (the choice is remembered):

  • Standard: the iPhone Calculator's own keys, ⌫ C % ÷ … ± 0 . =.
  • Scientific: ( ) x² xʸ eˣ 10ˣ 1/x √ ln log sin cos tan e π and DEG/RAD (remembered), above the standard keys.
  • Electronics: ( ), ∥ for parts in parallel, EE for a power of ten, and the prefixes p n µ m k M G, plus 1/x.

Keys build an expression, worked out on =. A result away from 1 to 1000 is also shown in engineering notation under the display: 0.001 reads "= 1 m", 1591.549431 reads "= 1.59155 k". A computer keyboard works too: digits, + − * / ^, | for ∥, E, and p n u m k M G for the prefixes.

Examples: 1k ∥ 2.2k, an RC time constant, a capacitor's reactance, a gain in decibels, the power in a resistor.

How an expression is read

  • Precedence, loosest first: + and −; then ×, ÷ and ∥ (and implicit multiplication, "2π" or "2(3+4)"); then a leading minus; then ^, from the right. So 6 + 3 × 2 is 12, 1k ∥ 2.2k + 100 is 787.5, and −2² is −4.
  • ∥ is a × b / (a + b): two resistors in parallel, or two capacitors in series.
  • A prefix straight after a number scales it: 4.7k is 4700, 100n is 1E-7, and u is accepted for µ. Capital M is mega, small m milli.
  • E after a number is a power of ten (1E-3). Lower-case e stays Euler's number, so a result like 1E-18 reads back as a number.
  • % works as on a phone: after + or −, it is a percentage of what comes before (50 + 10 % is 55); after × or ÷, or alone, the number over 100.
  • ± changes the number being typed, not the whole expression.
  • Degrees are reduced to a turn before sin, cos and tan, so the exact angles come out exact: sin 180° is 0, and tan 90° has no value (Error).

Assumptions and limits

  • Ten significant figures are shown. Past 1E12 and below 1E-9 a result is written with E.
  • Engineering notation stops at f and P: smaller or larger results get no second line.
  • Floating point: results carry the usual rounding of double-precision arithmetic past about 15 digits.

How it was checked

12 cases: 6 + 3 × 2, −2², sin 180°, tan 90°, 50 + 10 %, 5 − (−3) by ±, the ∥, RC and reactance examples (with their engineering lines), 1E3, 1n × 1n read back and multiplied by 1E18, and the remembered keypad.

The review made these changes: - Renamed Calculator. The title had wrapped. - The Electronics keypad, prefixes typed after numbers, the EE power of ten, ∥, and the engineering line, on Pierre's choice. - −2² had been 4, because the minus bound tighter than ^. - sin 180° had read 1.22E-16 and tan 90° a huge number. - % had divided the whole expression by 100: 50 + 10 % gave 0.6. - ± had negated the whole expression. - A result in E notation had used a small e, which read back as Euler's number. - At 375×812 the Scientific keypad ran 54 px under the tab bar. With a second keypad shown, keys and display are now tighter. - Remembering: the keypad and DEG/RAD are now remembered. - First cases, examples and this section.

Ohm's law

What it computes

Any two of voltage (V), current (I), resistance (R) and power (P) give the other two. These are the six pairs of the Ohm's-law wheel: V·I, V·R, I·R, P·V, P·I and P·R. A schematic marks each quantity where it is: V across the source, I along the wire, R and P on the resistor. Inputs are drawn blue, results green.

  • A resistance you enter has a tolerance (picked beside "Your inputs"). Its E-series slider steps through standard values, and the results show their spread at that tolerance.
  • A resistance worked out shows the nearest standard part instead.
  • Remembered: the pair, the tolerance and each quantity's unit.

Examples: 330 Ω on 3.3 V, a 0.1 Ω current shunt at 2 A, the limits of a ¼ W 1 kΩ resistor, 60 W at 120 V, and a resistance found from a measured voltage and current.

Why the formulas are these

V = I × R        I = V / R        R = V / I
P = V × I = I² × R = V² / R
I = √(P / R)     V = √(P × R)

Ohm's law, V = I × R, ties the first three. Power is the rate the resistor turns energy into heat, V × I. Putting one into the other gives the rest.

Tolerance: the result moves with R as its own power of R:

Pair Result goes as So at ±t
V·R I and P go as 1/R between V/(R(1 + t)) and V/(R(1 − t))
I·R V and P go as R ±t
P·R I goes as 1/√R, V as √R about ±t/2

Assumptions and limits

  • A resistor obeys Ohm's law only at a fixed temperature. A lamp filament's cold resistance is many times lower than the V²/P "working" value, and diodes and LEDs don't follow V = I × R at all.
  • DC, or AC in RMS values with a purely resistive load. With reactance, use impedance instead.
  • A spread is the tolerance alone. A resistor's temperature coefficient adds to it.

How it was checked

9 cases: - 12 V and 12 mA: 1 kΩ and 144 mW; - 330 Ω on 3.3 V: 10 mA, between 9.901 and 10.1 mA at ±1 %; - ¼ W in 1 kΩ: 15.81 V or 15.81 mA; - 60 W at 120 V: 500 mA and 240 Ω, nearest E96 237 Ω; - 4.98 V and 2.2 mA: 2.264 kΩ, nearest 2.26 kΩ; - P·I, 1 W at 100 mA: 10 V and 100 Ω; - 12 V shown in mV reads 12000; - a blank field; - the remembered pair, tolerance and unit.

The review made these changes: - Units: changing one kept the number and changed its meaning (12 V became 12 mV). Values are now held in SI, and the picker only re-expresses them. - Power as an input: the P·V, P·I and P·R pairs are new, with the tolerance spread through P·R. - Results pick their own unit: 144 mW, not 0.144 W. Large values had read like 1.20e+3. - A missing input says what is missing. - Remembering: the pair, tolerance and units are remembered. - Formula search had no Ohm's law card; it has one now. - Examples, the first cases and this section.

AC Ohm's law

(formerly AC Ohm's law (impedance form))

What it computes

Ohm's law for alternating current, V = I × Z, for a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in series or in parallel, by pill.

  • Inputs: R, L and C with their units, the frequency, and the source, given as a voltage or as a current (rms). A part at 0, or left empty, is not fitted: a plain wire in series, an open branch in parallel. So the same screen covers R-L, R-C, L-C or a single part.
  • Output, large:
  • the impedance |Z|, with its phase angle and whether the circuit is inductive, capacitive or resistive;
  • the current (or the voltage, when the current was given), with its phase against the source and whether it leads or lags.
  • Below:
  • Z in rectangular form, R + jX;
  • the reactances XL and XC;
  • the power factor, leading or lagging;
  • true power P, reactive power Q and apparent power S;
  • the voltage across each part in series, or the current through each branch in parallel;
  • the resonant frequency f₀ when both L and C are fitted.
  • Drawing: the source with the parts round the loop or in branches, a part not fitted shown as a wire or left out.
  • Remembered: the pill, whether a voltage or a current is given, and every unit.

Examples: Kuphaldt's series and parallel R, L and C, the power factor of an R-L load, series resonance, and a capacitor alone.

Source

Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Volume II, AC, 6th edition (2021), the free textbook (ibiblio.org/kuphaldt), read in review: - Reactance: XL = 2πfL and XC = 1/(2πfC). An inductive reactance is a positive imaginary impedance (+90°), a capacitive one negative (−90°). - Combining: series impedances add, Ztotal = ZR + ZL + ZC; parallel ones add as reciprocals, Ztotal = 1/(1/ZR + 1/ZL + 1/ZC). - Power, chapter 11: - true power P in watts; - reactive power Q in "Volt-Amps-Reactive (VAR)"; - apparent power S in volt-amps (VA); - P, Q and S form the power triangle, whose angle is the impedance's phase angle; - the power factor is P / S, "equal to the cosine of that phase angle". - Its examples, the tool's cases: - series: 250 Ω, 650 mH and 1.5 µF at 120 V, 60 Hz give 250 − j1.5233 kΩ, 1.5437 kΩ ∠ −80.680°, and 77.734 mA; - parallel: the same parts draw 480, 489.71 and 67.858 mA by branch, 639 mA in all at −41.31°; - power: 60 Ω with 160 mH on 120 V, 60 Hz give 119.365 W, 119.998 VAR and 169.256 VA, a power factor of 0.705.

Why the formulas are these

XL = 2πfL,  XC = 1 / (2πfC)
series:   Z = R + j(XL − XC)
parallel: 1/Z = 1/R − j/XL + j/XC
|Z| = √(R² + X²),  φ = atan(X / R),  I = V / Z
S = V × I,  P = S cos φ,  Q = S sin φ,  PF = P / S = cos φ
f₀ = 1 / (2π √(LC))

An inductor's opposition grows with frequency and a capacitor's shrinks, and they shift the current in opposite directions, so in a circuit they partly cancel. When XL = XC, at f₀, they cancel entirely. A series circuit is then only its R, and the voltage across L and across C can be many times the source's. A parallel L and C then draw no current between them from the source. A positive angle is inductive: the current lags the voltage, and the power factor is lagging. A negative one is capacitive and leading.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal parts: an inductor with no resistance of its own, a capacitor with no loss, as in the book's examples. A real coil's resistance can be typed into R in series.
  • Sine waves only, at the one frequency. Distorted waveforms carry harmonics that see other reactances.
  • Values are rms, the source taken as the 0° reference.
  • At exact resonance with no R, a series L-C is a short and a parallel one an open circuit; the tool says so instead of dividing by zero.

How it was checked

10 cases: - the book's series circuit: 1.544 kΩ at −80.68°, 77.73 mA, 250 − j1.523 kΩ; - the book's parallel circuit: 639 mA at −41.31°, branches 480, 489.7 and 67.86 mA; - the book's R-L load: power factor 0.705 lagging, 119.4 W, 120 VAR, 169.3 VA; - series resonance: 1 Ω, 0°, 10 V across L and across C, f₀ 159.2 kHz; - a capacitor alone: −90°, no true power; - given 1 A, the series circuit needs 1.544 kV; - R and L alone (C at 0): 350.1 Ω at +44.43°; - a unit change keeps the value; - nothing fitted is refused; - the remembered choices.

Kirchhoff's laws

What it computes

The one missing term that balances a node or a loop. Enter two to five known terms, each with a sign and a unit, and the tool gives the term that brings the signed sum to zero, with what it means.

  • KCL (current): + is a current flowing into the node, − one flowing out. The diagram draws each term as an arrow into or out of the node.
  • KVL (voltage): + is a rise, crossing a source from − to +, and − a drop, across a resistor in the direction of the current. The diagram is a real loop walked clockwise: each rise is a battery, met minus first; each drop is a resistor. They read in walking order, along the top and back along the bottom.

Known terms are drawn in the input blue and the missing one dashed in the result green. Each term is held in A or V, and its unit picker only changes how it is shown. The law chosen is remembered.

Examples: a node with three branches, a supply current split in mixed units, a 9 V battery with an LED and its resistor, two sources and two drops in one loop.

Why the formula is this

KCL:  ΣI = 0 at a node      (Σ in = Σ out)
KVL:  ΣV = 0 around a loop  (Σ rises = Σ drops)

Charge can't build up at a node, so what flows in flows out. Walking a loop back to where it started returns to the same voltage, so the rises and the drops cancel. Either way the missing term is minus the sum of the others.

Assumptions and limits

  • Lumped circuits: the laws hold where wires are short against the wavelength and no changing magnetic field threads the loop. At RF, or around a transformer's core, a "loop voltage" is induced.
  • Signs are yours: the tool can't see the circuit, so a wrong sign on one term gives a wrong answer with no warning.
  • Two to five known terms, plus the one solved for.

How it was checked

10 cases: - 2 A in and 1.2 A out leave 800 mA flowing out; - the three-branch node gives 1.5 A out; - mixed units give 30.5 mA; - 9 V minus a 2 V LED leaves 7 V for the resistor; - two rises and two drops leave 4.7 V; - a unit change keeps the value; - a flipped sign; - a blank term; - balanced terms give zero; - the remembered law.

The review made these changes: - Units: changing one kept the number and changed its meaning. Terms are now held in SI. - The KVL diagram had been ticks on a bare rectangle. It is now a real loop of batteries and resistors, with the walking direction. - Colours: the diagram had given each term its own colour, red among them. Known terms are now blue and the missing one green, as on every screen. Labels went from 10 px to 11 px. - Text: the detail line says when the known terms already balance, and what a rise or drop is like. - The rest: the remembered law, examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Calculators

SI prefix converter

(Scientific ↔ engineering notation was merged into it)

What it does

It writes one value in every SI prefix:

  • The input: a value typed as it is marked, 4700p, 0.1u, 2.2M, 32.768k or 1.5E-3, with u accepted for µ, and a unit picker (none, Ω, F, H, V, A, W, Hz, s).
  • The output: the value large in its best prefix, the one leaving 1 to 999 in front (4700 pF is 4.7 nF), and its plain value without a prefix.
  • Notation: the same value in scientific notation (one digit before the point, 4.7 × 10⁴), engineering notation (an exponent in steps of 3, the one a prefix names: 47 × 10³), and E notation as calculators, spreadsheets and code read it (4.7E4).
  • The grid: the value in each prefix. By default it shows the steps of 1000 from femto to tera, the ones electronics uses. The All 24 pill adds the rest, from quecto to quetta.

Values past a million or under a thousandth are written as × 10ⁿ. The unit and the grid choice are remembered.

Examples: 4700 pF, 0.1 µF decoupling, 2.2 MΩ, a 32.768 kHz crystal and a crystal's 3.4 fF motional capacitance.

Source

BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, as updated in 2022, read in review:

  • Table 7 lists the 24 prefixes, 10³⁰ quetta (Q) to 10⁻³⁰ quecto (q).
  • The 27th CGPM (2022) added ronna, ronto, quetta and quecto.
  • The rules: prefix symbols are upright and attached to the unit without a space. All multiple prefixes are upper-case except da, h and k, and all sub-multiples are lower-case. A prefix plus a unit symbol forms one new, inseparable symbol.

Why the formula is this

value in a prefix = value / 10ⁿ   (n the prefix's power)

Every prefix scales the same base quantity, so one value converts to all of them by dividing by each prefix's factor. The best prefix is the power of 1000 that leaves 1 to 999 in front.

Assumptions and limits

  • Only SI prefixes. The binary ones for bytes (Ki, Mi) belong to IEC 80000-13, not the SI, and are not here.
  • "u" for µ is the common stand-in when no µ is to hand. It is not SI, so the result always writes µ.
  • The best prefix stays within femto to tera, the range electronics uses.

How it was checked

11 cases: - 4700p F is 4.7 nF and 0.0047 µF; - 2.2u reads as µ; - 3da is 30, deca, not deci followed by atto; - 1.5E-3 is 1.5 mF; - 2.2M Ω is 2200 kΩ; - 3.4 fF is 0.0034 pF; - All 24 includes q and Q; - a malformed value is explained; - the remembered unit and grid choice; - 47k in scientific, engineering and E notation; - 999.9999999 rounds up to 1 × 10³ and 1 k.

The review made these changes: - More prefixes: femto (and with All 24, the full list of the SI Brochure). The tool had stopped at pico and tera. - Input: a value can be typed with its prefix, and a unit can be shown. - The best prefix is shown large. - × 10ⁿ replaces "1.000e+15". - Labels went from 10.5 px to 11 px. - The rules people trip on, in the note: k lower case, M not m, µ, no combined prefixes. - Scientific ↔ engineering notation is merged in, on Pierre's choice: it repeated what this screen shows, and its title wrapped. Its favourites and links open this tool. Its rounding put 999.9999999 at 10 × 10²; both notations now round first, then keep the mantissa in its band. - Examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Calculators

Tolerance & error

(formerly Percent tolerance / error)

What it computes

Three related questions, one per pill (the choice is remembered):

  • Tolerance: the range a part can land in, from its nominal value and its tolerance below (−) and above (+). A code picker fills both from the IEC 60062 letters: J for ±5 %, Z for −20 / +80 %. A lopsided tolerance with no letter can be typed. The output gives the range, the distance of each end from nominal, and the span.
  • Error: how far a reading is from a value taken as true, signed (+ reads high, − reads low), in % and in ppm.
  • Difference: how far apart two readings are when neither is the truth, as between two meters, taken against their mean.

Examples: 4.7 kΩ at ±5 % (J), 100 nF Y5V with code Z, a 5 V rail reading 4.93 V, a 1 % resistor measuring 99.2 Ω, and two meters reading 3.30 and 3.27 V.

Source

The tolerance letters are IEC 60062 clause 5, as the Ceramic capacitor code section reads them (checked in GOST IEC 60062-2014, the identical text of the 2004 edition):

  • Table 6: B ±0.1, C ±0.25, D ±0.5, F ±1, G ±2, J ±5, K ±10 and M ±20 %.
  • Table 7, the asymmetrical tolerances: Q −10/+30, T −10/+50, S −20/+50 and Z −20/+80 %.

Below 10 pF, a capacitor's B to G are absolute picofarads. That is the Ceramic capacitor code's business, not this screen's.

Why the formulas are these

min = nominal × (1 − below / 100)     max = nominal × (1 + above / 100)
error = (measured − expected) / expected × 100 %      1 % = 10 000 ppm
difference = |A − B| / ((A + B) / 2) × 100 %

A tolerance is a share of the nominal value, in each direction. An error is a share of the true value, so its sign says which way the reading is off. With no true value, the difference is taken against the mean, so it comes out the same whichever reading is A.

Assumptions and limits

  • A tolerance is the maker's worst case at its stated conditions, not a typical spread. Temperature and ageing come on top.
  • An error is only as good as the "true" value. It includes the meter's own error.
  • No units: the values are numbers in whatever unit you use, the same for each.

How it was checked

10 cases: - 4700 at ±5 % gives 4465 – 4935, recognised as J; - code Z sets −20 and +80; - a lopsided −3 / +7 % has no letter; - 4.93 V against 5 V is −1.4 %, −14000 ppm; - a high reading is signed +; - 3.30 and 3.27 V are 0.9132 % apart either way round; - an expected value of zero is refused; - a blank field; - the remembered mode.

The review made these changes: - Renamed Tolerance & error (Pierre's choice). With the examples' bulb, the old name wrapped. - New: asymmetric tolerances, the letter-code picker, the Difference mode, and ppm with high or low. - Blank fields: a blank or zero field had left a stale result. The output now says what is wrong. - Signs: a true minus sign and an explicit plus. - The rest: the remembered mode, examples, the first cases and this section.

dB ratio

(formerly Generic dB ratio calculator)

What it computes

The ratio of two values of one quantity, in decibels, both ways.

  • Kinds: power, voltage or current, by pill.
  • Inputs: a reference (P1, V1 or I1) and a compared value, each with its unit, in µ to k, or as dB against 1 of the unit (dBW, dBV, dB re 1 A). Typing a difference in dB solves the compared value instead.
  • Output: the difference large, signed (+ a gain, − a loss), with both the power ratio and the voltage or current ratio.
  • The table: −20 to +20 dB as power and voltage ratios.
  • Remembered: the kind and each field's unit.

Examples: twice the power, an amplifier from 10 mV to 1 V, half the voltage, a cable from 100 W to 79 W, and a 20 dB attenuator on 1 V.

Source

BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019, updated 2022), table 8, note (m), read in review:

  • The units: the neper, bel and decibel express values of logarithmic ratio quantities. "It is important that the quantity be specified, and that any reference value used be specified."
  • The definition: 1 dB = (1/10) B, and L_X = m dB means m = 10 lg(X/X0), "if X denotes a mean square signal or power-like quantity".

Why the formulas are these

power:            dB = 10 · log₁₀(P2 / P1)
voltage, current: dB = 20 · log₁₀(V2 / V1)
back:             X2 = X1 × 10^(dB / k),  k = 10 or 20

The decibel is defined on power. Into one resistance, P = V²/R = I²R, so a voltage or current ratio squared is the power ratio, and 10 lg of a square is 20 lg. That way ×2 in voltage and ×4 in power are both +6.02 dB. "3 dB is double" is a rounding: ×2 is 3.0103 dB, and an exact 3 dB is ×1.995.

Assumptions and limits

  • 20 log is a power ratio only across the same impedance. Between different impedances, compare the powers.
  • dBW, dBV and dB re 1 A are a value against 1 W, 1 V or 1 A. dBm, dBu and dBµV are in the dB / dBm tool.
  • Both values must be positive. A zero or negative ratio has no decibels.

How it was checked

9 cases: - 1 W to 2 W is +3.01 dB, ×1.414 in voltage; - 10 mV to 1 V is +40 dB; - half the voltage is −6.021 dB and a quarter of the power; - −20 dB on 1 V solves 100 mV; - a unit change keeps the value, and 2 W reads 3.0103 dBW; - the table's +3 dB row is ×1.995; - zero is refused; - the remembered kind and unit.

The review made these changes: - Renamed dB ratio (Pierre's choice). With the examples' bulb, the old name would have wrapped. - Units: there were only W, V and A, plus a "dB" relative to 1 that was never named. Real units µ to k, and that dB is now named for its reference (dBW, dBV). - Ratios: the output shows both the power and the voltage or current ratio, and so does the table. - Text: signs are explicit, and dB keeps its lower-case d. - The rest: remembered choices, examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Calculators

dB levels

(formerly dB / dBm / dBu / dBV conversion)

What it computes

A signal's level in decibels against a fixed reference, both ways, in six units, by pill:

Pill Kind Against
dBm power 1 mW
dBW power 1 W
dBV voltage 1 V rms
dBu voltage 0.7746 V rms
dBmV voltage 1 mV rms (cable TV)
dBµV voltage 1 µV rms (RF, EMC)
  • Inputs: a value (power µW to kW, or voltage µV to V as rms, peak or peak-to-peak) or a level typed in dB.
  • The impedance links power and voltage. It is typed, or picked from 8 Ω speaker, 50 Ω RF, 75 Ω video and TV, and 600 Ω telecom.
  • Output: the level large, the signal as watts and volts rms, and the same signal in the five other units and as Vrms, Vp and Vpp.
  • Switching from a power level to a voltage level keeps the same signal, and a new impedance keeps the level being looked at.
  • Remembered: the level, units, reading and impedance preset.

Examples: 0 dBm into 50 Ω, pro +4 dBu and consumer −10 dBV line levels, Wi-Fi at 20 dBm, a scope's 2 Vpp, and 0 dBmV on 75 Ω cable TV.

Source

ITU-R V.574-5 (08/2015), Use of the decibel and the neper in telecommunications (itu.int, free), read in review:

  • §4.2: an absolute level is written dB followed by its reference in parentheses, dB(mW), with "simplified symbols, such as dBm instead of dB(mW)" in common use.
  • §6.1: dBW is "decibels relative to one watt" and dBm "decibels relative to one milliwatt".
  • §6.5 Absolute voltage level: the nature of the voltage, e.g. r.m.s. value, "should be specified in every case". A reference voltage of 0.775 V r.m.s. "is generally adopted which corresponds to a 1 milliwatt power dissipated in a resistance of 600 ohms … The absolute voltage level is then expressed in dBu."

dBV, dBmV and dBµV are the same voltage rule against 1 V, 1 mV and 1 µV. dBu's reference is held as √0.6 V, 0.774597 V, the exact 1 mW in 600 Ω.

Why the formulas are these

power levels:   L = 10 · log₁₀(P / Pref)    dBm: 1 mW, dBW: 1 W
voltage levels: L = 20 · log₁₀(V / Vref)    V in rms
P = V² / R      sine: Vp = √2 · Vrms,  Vpp = 2√2 · Vrms

A voltage level uses 20 log because power goes as voltage squared. Moving between a power level and a voltage level needs the impedance, by P = V²/R. That is why 0 dBm is 0 dBu only across 600 Ω: across 50 Ω, 1 mW is 223.6 mV rms, −10.8 dBu.

Assumptions and limits

  • Peak and peak-to-peak readings are converted as for a sine. For another waveform, measure true rms.
  • The impedance only matters for crossing between power and voltage. dBu and dBV themselves are voltages, whatever the load.
  • Reference levels (dBr, dBm0, and dB(A) for weighted sound) are not here.

How it was checked

11 cases: - 1 mW is 0 dBm, 0 dBu and −30 dBW across 600 Ω; - 0 dBm into 50 Ω is 223.6 mV rms and +107 dBµV; - +4 dBu is 1.228 V; - a 2 Vpp sine is −3.01 dBV; - 0 dBmV at 75 Ω is −48.75 dBm; - switching to dBV keeps the signal (−2.218 dBV); - a unit change keeps the value; - a new impedance keeps the level; - 30 dBm solves to 1 W; - zero is refused; - the remembered level and impedance.

The review made these changes: - Renamed dB levels (Pierre's choice). The old name wrapped. - Units: changing one kept the number and changed its meaning (1 mW became 1 µW). Values are now held as the signal itself. - New levels: dBW and dBmV, and impedance presets. - Switching kinds keeps the same signal. - The other units are now in one block, with the signal's rms, peak and peak-to-peak voltage. - The formula card in Formula search was split into dB ratio and dB levels. - The rest: remembered choices, examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Calculators

RMS calculator

What it computes

A periodic waveform's peak, peak-to-peak, rms, mean and rectified average, from any one of peak, peak-to-peak, rms or rectified average.

  • Waveforms: sine, square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse (with its duty cycle D), and half-wave and full-wave rectified sines.
  • Inputs: the known value in mV, V, kV, µA, mA or A, and an optional DC offset under the shape.
  • Output: the rms large (the peak when the rms was typed), the other levels, and the lowest and highest points with the mean.
  • On a meter: what an average-responding meter reads and its error, the true rms a meter's AC range shows, the rectified average, and the crest and form factors.
  • Remembered: the waveform, the known value, the unit and the duty cycle. The DC offset has its own unit picker, which changes the value's too.

Examples: 230 V and 120 V mains, a square wave on a cheap meter, 1 A PWM pulses at 25 %, a 0 to 3.3 V clock, and a bridge rectifier at 17 V peak.

Source

Analog Devices AD737 datasheet, Rev. H, table 5 (read in review, from the RS Components copy):

  • Crest factor is "the ratio of the peak signal amplitude to the rms amplitude".
  • The table gives, for a 1 V peak, the crest factor, the true rms and the reading of an average-responding circuit calibrated to a sine's rms:
  • sine: 1.414, 0.707 V, 0 % error;
  • square: 1.00, 1.00 V, reading 1.11 V, +11.0 %;
  • triangle: 1.73, 0.577 V, reading 0.555 V, −3.8 %;
  • rectangular pulse: 2, 0.5 V, reading 0.278 V, −44 %;
  • pulse train: 10, 0.1 V, reading 0.011 V, −89 %.

The rectangular row is a 25 % pulse and the pulse train a 1 % one. The tool's cases reproduce every row. The datasheet's Gaussian noise and SCR rows are not shapes here; phase-controlled sines are in AC phase control. The IEC definitions (IEV 103) could not be fetched.

Why the formulas are these

Vrms = √(mean of v²)                   the DC value that heats a resistor the same
sine:     Vrms = Vp / √2,  Vavg = 2·Vp / π
square:   Vrms = Vp,       Vavg = Vp
triangle, sawtooth: Vrms = Vp / √3,  Vavg = Vp / 2
pulse:    Vrms = Vp · √D,  Vavg = Vp · D
half-wave: Vrms = Vp / 2,  Vavg = Vp / π
full-wave: as the sine
Vrms² = Vmean² + Vac²
crest factor = Vpeak / Vrms,  form factor = Vrms / Vavg

Vavg is the rectified average, the mean of |v|. Vmean is the plain mean, the DC level. Vac is the rms of what is left around the mean.

  • An average-responding meter rectifies, averages and multiplies by a sine's form factor, π/(2√2) = 1.111. It is exact on a sine and wrong on any other shape: the error is the shape's form factor over 1.111, less 1.
  • A meter's AC range blocks DC, so it reads Vac, not Vrms.
  • A DC offset adds to the rms in quadrature only for a zero-mean shape. For a pulse or a rectified sine the cross term 2·DC·Vmean,shape stays. The rectified average with an offset is summed numerically when the signal crosses zero.

Assumptions and limits

  • Ideal shapes: sharp edges, no ringing, a symmetric square and triangle. "Peak" is the height above the DC offset, from 0 for the pulse and the rectified shapes.
  • The meter readings use the datasheet's model: an average-responding circuit on the whole signal, DC included.
  • A real true-rms meter is limited in crest factor and bandwidth; the AD737 is specified to crest factor 5 (table 6). Check the meter's own data.

How it was checked

16 cases: - 230 V rms peaks at 325.3 V, and 120 V rms at 169.7 V; - AD737 table 5: square +11.1 %, triangle −3.8 %, 25 % pulse −44.5 % with crest factor 2, 1 % pulse −88.9 % with crest factor 10; - a 0 to 3.3 V clock: 2.333 V rms, 1.65 V on an AC range; - a full-wave 17 V peak: 12.02 V rms, 10.82 V mean; - a 5 V peak sine on 2 V DC: 4.062 V rms; - a rectified average with DC solves back to its peak; - switching what is known keeps the signal, and a unit change keeps the value; - an rms below the offset, and a 100 % duty cycle, are refused; - the remembered choices; - the DC offset's own picker changes the value's unit.

The review made these changes: - New shapes: sawtooth and a pulse with its duty cycle. The waveform is now a picker. - Units: changing one kept the number and changed its meaning. Values are now held in V or A, and volts and amps share one unit picker. - The result: the rms is large, the peak when the rms was typed. The peak was always large before, even when it was the typed value. - New: the average-responding meter's reading and error, and the AC range's true rms. - Fixed: "RMS of the AC part alone" was, for rectified shapes, the rms with their DC. The rectified average ignored the DC offset. - Text: true minus signs and 11 px drawing labels. - The rest: a formula card in Formula search, remembered choices, examples, the first cases and this section.

Unit converter

What it computes

One value shown in every unit of its quantity. All the fields are linked: type into any one and the rest follow.

Category Units
Length µm, mm, cm, m, mil, in, ft
Temperature °C, °F, K
Data bit, byte, kB, KiB, MB, MiB, GB, GiB
Time ns, µs, ms, s, min, h
Energy J, kJ, mWh, Wh, kWh, cal
Angle degree, radian, turn
Pressure Pa, hPa (mbar), kPa, bar, psi, atm
Force N, kN, gf, kgf, ozf, lbf
Mass mg, g, kg, oz, lb
Area mm², cm², m², in², ft²
Volume mL (cm³), L, m³, in³, ft³
Speed m/s, km/h, mph, ft/s
  • Shown to 6 significant figures, and 12 for data, so byte counts stay exact.
  • Remembered: the category.

Examples: a 10 mil trace, 85 °C, a 128 Mbit flash, an 18650 cell's energy, sea-level pressure, and a 90° phase shift.

Source

NIST Special Publication 811 (2008), Guide for the Use of the SI, appendix B (nist.gov, free), read in review. Its factors in bold are exact, and these are: - 1 in = 0.0254 m, 1 ft = 0.3048 m, 1 mil = 2.54 × 10⁻⁵ m; - 1 lb = 0.453 592 37 kg (footnote 22); - 1 lbf = 4.448 221 615 260 5 N (footnote 23), from 1 kgf = 9.806 65 N; - 1 atm = 101 325 Pa, 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa, 1 mbar = 100 Pa; - 1 calth = 4.184 J, against 4.1868 J for the International Table calorie; - 1 in³ = 1.638 706 4 × 10⁻⁵ m³ (footnote 13); - 1 mi/h = 0.447 04 m/s, 1 W·h = 3600 J; - T/K = t/°C + 273.15, and t/°C = (t/°F − 32)/1.8.

psi is built from them, as 1 lbf over 1 in²: 6894.757 Pa, as SP 811 lists.

BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019, updated 2022), read in review: - Table 8: the hour is "h", 1 h = 3600 s. - §3: SI prefixes "refer strictly to powers of 10. They should not be used to indicate powers of 2 (for example, one kilobit represents 1000 bits and not 1024 bits)". The prefixes for powers of 2 are kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi) and up, per IEC 80000-13.

Why the formulas are these

every unit but temperature:  value in base unit = value × factor
°F = °C × 1.8 + 32,   K = °C + 273.15
psi = lbf / in² = 4.448 221 615 260 5 N / (0.0254 m)²

A unit is a fixed multiple of the category's base unit, so each category holds one value in its base unit and every field shows it in its own. Temperature is the exception: °C, °F and K have different zeros, so it needs the offset.

Assumptions and limits

  • The calorie is the thermochemical one, and oz and lb are the avoirdupois ones.
  • gf and kgf are the weight of 1 g and 1 kg under standard gravity, 9.806 65 m/s².
  • A flash sold as "128 Mbit" counts in powers of 2: 128 × 2²⁰ bits, 16 MiB.
  • Below absolute zero is refused.
  • Not here: wire sizes (in Wire sizing), dB (in dB ratio and dB levels), and SI prefixes alone (in SI prefix converter).

How it was checked

14 cases: - 10 mil is 0.254 mm, and 1 in is 25.4 mm and 1000 mil; - 100 °F is 37.7778 °C and 310.928 K, and −1 K is refused; - 16 MiB is 16 777 216 bytes and 16.777216 MB; - 11.52 Wh is 41 472 J, and 1 cal is 4.184 J; - 1 psi is 6894.76 Pa, and 1 atm is 1013.25 hPa and 14.6959 psi; - 1 lbf is 4.44822 N, 16 ozf and 453.592 gf; - 1 in³ is 16.3871 mL; - 1 h is 3600 s; - 90° is 1.5708 rad and a quarter turn; - the remembered category.

The review made these changes: - Factors: the cubic inch and the pound-force had rounded values where SP 811 gives exact ones. - Symbols: "hr" is now "h", and the calorie is labelled. - New units: - ft; - ns; - mWh; - hPa (mbar); - bit and byte; - gf and ozf; - turn. - Layout: the fields are two per row, so every category fits the screen, and are shown to 6 figures instead of 4. - Notes: each category defines its units (mil, KiB, gf, the calorie). An unsupported claim about IP ratings and pressure was removed. - The rest: a formula card in Formula search, the remembered category, examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Converters

PPM converter

What it computes

Parts per million of a value, three ways, by pill:

Pill Inputs Output
Tolerance a value and a ± tolerance in ppm the ± deviation, the range
Error a nominal and a measured value the error in ppm, and the difference
Tempco a value, a tempco in ppm/K, two temperatures the change, and the value at the second temperature
  • Units: the value is in Hz, kHz, MHz, mV, V, Ω, kΩ, MΩ or none, held in SI.
  • Conversions: every result gives the same fraction in ppm, in % and as a power of ten.
  • For a frequency, the tool also gives the drift of a clock run from it, in seconds a day and a year.
  • The range is shown to as many figures as it takes for the deviation to show.
  • Remembered: the mode and the unit. In Error mode the measured value has its own unit picker, which changes the nominal's too.

Examples: a 16 MHz crystal at ±20 ppm, a counter reading 16.00032 MHz, a watch crystal at ±20 ppm, a 0.1 % resistor in ppm, and a 10 kΩ resistor at 100 ppm/K heated to 85 °C.

Source

BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019, updated 2022), §5.4.7, read in review: - ppm: the term "parts per million" or "ppm", "meaning 10⁻⁶ relative value, or parts in 10⁶, is also used. This is analogous to the meaning of per cent as parts per hundred." - ppb and ppt: their "meanings are language dependent. For this reason the abbreviations ppb and ppt should be avoided." The tool writes finer fractions as powers of ten instead.

The tempco is the linear temperature coefficient, R(T) = R0 (1 + α ΔT), as the resistor colour code gives it in ppm/K. Crystal budgets (tolerance, temperature, ageing, the tuning fork's parabola) are in Oscillator stability.

Why the formulas are these

deviation = value × ppm / 10⁶          1 % = 10 000 ppm
error (ppm) = (measured − nominal) / |nominal| × 10⁶
change = value × α × (T2 − T1) / 10⁶     α in ppm/K
clock drift = ppm × 10⁻⁶ × 86 400 s a day

A ppm is a fraction like a per cent, a ten-thousand times finer. A step of 1 K is a step of 1 °C, so ppm/K and ppm/°C are the same coefficient. A clock counts cycles, so a frequency off by some ppm makes it gain or lose that fraction of its time: 20 ppm is 1.728 s a day.

Assumptions and limits

  • The tempco is linear. Real parts curve, and a datasheet's figure is often a bound over its range rather than a slope. For crystals use Oscillator stability.
  • The tolerance is symmetric, ± the same both ways.
  • A zero value is refused, since ppm is a fraction of it.

How it was checked

13 cases: - 16 MHz at ±20 ppm: ±320 Hz, 15.99968 to 16.00032 MHz, ±1.728 s a day; - 16.00032 MHz read is +20 ppm, and 15.99984 MHz is −10 ppm; - 32.768 kHz at ±20 ppm is ±655.4 mHz; - 0.1 % is 1000 ppm, ±10 Ω on 10 kΩ; - 10 kΩ at 100 ppm/K gains 60 Ω at 85 °C and loses 65 Ω at −40 °C; - a unit change keeps the value, and with no unit the deviation is a plain number; - zero and a negative tolerance are refused; - the remembered mode and unit; - the measured value's own picker changes the nominal's unit.

The review made these changes: - New modes: Error (measured against nominal) and Tempco. The tool only applied a tolerance before. - Units: the value had none ("any unit"). It now has real units, and the result is shown in them. - Conversions: ppm, % and a power of ten, without ppb. - New: a clock's drift for a frequency. - The rest: a formula card in Formula search, remembered choices, examples, the first cases and this section.

Tools › Reference

Formula search

What it computes

Nothing: it finds. It holds the main formulas of 72 topics, one card each, searchable by a tool's name, by a formula or a symbol in it (fc, Vout, 2π × R × C), or by a word of its note (cutoff, duty).

  • Linked cards: 65 cards are for built tools. Tapping one opens the tool, and its lines are the tool's own Formula section, cut to the main ones.
  • Standalone cards: 7 cards are for tools not built yet (path loss, VSWR, antenna length, LDO, buck, boost, thermal resistance). They stand on their own, each sourced.
  • Left out: lookup tables, which have no formula to give: marking codes, packages, battery and button-cell sizes, cable colours, IP ratings, the Karnaugh map, constants and units.

Source

Each linked card follows its tool, whose manual section gives the source. For the standalone cards, read in review: - Path loss: ITU-R P.525-5 (11/2024), eq. 5, Lbf = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ), and eq. 6, Lbf = 32.4 + 20 log₁₀ f + 20 log₁₀ d, with f in MHz and d in km. The card gives the constant as 32.45, which is 20 log₁₀(4π × 10⁹/c). - LDO: TI LM317 datasheet, eq. 2, VO = VREF (1 + R2/R1) + IADJ × R2. IADJ is "typically 50 µA and negligible in most applications"; VREF is 1.25 V. - Antenna: 468 / f is 95 % of the free-space half wave, 491.8 / f in feet. No antenna handbook was read in review, so the card gives the arithmetic and says to trim on the air. - VSWR, buck, boost, thermal: the definitions and the ideal relations, stated as such.

Assumptions and limits

  • A card is a summary. The tool has the full set, the modes and the checks; open it for a number.
  • Search is plain text, case-insensitive, on the name, the formulas and the note.

How it was checked

7 cases: - the 72 topics, listed by name; - a formula finds its tool; - a symbol finds its tool; - a renamed tool's card opens under its new name; - a standalone card has no link; - the LM317 card's naming; - an empty search says what to try.

The check also fails any card whose tool is not in the app, by its name, its old name or a name merged into it, and any formula line that wraps on the phone.

The review made these changes: - Cards: 25 before, 72 now, one for every built tool that has a formula (Pierre's choice). The new ones are taken from each tool's Formula section. - Fixed: - the LDO card had R1 and R2 the other way round from the LM317 it named, and lacked the IADJ term; - path loss used 32.44; - the antenna note said 468 "ignores the velocity factor", where the 95 % is the end-effect allowance; - the thermal card now gives TJ = TA + P × θJA. - Links: cards also link through merged tool names. - Layout: each formula fits one line at 375 px; long ones were split. - Text: the subtitle and the empty-search hint no longer say the list is "still growing".

Tools › Reference

Physical constants

What it computes

A reference list of 15 constants electronics uses, searchable by name, symbol, unit or a word of the note. Tapping a card copies its plain value (8.8541878188e-12, in the unit shown).

Symbol Constant Kind
c, e, h, k speed of light, elementary charge, Planck, Boltzmann exact
eV, ħ, hc, F, σ electronvolt, h/2π, photon energy × wavelength, Faraday, Stefan–Boltzmann exact
ε₀, μ₀, Z₀, mₑ permittivity, permeability, impedance of free space, electron mass measured
Vt, Eg thermal voltage at 300 K, silicon bandgap at 300 K not constants
  • Values: shown with all their published digits, grouped in threes as CODATA prints them.
  • Measured values carry their standard uncertainty: in the last digits in brackets, (14), and spelt out as a fraction of the value.
  • Notes: each gives the constant's use in a circuit, such as thermal noise, a parallel-plate capacitor, a battery's ampere-hours per mole, or silicon's cutoff wavelength.

Source

CODATA 2022, NIST's "Fundamental Physical Constants — Complete Listing, 2022 CODATA adjustment" (physics.nist.gov/constants), read in review: - Exact: - c = 299 792 458 m/s; - e = 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; - h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J Hz⁻¹; - k = 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; - ħ = 1.054 571 817… × 10⁻³⁴ J s; - F = 96 485.332 12… C mol⁻¹; - σ = 5.670 374 419… × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴; - the inverse metre–electronvolt relationship, 1.239 841 984… × 10⁻⁶ eV (that is, hc). - Measured: - ε₀ = 8.854 187 8188(14) × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹; - μ₀ = 1.256 637 061 27(20) × 10⁻⁶ N A⁻²; - Z₀ = 376.730 313 412(59) Ω; - mₑ = 9.109 383 7139(28) × 10⁻³¹ kg.

Silicon bandgap: the Ioffe Institute's semiconductor database (NSM archive, Si band structure), "Energy gap 1.12 eV" at 300 K. It is not a CODATA constant, and the card says so.

Why the formulas are these

Vt = k T / e          25.852 mV at 300 K, 25.693 mV at 25 °C
hc / e = 1239.84 eV·nm,  so E (eV) = 1239.84 / λ (nm)
Z₀ = √(μ₀ / ε₀) = μ₀ c
F = NA × e,  96 485 C = 26.80 Ah per mole of electrons

Since the 2019 SI, c, h, e and k are fixed by definition, so they and anything made only of them are exact. ε₀ and μ₀ were exact before (μ₀ was 4π × 10⁻⁷) and are now measured, so their values change at each CODATA adjustment. They are within a part in 10⁹ of the old figures.

Assumptions and limits

  • Vt and Eg depend on temperature. The cards give 300 K (and Vt at 25 °C).
  • "…" marks an exact value whose digits go on. The copy gives the digits shown.
  • Left out: general-physics constants with no circuit use, such as G, gn, NA on its own, R and the proton mass.

How it was checked

11 cases: - c, ε₀, μ₀, Z₀ and mₑ exactly as CODATA 2022 prints them, with the uncertainties; - hc and the thermal voltage; - search by unit (F/m) and by a note's words (thermal noise); - a tap copies the plain value; - an empty search.

The review made these changes: - CODATA 2022: ε₀, μ₀, Z₀ and the electron mass were CODATA 2018 values. - Precision: values were cut to 6 figures, so even the exact c read 2.99792 × 10⁸. They now show every published digit. - New: - exact or measured on each card, with the uncertainty; - hc in eV·nm; - Vt at 25 °C; - tap to copy; - search by unit and by note. - Fixed: the bandgap note claimed it "sets the forward-voltage floor" of silicon diodes. It now gives what follows from it, the 1107 nm absorption edge, and its source. - Notes: rewritten around each constant's use in a circuit, with this manual section.

Tools › Reference

SI units

What it computes

A reference list of 25 SI units, searchable by name, symbol, quantity, a word of the note, or a unit expression (A/V finds the siemens).

  • Base units: the seven base units, each with the defining constant whose fixed value defines it.
  • Derived units: 18 of the 22 units with special names, each written in base units and in other SI units, as the SI Brochure's table 4 gives them (V = kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹ = W/A).
  • Notes: each gives the unit's use in a circuit.

Source

BIPM SI Brochure, 9th edition (2019, updated 2022), read in review: - Table 2 and §2.3.1: the base units and their definitions:

Unit Fixed constant
second ΔνCs = 9 192 631 770 Hz
metre c = 299 792 458 m/s
kilogram h = 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
ampere e = 1.602 176 634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
kelvin k = 1.380 649 × 10⁻²³ J/K
mole NA = 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
candela Kcd = 683 lm/W at 540 × 10¹² Hz
  • Table 4: the 22 units with special names, in base units in the order the CCU restored in 2013 (kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹), and in other SI units.
  • Its notes:
  • (b) one radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius, and phase advances 2π rad in a period;
  • (d) the hertz "shall only be used for periodic phenomena";
  • (e) electric potential difference is "also called voltage";
  • (f) a temperature difference has the same number in °C and K.
  • §2.3.4: angular frequency is given in rad/s, never Hz or s⁻¹: "Ignoring this fact may cause an error of 2π."
  • Chapter 3: prefixes go on the gram, not the kilogram (mg, not µkg).

Why the formulas are these

V = W/A,  Ω = V/A,  S = A/V,  F = C/V,  H = Wb/A,  Wb = V·s,  T = Wb/m²
lm = cd·sr,  lx = lm/m²
t / °C = T / K − 273.15

Every derived unit is a product of powers of the base units with a factor of one, which makes the set coherent: an equation between quantities, such as V = I × R, holds between their numbers with no factor when they are in volts, amperes and ohms.

Assumptions and limits

  • Left out of table 4: the becquerel, gray, sievert and katal, which are units of radiation and catalysis, not circuits.
  • Not here: the prefixes (in SI prefix converter) and the non-SI units that are accepted, such as the hour and the electronvolt (in Unit converter and Physical constants).

How it was checked

11 cases: - the second and the ampere's fixed constants; - the volt, farad, henry and tesla in table 4's forms and order; - a degree Celsius as a step of 1 K; - the base and derived groups; - search by expression (A/V), by quantity (inductance) and by note (the 2π warning); - an empty search.

The review made these changes: - Sourced: the cards cite the SI Brochure's tables 2 and 4. - Base units: each now gives the value its definition fixes. Before, only the constant's name was given, or a phrase. - Derived units: each gives its form in other SI units (W/A, C/V), as table 4 does, and the farad's base units are in the table's order. - New units: radian, steradian, newton, pascal, degree Celsius, lumen and lux. - New: the base and derived groups, and the hertz card's warning about rad/s. - Search: also by note and by unit expression. - The rest: keywords, the first cases and this section.
